@@138644368 <p> India 's climate adaptation efforts over the past decade have brought benefits to the country 's massive population . However , these initiatives have failed to address the particular vulnerabilities of India 's tribal communities , many of whom reside in ecologically fragile and climate-sensitive regions . This brief examines the inadequate consideration of tribal vulnerabilities within India 's climate adaptation framework despite existing national and state-level policies . It analyses primary policy documents such as the National Action Plan on Climate Change ( NAPCC ) and the State Action Plans on Climate Change ( SAPCCs ) , as well as various government reports and recent scholarly literature , and identifies challenges in the domains of data , institutional coordination , and decentralised governance . The brief proposes decentralised adaptation planning , climate-sensitive social protection , targeted funding , and improved institutional coordination to advance climate justice and resilience . <h> Introduction <p> Rising temperatures , irregular monsoon patterns , prolonged droughts , and extreme weather events -- all impacts of worsening climate change -- are reshaping livelihoods and development trajectories across India. 1 According to the India Meteorological @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ increased by approximately 0.7 ? C between 1901 and 2018 , while rainfall variability and climate-related extreme events have intensified across several regions . As a result , climate adaptation has become an important part of India 's climate policy through national frameworks , state plans , and climate-related welfare interventions. 3 Despite the growing policy focus on climate adaptation , its benefits remain unevenly distributed , with many of the most climate-vulnerable populations , including tribal communities , receiving little consistent support. 4 <p> Scheduled Tribes ( STs ) constitute 8.6 percent of India 's population , according to the 2011 Census. 5 India is also home to 75 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups ( PVTGs ) , many of whom reside in ecologically fragile and climate-sensitive regions . States such as Odisha , Jharkhand , Chhattisgarh , Madhya Pradesh , Maharashtra , and parts of the Northeast region are home to large tribal populations whose livelihoods depend heavily on forests , rain-fed agriculture , non-timber forest products ( NTFPs ) , and common property resources . Despite increasing adaptation initiatives , these communities continue to face multiple forms of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and often unaddressed climate risks . Many reside in ecologically fragile regions such as forested lands , hills , and rain-fed areas , with livelihoods closely tied to the surrounding ecosystem. 6 These groups include the Dongria Kondh of Odisha , the Baiga of Madhya Pradesh , the Koya of central India , and several PVTGs in the Eastern Ghats. 7 Climate-induced disruptions to agriculture , forests , and water resources , therefore , have direct and disproportionate effects on their food security , income stability , and quality of life. 8 In several tribal districts , irregular rainfall , biodiversity loss , declining forest productivity , and water scarcity have also contributed to livelihood insecurity and seasonal migration . <p> Even as tribal communities are highly climate vulnerable , they continue to be marginalised from the planning and delivery of India 's adaptation policies. 9 This reflects a broader policy challenge . Although India 's climate adaptation architecture has expanded in scope , it has not adequately internalised the differentiated vulnerabilities of tribal communities . Adaptation planning often relies on aggregate data , sectoral-based interventions , and standardised approaches @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 10 As a result , climate adaptation policies often do not effectively translate into on-the-ground resilience ; they tend to reinforce existing inequalities instead of addressing them . <p> The issue is particularly urgent as India seeks to scale up adaptation efforts in line with both domestic development priorities and global climate commitments . The success of these efforts will depend on their inclusion of and responsiveness to local contexts. 11 Neglecting tribal communities does not only undermine climate justice but also reduces India 's ability to adapt to climate risks . Climate risks in tribal regions have cascading implications for ecological sustainability , rural livelihoods , and regional development . <p> This brief argues that tribal communities continue to be policy blind spots within India 's climate adaptation framework due to governance gaps , institutional fragmentation , and limited decentralised planning . It examines the structural and administrative barriers that underpin this exclusion and identifies practical policy options to bridge India 's climate adaptation gap . Addressing these challenges is essential for developing a more resilient , fair , and effective adaptation strategy for India . <h> India 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has established an extensive institutional apparatus to provide support for climate adaptation over the last two decades . These institutions operate across different levels of governance and recognise the climate risks faced by different populations . However , their conceptualisation and implementation continue to show limitations in addressing the socially differentiated nature of vulnerability , especially among the country 's tribal communities. 12 <p> At the national level , the National Action Plan on Climate Change ( NAPCC ) , launched in 2008 and subsequently revised , provides the overarching framework for India 's climate response. 13 Initially focused largely on climate mitigation , the NAPCC has gradually incorporated adaptation through initiatives such as the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture , the National Water Mission , and the National Mission on Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change . While the missions identify vulnerability broadly , they typically do not develop targeted strategies for those whose livelihoods will be affected most by ecological changes , specifically tribal communities.10 <p> Supporting the NAPCC is the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change ( NAFCC ) , which aims to strengthen the adaptive capacity of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in vulnerable areas , project selection and design have generally followed technocratic and sector-driven approaches . Thus , adaptation initiatives frequently emphasise infrastructure and productivity enhancements over the social , cultural , and governance factors that shape vulnerability in tribal areas. 15 <p> The responsibility for implementation largely rests with the states , through their State Action Plans on Climate Change ( SAPCCs ) . All Indian states and Union Territories have created SAPCCs , tasked to translate national adaptation priorities into sub-national actions. 16 In practice , however , the quality of SAPCCs varies considerably , and they are rarely integrated with broader development and welfare planning processes. 17 Many identify tribal-dominated districts as climate hotspots but fail to provide tailored interventions or institutional mechanisms responsive to local needs . Moreover , the lack of clarity regarding the relationship between SAPCCs and Tribal Sub-Plans ( TSPs ) further complicates efforts to align adaptation priorities with social equity goals. 18 <p> Alongside climate-specific policies , a number of welfare and development programmes have become de-facto adaptation instruments . Schemes such as the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and crop insurance programmes play an important role in mitigating climate-related shocks in rural areas. 19 However , these programmes were not designed explicitly for climate adaptation , and their potential to strengthen resilience in tribal regions remains underutilised. 20 Limited flexibility , weak local planning , and inadequate integration of climate risk further reduce their effectiveness as adaptation tools . <h> Institutional Fragmentation and Poor Policy Integration <p> Institutional fragmentation further exacerbates the marginalisation of tribal communities within climate adaptation governance . Responsibility for climate policy primarily lies with environmental and climate ministries , while tribal welfare falls under separate administrative bodies. 25 As a result of the lack of coordination among these institutional domains , climate policy processes become fragmented . <p> At the state level , this is seen in the poor integration between State Action Plans on Climate Change and Tribal Sub-Plans . Although both instruments operate within the same geographical boundaries , they are developed through separate planning cycles and funding streams. 26 As a result , states are unable to integrate climate adaptation goals with other social justice and development goals in tribal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Although decentralised governance frameworks such as the Panchayats ( Extension to Scheduled Areas ) Act ( PESA ) establish institutional mechanisms for community participation in development planning in tribal areas , climate adaptation initiatives infrequently involve Gram Sabhas as decision-makers. 27 Instead , climate adaptation projects are frequently developed at higher administrative levels and include minimal opportunities for local consultation or co-production . The top-down nature of climate adaptation planning therefore fails to leverage the capabilities of decentralised institutions to increase adaptive capacity and incorporates localised knowledge and priorities into adaptation strategies . As a result , tribal communities are positioned as passive recipients of interventions rather than active agents in the development of climate resilience . <p> Together , the structural , informational , and institutional factors described above explain the continued lack of attention on tribal communities in India 's climate adaptation framework . Addressing this challenge requires more than just technical fixes and necessitates a paradigmatic shift in the way adaptation governance addresses issues of inclusiveness , coordination , and decentralised decision-making . <h> Governance and Implementation Gaps <p> Various studies have identified governance and implementation gaps @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tribal areas. 28 For example , while many Indian states have adopted climate adaptation plans and identified vulnerable groups for targeted support , institutional and administrative weaknesses often undermine implementation . A lack of institutional coordination , administrative inefficiencies , and inadequate accountability mechanisms all contribute to a situation in which tribal regions may be formally identified as climate-vulnerable but are effectively overlooked in the implementation of adaptation measures. 29 <h> Centre -- State Disconnect in Adaptation Planning <p> India 's climate governance framework is characterised by a division of responsibility between the Centre and the states . At the Centre , climate policies and missions establish broad priorities for mitigation and adaptation , while implementation is largely carried out by the states through the State Action Plans on Climate Change ( SAPCCs ) . 30 This decentralised approach was intended to enable states to design adaptation strategies suited to their specific circumstances . In practice , however , it has produced uneven levels of commitment , capacity , and implementation across states . <p> In tribal-dominated regions , this disconnect between the Centre and the states is even more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vulnerability into climate adaptation planning. 31 As a result , although states have discretion in designing adaptation strategies , they often lack the institutional support needed to address the specific conditions of tribal areas . Many SAPCCs developed by the states simply replicate the national templates for adaptation planning without tailoring them to the unique climate risks faced by tribal communities . Delays in the approval , financing , and revision of SAPCCs further reduce their effectiveness in a rapidly evolving climate-risk environment. 32 <h> Administrative Capacity Constraints at the Local Level <p> Limited administrative capacity at the district and block levels impedes the effective implementation of climate adaptation measures . Local officials are typically responsible for administering numerous development schemes while also responding to immediate constituency demands , leaving limited scope for long-term climate planning. 33 In tribal areas , these challenges are compounded by geographical remoteness , limited access to infrastructure , and high staff turnover . <p> Effective climate adaptation also requires specialised technical expertise in climate science , risk assessment , and participatory planning. 34 Unfortunately , such specialised knowledge does not evenly exist in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ adaptation initiatives often rely on traditional development schemes instead of context-specific measures to build resilience among tribal communities . This lack of administrative capacity reinforces a one-size-fits-all approach to climate adaptation planning that ignores the unique characteristics of tribal communities . <h> Fragmented Financing and Weak Resource Targeting <p> India has multiple funding sources for climate adaptation , including national funds , state budgets , and externally supported projects. 35 While these overlapping funding streams can encourage innovation , they also contribute to fragmentation and weak transparency . In other words , there is no guarantee that funds designated for vulnerable regions will reach the districts and communities most in need , nor is there an easy way to track adaptation spending comprehensively . <p> Tribal regions are disproportionately affected by these weaknesses in adaptation financing . The absence of dedicated adaptation budgets for tribal districts limits the scope for sustained and locally tailored interventions. 36 In addition , many adaptation projects are short-term and project-based , reducing their ability to generate lasting institutional change or strengthen community-level resilience . <h> Limited Monitoring , Evaluation , and Accountability <p> Monitoring @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ adaptation policies . However , few mechanisms currently exist to assess adaptation outcomes systematically . Most indicators focus on outputs , such as the number of green infrastructure projects completed , rather than outcomes such as reduced vulnerability or enhanced adaptive capacity . This limitation is particularly pronounced in tribal regions , where adaptation measures are rarely subject to systematic evaluation. 37 <p> Additionally , the current lack of strong accountability systems to ensure that policymakers are held accountable for the performance of adaptation policies in tribal areas also contributes to the poor performance of those policies. 38 Without clear standards or feedback mechanisms , policy failures in tribal areas are rarely recognised or addressed . Instead , adaptation policies are frequently continued or expanded without adequate consideration of their distributive impacts . <h> Bridging the Adaptation Gap : Policy Options <p> Addressing the exclusion of tribal communities from India 's climate adaptation framework will require a shift from fragmented , sector-specific interventions to a more integrated and inclusive governance approach. 39 The following policy options focus on building stronger institutional collaboration , more effective targeting , and greater decentralised @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unique vulnerabilities present in tribal areas . <h> Mainstream Tribal Vulnerabilities into Adaptation Planning <p> Bridging the adaptation gap requires the systematic incorporation of tribal vulnerabilities into national and state-level climate planning. 40 The existing framework of the NAPCC and the SAPCCs should move beyond broad vulnerability assessments towards mandatory tribal impact assessments . These assessments should identify climate-specific regional risks , livelihood dependence , and adaptive capacity within tribal districts . <p> Developing vulnerability maps at the district and sub-district levels would enable policymakers to prioritise interventions based on differentiated exposure and risk rather than broad aggregate indicators. 41 The use of traditional ecological knowledge in assessments will create better relevance and legitimacy of adaptation planning . A similar approach will create a paradigmatic shift in adaptation policy towards contextually designed adaptation policies . <h> Strengthen Decentralised and Community-Based Adaptation <p> Decentralised governance institutions remain underutilised in climate adaptation efforts in tribal areas . Local institutions like Gram Sabhas , especially in Scheduled Areas , should be formally included in adaptation planning and execution processes in accordance with existing legislative frameworks . Empowering local institutions to identify priorities , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ efficiency and accountability . <p> Community-based adaptation initiatives can also help incorporate local knowledge and practices that are typically excluded from top-down planning. 42 Enhancing capacity development programmes for local government representatives and frontline personnel will enable more authentic participation and less implementation gaps . Strengthening decentralised adaptation governance can , in turn , promote local ownership and the long-term sustainability of adaptation measures . <h> Align Social Protection with Adaptation Goals to Climate Shocks <p> Social protection programmes can serve as buffers against climate-related shocks but remain underutilised as adaptation tools. 43 Their adaptive potential could be strengthened through climate-sensitive redesigns of schemes such as the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act ( MGNREGA ) , food security programmes , and public health interventions . Redesigning social protection schemes could include flexibility in work provisions during extreme climate events , increased coverage in high-risk periods , and targeted support for climate-impacted livelihoods . <p> Aligning social welfare delivery with climate-related risk assessments will ensure that resources reach those most in need at times of high climate-related risk. 44 Coordination between climate-related and social sectors ' ministries will be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and district-level implementation of climate-related adaptations . <h> Improve Adaptation Finance and Resource Allocation <p> Effective adaptation in tribal regions will depend on predictable and targeted finance . Establishing dedicated funding windows for tribal districts within existing climate finance mechanisms could help address chronic under-investment. 45 Simplifying access to finance and strengthening local project preparation capacity would further improve the utilisation of adaptation funds . <h> Strengthen Monitoring , Evaluation , and Accountability <p> Bridging the adaptation gap will require robust monitoring and accountability frameworks . Outcome-oriented indicators that measure changes in vulnerability , livelihood security , and adaptive capacity are needed to assess the effectiveness of adaptation policies. 47 Regular evaluations of adaptation projects in tribal regions will generate data that will inform corrections to adaptation policies and the scale-up of successful approaches . <p> Increasing transparency and feedback mechanisms through community monitoring and public reporting will enhance accountability and policy responsiveness . Embedding learning and accountability into adaptation governance will ensure that tribal regions are no longer treated as peripheral to national climate resilience efforts . <h> Conclusion <p> The climate adaptation challenge in India is no longer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reach and effectiveness of adaptation frameworks . Although adaptation has gained increasing prominence in national and state-level policies , uneven implementation at the regional level has left tribal communities among the least equipped to cope with climate-related threats . The persistence of vulnerability in tribal regions is not accidental but rooted in structural marginalisation , fragmented governance , and inadequate decentralised planning within India 's adaptation framework . <p> The exclusion of tribal communities from effective adaptation planning also undermines India 's broader development and climate resilience goals . Tribal regions are both ecologically significant and socio-economically vulnerable , meaning that climate-related disruptions in these regions have cascading effects through livelihood loss , migration , food insecurity , and environmental degradation . As a result , the failure to address adaptation gaps in tribal regions represents a diminishing of the effectiveness of India 's national climate strategy and the weakening of India 's overall adaptive capacity . <p> A primary finding of this analysis is the need to shift adaptation governance from a predominantly top-down model towards a more inclusive and coordinated bottom-up approach . A more inclusive and regionally grounded approach to adaptation decision-making will not only enhance the resilience of communities that are most vulnerable to climate-related shocks but also contribute to a more equitable and effective climate response .

@@138656411 <h> Earth to reach its farthest point from the Sun on July 6 , yet the summer heat will not cool : Here 's why <p> Earth will reach its farthest point from the Sun on July 6 , a yearly astronomical event known as aphelion . At around 152.1 million kilometres from the Sun , the planet will be about 5 million kilometres farther away than it is in early January . Yet , despite this greater distance , the Northern Hemisphere will remain firmly in the grip of summer , with no drop in temperatures . The timing surprises many people because it seems to defy common sense . If Earth is farther from the Sun , should n't it be cooler ? Scientists say the answer is no . The seasons are shaped not by how far Earth is from the Sun , but by the way our planet is tilted as it journeys through space . <h> Why Earth reaching its farthest point from the Sun wo n't cool the summer heat <p> At first glance , it seems obvious that being farther from the Sun @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from a campfire makes you feel less warm.But space does not work quite like that.Imagine shining a torch onto a wall . Hold it straight and the light forms a small , bright circle . Tilt the torch and the same light spreads over a much larger area , making it less intense . The Sun behaves in a similar way.During July , the Northern Hemisphere is tilted about 23.5 degrees towards the Sun . Because of this tilt , sunlight strikes the ground more directly and daylight lasts much longer than it does in winter . <p> Those two factors deliver far more energy to the surface than the small reduction caused by Earth 's greater distance from the Sun.That is why cities across Europe , North America and much of Asia continue to experience warm summer days even when Earth is at its most distant point from the Sun . <h> Is n't it amazing what Earth is doing right now ? <p> Pause for a moment and think about where you are.You are standing , sitting or walking on a planet that is rotating at up to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ orbiting the Sun at an average speed of around 107,000 kilometres per hour.You can not feel either movement.At this very moment , someone could be relaxing beside a public swimming pool in Spain , Greece or Italy , soaking up the summer sunshine . Thousands of kilometres away , someone in Australia , New Zealand or Argentina may be pulling on a winter jacket before heading to work.They are all travelling through space together on the same planet , moving at incredible speeds , yet experiencing completely opposite seasons simply because Earth is tilted.It is one of the most elegant examples of how precisely our Solar System works . <h> What is aphelion ? <p> Aphelion is the point in Earth 's orbit where it is farthest from the Sun . This year , it occurs on July 6 , when Earth will be about 152.1 million kilometres ( 94.5 million miles ) away.The opposite point is called perihelion , which occurs in early January when Earth is about 147.1 million kilometres ( 91.4 million miles ) from the Sun.Although that sounds like a huge difference , it amounts to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from the Sun because our planet follows an orbit that is almost circular , not highly elongated . <h> Does Earth 's distance from the Sun matter at all ? <p> Yes , but far less than most people imagine.At aphelion , Earth receives about 7 per cent less solar energy than it does at perihelion because sunlight spreads over a slightly larger area . The Sun also appears around 3 per cent smaller in the sky , although the difference is too small for the human eye to detect.Even so , this slight reduction has little effect on everyday weather.The atmosphere , oceans and land absorb and slowly release heat , acting like a giant thermal reservoir . This natural buffering smooths out small changes in incoming sunlight , meaning the effect of Earth 's distance is largely overshadowed by the planet 's tilt . <h> Why does the Southern Hemisphere have winter in July ? <p> The explanation is beautifully simple.When the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun , the Southern Hemisphere tilts away from it . As a result , countries such as Australia , South Africa @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ while much of Europe , Asia and North America enjoy summer.Around six months later , the situation completely reverses.Interestingly , Southern Hemisphere summer occurs when Earth is actually closest to the Sun . However , because most of the Southern Hemisphere is covered by oceans , which warm and cool more slowly than land , its seasonal temperatures are generally less extreme than many people expect . <h> Earth even slows down during aphelion <p> Earth 's distance from the Sun also changes the speed at which it travels through space.According to Johannes Kepler 's Second Law of Planetary Motion , planets move fastest when they are closest to the Sun and slowest when they are farthest away.Near perihelion , Earth travels at about 30.29 kilometres per second , or nearly 109,000 kilometres per hour . Near aphelion , that falls to around 29.29 kilometres per second , or about 105,400 kilometres per hour.Because Earth moves a little more slowly during this part of its orbit , the Northern Hemisphere experiences the longest season of the year . Summer lasts almost five days longer than winter . <h> Why does @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? <p> Although aphelion usually occurs between July 3 and July 6 , the exact date changes slightly from year to year.Leap years , along with the gravitational pull of the Moon and the other planets , subtly alter Earth 's orbit . Over thousands of years , the orientation of Earth 's orbit also changes through a process called apsidal precession , causing aphelion and perihelion to slowly drift across the calendar . <h> A perfectly balanced system , now facing a new challenge <p> Earth 's annual journey around the Sun is a remarkable example of cosmic precision . A planet tilted by just 23.5 degrees , spinning on its axis while racing around the Sun at more than 100,000 kilometres per hour , has produced a stable cycle of seasons that has supported life for millions of years.Today , however , that natural balance is increasingly being disrupted by human-driven climate change . Global warming is not changing Earth 's orbit or its tilt , but it is making heatwaves more frequent , raising average temperatures and increasing the likelihood of extreme weather across many parts of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Sun on July 6 , remember that the summer heat has very little to do with distance . Instead , it is a reminder that the seasons depend on the remarkable geometry of our planet 's tilt , and that the climate we experience today is being shaped not by a changing orbit , but increasingly by the choices humanity makes . <p> The TOI Science Desk stands as an inquisitive team of journalists , ceaselessly delving into the realms of discovery to curate a captivating collection of news , features , and articles from the vast and ever-evolving world of science for the readers of The Times of India . @@138657541 <h> The New Climate Divide in Agriculture : Who Can Recover , and Who Can not <h> Key Takeaways <p> AI Summary <p> Analyzing article ... <p> The next food-security crisis may not arrive as a single failed harvest , but as a widening gap between farms that can absorb climate shocks and those that can not . With extreme weather becoming more frequent and destructive , agricultural resilience is emerging as one of the most important tests of climate governance . <p> A cross-country study published in Sustainability argues that climate change is already weakening Agricultural Production Resilience , or APR , across countries , with the strongest damage coming from extreme floods , followed by extreme heat and drought . The study , authored by Fangyan Bai , Chunyan Li , Qi Ban and Wenya Zhang , synthesizes 76 empirical studies published between 2005 and 2025 to compare how five climate factors affect farming systems across regions , production modes and agricultural structures . <h> Floods Are Now the Hardest Hit to Farm Resilience <p> Using network meta-analysis , the authors compare five climate factors : extreme high @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and temperature anomaly . All five significantly reduce APR , but their damage is not equal . Extreme flooding shows the strongest negative effect , with a standardized mean difference of -0.352 , followed by extreme heat at -0.327 , extreme drought at -0.304 , precipitation fluctuation at -0.218 and temperature anomaly at -0.105 . <p> The study 's ranking is reinforced by SUCRA values , a statistical measure used to compare the relative intensity of the shocks . Extreme flooding ranks first with a SUCRA value of 92.6 , ahead of extreme heat at 78.3 and extreme drought at 69.4 . The paper explains that floods damage agricultural production not only by destroying crops , but also by harming facilities , degrading soil fertility and disrupting recovery . Heat and drought remain major threats , but they operate through different channels , including heat stress on crops and restricted water supply . <p> In many countries , agricultural adaptation still focuses heavily on drought preparedness and water scarcity . Those remain essential , but the evidence suggests that flood resilience must move higher on the agenda , especially where @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ insurance remain weak . Climate adaptation for agriculture is no longer only about surviving dry years ; it is also about protecting production systems from too much water arriving too fast . <h> The Climate Burden Falls Where Farming Is Most Exposed <p> Low-latitude countries and tropical or subtropical regions suffer much stronger shocks than mid- and high-latitude regions . The pooled effect size for low-latitude countries is -0.452 , compared with -0.198 for mid- and high-latitude regions . In low-latitude areas , extreme flooding is the dominant risk ; in mid- and high-latitude areas , extreme high temperature is the main threat . <p> This uneven burden matters because many low-latitude countries are also developing economies with large rural populations , weaker agricultural infrastructure and higher dependence on climate-sensitive farming . The study 's evidence base includes 36 countries and regions across Asia , Africa , Europe , the Americas and Oceania , covering both developed economies such as the United States , Germany , France and Japan and developing economies including India , Brazil , South Africa , Thailand and parts of sub-Saharan Africa . <p> For the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ; they are development shocks . When floods , heatwaves or droughts reduce farm resilience , they can affect rural incomes , food prices , fiscal stability , nutrition outcomes and migration pressures . A resilience gap in agriculture can quickly become a governance challenge . This is why climate finance and technology transfer should not be treated as optional development support , but as core instruments for protecting food systems in the regions facing the sharpest climate exposure . <h> Rain-Fed Farms Are the Weak Link in Food Security <p> The study also shows that how food is produced strongly shapes how vulnerable it is . Rain-fed agriculture and crop farming suffer far greater climate impacts than irrigated agriculture and livestock systems . The pooled effect size for rain-fed agriculture and crop farming is -0.436 , compared with -0.209 for irrigated agriculture and livestock systems . The dominant shock for rain-fed crop systems is extreme flooding , while irrigated and livestock systems are more affected by drought . <p> Rain-fed farms depend heavily on natural rainfall and have limited control over water availability . When rainfall becomes erratic , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these farms have fewer buffers . Irrigation systems , livestock facilities and protected agriculture can reduce exposure by allowing more control over water , temperature and production conditions . This does not make them immune to climate risks , but it does improve their capacity to absorb shocks . <p> Agricultural structure also matters . Crop-dominated systems face the strongest climate impacts , with a pooled effect size of -0.468 . Balanced crop-livestock systems experience a smaller effect of -0.302 , while livestock and **31;2599;TOOLONG systems show the weakest effect at -0.185 . Within crop farming , the share of rain-fed agriculture is closely linked to vulnerability : high rain-fed systems show a pooled effect size of -0.512 , compared with -0.226 for low rain-fed and high-irrigation systems . The authors conclude that irrigation infrastructure acts as a core buffer against drought , precipitation variability , extreme heat and other climate shocks . <p> Governments do not have to wait for perfect climate models to begin reducing vulnerability . Investments in water-saving irrigation , drainage , rainwater harvesting , flood-control infrastructure , storage , logistics , climate-resilient seeds and diversified @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ banks and private investors , the study points to a large adaptation opportunity : the future of food security will depend heavily on infrastructure and technologies that help farms manage both water scarcity and water excess . <h> Adaptation Must Be Targeted , Not Generic <p> The study screens 3268 records and retains 76 valid empirical papers , including 38 Chinese and 38 English studies , from which 405 independent effect sizes are extracted for network meta-analysis . The authors also conduct quality checks , robustness tests and publication bias analysis . Their leave-one-out analysis finds that omitting any single study does not change the core conclusions , while a journal-only sensitivity test preserves the same ranking of climate hazards : extreme flood , extreme heat , extreme drought , precipitation fluctuation and temperature anomaly . <p> Still , the findings should be read with care . APR is measured differently across the studies included in the meta-analysis , and the authors acknowledge that converting diverse indicators into standardized effect sizes requires assumptions that can not be fully tested with the available literature . The literature search is also mainly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or non-English evidence may be missing . The paper further notes that it does not fully examine economic development , agricultural policy , technological investment or institutional environments , and that its analysis is more static than dynamic over time . <p> Despite these limitations , the policy direction is compelling . Agricultural climate policy must become more differentiated . <p> The world needs anticipatory adaptation : building agricultural systems that can absorb shocks before they become food crises . Floods , heat and drought will not affect all regions equally , and resilience will not emerge automatically . It will depend on choices made now about water systems , farm structure , technology , insurance , infrastructure and international cooperation .

@@138657705 <h> Cooperatives : The engine of inclusive growth and sustainable development <p> By Satish Marathe <p> From dairy to banking and housing , cooperatives have shaped India 's grassroots economy . As the government pushes the vision of Sahakar Se Samriddhi , modernising these institutions through better governance , technology and professional management can unlock inclusive growth , and build a more resilient economy <p> As the world grapples with widening inequalities , climate change , food insecurity , financial instability and the need for sustainable economic growth , the cooperative movement has emerged as one of the most effective models of people-centric development . Cooperatives are not merely business enterprises ; they are democratic institutions owned , managed and governed by their members . Built on the principles of self-help , mutual assistance , equality and collective prosperity , cooperatives have consistently demonstrated that economic growth and social justice can go hand in hand . <p> India has a rich cooperative tradition inspired by visionary leaders such as Mahatma Gandhi , Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel , Acharya Vinoba Bhave , Vaikunthbhai Mehta and Dhananjayrao Gadgil . They viewed cooperation not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for rural development , social harmony and empowerment of ordinary citizens . Today , as India aspires to become a developed nation by 2047 , the cooperative movement is once again acquiring strategic significance in shaping an inclusive and resilient economy . <p> The cooperative movement in India began with the enactment of the Cooperative Credit Societies Act of 1904 . Over the decades , it expanded far beyond agricultural credit to encompass dairy , banking , sugar , fertilisers , housing , fisheries , consumer services , handloom , marketing and numerous other sectors . Today , cooperatives have one of the largest grassroots institutional networks in the country , reaching almost every village and serving millions of members across urban and rural India . <p> Agriculture continues to provide livelihoods to a substantial proportion of India 's population while supplying raw materials to numerous industries . Small and marginal farmers , who constitute the overwhelming majority of cultivators , often face fragmented landholdings , inadequate access to markets , volatile prices and climate-related uncertainties . Cooperatives provide an institutional mechanism through which these farmers can pool resources , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ marketing and strengthen their bargaining power . <p> Primary Agricultural Credit Societies ( PACS ) , dairy cooperatives and farmer producer organisations have become indispensable pillars of rural development . Beyond credit delivery , modern cooperatives are increasingly participating in food processing , warehousing , value addition , cold storage and exports , enabling farmers to capture a larger share of the value chain . This transformation is particularly significant at a time when global food demand continues to rise and agricultural sustainability has become a worldwide concern . <p> The Government of India 's decision to establish a dedicated Ministry of Cooperation under the vision of " Sahakar Se Samriddhi " marks an important milestone in revitalising the sector . The computerisation of PACS , expansion of multipurpose cooperative societies , creation of a national cooperative database , promotion of cooperative exports and initiatives for the world 's largest grain storage programme through cooperatives reflect a renewed policy commitment to strengthening grassroots institutions . The cooperative model is equally significant in financial inclusion . Cooperative banks and credit societies have historically extended banking services to areas where commercial banks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ providing affordable credit , they have supported agriculture , micro-enterprises , artisans , self-employed workers and rural entrepreneurs . Unlike purely profit-driven financial institutions , cooperatives operate on the principle of member welfare , ensuring that financial services remain accessible to economically weaker sections . <p> Housing cooperatives have enabled millions of middle-class families to own affordable homes , while consumer cooperatives have protected members from exploitative market practices . Dairy cooperatives have transformed India into one of the world 's largest milk producers , demonstrating how collective ownership can create globally competitive enterprises . Despite these achievements , the Indian cooperative sector faces several structural challenges . Many societies suffer from dormant membership , inadequate member participation , weak governance , political interference , insufficient professional management and excessive dependence on government financial support . Financial stress arising from loan defaults , limited capital mobilisation and inadequate technological adoption has also affected the competitiveness of several cooperative institutions . <p> Addressing these challenges requires comprehensive reforms rather than greater governmental control . Cooperative autonomy , democratic functioning , professional management , transparent governance and accountability must remain the cornerstones @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ preserving the unique identity of cooperatives as member-owned enterprises . <p> The constitutional recognition accorded to cooperatives through the Ninety-Seventh Constitutional Amendment reinforced the importance of voluntary formation , democratic control and autonomous functioning . Although constitutional developments have refined its scope , the amendment remains an important milestone in recognising cooperatives as essential institutions of democratic economic development . Globally , the cooperative movement represents one of the largest socio-economic networks in the world . More than one billion people across over one hundred countries are members of cooperatives operating in diverse sectors including agriculture , finance , insurance , healthcare , retail , housing , fisheries , renewable energy and telecommunications . Millions of jobs worldwide are directly or indirectly supported by cooperative enterprises . <p> Countries such as Finland , Canada , New Zealand , Singapore and Norway demonstrate exceptionally high levels of cooperative participation . Kenya derives a significant share of its GDP from cooperative enterprises , while New Zealand 's dairy industry owes much of its global competitiveness to farmer-owned cooperatives . Cooperative banks in Europe have consistently demonstrated financial resilience , often weathering global @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ prudent lending practices and long-term orientation . Health cooperatives have become important providers of affordable healthcare in countries such as Brazil , Japan , France , Germany and the Netherlands . Consumer cooperatives dominate retail markets in Switzerland , Italy and Singapore , while housing cooperatives have successfully addressed urban housing challenges in Scandinavia , the United Kingdom and the United States . Electricity cooperatives continue to deliver reliable power to rural communities in the United States , Bangladesh and Argentina where private utilities have limited commercial incentives to operate . International experience also demonstrates the remarkable resilience of cooperatives during periods of conflict and economic disruption . In countries recovering from civil wars , cooperatives have helped rebuild livelihoods , restore agricultural production , revive financial systems and strengthen community trust . Their democratic character enables them to bridge social divisions and foster inclusive local development . <p> As India advances towards becoming a developed economy , cooperatives can serve as powerful engines of inclusive growth by reducing inequalities , empowering farmers , generating employment , strengthening rural industries , promoting women 's economic participation and ensuring equitable distribution @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is created through collective participation . <p> The cooperative movement may not be the sole answer to every developmental challenge , but it undoubtedly constitutes one of the most effective pathways towards sustainable and inclusive progress . By combining economic efficiency with social responsibility and democratic governance , cooperatives embody the vision of development that leaves no one behind . Strengthened by progressive policies , modern technology and active member participation , India 's cooperative sector can become a defining pillar of national development , transforming the philosophy of " Sahakar Se Samriddhi " into a lasting reality for millions of citizens . <p> The writer is a founder member of Sahakar Bharti , Director Central Board RBI , NABARD &amp; NHB ; Views presented are personal . 
@@138657801 <p> Modern human civilisation , industrialisation , urbanisation , and rapid economic growth and prosperity are inextricably linked to ever-increasing energy consumption . Animals consume energy in the form of food for survival . Only modern humans consume most energy not for food but for convenience , comfort , and the consumption of various goods and services . We consume about 2,500 kcal of food per day per capita . That is roughly equivalent to 3 kWh of energy . <p> Every year , a person consumes about 1,000 kWh of energy as food . All humanity ( 8.3 billion ) thus consumes about 8,300 terawatt hours ( TWh ) of energy per year as food . Considering that global primary energy consumption in all forms by humanity is about 200,000 TWh , we consume about 25 times the energy that we eat as food for survival . In a fundamental sense , our energy consumption distinguishes us from all other animals and has enabled us to enjoy a measure of comfort , convenience , and quality of life unmatched by any other species . <p> Rise Of Modern Energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ limited to firewood for cooking and heating . With the advent of the Industrial Revolution , things changed rapidly . In 1804 , Richard Trevithick designed the first steam-powered railway locomotive . From the 1850s , rail transport took off . In India , the first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853 . In the US , the first transcontinental rail track was completed in 1869 . The use of coal kept increasing for railways from 1850 onwards . <p> With Thomas Edison 's invention of the electric bulb in 1879 , and with alternating current winning the " War of the Currents " in 1895 as an efficient mode of transmission of power over long distances , the age of electricity dawned . Coal became the fuel of choice for the production of electricity , and coal consumption took off . <p> With Henry Ford 's remarkable success with assembly lines and the mass production of automobiles from 1908 , the era of oil began . From the 1950s , natural gas consumption grew dramatically for heating , cooking , and use as industrial fuel and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ massive consumption of energy , without which life comes to a standstill and economies collapse . Oil consumption , which constitutes 30% of our primary energy consumption , was 11 million barrels per day ( mbd ) in 1950 and now stands at 103 mbd . Global coal consumption , mostly for thermal power , stands at 8.8 billion tonnes per year and accounts for about 27% of the global energy supply . Natural gas consumption of 4 trillion cubic metres ( bcm ) accounts for about 23% of primary energy consumption . Renewable energy -- nuclear , hydropower , solar , wind and biofuels -- accounts for about 19% of energy , and this segment is growing rapidly . <p> Climate And Energy Challenge <p> In the past four decades , climate scientists have concluded that atmospheric carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) levels are rising ( 280 ppm in the pre-industrial era ; about 432 ppm now ) and are causing global warming due to the greenhouse effect , and this rise is very likely due to human activities . Since then , there have been serious concerns about @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Concerted efforts are being made to reduce CO2 emissions . <p> But given our critical dependence on energy consumption for economic activity , we are always falling short of our targets . Climate sceptics dismiss the concerns of global warming as alarmist and argue that changes in temperature are part of natural cycles throughout the planet 's history and that reducing consumption of fossil fuels ( coal , oil and gas ) would be painful and unnecessary . Irrespective of which argument is right , prudence and the precautionary principle demand that we reduce CO2 emissions and switch over to alternative , renewable energy sources . <p> Until about four decades ago , the concern all over the globe was " peak oil/gas/coal production " and the likelihood of depletion of these fuels , posing an existential threat to humanity , as they are finite in quantity and will eventually be exhausted . Estimates indicate that global oil and gas reserves may last about 50 to 55 years and coal reserves about 130 years . Experience has shown us that new deposits may be found through exploration . A new analysis from ClimaMeter reveals that 327 million people and US$15.6 trillion of assets were exposed to heat intensified by climate change in the late June @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ people and 86 per cent of those assets exposed to the highest category of heat . <p> ClimaMeter is an observation-based , rapid climate attribution framework designed to analyse extreme weather events in real time . Developed by scientists at the Institut Pierre-Simon Laplace ( IPSL ) and the French National Centre for Scientific Research ( CNRS ) , the platform contextualises ongoing extreme weather by comparing it directly to similar historical weather patterns . <p> Beginning in late June 2026 , Europe experienced an exceptionally intense and record-breaking heatwave driven by an atmospheric phenomenon known as a " heat dome " . Such a heat dome is associated with a stable atmospheric blocking pattern that inhibits the typical west-to-east progression of weather systems . This persistent blocking high-pressure system , referred to as an " Omega block " , forms when a persistent area of high pressure traps hot air over a large region , preventing cooler air from entering , inhibiting local convection , cloud formation , and precipitation , and allowing temperatures to rise continuously for several days . A surface low-pressure system to the west of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advecting warm , dry air from North Africa towards Western Europe . <p> " Heat domes like the one behind the June 2026 Western European heatwave are not new : quasi-stationary blocking anticyclones have always formed over the continent . What has changed is the baseline on which they act , " said Marco Zanchi , CNRS- IPSL , France . <p> " ClimaMeter 's analogue analysis shows that meteorological configurations of this type are today up to 2.5 ? C warmer than they were a few decades ago , and that they now persist for longer . The same circulation that once produced a hot but manageable spell now delivers record-breaking temperatures over dry land , because the atmosphere it draws on has been thermodynamically amplified by human-driven climate change , " said Zanchi . <p> According to Haosu Tang , University of Sheffield , UK : " One of the most overlooked aspects of events like the June 2026 heatwave is that they are becoming increasingly predictable from a meteorological perspective , yet remain socially disruptive . " <p> " The sequence of exceptional heatwaves striking Europe is unprecedented . @@138658269 <h> At the national level , no single agency has the mandate , the legal authority , and the public accountability to tell India what wildlife crime actually looks like . <p> In August 2025 , the Ministry of Environment , Forest and Climate Change placed a set of numbers before the Lok Sabha that , on the surface , read like good news . Wildlife crime in India , the government said , had fallen sharply . From 820 registered cases in 2020 , the count had dropped to 349 in 2023 and edged up slightly to 354 in 2024 . Total cases between 2020 and 2024 were 2,701 . In a country that hosts 106 national parks , 573 wildlife sanctuaries , and over 70 per cent of the world 's wild tiger population , the trend appeared reassuring . <p> It should not . <p> The data placed before Parliament comes almost entirely from the police . It excludes the majority of wildlife crime cases registered in India , which are filed not by the police but by state forest departments . <p> The National Crime Records @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ official crime statistics annually , captures only one of two enforcement streams . The other , far larger stream flows largely in the dark , uncounted , and unchecked . What the government presented as a declining crime rate is , in practice , a declining count of the fraction of crimes that one agency bothers to report to a central database . <h> Two databases , one black hole <p> The structure of India 's wildlife crime data problem is not complicated , even if the institutional complacency that sustains it has persisted for over a decade . The Wildlife ( Protection ) Act , 1972 gives both the police and forest department officials the power to register wildlife offences . The NCRB collects crime data through a chain that runs from district records bureaus to state bureaus and then to the national level . This chain runs through the police . <p> Forest department cases , however , flow into a separate system managed by the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau ( WCCB ) , a statutory body under the Ministry of Environment , Forest and Climate Change established @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Database Management System . That database is not in the public domain . <p> Researcher Shankar Prakash Alagesan laid this problem out with precision in a 2020 peer-reviewed paper published in the Indian Journal of Environmental Education . Alagesan found that two enforcement agencies operate parallel databases with no mandatory integration point . His conclusion was direct : <p> " In order to measure the extent of enforcement of WPA , wildlife crime data becomes a crucial indicator . As discussed elsewhere , wildlife crime databases are vital information system that helps enforcement officers to detect , prevent , and pursue criminals . Hence , a centralised , integrated wildlife crime database becomes the need of the hour . " <p> His recommendation , that the WCCB act as a nodal integrator and publish consolidated data in the manner of the NCRB 's annual ' Crime in India ' report , remains unimplemented five years on . <p> The Citizen consumer and civic Action Group made the same argument in a detailed 2022 analysis , noting that NCRB data on wildlife crime " can not make any meaningful assessment of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are invisible to it . This is not a marginal technical flaw . The NCRB 's own publication acknowledges that the chapter on environment-related offences " only includes wildlife crime cases registered by police alone " . <h> What the numbers actually show <p> The gap between what forest departments register and what the NCRB records is not marginal . Karnataka provides a concrete documented illustration . According to documents reviewed by Deccan Herald and corroborated by state officials , Karnataka 's forest department recorded 1,956 wildlife offences between 2018-19 and 2021-22 . Over 3,520 cases remained pending before courts , a figure that itself reveals the volume of actual enforcement actions that never enter the national database . In the same years , Karnataka 's contribution to NCRB national totals was a small fraction of that number . Across the five years from 2020 to 2024 , the NCRB counted just 84 wildlife crime cases from Karnataka . <p> The gap between 1,956 forest-department offences over roughly four years and 84 police-registered cases over five years is not a statistical curiosity . It is the difference between what actually @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ record books say happened there . <p> " The forest department underreports cases of poaching , animal death , conflicts , encroachment and forest fire areas , " said BK Mukherjee , then Accountant General ( E&amp;RSA ) , while speaking about the report in 2017 . <p> The CAG auditors noted that encroachment data in official records was a fraction of what satellite maps showed on the ground , and that management plans were absent for most protected areas . <p> Kerala 's record is equally telling . A separate CAG audit found that the state registered 630 wildlife offences over 17 years , of which only 20 resulted in convictions . The auditors traced this to failures in evidence gathering , forensic incapacity , and procedural lapses at the forest department level . <h> A 2 per cent conviction rate <p> The data black hole does not exist in isolation from what happens when cases do reach the courts . Between 2012 and 2018 , over 9,253 poachers were arrested across India in wildlife crime cases . The conviction rate , according to a 2023 peer-reviewed study by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Biodiversity and Conservation , was 2 per cent . Thousands of arrests resulted in fewer than 200 convictions , which is low enough to function as an effective impunity guarantee for organised trafficking networks . <p> " The number of cases detected are high but it is nearly impossible to secure conviction . Lack of trained and specialised staff in investigating and handling such seizures , and the shortage of resources and poor maintenance of records of habitual offenders affect the rate of conviction , " he told Deccan Herald . <p> Those words , " poor maintenance of records " , carry particular weight here . Records that are scattered across two parallel systems , incomplete at the point of registration , and then never integrated can not build a prosecution . The data gap is not merely a statistical inconvenience . It is the institutional precondition for persistent impunity . <h> A bureau running on Rs 15.14 crore <p> The WCCB , the nodal enforcement body that should be integrating and publishing this data , operates on a budget that reveals exactly how seriously the central government treats @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2026-27 is Rs 15.14 crore . For an agency mandated to combat transboundary wildlife crime across a country with over 1,000 protected areas and a coastline of 11,098 kilometres , this figure is structurally inadequate . <p> The WCCB operates through five regional offices located at New Delhi , Mumbai , Jabalpur , Chennai , and Kolkata , three sub-regional offices , and five border units . All positions are filled through deputation , meaning the bureau draws its officers from other services rather than building a permanent , specialised cadre trained in wildlife crime investigation . In this context , the WCCB 's own acknowledgement that 30 to 40 per cent of wildlife incidents go unreported because villagers living near forests fear retaliation should be read as a confession of institutional reach , not just a community policing gap . <p> Uttar Pradesh , which recorded 297 wildlife crime cases in the NCRB dataset between 2020 and 2024 and sits along trafficking corridors connecting Nepal to domestic markets , has one forest guard for every 50 square kilometres of forest . With that kind of coverage , the cases @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ proportion of what is actually happening on the ground . <h> When conservation criminalises the wrong people <p> In May 2025 , 52 Jenu Kuruba families marched back into the Nagarahole Tiger Reserve in Karnataka , returning to lands from which their community had been evicted nearly four decades earlier . Their ancestors were displaced when the area was first sealed off in the 1970s and 1980s to create the national park and later , the tiger reserve . The Jenu Kuruba , classified as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group , had submitted claims under the Forest Rights Act , 2006(FRA) as far back as 2009 . By 2025 , those claims remained unprocessed . <p> The forest department 's response was swift . On 17 June 2025 , officials issued notices to the families under the Wildlife Protection Act , 1972 , citing illegal occupation . The following afternoon , around 250 personnel from the forest department , the Special Tiger Protection Force , and the police tore down six of the community 's newly built huts . The Karadikallu Gram Sabha , which had passed a resolution supporting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forest department has imposed several projects on our lands -- wildlife sanctuaries , protected areas , tiger reserves , national parks -- all in the name of conservation . We are not the occupiers ; we are the original inhabitants , " Thimanna who has been part of several movements to save tribal land in Nagarahole , including the fight against Taj Hotels , told Maktoob Media in January 2026 . <p> This dynamic carries direct consequences for wildlife crime data . When forest communities lose their legal recognition and their formal relationship with the forest , they also lose the standing to report what they see . A Jenu Kuruba community member who witnesses poaching inside Nagarahole is simultaneously a person whom the forest department has just served a notice under the Wildlife Protection Act . That person does not file a complaint with the department that just demolished her home . Wildlife crime that forest communities know about and could report remains invisible because the enforcement system has made adversaries of those best positioned to provide intelligence . <p> The criminalisation runs deeper than just the chilling of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs documented , in Nagarahole Tiger Reserve specifically , Individual Forest Rights were recognised primarily for the Yerawal community but not for the Jenu Kuruba . This selective recognition reflects the forest bureaucracy 's persistent preference for a people-free conservation model . It removes communities precisely where their presence would most complicate the government 's infrastructure and tourism concessions . <h> The politics of the data gap <p> The situation of the Jenu Kuruba community in Nagarahole is not an isolated case of local implementation failure . It reflects a broader direction in India 's forest governance that the data gap actively conceals . The Forest Conservation Amendment Act of 2023 introduced a new definition of " forest " that excludes large areas from legal protection , opening them to industrial and infrastructure use without requiring Gram Sabha consent . In May 2025 , the Chhattisgarh state forest department declared itself the " nodal agency " for Community Forest Resource management , an order that would have displaced Gram Sabha authority entirely . The order was placed in abeyance in July 2025 after protests @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ These moves make the data gap wider , not smaller . When forest communities lose legal recognition , they stop functioning as intelligence sources for wildlife crime . When Gram Sabha authority over forest management is displaced , the collective surveillance that communities provide over who enters and exits the forest , and with what , collapses . The forest becomes monitored only by an understaffed department with one guard per 50 square kilometres , a WCCB with a budget of Rs 15.14 crore , and a database that nobody outside the ministry can access . <p> The organised wildlife trafficking networks that move tiger bones from Madhya Pradesh to China , pangolin scales from Mizoram to Southeast Asia , or red sanders from Andhra Pradesh to ports in Tamil Nadu do not operate in the villages of Nagarahole . They operate through supply chains that intersect the forest at its boundary . Those boundaries are guarded most effectively by the people who live inside the forest and know who does not belong . Strip those people of their rights , criminalise their presence , and the trafficking corridor widens @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ count . <h> Who is accountable for the numbers <p> At the national level , no single agency has the mandate , the legal authority , and the public accountability to tell India what wildlife crime actually looks like . The NCRB counts only police cases . The WCCB collects forest department data that it does not publish . The Ministry of Environment makes selective disclosures to Parliament . The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence , which handles seizures at ports and airports , maintains its own separate data stream , also not integrated . Researchers who file RTI queries force partial disclosures . All these factors confirm what the academic literature has been arguing since 2020 : the official wildlife crime picture is a fraction of the actual one . <p> India 's forests are not safer just because official numbers are falling . The wildlife crime that threatens tigers in Jim Corbett , pangolins in Mizoram , star tortoises in Andhra Pradesh , and river dolphins in the Gangetic plains continues largely undocumented , underprosecuted , and unaccounted for . The communities who know these forests best , who @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ snares , have been systematically excluded from both the data systems and the governance structures that could make those systems better . <p> The numbers the government presents to Parliament are not a measure of what is happening in India 's forests . They are a measure of how much the state has chosen to see . <p> Ankit Mishra is an ICSSR Fellow at Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute , Prayagraj . @@138668803 <h> The Freshwater Crisis Is Bigger Than Running Out of Water <p> Every summer , headlines warn of another Indian city running short of water . Bengaluru 's reservoirs shrink . Delhi faces shortages . Farmers in Punjab drill deeper wells , while Himalayan glaciers continue to retreat . These are usually reported as separate crises driven by rising demand , population growth , or climate change . All of that is true . But taken together , they point to something much larger : we are no longer just using more water than before ; we are beginning to alter the natural processes that store , circulate , and replenish water across the Earth system itself . That is what the freshwater planetary boundary seeks to measure , and scientists now conclude that humanity has already crossed it . <p> Two Kinds of Water , Both Boundaries Broken <p> For most of the planetary boundaries framework 's history , the freshwater boundary tracked only what scientists call blue water -- the water found in rivers , lakes , reservoirs and underground aquifers . This is the water most people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ assessment led by Katherine Richardson at the Stockholm Resilience Centre -- the first time all nine planetary boundaries were fully quantified simultaneously -- expanded this significantly . It added green water to the measurement : the moisture stored in soils , the water absorbed by plant roots , and the evapotranspiration that forests and grasslands return to the atmosphere . According to the assessment , published in Science Advances , the freshwater boundary is now transgressed for both components . <p> That second category matters enormously and receives almost no public attention . Green water is what allows forests to function , crops to grow , and the atmosphere to carry moisture from one region to another . It is not the water pumped from a well or diverted from a river , but the water that moves invisibly through soils and plants , regulating how much rainfall a landscape generates and retains . When forests are cleared and soils degrade , this cycle begins to weaken . The land becomes drier , absorbs less rain , and returns less moisture to the atmosphere through evaporation and transpiration . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ enormous amounts of water back into the air , creating vast streams of water vapour -- often called ' atmospheric rivers ' -- that winds carry hundreds and even thousands of kilometres inland . That recycled moisture later falls as rain over distant regions , sustaining agriculture , rivers , and ecosystems far beyond the forest itself . Remove enough of the forest , and the consequences are no longer confined to where the trees once stood ; rainfall patterns across entire regions begin to shift . <p> Water Is Always Moving <p> This runs against the intuition most people bring to water discussions . We tend to think of water as something stored -- in a reservoir , an aquifer , a glacier , a lake . In reality , water is perpetually in motion : evaporating from oceans , carried inland by winds , falling as rain and snow , absorbed by soils and plants , transpired back into the atmosphere , flowing through rivers to the sea , and recharging aquifers slowly over years or decades . This circulation is what makes freshwater available at all . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It is a set of processes , each linked to the other and each dependent on conditions such as vegetation cover , soil health , temperature , and land use , all of which keep the circulation functioning . <p> The 2022 study that defined the green water boundary , led by Lan Wang-Erlandsson , found that soil moisture patterns are shifting across the planet , from the boreal forests of the north to the tropical rainforests nearer the equator . Regions that once experienced relatively stable wet and dry cycles are now seeing soils become unusually dry in some places and unusually wet in others . In other words , the natural rhythms governing how water moves through landscapes are becoming less predictable . That is what crossing the green water boundary actually means . It is not simply that humanity is using too much water , but that the processes controlling how moisture is stored in soils , recycled by plants , and returned to the atmosphere are being disrupted on a planetary scale . <p> Urban flooding and urban water scarcity are therefore not opposite problems @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the same hydrological instability expressing itself at different moments of the same disrupted cycle -- too much water arriving faster than degraded soils can absorb , followed by too little stored in the systems that should carry communities through the dry months . Both are symptoms of a water cycle under pressure from land use , extraction , and a warming atmosphere simultaneously . <p> A Different Way of Seeing Water <p> For centuries , humanity assumed the water cycle was one of the planet 's permanent features that rivers would flow , monsoons would return , and aquifers would gradually refill . The freshwater planetary boundary reminds us that this was only possible because the forests , soils , wetlands and climate that keep water moving through the Earth system remained broadly stable . Those conditions are no longer guaranteed . <p> The challenge ahead is not simply to use water more efficiently , important though that is . It is to manage forests , soils and landscapes in ways that keep the Earth 's natural water cycle functioning . Water scarcity is real , but it is only @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ itself is beginning to change . Cities that swing from severe summer shortages to devastating monsoon floods are not experiencing separate crises ; they are living through the consequences of a water system that is becoming increasingly unstable . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Utkarsh Mishra is a journalist based in Ranchi writing on law , labour rights , and the environment . His work has appeared in Feminism in India , The India Forum , Down to Earth , The Policy Circle , Verdicto News and Zee News . <p> Without synthetic fertiliser , modern civilisation probably could n't exist in its current form . Scientific institutions have repeatedly warned that the Himalayas are among the world 's youngest and most unstable mountain systems , making them exceptionally vulnerable to geological disturbances . Rising temperatures are altering rainfall patterns across the Himalayas , producing shorter but far more intense bursts of precipitation . Glacial retreat is changing river behaviour , while warming slopes increase the likelihood of rockfalls and landslides .
