@@138741756 <h> Forests Are Not Just Trees . They Are How the Planet Works <p> Every year , satellite images reveal another stretch of forest disappearing . The debate that follows usually centres on wildlife habitat or carbon storage . Both matter . But forests do far more than shelter species or absorb carbon . They regulate rainfall , stabilise soils , protect biodiversity , and shape the water cycle itself . The planetary boundaries framework captures this broader role through the land-system change boundary , which asks not simply how many trees have been lost , but how much of the Earth 's living surface has been transformed into landscapes that can no longer perform the ecological functions they once did . <p> The popular framing of deforestation as a carbon problem is accurate but incomplete . Forests regulate rainfall , stabilise soils , recharge groundwater , moderate temperatures , and support the web of species this series examined in its article on biosphere integrity . Remove them , and each of those functions begins to unravel -- often in ways that appear , on the surface , as separate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the most direct . Forests do n't simply absorb rainfall ; they generate it . Trees draw water from the soil and release it through their leaves into the atmosphere , where it condenses and falls again elsewhere . The Amazon rainforest , through this process , generates rainfall hundreds of kilometres from the forest itself , sustaining agriculture across South American interior regions that receive no direct oceanic rainfall . Deforest enough of it and the rainfall it produces disappears with it , turning the water boundary and the land boundary into the same problem expressed in two different places . <p> The connection to soil is just as important . Tree roots hold the soil together , while fallen leaves and organic matter keep it porous enough to absorb rainfall rather than rushing away . Remove the forest , and heavy rain is far more likely to cause flooding than to recharge groundwater . Water that would have soaked into the earth instead races across the surface , carrying away fertile topsoil , silting up rivers downstream , and leaving the surrounding landscape both more vulnerable to floods @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the rains end . <p> Forests also cool the land through evapotranspiration -- the same process that helps generate rainfall . Once they are cleared , the exposed ground absorbs more heat and loses much of that natural cooling effect , pushing local temperatures higher . This is why land-system change is closely linked to the climate boundary : deforestation not only releases the carbon stored in trees but also removes one of nature 's most effective systems for cooling the landscape . <p> India 's Forests in Numbers and in Practice <p> India 's official forest cover story is more complicated than the headline numbers suggest . The Forest Survey of India 's 2023 State of Forest Report says the country 's total forest and tree cover has risen to 25.17 per cent of its geographical area . But a closer reading reveals a different pattern . Ecologically important landscapes , including the Western Ghats , the northeastern states , and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands , have all recorded declines in natural forest cover . Much of the reported increase comes from plantations and agroforestry , which can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ regulation , and ecological functions of old-growth forests . <p> The drivers vary by region and are worth naming specifically because they are not uniform across regions . In Hasdeo Arand , one of central India 's last large contiguous forest tracts and the source of several major rivers in Chhattisgarh , coal mining has already claimed forest land and the Parsa Kente Basan coal block clearance is set to require the felling of 3.68 lakh trees . In the Andaman and Nicobar Islands , the government 's planned infrastructure project on Great Nicobar -- involving a transhipment port , airport , and township -- is projected to clear 130 square kilometres of one of India 's last intact forest landscapes , between one million and ten million trees , on an island whose forests have developed in isolation over millions of years . The Western Ghats Eco-Sensitive Area has lost 58.22 square kilometres of forest cover over the past decade . The northeastern region saw a 327-square-kilometre decrease in its last assessment . <p> What these cases have in common is not the cause of clearing but its consequence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ millions of people depend on for water , for stable soil , for flood regulation , and for the livelihoods tied to forest produce , fishing , and farming downstream . <p> The Cascading Logic <p> The planetary boundaries framework uses forests as its primary measure of land-system change because they influence so many other Earth-system processes at once . Clearing forests releases carbon into the atmosphere , intensifying climate change . It reduces rainfall and limits groundwater recharge , placing greater pressure on freshwater systems . It destroys habitats and fragments ecosystems , accelerating biodiversity loss . In other words , deforestation is not a single environmental problem . It is a force that amplifies many of the others this series has already explored . <p> That is what the framework means by Earth-system change . The point is not simply that forests are ecologically important -- that has long been recognised . It is that forests , water , soils , biodiversity and climate function as one interconnected system . Clearing land in one place can alter rainfall somewhere else , raise temperatures across an entire region , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Land is not simply space waiting to be developed . It is part of the living infrastructure that keeps the planet functioning , and we are transforming it faster than those systems can adapt . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Utkarsh Mishra is a journalist based in Ranchi writing on law , labour rights , and the environment . His work has appeared in Feminism in India , The India Forum , Down to Earth , The Policy Circle , Verdicto News and Zee News . <p> Human civilisation has always made new materials . Bronze , steel , concrete , glass -- each transformed what societies could build and how they could live . @@138741769 <h> The American Promise at 250 : Between International Legitimacy and the Reality of Power <p> For 250 years , the United States has carried one of the most influential political promises in modern history : the belief that human beings can govern themselves , that rights are inherent rather than granted , and that power must be accountable to the people . This promise emerged in a world ruled by empires , monarchies , and coercive authority , making it at the time a radical declaration of human dignity and political possibility . Yet the distance between the ideals proclaimed at the nation 's founding and the realities of its global conduct remains a subject of enduring debate . <p> From the outset , America announced liberty while denying it to millions , spoke of equality while sustaining slavery , and built a constitutional order that protected rights while leaving each generation with the unfinished task of making those rights universal . As observers often note , " The strength of a promise lies not in its beauty , but in its fulfillment . " Today , admiration for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Over decades , the world has witnessed wars , occupations , and sanctions that have destabilized entire regions . Political and military decisions have weakened prospects for peace and strained the principles of international humanitarian law . Fear and mistrust have reshaped societies , often imposing costs on civilians who bear no responsibility for geopolitical calculations . As one humanitarian scholar wrote , " When power speaks too loudly , humanity becomes difficult to hear . " <p> At the same time , global challenges demand unprecedented cooperation : climate change , pandemics , food insecurity , artificial intelligence , outer space governance , and cyber stability . In these arenas , gaps persist between American rhetoric and practice . The United States withdrew from the Paris Climate Agreement before rejoining it , resisted binding frameworks for cyber governance , and opposed international rules for the peaceful use of outer space . <p> It is also important to recognize that the United States has played constructive roles in building peace and supporting global recovery . After World War II , it contributed to rebuilding Europe and Japan , supported @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ financial institutions , and backed development programs that shaped global stability for decades . These achievements form part of the American promise . Yet this article examines whether that promise , after 250 years , still aligns with the principles of international legitimacy and human dignity . <p> Today , the performance of major powers is increasingly measured against the Sustainable Development Goals , especially good health and well-being , climate action , reduced inequalities , and strong institutions . Principles such as Health for All and Universal Health Coverage are no longer technical aspirations ; they are pillars of human security . Access to healthcare , food , water , and a safe environment now shapes the security of nations more profoundly than military strength . Climate change has become a direct threat to millions and a test of global responsibility , including that of the United States . <p> In the field of disarmament , a cornerstone of human security , the United States remains outside several key treaties designed to protect civilians and reduce the brutality of war : <p> * The Mine Ban Treaty* The Convention @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Weapons* The Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty <p> It has also not ratified major human rights instruments , including : <p> * The Convention on the Rights of the Child* The Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women* The Convention on Enforced Disappearances <p> These omissions are not procedural details ; they reflect structural hesitation toward emerging global consensus on human dignity and civilian protection . <p> In practice , the consequences have been profound . From the Vietnam War to the 2003 invasion of Iraq without UN authorization , from the prolonged conflict in Afghanistan to covert operations in Iran , Libya , and Syria , interventions have occurred outside the boundaries of international legitimacy . These actions have left deep societal scars and weakened global confidence in the norms the United States claims to defend . <p> Unilateral decisions have further strained the international order , including : <p> These decisions were rejected by the overwhelming majority of UN member states of the principle that territory can not be acquired by force . <p> Additionally , unilateral sanctions outside the UN framework , withdrawals from key international @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ resolutions aimed at protecting civilians , especially in Palestine , have widened the gap between moral discourse and political behavior . As one diplomat observed , " Legitimacy is not a possession ; it is a practice . " <p> This article does not seek to condemn but to analyze . It aims to understand how global security is shaped by the tension between declared principles and actual policies . The world stands at a critical juncture requiring a redefinition of the legitimacy of power , one rooted in adherence to international humanitarian law and in recognizing disarmament , especially nuclear disarmament , as essential to sustainable peace . <p> The future of the international system will not be built on military superiority but on the collective ability of nations to uphold law , protect civilians , and expand justice . In this context , the renewal of the American promise depends on the willingness of the United States to close the gap between its ideals and its actions , and to engage in a global order that places human dignity above all other considerations . <p> CONCLUSION <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moment to celebrate history but an opportunity to reassess it . The global future requires major powers , foremost among them the United States , to redefine their role in advancing peace , commit to international humanitarian law , join key disarmament treaties , and abandon unilateral policies that weaken the international system . Humanity today needs leadership measured not by the weapons it possesses but by the lives it protects . If the United States seeks to redefine its global leadership for the next quarter century , its strongest advantage will not be unmatched military power but unmatched credibility in defending international law , humanitarian disarmament treaties , and the protection of civilian life . Acknowledging past errors and correcting course in line with international legality and human justice is essential for any responsible global role , and for any promise seeking to regain its credibility . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Dr. Ghassan Shahrour , Coordinator of the Arab Human Security Network , is a medical doctor , prolific author , and human rights advocate specializing in health , disability , humanitarian disarmament , and human security @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ disarmament , and the rights of persons with disabilities . <p> The International Year of Volunteers 2026 comes at a time when communities worldwide face rising pressures from climate shocks to displacement , inequality , and social fragmentation . @@138759136 <h> Explained : The 12 reasons why Mumbai floods year after year <p> MUMBAI : Mumbai 's roads get flooded , train services get disrupted , traffic snarls and daily life come to a standstill every monsoon season . Heavy rain is the immediate trigger , but experts say it 's a combination of natural and man-made causes behind the city 's annual flooding.Because of the increased frequency of extreme rainfall events , which often take place at the same time as high tides , stormwater is less able to get out to sea . <p> The city 's vulnerability is compounded by its low-lying geography , ageing drainage network , stressed rivers and nullahs , shrinking wetlands and mangroves and rapid urbanisation . Blocked drains , ongoing infrastructure projects and long periods of rain with strong winds are also causing widespread disruption.Read also : Mumbai Rains Live Updates : Localized flooding alone can cripple Mumbai 's transport network and affect millions of commuters . This is made more difficult by the expected rise in the number of heavy rainfall events due to climate change . Here we examine 12 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and why creating a more flood-resilient city will take long-term planning , stronger infrastructure and better environmental management . <p> 1 . Greater incidence of extreme rainfallMumbai has always experienced heavy monsoon rains but the intensity of rainfall is increasing over shorter durations , experts say . Even well-functioning infrastructure is hard pressed to cope when 150 -- 300 mm falls within a few hours.2 . Mumbai is a coastal city and is low-lying.Much of Mumbai is only a few meters above sea level . These low-lying areas are vulnerable to water flow and localities such as Hindmata , Sion , Kurla and Milan Subway are particularly vulnerable.3 . High tides stop rainwater from draining into the seaThe storm water drains of Mumbai finally discharge into the Arabian Sea . During high tide this seawater slows or stops the outflow . When it rains hard at high tide that water stays in the city for hours . <p> 4 . Stormwater drains have a limited capacity to carryAlthough the drainage network has been upgraded over the years , many areas of the city still receive rainfall that exceeds the rate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are full , water begins to collect on the roads.5 . Rivers and natural channels under pressureImportant flood channels are Mithi River , Dahisar River , Poisar River , Oshiwara River and many nullahs . Siltation , encroachments and waste reduce their capacity to carry huge volumes of rainwater during peak monsoon.6 . Wetlands and mangrove lossMangroves and wetlands once absorbed excess water and slowed runoff , acting as natural flood buffers . As urbanisation has increased , many of these natural protections have been reduced or fragmented , increasing flood risk.7 . The fast growth of cities has put more pressureMumbai today has many more people , vehicles and buildings than it did a few decades ago . Infrastructure upgrades often have not kept pace with this growth , leaving many systems working under constant pressure during heavy rains . <p> 8 . Blocked drains -- a constant headacheStormwater drains are often clogged with plastic waste , construction debris , silt and household garbage . A modern drainage system will be useless if water can not get into it or flow through it.9 . Major infrastructure projects lead to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ redevelopment and utility projects are common for excavation and traffic diversions . Poor temporary water management practices during construction can change local drainage patterns.10 . Trees can fall victim to high winds , and prolonged rainContinuous days of rain soften the soil , which decreases root stability . High winds could bring down trees , blocking roads , damaging vehicles and cutting power supplies . <p> 11 . Mumbai 's transport system can not afford to be disruptedThe city is largely dependent on suburban railways and a few major arterial roads . Flooding at just a few critical spots can quickly affect trains , buses , taxis and private cars , creating cascading delays across the metropolitan region . <p> 12 . Climate change increases uncertaintyMore and more scientists are linking global warming to the increasing frequency of extreme rainfall events along India 's west coast . Mumbai 's flood management may become more difficult in the coming decades with rising sea levels and changing weather patterns .

@@138759257 <p> Europe witnessed its deadliest heatwave in June , with France , Belgium and the Netherlands recording 3,700 excess deaths . The heatwave , which lasted between June 20 and 28 , was among the worst-recorded in Europe , saw rising temperatures cause disruptions to power supply and infrastructure damage , while overwhelming the healthcare system . Scientists have attributed the extreme heat almost entirely to climate change . <p> The US , currently a co-host of the ongoing Football World Cup , is also in the midst of a heatwave that scientists have attributed to a heat dome , causing warm air to be trapped in the atmosphere for a prolonged period . At least 25 people have died over the Fourth of July weekend , while over 20 states experienced temperatures exceeding 38 ? C. <p> The heatwaves have spurred comparisons with India , where heatwaves are more frequent , longer-lasting and expose hundreds of millions of people each year . Yet unlike Europe , which estimates excess deaths during extreme heat events , India still lacks a comprehensive system to measure heat-related mortality , leaving the true @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is heat mortality difficult to measure and track accurately in India ? What do current estimates likely miss ? <p> Heat is seldom recognised as a cause of death and rarely appears on a death certificate . This is chiefly because heat is treated as a contributing factor , not as a cause . People who die of heat generally suffer from other underlying illnesses or co-morbidities , and heat acts as a hidden trigger , exacerbating these problems . So when extreme heat strains a weak heart , the recorded cause is a heart attack . <p> The bare-bones definition of heat mortality is one critical source of confusion . Currently , the official data only counts heatstroke deaths and not the broader category of ' heat-related ' deaths . Separately , official data does not account for undigitised records and excludes data from the private health sector , which delivers nearly two-thirds of all inpatient care . Therefore , current estimates exhibit large variation due to fragmented sources , each with its own definition of heat mortality . <p> Tracking data accurately , and juxtaposing heat-related deaths to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ base for policymakers to design tailor-made heat management solutions that reduce heat mortality . <p> Story continues below this ad <h> There is a common perception that Indians are more accustomed to extreme heat than Europeans . From a public health perspective , how true is that ? Does living in a hot climate protect people from the health risks of prolonged heat exposure ? <p> This perception is not entirely true . Indians have not evolved to become biologically accustomed to heat ; however , they have become better adapted to it . <p> India has historically been hot . Therefore , habits and infrastructure have evolved around heat being an integral part of Indian lives . This includes ventilated architecture , coolers , fans , widespread air-conditioning , and traditional evaporative cooling methods such as clay matkas . <p> Europe , on the other hand , was never built for heat , and temperature is now rising faster than it can adapt . This is why European heatwaves have proven deadly . <p> Biological evolution by itself offers limited protection against heat . Pertinently , absolute temperature does @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ now report a " feels like " temperature . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> One such factor is the " wet-bulb " temperature . This temperature tracks humidity alongside heat . Sweating , the body 's natural cooling mechanism , must evaporate to cool . Increased humidity reduces this evaporation . Therefore , the same temperature is far more dangerous on a humid coast than in a dry environment . Irrespective of acclimatisation , prolonged exposure to wet-bulb temperatures above 35 ? C can prove fatal . <h> Who are the Indians most vulnerable to extreme heat today ? Are there particular occupations , age groups , income groups , or regions that face disproportionate risks , and why ? <p> The occupational groups most at risk are outdoor workers who are directly impacted by any increase in temperature . Farmers , construction workers , manual labourers , street vendors and delivery riders are most vulnerable . Making matters worse , such workers belong to lower-income groups and work in the informal sector and fall beyond the purview of protection measures . Consequently , with no paid sick @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , such workers are forced to work through dangerous heat with no protection . <p> Research suggests other demographics which face disproportionate risks of heat mortality are infants , the elderly , pregnant women and people with chronic illnesses . <p> Geography concentrates the danger . A 2026 mortality study found that five states -- Uttar Pradesh , Bihar , Madhya Pradesh , Rajasthan and Gujarat -- account for more than 60% of estimated heatwave deaths . Poverty runs through all of it : those who can not afford cooling or rest bear the greatest risk . <p> Story continues below this ad <h> India has increasingly adopted heat action plans in cities and states over the past decade . What lessons have we learned from these efforts ? Which interventions have been shown to work , and where do the biggest gaps remain ? <p> India now has numerous Heat Action Plans ( HAPs ) , which include early-warning systems , cooling centres , public-awareness drives , and adjusted hours for outdoor work and schools . This approach works and is inexpensive . An evaluation of Ahmedabad 's HAP @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a year . <p> Newer tools such as parametric heat insurance are emerging as well . SEWA 's parametric insurance product for women in the workforce compensates for some of the lost wages when the temperature exceeds a certain threshold for three consecutive days . This program covers 50,000 women across 22 districts in the country . <p> The biggest gap is implementation . Manual labourers can not afford to stop working when heat alerts are sent . Thus , alerts that connect with an on-ground mandatory action are imperative . Reducing heat mortality could also include curbing short-lived climate pollutants like black carbon that heat the planet thousands of times more than carbon dioxide in a shorter period . Such measures would treat the underlying disease of heat stress itself , and not just its symptoms . <h> As climate change makes heatwaves more frequent and intense , what should India be doing differently over the next decade ? Are we still treating heat as a seasonal inconvenience rather than a major public health threat ? <p> Heat is largely treated as a seasonal nuisance and not a notified @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cyclones , which keep it outside dedicated relief funding . Treating heat as a standing public-health threat means expanding the scope and our understanding of true heat-related mortality ; actively prioritising and implementing funding plans ; protecting outdoor workers with rest and water ; and cooling cities through shade , trees and reflective roofs . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> India can also pull a faster lever : cutting short-lived climate pollutants ( SLCPs ) . These warm the planet many times more than carbon dioxide , but last only a short time in the air . Therefore , reducing SLCPs slows warming within years , not centuries . A UNEP -- WMO assessment found global action on SLCPs could avoid about 0.5 ? C of warming by 2050 . This would mean preventing millions of heat-related mortalities . Therefore , choosing climate-friendly refrigerants and curbing black carbon offers relief that can be felt within our lifetimes . <p> Himanshu is a Senior Policy &amp; Research Associate at Gateway Research . @@138760254 <h> Key Takeaways <p> AI Summary <p> Analyzing article ... <p> A new editorial synthesis in Water examines how freshwater use and energy sustainability are increasingly linked across agriculture , industry , irrigation , hydropower , wastewater treatment , and climate adaptation . Authored by Winnie Gerbens-Leenes and Santiago D. Vaca-Jim ? nez , the article reviews five contributions from Sudan , China , Ecuador , Greece , and Spain , each applying water footprint methods or related assessment tools to improve resource efficiency . <p> The reviewed studies show that water efficiency gains are possible , but they often involve trade-offs . For instance , drip irrigation can reduce blue water footprints , yet it requires energy . Wastewater treatment can reduce blue and grey water footprints , but deeper treatment can raise energy use . <p> The future of sustainability will depend not only on saving water or producing cleaner energy , but on designing systems that understand the cost of both , the study asserts . <h> Efficiency Is Not Free <p> According to the study , more efficient " does not always mean " more sustainable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ irrigation , for example , is widely promoted as a water-saving technology . The editorial describes it as a promising way to reduce blue water footprints , but also notes that it requires energy . One reviewed contribution studies filtration cycle patterns in drip irrigation systems to identify a better balance between water filtration and filter backwashing , with the goal of reducing both water and energy consumption . <p> Irrigation modernization can raise yields and protect farmers from erratic rainfall , but it can also increase electricity demand , diesel use or operating costs . If smallholders can not afford the energy bill , the technology may deepen inequality rather than reduce vulnerability . If the energy comes from fossil fuels , water savings may be partly offset by higher emissions . The editorial suggests one possible pathway : renewable energy , such as solar pumps , could support irrigation efficiency while avoiding carbon dioxide emissions linked to fossil energy use . <p> Industrial water reuse carries a similar lesson . A contribution from Greece applies a decision-support framework to wastewater treatment and reuse in a brewery . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , reducing the blue water footprint , while also lowering the grey water footprint . But deeper treatment brings a trade-off : higher energy use . <p> For businesses and regulators , this means sustainability claims need sharper scrutiny . A factory can not simply say it reduced water withdrawals . It must also ask how much energy was required , what kind of energy was used , whether emissions rose , and whether the system is economically viable over time . The same logic applies to cities , farms and export supply chains . Sustainability is not a single metric . It is a balance sheet . <h> The Hidden Water Footprint Runs Through Supply Chains <p> The editorial also shows why water policy must look beyond the obvious point of use . In Ecuador 's Guayas region , one reviewed study examines banana export systems using the water footprint method . Importantly , it includes not only agricultural water use but also the post-harvest packaging stage . The finding is striking : 75% of the grey water footprint is attributed to agriculture , while 25% comes from packaging @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ banana on an overseas supermarket shelf carries with it not only the water used in cultivation , but also the pollution burden and processing footprint embedded in the export chain . For producing countries , this raises questions about certification , industrial standards , wastewater rules and the environmental terms of trade . For importing markets , it challenges the idea that sustainability can be verified only through farm-level indicators . <p> The China case adds another layer . A contribution on fruit trees in the Tarim River basin uses water footprint analysis to quantify irrigation needs in a water-scarce but agriculturally important region . The editorial notes that an improved irrigation method could be more efficient than traditional drip irrigation , while drip irrigation itself may save around 39% to 56% of water . <p> For water-stressed agricultural regions , such evidence points to a practical strategy : map the water footprint , identify where losses and pollution occur , then target interventions where they deliver the greatest savings . But it also underlines the danger of one-size-fits-all policy . What works in one basin , crop system or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ local , even when the global stakes are shared . <p> The Sudan case reinforces this point under climate stress . The reviewed contribution assesses green water footprints of sugar cane under climate change conditions and finds that effective precipitation can vary by a factor of four between years . Traditional water sources that once ran year -- round now dry up in summer . Sudden cloudbursts and intense downpours have become more frequent , heightening the risk of flash floods and landslides . @@138761223 <h> E20 Petrol in India The controversy behind the biofuel revolution and its environmental implications <p> 07-Jul-2026 <p> <p> Nicholas KhundrakpamIndia has accelerated its transition towards cleaner and renewable energy through the Ethanol Blended Petrol ( EBP ) Programme , which aims to blend 20% ethanol with petrol ( E20 ) to reduce crude oil imports , lower greenhouse gas emissions , and strengthen the agricultural economy by creating additional income opportunities for farmers . The programme is part of India 's broader strategy to address climate change , driven by rising atmospheric carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) concentrations , to which human activities make a significant contribution . Despite these objec- tives , the E20 programme has sparked widespread debate among scientists , automobile experts , environmentalists , and consu- mers . Critics have raised concerns over vehicle compatibility , engine durability , reduced fuel efficiency , increased water use , food security , air pollution , and the overall environmental sustainability of large-scale ethanol production . Others argue that despite increasing ethanol blending , consumers have not benefited from lower petrol prices . These concerns , widely discussed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to label the initiative the " E20 petrol scam . " Some critics also argue that people are being exposed to hazardous , pollution-related health risks in the name of promoting cleaner fuel . The controversy highlights the challenge of balancing India 's energy security and climate goals with environmental protection , consumer interests , and sustainable development , making a critical assessment of the E20 programme both timely and necessary.The Growing Controversy Surrounding E20 PetrolThe introduction of E20 petrol has become one of India 's most debated energy policies . Critics question whether these benefits outweigh the economic , technical , and environmental costs . A major concern is vehicle compatibility . Ethanol is hygroscopic , meaning it readily absorbs moisture , and it has a lower energy content than petrol . It can also affect rubber , plastic , and metal components in older fuel systems . While newer E20 compatible vehicles are designed to handle these properties , many older vehicles ( before 2023 ) built for E5 or E10 fuel blends may experience increased wear , corrosion , and higher maintenance requirements with prolonged use . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to handle this E20.Another concern is fuel efficiency . As ethanol has a lower energy content ( 24 MJ/L ) than petrol ( 34 MJ/L ) , E20 fuel may reduce vehicle mileage , especially in older vehicles , although modern engines can partly offset this through improved combustion . Critics argue that inadequate consumer awareness and inconsistent communication from automobile manufacturers and Government agencies regarding ethanol blending , vehicle compatibility , and warranties contributed to public confusion and the emergence of the term " E20 petrol scam . " Another major concern is the food-versus-fuel debate , as expanding ethanol production from crops such as sugarcane , maize , rice , and wheat may compete with food production for land , water , and fertilizers . During droughts or poor harvests , this could increase food prices , worsen water scarcity , and challenge the long-term sustainability of ethanol production.Ethanol Production : From Agricultural Crops to Transportation FuelEthanol is a renewable biofuel produced by converting carbohydrates into alcohol through biochemical processes . In India , it is mainly produced from sugarcane juice , molasses , maize , rice , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ residues . The production process involves four main steps : feedstock preparation , where starch-rich materials are converted into fermen-table sugars ; fermentation , in which yeast ( Saccharomyces cerevisiae ) converts sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide ; distillation , which separates ethanol from the fermented mixture ; and dehydration , which removes residual water to produce fuel-grade ethanol suitable for blending with petrol . Based on the feedstock used , ethanol production is classified into three generations . First-generation ( 1G ) ethanol is produced from edible crops such as sugarcane , maize , rice , and wheat . It is commercially established and cost-effective but competes with food production . Second-generation ( 2G ) ethanol is produced from non-edible agricultural residues , including rice straw , bagasse , bamboo , and corn stalks . Although more environmentally sustainable because it utilizes agricultural waste and reduces competition with food crops , its production is technologically complex and relatively expensive . Third-generation ( 3G ) ethanol is derived from algae and offers high production potential without requiring agricultural land ; however , it is still in the early stages @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Ethanol BlendingEthanol blending offers several economic and environmental benefits . By partially replacing petrol with domestically produced ethanol , India can reduce its dependence on imported crude oil , strengthen energy security , lower foreign exchange expenditure , and provide additional income to farmers through increased demand for feed- stock crops . Since India imports over 80% of its crude oil , ethanol blending helps reduce vulnerability to global oil price fluctuations . Environmentally , ethanol is considered a renewable fuel because the crops used for its production absorb atmospheric carbon dioxide during growth , partially offsetting the emissions released during combustion . In addition , ethanol contains oxygen , which promotes more complete combustion and can reduce emissions of carbon monoxide , unburned hydrocarbons , and particu-late matter , thereby impro- ving urban air quality . The expansion of second-generation ( 2G ) ethanol further enhances these benefits by utilizing agricultural resi-dues such as rice straw and bagasse instead of food crops . Converting these residues into biofuel reduces open-field biomass burning , a major source of seasonal air pollution , while producing cleaner and more sustainable renewable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ethanol production poses several environ- mental challenges . Sugar-cane , the primary feedstock in India , is a highly water-intensive crop , and its expansion can increase groundwater depletion and water scarcity , particularly in drought-prone regions . India is already facing serious water stress and many regions are struggling for drinking water . Studies reported that 21 major Indian cities including Delhi , Mumbai , Chennai could run out of water by 2030 if water is used at the presents pace . Studies reported that for every litre of ethanol produced , 10000 litres of water is used . Large-scale cultivation may also drive land-use change , leading to deforestation , biodiversity loss , and increased use of fertilizers and pesticides , which contribute to soil and water pollution as well as greenhouse gas emissions . Etha- nol distilleries require substantial amounts of thermal energy , often generated using coal-fired boilers or biomass combustion , resulting in emissions of parti- culate matter and greenhouse gases . Distillation processes may also emit volatile organic compounds that contribute to local air pollution if not properly controlled . Another major concern is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , maize , rice , and wheat for ethanol production may increase competi- tion for land and water , raise food prices , and threaten food security during periods of poor harvest . Byrnihat , located on the Assam -- Meghalaya border , has emerged as one of the world 's most polluted industrial regions . As a result , PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations exceed the WHO permissible limit by nearly 25 times . Industrial emissions release particulate matter , sulphur dioxide ( SO2 ) , nitrogen oxides ( NO ? ) , and volatile organic compounds ( VOCs ) , while studies have also reported @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ WHO and BIS permissible limits . In 2024 , IQ Air Quality Report shown that the city was reported as the World 's most polluted metropolitan area . Although the Meghalaya State Pollution Control Board ( MSPCB ) has strengthened inspections , closed non-compliant industries , and mandated zero- liquid discharge and improved emission moni- toring , residents continue to suffer from respiratory diseases , cardiovascular dis- orders , and reduced lung function . Locals are waiting for the right to live with clean air and water.Air pollution also affects agriculture by damaging plant tissues and reducing crop productivity . Social media influencers and National media like BBC and India Today have criticized the authorities for allegedly ignoring on-ground reports from the region . Videos showing thick black smoke settling on houses , roads , and vegetation have been presented as evidence , with some describing the area as resembling an industrial dumping ground rather than a model green village . The imprint of pollution is on every surfaces . Local residents also claim that clothes hung out to dry quickly become coated with black dust , highlighting the severity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fuels alone can not solve India 's pollution problem ; effective industrial regulation , continuous monitoring , and strict enforcement of environmental standards are equally **27;804;TOOLONG all these together the E20 story is not only about cleaner fuel in vehicles , also about polluting air , looting ordinary people , and pushing policies that favours interest close to the political connections , pointing to the rapid growth of certain ethanol companies where the stock went from 18 crores to 523 crores in just 1 year , while consumers are facing higher fuel price and lower mileage . @@138772471 <h> How Air Pollution Is Changing Rainfall , Monsoons and the Climate <p> Every winter , Delhi disappears beneath a blanket of smog . The conversation that follows usually centres on health : dangerous PM2.5 levels , rising hospital admissions , school closures , and emergency restrictions on construction and traffic . Those concerns are real . But the haze hanging over the Indo-Gangetic Plain is doing more than making the air unsafe to breathe . The tiny particles suspended in it are also influencing how clouds form , when the monsoon arrives , how much rain falls , and even how quickly Himalayan glaciers melt . That is why the planetary boundaries framework includes atmospheric aerosol loading . The concern is not only what these particles do to our lungs , but what they are beginning to do to the Earth 's climate and water systems . <p> What Aerosols Actually Are <p> Aerosols are tiny particles or liquid droplets suspended in the atmosphere . Some occur naturally , such as volcanic ash , sea salt and desert dust . The planetary boundary , however , is mainly concerned @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , diesel engines , crop residue burning , brick kilns , industrial emissions , and the widespread use of biomass for cooking . <p> Not all aerosols behave in the same way . Sulphate particles , released mainly from burning coal , reflect sunlight back into space and temporarily cool the Earth 's surface . Black carbon , or soot , does the opposite , absorbing heat and warming both the atmosphere and anything it settles on , including snow and glacier ice . These contrasting effects make aerosol loading one of the most complex planetary boundaries to understand . A region may experience some short-term cooling from sulphate pollution while simultaneously disrupting rainfall patterns and contributing to glacier melt elsewhere . <p> What Aerosols Do to Weather and Climate <p> The health effects of air pollution are the part of this story most people already know . The larger Earth-system story is far less familiar -- and perhaps even more worrying . <p> When large numbers of aerosol particles enter the atmosphere , they become tiny surfaces around which water droplets form , creating clouds . As the number @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ much smaller , droplets . These clouds reflect more sunlight back into space , yet are often less efficient at producing rain . The result is that air pollution can influence not only how much rain falls , but also where and when it falls . A growing body of evidence indicates that heavy aerosol pollution influences the timing , intensity and regional distribution of the Indian monsoon , although the magnitude of these effects remains an active area of research . Smoke from crop residue burning , brick kilns , coal-fired power plants and diesel vehicles changes how clouds behave , affecting the timing and distribution of rainfall . Research by the Indian Institute of Science , which contributed to the 2023 planetary boundaries assessment , found that differences in aerosol pollution between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres can even shift the tropical rainfall belt , reducing monsoon rainfall in some regions . <p> The impact is equally visible in the Himalayas . Black carbon -- or soot -- is carried by winds from the Indo-Gangetic Plain to snowfields and glaciers high in the mountains . A 2025 study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research : Atmospheres found that dust mixed with black carbon darkens snow more than twice as much as cleaner dust . Research by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology has similarly shown that black carbon significantly reduces the reflectivity of Himalayan snow and ice , accelerating glacier loss . A 2025 Mongabay analysis , drawing together several scientific studies , concluded that nearly one-third of recent changes in the Himalayan cryosphere can be linked to short-lived pollutants such as black carbon , with the main sources being cooking stoves , brick kilns , diesel engines and crop burning across South Asia . Unlike carbon dioxide , black carbon remains in the atmosphere for only days or weeks , meaning cutting these emissions could slow glacier melt . <p> The Boundary That Is Both Crossed and Complicated <p> The atmospheric aerosol boundary is different from the others in this series . As a result , this boundary is not considered crossed globally in the same clear-cut way as several of the others . <p> But the Stockholm Resilience Centre is explicit that this global average masks a severe regional picture . In South Asia and parts of East Asia , aerosol concentrations already exceed safe levels -- affecting health , disrupting weather patterns , and altering ecosystems -- even as the global metric shows apparent improvement . The planetary boundary for aerosols is therefore best understood as a regional warning for South Asia even when the global number looks less alarming : the Indo-Gangetic Plain , including the states of Bihar , Uttar Pradesh , Punjab , Haryana and Delhi , is one of the world 's most documented aerosol hotspots . <p> The System This Connects To <p> What makes aerosol loading consequential beyond its direct health effects is how thoroughly it connects to every other boundary in this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ freshwater boundary crisis this series examined earlier , shrinking the glacial buffer that river systems and agriculture depend on . Aerosol-driven changes to monsoon timing and intensity worsen agricultural productivity and compound the food security pressures examined in the nitrogen piece . The cooling effect of sulphate aerosols has partially masked the true scale of greenhouse-gas-driven warming , meaning that as coal burning declines and sulphate levels fall -- a necessary climate intervention -- some of the warming they were temporarily suppressing will become visible . Aerosol loading is not a standalone problem . It is woven into the same fabric as every boundary this series has examined . <p> The smoke rising from a brick kiln in Jharkhand or a crop fire in Punjab does not simply disappear when it leaves the chimney . It enters a planetary atmosphere that carries it into cloud formation over the Bay of Bengal , deposits it on ice fields above Gangotri , and returns it to earth in rainfall whose timing and intensity have both shifted from what the agriculture beneath them was built around . @@138777707 <h> Energy News Monitor Volume XXII , Issue 48 <h> Published on Jul 07 , 2026 <h> Quick Notes <h> Strategic Petroleum Reserves : Balancing Costs and Benefits <p> Source : Energy Information Administration <p> Strategic petroleum reserves ( SPRs ) are government-held stockpiles of crude oil ( sometimes petroleum products ) designed primarily as a buffer against short-term supply disruptions from geopolitical events , natural disasters , or other shocks . They aim to ensure energy security , stabilise prices temporarily , and support economic continuity . SPRs provide a cushion during disruptions . For import-dependent economies , even 10 to 20 days of oil demand in storage can prevent immediate shortages , refinery shutdowns , and panic . Releases can signal market confidence and deter hoarding . In administered-price or subsidy-heavy systems , which are common in developing countries , SPR drawdowns can mitigate spikes that hit inflation , transport , agriculture , and poor households hardest . <p> The Indian government , through a special purpose vehicle called Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserve Limited ( ISPRL ) , has established SPR facilities with a total capacity of about 39 million barrels ( mb ) of crude oil at Visakhapatnam ( 9.75 mb ) , Mangaluru ( 10.99 mb ) and Padur ( 18.33 mb ) . In phase II , the government has approved the establishment of two additional commercial-cum-strategic petroleum reserve facilities with a total storage capacity of 47.65 mb at Chandikhol ( 29.32 mb ) in Padur ( 18.33 mb ) , on a public-private partnership ( PPP ) mode at an estimated cost of US$1.75 billion . <p> Under the PPP model , the concessionaire will have rights over the crude oil inventory as per agreed terms . This will allow the concessionaire to generate revenue by leasing storage capacity to the government or domestic oil companies , and by commercially trading the crude held in the facility . In times of crisis , the Government of India will hold the first right of refusal on the inventory . In a parallel and separate development , the government has also directed the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation ( ONGC ) , a public sector undertaking , to build a new strategic petroleum reserve facility in Mangaluru at an estimated cost of around US$1.8 billion . Abu Dhabi National Oil Company ( ADNOC ) is currently the only overseas company storing oil in India 's reserves . ADNOC currently stores 5.86 mb of crude oil in India 's Mangalore SPR . This arrangement is part of India 's broader strategy to strengthen its emergency oil buffer while allowing ADNOC commercial flexibility to re-export some of the crude if needed . Recent agreements between ADNOC and the Indian government include plans to expand storage to around 30 mb across multiple SPR sites , including Mangalore , Visakhapatnam , and Chandikhol . This would represent a nearly fivefold increase in UAE-linked crude reserves inside India . India can draw on the reserves in emergencies , while ADNOC retains rights to trade part of the stock commercially . ADNOC 's planned 30 million barrels would cover nearly three-quarters of India 's current SPR capacity . Media reports suggest that Kuwait Petroleum Corporation ( KPC ) and Saudi Aramco have expressed interest in storing crude oil in India 's strategic reserves . <p> India 's Phase I SPR of about 39 mb provides about 9.5 days of net import cover when full . According to reports , if commercial stocks are included , 74 days of cover is available . For oil-importing developing countries like India , maintaining SPRs involves a classic trade-off between energy security and fiscal prudence . First , there are construction and capital costs . Underground caverns , which are preferred for safety , are expensive . India 's Phase I SPR cost is estimated at more than US$600 million . This is more than twice the US$300 million allocated in the Indian budget 2026-27 for improvement of health care facilities in 50 districts or the US$240 million allocated for construction of schools in underserved districts . A wealthy country can afford to immobilise tens of billions of dollars in underground oil caverns . A developing country must weigh that expenditure against schools , hospitals , power infrastructure , and economic development . Consequently , the optimal reserve size for poor countries is likely to be significantly smaller than that of wealthy nations , complemented by supplier diversification , commercial inventories , and demand-management capabilities . <p> Buying oil for filling SPRs is an important cost item . If filled opportunistically during periods of low oil prices , the cost of buying can be contained . But even at US$60/barrel ( b ) , filling the SPR with 30 million barrels of oil will cost over US$1.8 billion , which means tying up scarce foreign exchange . Full IEA ( International Energy Agency ) scale builds providing cover for 90 days are likely to be prohibitively expensive . <p> Then there are operations &amp; maintenance ( O&amp;M ) costs . Ongoing pumping , monitoring , securing cavern integrity , general security , and rotation required to avoid degradation involve significant costs . ISPRL is reported to have run losses of about US$12 million in 2019-20 . In addition , evaporation and maintenance failures can reduce the volume of stored oil in the short term . In the longer term , storage degradation can reduce the value of SPR . Successful electrification of transport or even a switch to natural gas can render SPR a stranded asset . SPR releases may have muted price impact if expectations dominate . <p> Developing countries have higher marginal utility for spending on immediate needs ( food security , infrastructure ) than on SPRs . Many non-IEA developing countries hold limited SPRs , relying on global responses and private or commercial inventories . Wealthy IEA member countries have more fiscal space , better infrastructure , and geopolitical incentives to maintain large SPRs . SPR releases by rich countries create global public goods such as lower oil prices , which will benefit all countries . As opportunity costs ( reduction of spending on poverty alleviation and on basic infrastructure ) are high for developing countries , full SPR duplication is inefficient . Historical precedents ( non-IEA nations relying on global responses ) support this . Moreover , developing countries contribute little to geopolitical triggers as they are not primary sources of sanctions or political interventions . And yet they bear a disproportionally high cost of oil price increases . For developing countries like India , a modest SPR providing cover for 10 to 30 days , excluding commercial reserves , makes sense as targeted insurance , ideally via PPPs or international partnerships to share costs , may be ideal . <p> Maintaining SPRs is thus a complex balancing act for a developing economy like India . From an energy security perspective , an SPR acts as a sovereign insurance policy , but one that comes with substantial capital and opportunity costs . While individual SPRs are small relative to the global market , they signal market resilience . A country with reserves is less susceptible to ' panic buying ' during crises , which can help moderate extreme price spikes . In the event of a sudden , severe supply disruption , the SPR provides a physical ' breathing room ' to maintain essential services and industrial activity while diplomatic or alternative supply efforts are launched . Owning physical oil provides the government with a tool for active market management -- buying when prices are low and potentially releasing into the market during severe price volatility . SPRs are a classic insurance good . They are expensive , rarely used , but potentially invaluable during extreme events . For developing countries , however , the key issue is not whether SPRs provide security because they do to a certain extent , but whether the security gained justifies the immense fiscal and opportunity costs . <p> The challenge for countries like India is therefore not maximising strategic stocks , but finding the point at which additional barrels of stored oil provide less security than alternative investments in economic and energy-system resilience . SPRs are an expensive insurance policy , not a substitute for broader energy sector reforms . <h> Monthly News Commentary : OIL <h> Blended Fuels for Energy Security &amp; Emission Reduction <h> India <p> Blending <p> India may soon allow consumers to choose from different ethanol-blended petrol variants at fuel stations , giving vehicle owners the option to select fuel based on engine compatibility . @@138779376 <p> Every time a herd of wild elephants enters a village in Assam , the immediate response is predictable . Forest officials scramble to drive the animals back , frightened residents try to protect their homes and crops , and news reports describe yet another episode of " human-elephant conflict " . <p> Every time a herd of wild elephants enters a village in Assam , the immediate response is predictable . Forest officials scramble to drive the animals back , frightened residents try to protect their homes and crops , and news reports describe yet another episode of " human-elephant conflict " . Such incidents are increasingly viewed as isolated crises requiring rapid intervention . In reality , they are manifestations of a deeper ecological imbalance that has been unfolding over decades . The conflict is not simply between humans and elephants ; it is between development that fragments landscapes and conservation that struggles to keep pace . <p> Assam is home to one of India 's largest populations of the endangered Asian elephant ( Elephas maximus ) , a species classified as Endangered by the International Union for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 60% of the world 's remaining wild Asian elephants , and the forests of the Northeast constitute one of their most significant strongholds . These elephants are not confined to protected areas . They move across vast landscapes following traditional migratory routes that have evolved over centuries , connecting forests , grasslands and riverine ecosystems . Their movement is essential for maintaining ecological balance , dispersing seeds , regenerating forests and sustaining biodiversity . <p> The growing frequency of encounters between elephants and humans reflects the steady erosion of these ecological pathways . Assam 's forests have undergone profound changes owing to expanding agriculture , tea plantations , highways , railway lines , mining , urbanisation and other infrastructure projects . While these developments have contributed to economic growth , they have also fragmented habitats into isolated patches . Elephant corridors that once enabled seasonal migration have been narrowed , blocked or degraded , forcing herds to move through villages and cultivated fields in search of food and water . <p> This is not merely a conservation concern but a governance challenge . Wildlife can not be managed in isolation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inevitably transfer costs to both people and wildlife . When railway tracks cut through elephant habitats without adequate mitigation measures or highways dissect migration routes without wildlife crossings , conflict becomes an expected consequence rather than an unfortunate accident . <p> The ecological significance of elephants often receives less attention than the damage associated with their movement . As one of nature 's foremost ecosystem engineers , elephants shape the landscapes they inhabit . By dispersing seeds across long distances , opening dense vegetation , creating water holes and maintaining forest diversity , they support countless other species . The health of tropical forests is closely linked to the survival of large herbivores such as elephants . Their decline would have cascading consequences that extend far beyond the loss of a single species . <p> Climate change has added another layer of complexity . Erratic rainfall , prolonged dry spells and recurring floods increasingly influence the availability of food and water within forests . Assam 's annual floods , while ecologically important , often displace wildlife , including elephants , from protected areas into nearby human settlements . Simultaneously , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ compelling herds to seek highly nutritious crops such as paddy , maize and sugarcane . What appears to be crop raiding is often an adaptive response to shrinking ecological resources . <p> The response to these challenges can not rely solely on reactive measures such as driving elephants back into forests . Such interventions may offer temporary relief but fail to address the underlying causes . The long-term solution lies in restoring ecological connectivity . India has identified more than one hundred elephant corridors , several of them located in the Northeast . Yet many remain without adequate legal protection . Securing these corridors through land acquisition , voluntary relocation where appropriate , conservation agreements and careful regulation of infrastructure development must become a national priority . <p> Equally important is the integration of conservation into development planning . Environmental impact assessments should evaluate not only the immediate footprint of projects but also their implications for wildlife movement over decades . Where roads and railway lines intersect elephant habitats , scientifically designed overpasses , underpasses and sensor-based warning systems should become standard practice rather than exceptional measures . Experience from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wildlife conservation can coexist when ecological planning informs infrastructure design from the outset . <p> Technology also offers new opportunities . GPS collars , satellite tracking , artificial intelligence-based monitoring , thermal drones and mobile phone alert systems can provide communities with advance warning of elephant movement . Assam has already begun experimenting with some of these tools , but their deployment remains uneven . Technology , however , is only as effective as the institutions and communities that use it . Strengthening local response teams , improving coordination among forest departments , district administrations and village committees , and ensuring timely dissemination of information are equally critical . <p> The human dimension of conservation deserves far greater attention . Communities living near forests often bear disproportionate costs while contributing significantly to wildlife protection . Compensation for crop losses , property damage and human casualties frequently suffers from procedural delays and inadequate valuation . A more transparent and time-bound compensation mechanism would not only reduce hardship but also strengthen public support for conservation initiatives . Equally valuable is involving local communities in habitat restoration , monitoring and eco-tourism programmes that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ example of grassroots commitment can be found in Assam itself . Dr Shatabdee Roy , Medical Officer at G.B. Primary Health Centre in Kukurmara , Chaygaon , has often witnessed how environmental disruptions influence public health in rural communities . While her primary responsibility is healthcare , her engagement with local populations illustrates the interconnectedness of ecological stability and human well-being . Communities facing recurring encounters with wildlife also experience psychological stress , economic insecurity and disruptions to daily life , reminding policymakers that conservation and development can not be pursued in isolation . <p> Ultimately , Assam 's elephant crisis is neither an inevitable consequence of population growth nor an unavoidable conflict between humans and wildlife . It is the outcome of policy choices that have undervalued ecological connectivity in the pursuit of development . Reversing this trajectory will require viewing forests not as isolated protected islands but as living landscapes linked by functional corridors . Conservation must move beyond protecting species to protecting the ecological processes that sustain them . <p> India has demonstrated through initiatives such as Project Tiger that determined political commitment , scientific management and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vision is now required for elephants . The future of Assam 's forests , biodiversity and rural communities will depend not on how effectively elephants are chased away from villages but on whether the landscapes they have inhabited for millennia are restored to ecological health . Protecting elephant habitats is therefore not simply a conservation imperative ; it is an investment in environmental security , climate resilience and sustainable development itself . 
@@138779428 <h> An Ocean of Data : The Future of Cloud Computing <p> With climate change at the doorstep , Adarsh looks into the potential future of data centers <p> Citing environmental concerns , operational costs and the need for superfast connectivity , major market players like Microsoft and Google are looking to shift their data centers underwater . <p> A study by Datareportal earlier this year revealed that over 5 billion people around the world use the internet every day . In other words , 63.1 per cent of the world 's total population is accessing data online . <p> The study also revealed that internet users are increasing at an annual rate of almost 4 per cent . This means that two-thirds of the world 's population should be online sometime in the second half of 2023 . <p> As the number of people accessing the internet continues to increase , there is a need to improve the physical infrastructure that 's needed to support all that data . Cloud computing is an integral part of every software solutions provider and has seen a surge in demand over the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ go Underwater <p> The multitude of server networks in these data centers consume a lot of power and pump out a lot of waste . They are also high maintenance and suffer a lot of corrosion due to the oxygen and humidity on land . Temperature fluctuations and power failures also affect the effectiveness of the data centers and the maintenance cost for this is unimaginably high . <p> That 's not all ! Another area of concern is the scarcity of space . With the surge in the need for more data centers around the globe , on-land options are bound to run out in the next 10 years . <p> This is why the outrageous idea of underwater data centers was first proposed . <p> The Out-of-the-box Idea ! <p> Microsoft hosts an annual event called ThinkWeek where it urges employees to share out-of-the-box ideas . During the 2014 ThinkWeek , an underwater data center was proposed as a potential way to provide lightning-quick cloud services to coastal populations while also saving energy . <p> The reasoning was that more than fifty percent of the world 's population @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ data centers near coastal cities , the data would only have to travel a shorter distance , thereby speeding up the surfing and streaming requirements of the masses . <p> The Switch to Underwater <p> After the idea was received and researched , phase 1 of Project Natick was conducted in the Pacific Ocean in 2015 . A relatively small data center -10 ? 7 feet in dimensions and weighing 38,000 pounds -- was deployed underwater for just over 3 months . <p> Microsoft 's underwater data center experiment Project Natick <p> After 105 days , it was retrieved from the ocean bed and extensive studies revealed that it had delivered expected results with minimal complications and drastically less power consumption . <p> So in 2018 , Microsoft launched phase 2 of Project Natick . This was an extensive three year project which would involve submerging a full-fledged data center with 12 racks and 864 servers underwater . Scotland 's Orkney Islands was chosen as the location because of its popularity as a renewable energy research destination . Tidal currents that are 9 miles per hour and waves that reach @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the economic viability of a fully submerged data center . <p> For the next two years , researchers tested and monitored the performance and reliability of the data center 's servers . When this data center was retrieved at the start of 2020 , it was noted that there were just a handful of failed servers and related cables . <p> Though all the reasons for the same are still being researched as to why , the underwater data center was found to be 8 times more reliable than its on-land counterpart . So as far as Microsoft is concerned , Project Natick has been a grand success . <p> The War for Water <p> From 2007 to 2012 , Google was using regular drinking water to cool its data center in Douglas County , Atlanta . But after environmental conversationalists started filing lawsuits , the company switched to recycled water to help conserve the Chattahoochee River . But this is proving difficult as recycling options are not available in all the locations where they have data centers . <p> Google 's recycled water use in green data center <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It considers it a proprietary trade secret but information continues to leak out as part of legal battles and lawsuits . In 2019 alone , it was reported that Google either requested or was granted over 2.3 billion gallons in three different states in the USA . Google however has insisted that they do n't use all the water they are granted . <p> As the company continues to chase Microsoft and Amazon in the cloud-computing market , things are bound to get more complicated in the future . As of now , Google has 21 data centers but it intends to spend USD 10 billion on data centers in the next year alone . <p> The Future of Underwater Centers <p> The overall reliability of a data center in a sealed container on the ocean floor is great for environmental , economical and connectivity reasons . <p> Microsoft , Google and Amazon are already looking to serve customers who need to deploy and operate tactical and critical data centers anywhere in the world . Wherever possible , they are looking to deploy these centers off the coast . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ aim to being carbon-negative by 2030 . The company intends to do this by developing long-term cloud infrastructure . In addition , it hopes to have entirely shifted its technical reliance on renewable energy sources by 2025 . <p> All in all , just like cloud computing is here to say , so are underwater data centers . It might seem intriguing now but very soon , it looks like it is going to become the norm ! 
@@138780945 <h> Neolissochilus pnar : The Pride of Meghalaya <p> Meghalaya is renowned not only for its breathtaking landscapes but also for its extraordinary underground world . Its heavy rainfall and vast limestone deposits have , over millions of years , created one of the largest and most spectacular cave systems in India , earning it the title of the " Caving Capital of India . " These caves are home to a remarkable diversity of rare and endemic species , including Neolissochilus pnar , the world 's largest known subterranean fish . Together , they make Meghalaya a globally important centre for cave biodiversity and scientific research . These cave systems have become a source of pride for the state , as the study and exploration of caves in Meghalaya have attracted scientists , geologists , and cave explorers from around the world . Formation of Caves in Meghalaya Most caves in Meghalaya are formed through a natural process known as karst formation . Karst topography develops when rainwater , which is slightly acidic , dissolves soluble rocks such as limestone over thousands of years . This process creates underground @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Most of these caves are limestone caves , and they occur in areas that have large deposits of limestone . Meghalaya 's heavy rainfall accelerates this process . Water seeps through cracks in limestone rocks , gradually widening them into large underground passages . Over time , these passages become extensive cave systems . While most caves in Meghalaya are limestone caves , some are formed in sandstone , which is rare and scientifically important . While one can find many sandstone caves in the state , the most remarkable example is Krem Puri , which is recognised as the longest sandstone cave in the world , stretching over 25 kilometres . Exploration of Caves in Meghalaya Although local communities have known about many caves for centuries , scientific exploration began only in the late twentieth century . In 1992 , a small team of European cave explorers visited Meghalaya and recognised the enormous potential for cave exploration in the Khasi , Jai ? tia , and Garo Hills . In 1994 , they partnered with the Meghalaya Adventurers ' Association , led by Brian D. Kharpran Daly and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Caving in the Abode of the Clouds , which has continued for more than three decades . Through this collaboration , approximately 1,700 caves have been recorded in Meghalaya , and over 1,000 have been explored or partially mapped . These discoveries have placed Meghalaya on the global map of cave exploration . These many expeditions have also helped establish the fact that most of the longest and deepest caves in the Indian subcontinent are found in Meghalaya . Importance of Caves The caves of Meghalaya are important for several reasons . They preserve evidence of Earth 's geological history and help scientists understand climate change and environmental changes over thousands of years . They are home to many rare and endangered species , some of which are endemic to the region and therefore contribute significantly to biodiversity conservation . Caves also attract tourists , researchers , and adventurers , which support the local economy and create employment opportunities . Additionally , the caves are an important part of Meghalaya 's natural heritage and must be protected for future generations . Dr. Khlur Baiaineh Mukhim , one of the experts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tia Hills , said , " Caves like Krem Liatprah Um-im-labit are a factory of time-taking speciation , where new species are being formed over millions of years . If the Shillong Plateau ( including both Jai ? tia and Garo Hills ) was raised some 50 million years ago from the Tethys Sea , nature could have taken at least 5 -- 10 million years to create such extensive caves of great magnificence that are often visited with a sense of respect , wonder , and awe ! These are humongous natural assets ( belonging to our past ancestors , to us today , and to many future generations of our children , grandchildren , and their children ) that have to be responsibly respected . " The Meghalayan Age In 2018 , the International Commission on Stratigraphy officially named the present geological age the Meghalayan Age . This was based on scientific evidence collected from a stalagmite found in Mawmluh Cave . This discovery gave Meghalaya international recognition and highlighted the scientific importance of its caves . Biodiversity in Meghalaya 's Caves Although caves appear dark and lifeless @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ animals have adapted to survive in these dark and isolated environments . The caves of Meghalaya provide shelter to more than eleven species of bats . These include the Greater Large-eared Horseshoe Bat , Pomona Leaf-nosed Bat , and Eastern Bent-winged Bat . One of the rarest species found here is Wroughton 's Free-tailed Bat , and Meghalaya is believed to hold more than half of the world 's known population of this species . Animals that live in caves are called troglofauna ( from the Greek trogle , meaning " hole " ) . They are divided into three groups based on their dependence on caves . The first group is called trogloxenes . These animals use caves temporarily for shelter or breeding but do not spend their entire lives there . Bats are a common example . The second group is troglophiles . These animals prefer living in caves but can also survive outside them . Examples include certain frogs , spiders , and insects . The third group is troglobites , which are true cave animals . They are fully adapted to cave life and can not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reduced eyes or no eyes , and enhanced senses of touch and smell . Neolissochilus pnar and Other Cave Fish The caves also contain rare fish species adapted to life in darkness . Among these rare species are Schistura larketensis , Schistura papulifera , and Neolissochilus pnar , discovered in East Jai ? tia Hills . These animals have reduced eyesight or no eyesight at all , as vision is not necessary in total darkness.Scientific information about Neolissochilus pnar was first published in Vertebrate Zoology 73:141 -- 152 on February 6 , 2023 . The paper was co-authored by Neelesh Dahanukar , Department of Life Sciences , School of Natural Sciences , Shiv Nadar Institution of Eminence , Delhi-NCR , India ; Remya L. Sundar and Rajeev Raghavan , Department of Fisheries Resource Management , Kerala University of Fisheries and Ocean Studies ( KUFOS ) , Kochi , India ; Duwaki Rangad , Department of Zoology , St. Edmund 's College , Laitumkhrah , Shillong , India ; and Graham Proudlove , Department of Entomology , The Manchester Museum , University of Manchester , Manchester , United Kingdom . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was tentatively identified as a troglomorphic form of the golden mahseer , Tor putitora . Detailed analyses of its morphometric and meristic data , together with results from molecular analyses , revealed that it is a new species of the genus Neolissochilus , the sister taxon of Tor . The study formally described the new species as Neolissochilus pnar , honouring the tribal communities of East Jai ? tia Hills in Meghalaya , Northeast India , where it was discovered . Neolissochilus pnar possesses a number of characters unique among species of Neolissochilus , with the exception of the similarly subterranean N. subterraneus from Thailand . The unique characters that distinguish N. pnar from all epigean congeners include highly reduced eye size or the complete absence of externally visible eyes , complete lack of pigmentation , long maxillary barbels , long pectoral-fin rays , and a distinct scalation pattern .
