This recognition led the ministry to support the protection and conservation of this very unique fish species . Later , the Central Government , through the Ministry of Fisheries , sanctioned Rs 1 crore to the department of Fisheries , Government of Meghalaya for the protection and conservation of Neolissochilus pnar in its only known habitat in East Jai ? tia Hills . With the funds now available , it is hoped that the government , through the Fisheries Department and with the support of the Meghalaya Adventurers ' Association , will be able to protect this endemic species . Threats to the Caves Despite their importance , Meghalaya 's caves face several threats . Limestone mining and quarrying can damage or destroy cave systems . Pollution from human activities can harm delicate cave ecosystems . Unregulated tourism can also damage cave formations and disturb wildlife . Deforestation around cave areas affects water flow and increases erosion , further threatening these fragile environments . Therefore , conservation and responsible tourism , instead of promoting the cement @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Conclusion The caves of Meghalaya are among the state 's greatest natural treasures . They tell the story of the Earth 's geological past , support unique forms of life , and contribute to the cultural and environmental heritage of the region . Protecting these caves is the responsibility of every citizen so that future generations may continue to learn from and appreciate this remarkable natural heritage . Hopefully , the government will accord due recognition to these natural phenomena and ban mining and any activities that could put the caves in danger . <h> Follow us <h> About Us <p> Since 1945 , The Shillong Times has evolved from a weekly tabloid to a prominent daily , launching regional editions and embracing technological advances , consistently delivering news that matters to Meghalaya and beyond . 
@@138780953 <h> Moving forests to save them : The risks and rewards of tree migration <p> Climate change is shifting forest conditions faster than local tree species can adapt . Higher temperatures , more frequent droughts and less predictable winters can weaken species that have been established in a region for centuries . In light of this , one idea is gaining ground : assisted migration . Assisted migration involves deliberately moving tree species or populations to regions where the future climate is expected to be more favourable . The aim is to anticipate changes rather than wait for forests to decline . While this approach may sound logical , it raises several important questions . Helping forests adapt is a legitimate ambition , but ecosystems are complex , and any intervention has its limits . Five key issues help us better understand the potential of assisted migration and the precautions it requires . As an assistant professor at the Eau Terre Environnement ( ETE ) Research Centre at the Institut national de la recherche scientifique ( INRS ) , I have been working on the DREAM project , specifically on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? tou Diouf , is a specialist in tree ecophysiology , and Alison Munson is currently working on several assisted migration projects for trees in Qu ? bec . <p> The risk of invasion <p> The primary concern relates to the risk of ecological invasion . Moving a species outside its natural range can , in some cases , disrupt the balance of local ecosystems . Some newly introduced species can spread rapidly and take over at the expense of existing vegetation . However , this does not happen systematically , since the establishment of a tree depends on numerous factors that change over time , including soil quality , the local climate , interactions with other living organisms and the specific characteristics of the species itself . Studies have shown that some displaced species struggle to establish themselves or have lower survival rates in their new environment , while others benefit from favourable conditions that facilitate their establishment . So far , most assisted migration projects have been experimental , which limits the observation of potential impacts in different contexts . International studies have demonstrated that certain species introduced @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ influence how other species establish themselves , sometimes several years after introduction . This possibility highlights the importance of proceeding with caution and closely monitoring transplant sites . <p> Surviving today , but withering tomorrow <p> Even when a tree successfully establishes itself , there is no guarantee that it will adapt to future conditions . The climate continues to change , sometimes more rapidly than anticipated . Scientists use climate models to anticipate these changes and guide planting decisions . These tools are valuable , but they can not predict the future with certainty . Some trees may find themselves ill-suited to new climate extremes , such as intense heatwaves or late frosts . Researchers favour using a step-by-step approach to limit this risk . They test different populations of the same species , sourced from various climatic regions , and observe how they behave in new environments . Experimental programs in North America illustrate this cautious method , based on learning over time . This is the case with the DREAM project , as well as initiatives such as the Assisted Migration Adaptation Trial and TransX , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sites and climates . Despite these efforts , some uncertainty remains , particularly in fragmented landscapes where forests have fewer opportunities to adapt naturally . <p> Invisible effects on the soil <p> When we talk about assisted migration , we often think of the trees themselves , but the soil plays an equally important role . Roots interact with an underground world of bacteria , fungi and other microorganisms that are essential to forest health . These organisms help trees absorb water and nutrients , and strengthen their resistance to environmental stresses . If a tree is moved to a site where these partners are absent or different , its growth may be hindered . Conversely , the presence of certain species can permanently alter the soil and , as a result , shape future vegetation through what 's known as the ecological legacy effect . These changes are often invisible in the short term , but can have long-term consequences for the entire ecosystem . To better understand these subtle yet crucial interactions , assisted migration projects incorporate soil analyses and preliminary trials . <p> Interactions with herbivores <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the survival and growth of young plants . Although assisted migration can help certain vulnerable wildlife species adapt to habitats disrupted by climate change , relocated trees still have to contend with local wildlife . Some newly introduced species may be tasty to local herbivores , leading to significant damage . Other species , meanwhile , may be consumed less frequently , thereby altering existing food balances . In any case , these interactions play a key role in the success or failure of tree migration . To address this , researchers are working with forest managers to test various solutions , such as temporary fencing , selecting more resilient seedlings and management practices that promote better coexistence with wildlife . These approaches show that assisted migration is not limited to climate , but involves the entire ecological network . <p> Logistical constraints , economic risks <p> Even when ecological aspects are taken into account , assisted migration poses practical challenges . Producing seedlings , transporting them , planting them and monitoring them represent a significant investment of time and resources . On a large scale , these costs can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ roads and agricultural or urban areas , complicating the planning and implementation of plantations . Assisted migration also raises economic issues related to risk-taking . Introducing unfamiliar species creates new uncertainties that forest owners -especially private ones -- must learn to manage . This raises questions about the allocation of investments and the role of public land in implementing these strategies . Social and ethical questions then arise : Which species should be prioritized ? Who decides ? And how can climate adaptation , biodiversity and local forest uses be reconciled ? Guiding the forests of tomorrow Assisted migration offers promising prospects for protecting forests from climate change . It is based on a simple idea : anticipating and acting rather than suffering the consequences . However , challenges relating to invasions , long-term adaptation , interactions with soil and wildlife and practical constraints serve as a reminder that forest ecosystems are complex . By recognising the limitations of assisted migration and integrating it into a broader forest management strategy , it becomes possible to use it as a complementary and flexible tool . Helping forests adapt to climate change @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to intervene with discernment while respecting the diversity and dynamics of living systems . @@138790729 <p> In middle school , I decided to spend my life 's net worth in saved-up coins . Not because melting is surprising . Of course it melts . The disappointment is how little time it takes to give up . The product sold today feels like it was never designed for the place it lives @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ice cream here moves through heat , only briefly interrupted by refrigeration . Consider the journey of an ice cream tub . It leaves the factory in a refrigerated truck to reach the distributor , from where it goes to a petti kada freezer or a street vendor 's cart , eventually to reach the customer 's home on a bike ride . <p> Each step offers an opportunity for heat to creep in . Repeated cycles degrade its quality even if the product remains frozen . <p> If we take India thermodynamically seriously , what could ice cream look like ? <p> To answer that , we have to start with what ice cream actually is . <h> Ice cream as a material <p> As a lover of ice cream but a hater of its melted form , I would try freezing the melted portion of my bowl , hoping to reconstruct what it once was . It never worked and always resulted in either a hard block of ice or an even weirder soup . This is because , counter to its name , ice cream is n't @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ together just long enough . The texture depends on the size and arrangement of these phases . <p> The first thing holding ice cream together is ice itself , which shares the same lattice structure as regular ice called Ice I. When ice cream melts and refreezes , water molecules deposit onto existing crystals . You might have experienced this as a grainy tasting ice cream . Second , a concentrated sugar solution stays liquid even below zero , without which the ice cream would freeze into a solid block . <p> The third phase is the least obvious one : air . Churning folds air into the mixture and is called overrun , which gives ice cream its lightness . Sometimes , nearly half of what you 're eating is nothing but air . The air improves mouthfeel and cuts cost per unit volume , but also increases surface area and structural fragility . Finally , fat from milk or cream partially crystallises , which forms a network around air bubbles that keeps them from collapsing and gives the ice cream body . <p> It is impressive that we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to see ice crystals or crystallography to study their growth . Remove any one of these constraints , and you do not get ice cream . <h> How the world does it <p> Long before refrigeration , the logistics of cold were already a prestige problem . The Achaemenid Persians were making dessertchilled with snow around 400 BC . They stored ice year-round in cone-shaped desert structures engineered to beat the heat called yakhchals . The sharbat tradition grew from this and traveled the Silk Road eastward and southward for centuries . <p> By the 16th century , it had reached the Mughal court , where the court dispatched riders to carry ice back to the capital for fruit sorbets . The sharbat reached Europe -- in part through Muslim Sicily , where sugar culture took root and early frozen drink traditions first arrived on the continent -- and continued travelling west . <p> Different regions began making it their own as ice cream spread globally . It 's particularly interesting how heat influenced new forms of ice cream in equatorial countries . <p> Turkish dondurma is the eccentric aunt @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tuber ) and mastic ( a tree resin ) that gives it a chewy , elastic texture that lets vendors stretch it like taffy . It can be cut with a knife and fork , resists melting and is often hung on meat hooks to prove this point . <p> The classic Indian kulfi originated in 16th-century Delhi during the Mughal era , and it is made by simmering milk until it 's thick and caramelised , and frozen without any churning at all . Without any overrun or foam , it has almost nothing in common ( structurally ) with a scoop of H ? agen-Dazs and stays stable longer . <p> Some newer Indian brands are closely competing with the dondurma in theeccentric ice cream game . Hocco Ice Cream dropped a barfi-flavored ice cream with the snack industry mogul Haldiram 's and also a modak edition timed with Ganesh Chaturthi . These come with a denser composition , making them more stable . <p> India 's ice cream market generates roughly Rs 30,000 crore annually , with projections pointing to Rs 45,000 crore within three years , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <h> Cold-chain infrastructure <p> India 's cold chain is built on small logistics operators with , until recently , almost no real-time visibility into temperature across the journey from factory to shelf . According to Varun Sheth of NOTO , distributors now run their own Internet of Things dashboards , and some brands place independent data loggers inside their shipments . <p> A number of specific design choices matter for the ice cream that ends up in your hand . For example , many retail freezers in India are front-opening . But Seth pointed out that a chest freezer with its lid lifted toward the face loses far less cold air than one with a door that swings open horizontally , because cold air sinks rather than spills out . <p> Similarly , in warehouse design , if ice cream goes directly from -20 ? C storage to ambient conditions , the temperature abuse has already begun , and a refrigerated truck can not undo it . Roli Shrivatsava , Hocco 's VP , seemed to think of packaging as a part of the products . They created more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their cassata . <h> Postponing melting ( or freezing , sometimes ) <p> NOTO ice cream is built around high-protein , low-sugar formulations . Their earliest formulations had extremely low fat levels , making them more sensitive to temperature shocks . The fix was to increase protein levels and prebiotic fibers . Protein improves water binding and structural stability , partially compensating for reduced fat . Fibre adds body and mouthfeel that helps close the textural gap . <p> Combined with a carefully designed stabiliser system , the product gets close to traditional ice cream texture despite lower sugar and fat . <p> An elegant solution to ice cream 's cold chain problem might be to stop making ice cream altogether . At least in the traditional sense . And instead , to postpone freezing until the very last possible moment . <p> Soft serve -- or softies as they 're colloquially known across India -- are an entirely distinct product category from ice creams . Manufacturers heat-treat the mix rather than freeze it , which gives it a shelf life of up to nine months at ambient temperatures . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the outlet , which freezes the product at the moment of dispensing . The product does n't exist as ice cream until the customer orders it . <p> Arnav Bajaj , the Director of Amrit Food , says these commercial machines could cost anything between Rs 1.5 lakh at the low end and more than Rs 12 lakh for higher-end units . The upfront cost helps explain why the format remains concentrated in quick service restaurants despite its logistical appeal . <p> " If you go to the Thikse Monastery in Ladakh , you 'll actually find a soft serve machine there on the first floor , " Arnav explained , clearly pleased . " They can store the TetraPak at ambient temperature . Now whenever you want , if there 's electricity switched on , turn on the machine , sell ice cream , get it done with . " <p> The economic drag from melty ice cream may be less dramatic than it sounds . One founder I spoke with estimated their heat-related inventory loss at 2% to 3% on the high side and shared that most of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The supply chain problem is going to improve over time , even as temperatures rise due to climate change , eventually paving the way for better cold chain logistics . What is not on a trajectory of getting better is the experience of eating an ice cream bar on a 42 ? C afternoon . That is a different kind of failure that happens in the hand . One that hardly holds it together long enough to eat . <h> What ice cream could be <p> Heat-stable ice cream is not just a future possibility . Researchers say these changes could affect river ecosystems , agriculture , and drinking water supplies downstream . <p> The Himalayas , often called the " Water Tower of Asia " , store vast freshwater reserves in glaciers and snowfields that sustain major river systems supporting over a billion people . By examining these dissolved chemicals , hydrochemists can determine where the water came from , how it evolved , whether it is safe for drinking or agriculture , and what it reveals about environmental and climatic conditions . <p> Riyaz Mir , a scientist at the National Institute of Hydrology , Western Himalayan Regional Centre , Jammu explains , glacial meltwater plays a fundamental role in shaping the hydrochemistry of Himalayan rivers because it acts as both a source of freshwater and a carrier of dissolved minerals , sediments , and nutrients derived from intense water -- rock interaction beneath and around glaciers . <p> " As glaciers melt , the cold @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ erosion , allowing rapid chemical weathering . This process enriches the meltwater with dissolved ions such as calcium , magnesium , bicarbonate , sulfate , sodium , and silica , which strongly influence the chemical composition of downstream rivers , " he says . <p> Scientists studying the Rulung Glacier in Ladakh found that climate warming is changing not only how fast glaciers melt , but also the chemical composition of the meltwater flowing into the Indus river basin . Trace elements are chemical elements that occur in very small concentrations in water , rocks , soil , or living organisms . <p> The meltwater of Rulung Glacier initially acquires dissolved ions from carbonate-rich metamorphic rocks . @@138791516 <p> India 's ethanol-blending programme has evolved rapidly over the last decade from a limited effort to blend with petrol to now one of the central pillars for India 's energy security and clean mobility strategy . The country has already achieved E20 blending ahead of schedule , increasing it gradually from 1.5% in 2014 . The central government is now preparing for higher blends through the recent notification and recent launch of flex-fuel vehicles ( FFVs ) . <p> The rationale for ethanol blending has been to reduce fossil oil imports and thus provide a degree of insulation from global oil price volatility , supply shocks and geopolitical disruptions . According to government reports , this transformation has helped save over Rs 1.84 lakh crore in foreign exchange over the years and substituted more than 300 lakh metric tonnes of oil imports . Ethanol blending has thus been positioned as a strategic tool to reduce fossil oil consumption , lower foreign exchange outflows , build domestic fuel resilience and at the same time create additional income for farmers . However , the blending has also been questioned by critiques @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for better acceptance of the programme . <p> On the consumer side , an often-cited challenge is the issue of fuel efficiency and impact of fuel blends on the engine . As ethanol has 30% lower energy density than petrol , ethanol blends reduce vehicle mileage , particularly for vehicles that are non-E20 compliant . Furthermore , the hygroscopic property of ethanol can lead to moisture accumulation , corrosion of fuel system components , and potential breakdowns of non-compliant vehicles . In this scenario , the recent FFV notification is an important policy step . By introducing engine compliance standards , the government has recognised that higher blending requires compatible vehicle systems . <p> On the supply side , India 's ethanol ecosystem today remains dominated by first-generation ( 1G ) feedstocks , particularly sugarcane , maize and broken rice . This has generated important gains for the farmers , as sugar mill arrears , historically a major source of farmer distress , have reduced significantly . Because of the rising demand from the distilleries , maize cultivation has expanded . For policymakers , ethanol has become an instrument that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ agricultural market stability . <p> While a higher blend beyond E20 for the FFV has the potential to further reduce our fossil oil consumption and thus foreign exchange outflows , the next phase of India 's ethanol programme must be evaluated through a broader ' systems ' perspective that considers not only energy security but also ecological sustainability and long-term resource resilience . Sugarcane is among the most water-intensive crops cultivated in India and is often grown in regions already experiencing groundwater stress . Its cultivation is supported by significant electricity subsidies for irrigation and high fertiliser inputs . <p> Furthermore , while ethanol may reduce tailpipe emissions , a rigorous comparative life cycle assessment ( LCA ) is essential to account for the full production chain , including fertiliser manufacture and use , groundwater extraction , electricity consumption for irrigation , transportation , distillation energy , land-use changes associated with feedstock cultivation , waste generation and treatment , and emissions across the value chain . Only such a cradle-to-grave assessment can determine whether higher ethanol blends deliver genuine net environmental gains under Indian conditions . <p> The environmental assessment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Distilleries reportedly generate large volumes of effluent with significant pollution potential if inadequately treated . Although regulatory norms mandate treatment and reuse through bio-methanation , concentration or composting , a rapid expansion of ethanol production will proportionately increase waste volumes . <p> A major concern is also on the long-term impact on agricultural patterns . If ethanol demand continues to incentivise sugarcane and maize cultivation , what happens to crop diversification and soil resilience ? Monoculture expansion may improve short-term farmer incomes , but over time weaken ecological stability and increase resource stress , thereby impacting the farmers themselves . There is also an implicit food security dimension . The current policy support still disproportionately favours rapid expansion of 1G infrastructure because it is easier to scale quickly . That may help India achieve blending targets and reduce foreign exchange outflow , but it risks locking into a resource-intensive biofuel pathway with longer-term impacts on soil and groundwater . While surplus and waste IG feedstocks should be used to produce ethanol , any expansion through additional cultivation must be preceded by a comprehensive and rigorous life cycle assessment ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ work on prioritising second-generation ( 2G ) biofuels . India generates up to 500 million tonnes of agricultural residues annually , much of which is burned , contributing to severe air pollution . Converting crop residues , municipal waste , and non-food biomass into ethanol offers a far more sustainable pathway than indefinite expansion of first-generation feedstocks . However , 2G ethanol remains commercially challenging due to high capital costs of pre-treatment and lower yields . Going forward , the policy should simultaneously focus on enabling 2G systems through targeted financial incentives , innovation support , technology partnerships , and long-term procurement certainty . The objective should not merely be increasing ethanol percentages but creating a genuinely sustainable low-carbon fuel ecosystem . <p> While India 's ethanol programme has undoubtedly supported rural incomes , its next phase should be guided by a ' systems ' perspective rather than blending targets alone . Energy security can not be separated from groundwater stress , fertiliser dependence , agricultural resilience , waste management , and long-term resource sustainability and security . International experience , particularly Brazil 's , offers valuable lessons but should @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cultivation is rain-fed and takes place under agro-climatic conditions that differ from India 's , where irrigation and groundwater extraction play a larger role . Also , Brazil vehicle ecosystem for using blended fuels was simultaneously developed . India 's biofuel strategy must be tailored to its own resource constraints and conditions . Ultimately , the next phase of India 's ethanol transition should be evaluated not only as an energy security initiative but also as a resource security strategy without impacting the vehicle users . <p> While India 's ethanol programme has undoubtedly supported rural incomes , its next phase should be guided by a ' systems ' perspective rather than blending targets alone . Energy security can not be separated from groundwater stress , fertiliser dependence , agricultural resilience , waste management , and long-term resource sustainability and security <p> Dr. Akanksha Jain is a Research Associate and Dr. Debajit Palit is the Centre Head at the Centre for Climate Change and Energy Transition at Chintan Research Foundation ; Views presented are personal .

@@138792378 <p> Loktak lake is northeast India 's largest freshwater wetland and is the ecological heart of Manipur . The lake spans about 287 square kilometres , about half the size of the capital Imphal , and is already under growing stress from pollution , altered hydrology and catchment degradation . Using predictive methods , researchers have mapped out how a changing climate will fundamentally alter the lake 's water depth , temperature , and oxygen levels . <p> Loktak is an indelible part of the Manipuri identity -- lives , lore , legends , history , and aquatic ecosystems . @@138803574 <h> How the World Saved the Ozone Layer -- and Why We Have n't Repeated It <p> Ask someone under 25 about the ozone hole , and you 'll probably get a vague memory from a school science class . That , in itself , is remarkable . In the late 1980s , the ozone hole was one of the world 's biggest environmental fears . Scientists warned that if the ozone layer continued to thin , more harmful ultraviolet radiation would reach Earth 's surface , increasing skin cancer , damaging crops , disrupting ecosystems , and threatening the protective shield that had made life on land possible . Governments responded . Industries replaced the chemicals responsible . Today , most people under 30 have never experienced the ozone hole as an unfolding global crisis . <p> Not because the threat went away on its own . It did n't . It faded because the world acted . That makes the ozone story unique in humanity 's relationship with the planet . It is one of the few examples of a global environmental crisis that was confronted before it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that feels more relevant than ever : if the world could solve this problem , why has it struggled to do the same with so many others ? <p> What Was Actually Happening <p> Chlorofluorocarbons -- CFCs -- were , when first developed in the 1930s , celebrated as a chemistry marvel . Non-toxic , non-flammable , chemically stable , they were ideal for refrigerators , air conditioners and aerosol sprays . Their stability was precisely the problem . CFCs persisted long enough to drift into the stratosphere , where ultraviolet radiation broke them apart and released chlorine atoms , each capable of destroying tens of thousands of ozone molecules in a chain reaction the lower atmosphere can not interrupt . <p> In 1974 , chemists F. Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina first calculated that CFC emissions posed a serious threat to the stratosphere . A decade later , British Antarctic Survey scientist Joseph Farman published measurements showing dramatic seasonal thinning of ozone above Antarctica . NASA satellite data confirmed the scale . The scientific response was unusually fast : the Vienna Convention followed in 1985 , and the Montreal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in September 1987 . <p> What the Protocol Actually Did <p> The Montreal Protocol is now the only treaty in UN history to achieve universal ratification -- 198 parties . It phased out nearly 100 ozone-depleting substances , starting with the most damaging CFCs , progressively expanding to cover related chemicals , and , through the 2016 Kigali Amendment , addressing hydrofluorocarbons -- replacement chemicals that turned out to be potent greenhouse gases . Developed countries phased out CFCs by 1996 . Developing countries received extended timelines and access to a Multilateral Fund , ultimately disbursing over $4 billion to finance the transition to alternatives . <p> The honest answer to why the Montreal Protocol succeeded where other environmental agreements have struggled involves recognising that the conditions enabling it were unusually favourable , and most do not automatically transfer to other crises . <p> The science was clear and fast . The causal chain -- chlorine atoms from CFCs destroying ozone -- was chemically specific and testable . From Rowland and Molina 's 1974 calculations to the 1987 treaty took thirteen years . Climate science involves a larger , noisier @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ no less real but considerably harder to communicate with equivalent simplicity . <p> The number of actors who needed to change was small . CFC production was dominated by a handful of large chemical companies . Once DuPont concluded that viable alternatives could be developed and that regulation was arriving regardless , it shifted from opposing to supporting the treaty . The commercial logic of a manageable transition has no parallel in fossil fuels , where economic interests span every sector of every economy on Earth . <p> Crucially , the alternatives to CFCs either already existed or were chemically close enough to develop within a few years . The alternative to fossil fuels involves rebuilding energy infrastructure across entire economies -- a transformation several orders of magnitude larger in cost , complexity and disruption . <p> The benefits were also visible , personal and nearly universal . Everyone understood the connection between ozone depletion and skin cancer . The harms of climate change , by contrast , are diffuse , delayed and unevenly distributed in ways that are much harder to connect to specific policies and choices . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It means the achievement was enabled by a specific set of structural conditions -- and that recreating those conditions for other planetary boundaries is the actual challenge , not simply summoning more political will . <p> What It Proves <p> The planetary boundaries framework , which this series has used to examine everything from nitrogen cycles to ocean chemistry to the living web of species , identifies Earth-system processes that can be pushed beyond their stable range into zones of growing and potentially irreversible risk . The ozone story demonstrates that this trajectory is not always permanent -- that recovery is sometimes possible , and that the mechanism is not mysterious . It requires early science , binding treaty targets , real monitoring , technology transfer , finance for poorer countries , and sustained commitment over decades . <p> Even this success remains incomplete . An April 2026 MIT study found that chemicals still legally used as industrial feedstocks are leaking into the atmosphere at rates that could slow ozone recovery -- a reminder that even the most successful environmental treaty requires continued vigilance rather than a single act of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is unmistakably one of collective action producing measurable results in an Earth-system process that was heading toward catastrophe . Children born today will live into a world where the ozone layer , barring unforeseen violations , has substantially healed . <p> The planetary boundaries framework does not only issue warnings . It also sets tests . Humanity has already passed one imperfectly , incrementally , over decades of science and diplomacy , but passed it nonetheless . The remaining seven boundaries pose the same fundamental question : whether the conditions that made this success possible can be built for crises that are structurally harder in almost every dimension . The ozone layer 's slow , measurable recovery is the only evidence available that the answer might be yes . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Utkarsh Mishra is a journalist based in Ranchi writing on law , labour rights , and the environment . His work has appeared in Feminism in India , The India Forum , Down to Earth , The Policy Circle , Verdicto News and Zee News . <p> Human civilisation has always made new materials . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what societies could build and how they could live . @@138803586 <h> Why Did We Stop Repairing ? <h> We went from ' repair ' to ' replace ' in a single generation . We built a movement around recycling . But repair ? Repair is the revolution we forgot <p> Twenty years ago , when our mixer stopped working , my mother would call the local electrician . He 'd open it up , fix whatever had gone wrong , and it would run perfectly for another decade . Today , when my mixer dies , I open Amazon or Flipkart and exchange it for a new one without a second thought . But somewhere between that workshop and my shopping cart , something changed . We stopped fixing the things we owned and started replacing them instead . This was never really about better technology . It was a quiet shift in what we value . <p> So , what caused this shift ? <p> Consider fixing something today . You call a technician . You wait for him to arrive . He takes one look , decides he needs a part , and leaves . You wait again @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is no warranty on the work , and no promise that it wo n't break again next month . Now think about the alternative . Click . Pay . Delivered tomorrow . Consumers are simply choosing convenience . <p> There is also trust -- or rather , its absence . My mother knew the technician who repaired her appliances . She trusted him to use genuine parts and to stand behind his work , not because of any contract , but simply because she knew him . That relationship , built over years of small fixes and familiar faces , was its own kind of warranty . Today , we hand our things to strangers , brace for disappointment , and half-expect to call him again the following week . <p> Two decades ago , an electrician would have charged somewhere between ? 100 and ? 300 . Today , that same visit can run anywhere from ? 3,000 to ? 8,000 . But labour is only part of it . Spare parts are increasingly proprietary and expensive , and many products today are barely designed to be opened . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at nearly 50% of the cost of buying a new one . <p> In essence , both the economics and the emotions point in the same direction -- replacing is probably the better choice . <p> Do numbers tell the same story ? <p> India is the world 's third-largest generator of e-waste , producing 3.2 million metric tonnes every year -- and only about a third of that is formally recycled . A 2023 study by Toxics Link , titled ' A Stitch in Time ' , traced repair habits across Delhi , Hyderabad , Kolkata , Nagpur , and Ranchi . The findings were not surprising ; high costs and the scarcity of genuine spare parts were the two biggest reasons people walked away from repair . Smaller cities such as Nagpur and Ranchi had held on to repair culture far better than the metros . And the starkest divide ran along income lines : the less you earned , the more likely you were to repair . In essence , rising income levels did n't just change what we could buy ; they also changed what we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ attempt to deal with the mess we have already made , and it deserves credit for that . Every tonne of e-waste that gets formally processed , rather than buried in a landfill or quietly dismantled in an informal scrapyard , represents a real environmental gain . But recycling does not nip the problem in the bud , because by the time it enters the picture , a product has already been manufactured , shipped , consumed , and discarded ; the waste already exists . Recycling is , at best , our most organised response to a problem that should never have reached that point . <p> Repair asks an entirely different question : ' Can we stop creating waste ? ' That shift , from managing the end of a product 's life to actively extending it , is what a circular economy actually means in practice . A linear economy runs on a straightforward and , for a long time , unquestioned logic : things are made , used , and discarded , and the cycle repeats . A circular economy insists that the loop must close @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as long as possible , and anything that breaks should be fixed rather than replaced . When a thing can no longer be used in one form , it should find a new purpose in another . Repair is where this circle begins . <p> How can we make repair great again ? <p> The answer lies not just in changing mindsets but also in changing the system itself . In fact , several of the changes may not even be radical or expensive . <p> For instance , consider standardising repair warranties across independent repair shops . Today , a service centre visit comes with a 90-day guarantee ; a neighbourhood electrician 's work comes with nothing . A minimum warranty standard , even a month , changes the consumer 's risk perception and begins rebuilding the trust that has quietly eroded over two decades . <p> Manufacturers have the power to price components out of reach for independent repairers or withhold them entirely . This leaves local shops with grey-market alternatives . A right-to-repair framework that mandates fair access to parts at reasonable prices can level the playing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ today are built to resist being opened : glued casings , non-standard screws , and batteries that can not be removed without specialist tools . Making key components such as batteries , screens , motors , and switches serviceable extends product life by years . None of this is inevitable ; these are deliberate choices , and they can be regulated . <p> Repair subscriptions and repair insurance could take much of the uncertainty out of fixing things by spreading the cost , reducing upfront hesitation , and making repairs feel like something you can depend on rather than a gamble you 'd avoid . A certified network of neighbourhood technicians would restore what has quietly disappeared over the years : someone who shows up prepared , does the job properly , and can be held accountable . That kind of reliability is what the repair economy needs to earn back its place . <p> Technology can also solve the multi-visit problem that drives most people away from repair . For instance , a diagnostic app , a quick video call , or a sensor built into the appliance could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ comes over . So , he shows up with the right part and fixes it on the first visit . If done right , getting something fixed can be as fast and certain as ordering a replacement . <p> Sustainability became fashionable only after we abandoned it as a way of life . The most sustainable generation never attended climate conferences , calculated carbon footprints , or observed Earth Day . They repaired what broke , reused what remained , and recycled only as a last resort . The circular economy is not a new invention waiting to be discovered . It is an old habit waiting to be remembered . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Dr. Rangapriya Saivasan is an Associate Professor of Finance and Analytics at CHRIST ( Deemed to be University ) , Bengaluru . @@138803598 <h> Those Displaced by Climate , Abandoned by Policy <p> In the shrinking coastlines of the Sundarbans , fishermen do not return to the delta , for the embankment near their village has breached for the third time in five years . They do not leave because they wanted to , they did n't have a choice anymore . Amidst coastal erosion , natural disasters , water contamination and saline soil and water , the people of Sundarbans follow what is slowly becoming a familiar route , to move north , to move away into a cluster of tarpaulin and corrugated iron that is called , on no official map , home . There is no government record of why they left . There is no scheme designed for what happens next . <p> India 's climate refugees are no longer a projection . They are already here , here in the jhuggi clusters of Delhi , in the construction sites outside Pune , in the seasonal labour camps that appear and disappear on the edges of cities that have no interest in counting them . They have arrived from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Assam and from the parched interiors of Bundelkhand . What connects these geographies is not merely ecological catastrophe , it is a political economy that has , for decades , extracted from these landscapes without returning to them , and then turned away when the bill arrived in the form of displacement . <p> The Geography of Expulsion <p> The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre ( IDMC ) recorded 5.4 million displacements in India in 2024 , the highest in twelve years . Globally , 99.5 percent of disaster-induced displacements in the same period were linked to climate-related extreme weather . These are not abstract numbers . They correspond to specific embankments that broke , to specific monsoons that did not come , to farms where the borewell went dry and the loan did not get repaid . The Centre for Science and Environment found that India experienced extreme weather events on 314 out of 365 days in 2024 , killing nearly 3,000 people and destroying two million hectares of cropland . When land fails , people leave . They accumulate from the moment the decision to leave is made ; in the weeks of distress migration without food security or medical access , in the physical deterioration of travel undertaken without money . What awaits is a slum . Not metaphorically , literally . Metal-roofed , unplanned , overcrowded , without reliable water or sanitation . A 2024 survey by People 's Courage International found that heat and excess rain are the primary climate stressors facing internal migrants at their destinations , reported by 77 and 59 percent of respondents respectively . The informal settlement is not a place of recovery from ecological disaster ; it is a continuation of it by other means . The same bodies that fled waterlogging in the delta now live beside open drains . The same lungs that breathed sea air now breathe particulate matter . <p> There is also the subtler problem of immunological exposure , that is , the transition from a rural disease environment to an urban one , encountering local variants of dengue or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ then there is what researchers are beginning to call solastalgia : the particular grief that comes not from leaving home , but from watching home be destroyed . A 2021 study by researchers at the Central University of South Bihar found that rural communities experiencing climate change in the form of erratic monsoon , heatwave , loss of particular bird and tree species , reported emotional distress , reduced self-worth , and severed cultural and religious practices as direct consequences . This is not sentiment . A 2025 scoping review in BMJ Mental Health found consistent associations between solastalgia and depression , anxiety , and post-traumatic stress disorder . The quiet epidemic in India 's climate settlements is not only physical . <p> The Architecture of Exclusion <p> India 's welfare architecture is territorial . Its benefits are tied to addresses , to ration cards registered in districts that the migrant has left , to identity documents that prove belonging to a place they may never return to . When they move , the entitlements do not follow . Only 35 percent of urban local bodies meet the AMRUT water supply benchmarks . The cities receiving millions of climate migrants are not equipped to receive them , and the national budget has not decided that equipping them is a priority . <p> The Fix Exist , The Will Does Not ! <p> The International Institute for Environment and Development ( IIED ) noted in 2025 that migrants drive India 's development but are systematically excluded from programs designed to prevent climate-induced shocks . This is not an administrative oversight . It is a consequence of treating migrants as labour inputs rather than as citizens with rights that travel with them . A genuine response requires portability that actually functions ; health entitlements , ration access and social security across state lines , without a bureaucratic queue . It requires primary care in informal settlements that do not ask for a local address . It requires legal recognition that climate displacement is a category of harm distinct from economic migration . <p> There are approximately 14 million @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the IDMC , without Ayushman Bharat coverage in the cities where they now live , without legal recognition as displaced persons , without recourse if the corrugated iron roofs they sleep under give them heatstroke in May . They are a present political and environmental protection failure . More will arrive with every monsoon season that does not come , every summer that runs past what the land can hold . @@138804801 <p> At Ladakh , 11,500 feet above sea level , the air is so thin that each breath feels like a conscious effort . The landscape is a stark , brutalist canvas of ochre mountains and piercing blue skies . There , in the cold desert of the Indian Himalayas , I sat with an elder in the Aryan Valley , sipping butter tea from a hand-carved wooden cup . <p> I asked him about the changing seasons . He paused , looked towards the distant , snowless peaks , and said quietly , " Everything seems to be delayed now . " <p> In that single sentence , the entire sustainability narrative of the global textile industry seemed to unravel . For the past three decades , the fashion world has been obsessed with ' sustainable materials ' : organic cotton , recycled polyester and lab-grown leather . Yet , in Ladakh , a culture that has worn wool for a millennium achieved sustainability without a single ESG report , carbon credit or green certification . The difference is not technology ; it is culture . <p> To understand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strip away the Western concept of ' environmentalism ' and look instead at necessity . In a region where temperatures drop to -30 ? C and the growing season lasts barely three months , waste is not a sin ; it is a death sentence . <p> Take the traditional Goncha , the heavy woollen robe worn by Ladakhi men . It is not designed by a fashion house in Paris . It is designed by the landscape . Woven from the coarse wool of local sheep and pashm ( cashmere ) from the Changthangi goat , a single Goncha is worn daily for 15 to 20 years . It is patched , mended and eventually recycled into floor rugs . When it finally disintegrates , it returns to the earth as organic carbon . <p> This is the circular economy , not as a marketing buzzword , but as a biological inevitability . The monks in the ancient gompas ( monasteries ) institutionalised this approach further , embedding Ulg-pha ( voluntary community labour ) into the social fabric . Harvesting , threshing and building are all communal activities , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of sufficiency rather than accumulation . <p> In contrast , modern urban consumers often purchase synthetic fleece jackets for a single winter , wear them only a limited number of times and then discard them . Garments are frequently viewed as expressions of identity or fashion . In Ladakhi culture , however , clothing is regarded as a second skin : valuable , repairable and irreplaceable . Here , utility and longevity take precedence over consumption . <p> While Ladakh operates on a rhythm dictated by glaciers and solar cycles , the global fast-fashion machine moves to a rhythm driven by quarterly earnings and ever-changing micro-trends . The consequences are profound : <p> Volume : The average consumer now buys 60 per cent more clothing than in 2000 but keeps each garment for only half as long . <p> Waste : Every second , the equivalent of one truckload of textiles is sent to landfill or incinerated . By 2050 , the fashion industry is projected to consume a quarter of the world 's carbon budget . <p> Water : Producing a single cotton T-shirt requires around 2,700 litres of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one person for approximately 2.5 years . Ladakh 's entire irrigation system operates on a fraction of that amount . <p> The tragedy is that fast fashion has extracted textile knowledge from cultures such as Ladakh while discarding the cultural safeguards that made those practices sustainable . The industry adopted pashm ( cashmere ) and industrialised it , severing the traditional relationship between herders and their animals , while high-density production systems contributed to the degradation of grasslands in regions such as Inner Mongolia ( Chinese autonomous region ) . It took the handloom and replaced it with power looms capable of producing , in a single hour , what an entire village might once have created in a month . <p> The result is a world in which a $3 T-shirt can exist . This is a price so low that it ignores the environmental cost of water extraction , the social cost of exploited labour , and the long-term consequences of landfill methane emissions . <p> However , my journey to the Aryan Valley revealed a sobering truth . Culture-driven sustainability works brilliantly , until the climate breaks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " are the canary in the coal mine for the entire textile world . The apricot blossoms are arriving three weeks late . The barley ripens outside the optimal window . The glaciers melt violently , causing flash floods in June and drought in August . <p> The Ladakhis have no backup global supply chain . When their cultural predictions fail , they do not import a substitute . They go hungry . Their culture is adapting , but adaptation takes generations and climate change moves in decades . The young Ladakhi , seeing his grandfather 's weather-reading skills fail , begins to view the traditional woollen Goncha as ' backward ' and reaches for the synthetic puffer jacket . He believes that manufactured polyester is more ' modern ' and reliable . <p> What can a cold desert in the Himalayas teach the textile industries of Mumbai , New York and London ? The lessons are surprisingly relevant in an era of mounting environmental pressures and shifting consumer expectations . <p> Durability as the Ultimate Sustainability Metric : The industry needs to shift its focus from volume to longevity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emphasis should be placed on their lifespan , repairability and continued use . Brands can support this transition by designing products for durability , disassembly and easy repair , with the goal of extending garment life from seasons to decades . <p> Localising the ' Invisible ' Supply Chain : In Ladakh , wool is sourced from goats grazing on the Changthang Plateau , often within a relatively small geographic radius . This localised model highlights the potential benefits of regional sourcing and decentralised production . As the industry seeks to reduce its environmental footprint , greater attention may need to be paid to shortening supply chains and reducing the carbon costs associated with transporting materials and products across multiple continents . <p> Prioritising Sufficiency Over Efficiency : The industry 's longstanding pursuit of efficiency ( producing more , faster and at lower cost ) has contributed to significant environmental pressures . Ladakh offers a contrasting perspective centred on sufficiency : producing and consuming what is necessary rather than what is possible . This approach encourages a greater appreciation of value , fair compensation for artisans and more responsible resource @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ proposed Digital Product Passports represent an important step , but their effectiveness will ultimately depend on a broader cultural shift in consumer attitudes and purchasing behaviour . <p> As I left the Aryan Valley , the elder smiled and offered me a piece of dried apricot . I asked him , " What do you watch now , if the old signs are failing ? " He pointed to the youngest child playing nearby . " We watch them . We teach them to watch harder . And we pray . " <p> The fashion industry can not rely on prayer , but it can learn the value of paying closer attention . The sector must monitor the declining water tables of cotton-growing regions , address concerns around forced labour in fast-fashion supply chains , and confront the growing volumes of discarded clothing accumulating in places such as Chile 's Atacama Desert . Ladakh demonstrates that sustainability is not merely a technological challenge but a cultural inheritance . The future of the industry may depend less on discovering new materials and more on rediscovering enduring values , and a simple @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ clothes humanity . <h> Conclusion <p> Ladakh offers a powerful reminder that sustainability is not solely a matter of materials , certifications or technology . Its textile traditions show how longevity , repairability , community participation and respect for natural limits can create genuinely circular systems . While climate change is testing even these resilient practices , the broader lesson for the global fashion industry remains clear : lasting sustainability will depend as much on cultural values and responsible consumption as on technological innovation . <p> Sulagna Saha is an assistant professor at the National Institute of Fashion Technology ( NIFT ) , Bhubaneswar . She holds a PhD in Sustainability Studies from XIM University , Bhubaneswar , Odisha . @@138807405 <p> Long before the age of fossil fuels and centralised power grids , ancient Indian societies met their energy needs through a resilient system based on local renewable resources and ecological stewardship . By integrating community resource management with environmental ethics , ancient Indian societies followed a sustainable energy framework that supported agriculture , industry and livelihoods while maintaining harmony with nature . Early societies utilised wind energy and rudimentary water mills to capture kinetic energy for tasks like grinding grain . Meanwhile , advanced metallurgy , exemplified by achievements such as the Delhi Iron Pillar , depended on specialised charcoal-fired furnaces and sophisticated metallurgical knowledge . Foundational elements of energy , water and agriculture were revered as sacred forces : Surya ( Solar Radiation ) as the primary life force driving climate cycles and crop production , Vayu ( Air ) and Varuna ( Water ) as vital forces necessary to sustain civilisations . <p> The following Bhumi Suktam from the Atharvaveda shows this reverence : <p> ( Atharva Veda , 12.1.12 ) <p> " Earth is our mother and we are her children . The life-giving rain is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " <p> Further , energy security was treated as a centralised state responsibility . @@138808996 <p> India 's heatwaves are no longer just public health emergencies ; they are increasingly becoming electricity system events . In the last five years , the country 's peak demand has risen from 183 GW in December 2020 to over 270 GW in May 2026 . The primary driver is the rapid growth in cooling demand . This already accounts for over 40 percent of residential electricity consumption and roughly 26 percent of national peak load in summer . In 2025 , 15.4 million air conditioners were sold , and this number is projected to double to 28 million by 2030 . The policy response has largely focused on demand-side reforms , such as slowing the growth of cooling energy use through measures like efficiency standards , star-labelling of ACs , and building codes . While helpful , they can not eliminate the underlying challenge of rising cooling demand during peak hours . <p> The dependence on a coal-led electricity system amplifies this challenge , as coal continues to supply 75 percent of India 's electricity . As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of heatwaves , thermal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ To reliably meet the cooling electricity demand , integrating renewable energy into India 's power system is an immediate imperative . Yet its integration remains constrained by system-level bottlenecks in the grid , storage and transmission infrastructure . Currently , it meets only about one-third of India 's daytime demand , and even less during evening periods when solar energy is unavailable . <p> Three interconnected pathways will help address these challenges : modernising the grid with storage to better integrate renewable energy and meet cooling demand ; improving transmission and distribution networks so that renewable energy can reach demand centres ; and securing the financing required to support the power ecosystem 's transition . <p> Figure 1 : Share of Cooling in total electricity consumption in May 2026 <h> Modernising Grid Resilience with Storage <p> Extreme heat and rising cooling demand are testing the ability of India 's grid system to provide round-the-clock power , let alone generate reliable power from renewables . <p> India 's grid , designed for coal-based plants , relies on those plants operating above a Minimum Technical Load ( MTL ) . Most Indian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , forcing them to continue generating even when cheaper solar power is available . The Central Electricity Authority ( CEA ) has proposed reducing the MTL to 40 percent , thereby enabling the grid to absorb more renewable energy . This write-up aims to share that experience . Drought is a natural disaster with a difference . Others like floods , hailstone , earthquakes or even fires occur suddenly , casualties occur and collateral damage happens in the twinkling of an eye . One is then usually left only with the task of relief disbursement . The onset of drought is different . It does not come with a bang . The calamity creeps with terrifying slowness over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is erratic , declining rainfall and unusual higher temperatures ( already happening to Meghalaya ) . These are the characteristics of a drought . Precursors of a famine perhaps . The question is how prepared is Meghalaya on dealing with this unknown natural calamity ? Drawing from my own experience , there are two ways people approach the onslaught of drought . The first approach advocates passive reaction , by responding to each phase of the drought as and when it happens and hope for the best . This is a knee jerk reaction which can only result in greater confusion amidst the chaos that drought brings along . The second approach is based on a preconceived roadmap on how to manage a drought . It 's unplanned reaction vs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ appears to focus on the second approach . Why do I say this ? I say it because the victim of any natural disaster is the common man . The ordinary citizen will be completely bewildered and stumped as he sees the failure of nature around him . Panic and confusion will be his initial reaction , which if not handled in the initial phase can lead to serious law and order issues . However , people will tend to maintain their calmness and composure if they are assured by physical evidence or audio devices that the Government is working to help them through the turmoil . @@138821550 <p> Mangrove forests rank among the world 's most valuable coastal ecosystems , shielding communities from storms , storing vast amounts of carbon and providing nurseries for countless marine species . ( Photo : Windy ) <p> Climate scientists say a warmer atmosphere can hold substantially more moisture . @@138823482 <h> As temperatures rise across the Valley , simple precautions , public awareness , and timely care can prevent a seasonal discomfort from becoming a public health concern <p> The Kashmir Valley , long associated with cool breezes and a forgiving summer climate , is increasingly feeling the strain of rising temperatures . What was once a brief seasonal inconvenience is now turning into a public health and daily life concern , especially for children , the elderly , outdoor workers , and patients with existing illnesses . In such conditions , summer heat precautions are no longer a matter of personal comfort alone ; they have become a civic necessity . <p> Every year , the first intense spell of heat exposes the same weaknesses : poor hydration habits , unnecessary exposure to the sun , delayed medical response , and a general underestimation of heat-related illness . Many people continue to treat summer fatigue , dizziness , dehydration , and heat exhaustion as minor discomforts . In reality , these can quickly become serious if ignored . The body under high heat loses fluids faster , the risk @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . What looks like a routine hot day can become a medical emergency for someone who is already fragile . Regular fluid intake throughout the day , avoiding too much tea or sugary drinks , and eating water-rich fruits and light meals can make a significant difference . Equally important is avoiding direct sun exposure during peak afternoon hours . @@138834538 <h> Climate Change at the Tipping Point : Global Disruptions and the Growing Crisis in the Indian Subcontinent <p> Climate change is no longer a distant warning or a future possibility . It is a present-day reality that is reshaping the Earth 's ecosystems , economies , and societies . The effects are visible across continents , from record-breaking heatwaves and devastating floods to shrinking glaciers and collapsing ecosystems . Human-induced greenhouse gas emissions , combined with natural climatic variations such as the recent strengthening of El Ni ? o , have accelerated global warming to dangerous levels . <p> The global average temperature has now reached approximately 1.46 ? C above pre-industrial levels , placing humanity perilously close to the internationally recognised 1.5 ? C threshold beyond which climate impacts are expected to become significantly more severe and , in some cases , irreversible . <p> The consequences are unfolding simultaneously across multiple sectors , making climate change one of the defining challenges of the twenty-first century . <p> Oceans Under Stress and Intensifying Extreme Weather <p> The world 's oceans have absorbed unprecedented amounts of heat , with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ heatwaves . Temperatures are repeatedly reaching record levels , while high humidity is pushing human tolerance to dangerous limits . In several locations , wet-bulb temperatures -- where the human body struggles to cool itself through perspiration -- are approaching thresholds that pose serious risks to human survival . <p> Rising temperatures have dramatically increased global demand for cooling . Air conditioning , once considered a luxury in many regions , is becoming an essential requirement for survival during increasingly severe heatwaves . <p> The vulnerability of modern electricity grids is emerging as one of the major challenges of climate adaptation . <p> Ecosystems and Food Production Under Threat <p> Natural ecosystems are changing faster than many species can adapt . @@138838296 <h> Resource Race <p> The Arctic is no longer a distant , frozen frontier at the edge of global politics . It has become one of the world 's most consequential strategic theatres , where climate change , great-power rivalry and technological competition are converging . At the centre of this transformation stands Greenland , an island of barely 56,000 inhabitants but immense geopolitical significance . United States President Donald Trump 's repeated insistence that Greenland should come under American control has reignited a debate that extends far beyond one island or one presidency . While his rhetoric has alarmed allies and unsettled diplomatic norms , it has also exposed a reality that many policymakers have preferred to ignore : the Arctic is rapidly becoming a decisive arena in the emerging global order . The question , however , is not whether Greenland matters strategically -- it unquestionably does -- but whether strategic necessity can ever justify overriding the principles of sovereignty , self-determination and alliance solidarity that have underpinned international stability for decades . <p> Greenland 's value is rooted primarily in geography . Situated between North America and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ island has long served as a military outpost guarding the North Atlantic . During the Second World War , it became vital to protecting Allied shipping routes , while throughout the Cold War it functioned as a crucial early-warning station against Soviet missile threats . Today , the United States already operates the strategically important Pituffik Space Base , supporting missile defence , space surveillance and NATO operations . Greenland also overlooks the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom ( GIUK ) Gap , a maritime chokepoint critical to monitoring Russian submarine activity . Yet the island 's significance has expanded dramatically because climate change is reshaping the Arctic itself . Shrinking sea ice is gradually opening previously inaccessible shipping routes , potentially shortening trade links between Asia , Europe and North America . Simultaneously , melting ice is exposing vast deposits of rare earth elements and other critical minerals indispensable for semiconductors , electric vehicles , renewable energy technologies and advanced defence systems . Geography that was once frozen into strategic irrelevance is now becoming central to the economic and military competition of the twenty-first century . <p> The renewed interest in Greenland @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rivalry among the world 's major powers . Russia has steadily rebuilt its Arctic military infrastructure , modernised old Soviet-era bases and strengthened the capabilities of its Northern Fleet . China , although geographically distant , has declared itself a " near-Arctic state " and incorporated the region into its ambitious Polar Silk Road initiative , seeking future commercial access while expanding its global strategic footprint . Western governments , meanwhile , remain increasingly concerned about China 's overwhelming dominance in processing rare earth minerals , creating vulnerabilities in supply chains essential for high-technology industries . These developments have understandably pushed Arctic security higher on the agenda of NATO and Western capitals . However , recognising Greenland 's importance should not be confused with endorsing unilateral acquisition . The United States already enjoys extensive military access through agreements with Denmark and Greenland , and security experts themselves have noted that formal ownership would add little to Washington 's existing strategic advantages . In reality , what is at stake is less about immediate defence requirements than about geopolitical symbolism and long-term resource competition in an increasingly contested Arctic . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ powers often determine the legitimacy of their objectives . Denmark remains a longstanding NATO ally , while Greenland enjoys extensive self-government under the Danish Crown . Its elected leadership has consistently maintained that the island 's future will be determined solely by the Greenlandic people . Suggestions of military force or territorial acquisition , even when later softened , undermine the very principles that democratic nations invoke when criticising similar behaviour elsewhere . If powerful states begin treating strategic geography as a commodity to be acquired rather than territory governed by international law and popular consent , the consequences will extend well beyond the Arctic . Such precedents weaken the credibility of alliances , encourage revisionist ambitions elsewhere and create unnecessary distrust among partners facing common security challenges . Ironically , they may also strengthen the narratives of rival powers who frequently accuse the West of applying different standards depending on whose interests are involved . Effective deterrence against Russia or strategic competition with China requires stronger alliances , not avoidable disputes within them . <p> Greenland therefore represents a defining test of how democracies respond to an era of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , stronger infrastructure , scientific cooperation and coordinated security arrangements among like-minded nations . The region 's critical mineral reserves should be developed responsibly to diversify global supply chains without sacrificing environmental safeguards or indigenous rights . Above all , the voices of Greenland 's people must remain central to every decision concerning their future . Strategic importance does not erase the principles of sovereignty , nor should resource wealth become a licence for geopolitical opportunism . The Arctic 's future will shape global trade , technological competition and military balance for generations to come . Whether it becomes another theatre of confrontation or an example of responsible international cooperation will depend on whether nations choose partnership over possession , diplomacy over coercion , and international law over the temptations of power politics .

@@138839103 <p> If cities have long known their vulnerabilities , why do they continue to flood ? Rainfall may initiate the event , but the dominant model of urban development systematically converts precipitation into a human-made catastrophe . The crisis is not natural . It is engineered . <p> Is heavy rainfall alone responsible for urban flooding ? <p> No . Rainfall may trigger flooding , but the scale of urban inundation is largely determined by how cities are planned and built . The dominant model of urban development systematically converts precipitation into disaster by steadily reducing the landscape 's ability to absorb water . <p> Unlike fluvial flooding , which is shaped by regional hydrology and climatic vagaries , pluvial flooding is directly produced by local land-use decisions and the aggressive transformation of natural topography into impermeable concrete . <p> Rapid , uncontrolled urban sprawl has systematically forced these ecosystems toward what researchers describe as a forced death , erasing living hydrological systems in the service of real estate extraction . <p> What does the evidence show ? <p> The pattern is strikingly similar across cities . <p> Bengaluru recorded @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in water bodies between 1973 and 2010 . Chennai 's Pallikaranai marshland had shrunk to just 12% of its original extent by 2011 . Mumbai 's reclamation of coastal wetlands and mangroves has drastically reduced tidal drainage capacity . Hyderabad 's encroachment on lakes and natural nalas has produced recurring waterlogging , while Kolkata 's wetlands and historic canal networks have been diminished by real estate pressure . <p> In each case , the ramifications of ecological erasure are identical : water that once percolated slowly through living soil now accelerates across paved surfaces , generating immense peak runoff that ageing , choked drainage infrastructure can not absorb . <p> Recovery in informal settlements stands in stark contrast to the relatively swift restoration of services in wealthier urban enclaves . Urban flooding remains a perfect reflection of the existing structural inequalities on muddy water . <p> Why does governance continue to dither ? <p> The persistence of urban flooding is rarely a failure of engineering knowledge . It is a crisis of governance and political rectitude . <p> Responsibility for urban waterscapes is fractured across municipal corporations , development authorities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ agencies . Operating in institutional silos , drainage upgrades are planned independently of land-use blueprints , while environmental conservation remains disconnected from infrastructure development . <p> How do spending priorities make matters worse ? <p> Municipal spending continues to favour highly visible , politically rewarding projects such as flyovers , metros and expressways over the invisible work of maintaining stormwater systems . <p> As a result , cities often desilt drains only after floods rather than before the monsoon . <p> Yes . After catastrophic flooding , Surat established the Surat Climate Change Trust , bringing together government agencies , businesses and researchers to coordinate real-time early warning systems and resilience planning . <p> Ahmedabad 's Heat Action Plan , although designed for extreme heat rather than flooding , demonstrated that coordinated governance and cross-agency communication can substantially reduce disaster-related mortality by overcoming institutional fragmentation . <p> Can cities rely only on bigger drains and concrete infrastructure ? <p> No . For decades , flood control relied primarily on structural grey engineering through larger drains , embankments , pumps and massive infrastructure projects . While these remain necessary , they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ offer perhaps the most pellucid example . The internationally recognised wetland system functions simultaneously as Kolkata 's natural kidney and flood buffer . It naturally treats a substantial share of the city 's sewage before the nutrient-rich water supports fish farming and vegetable cultivation . Livelihood stability and flood mitigation thus coalesce in a single living system at negligible cost compared with the billions spent on grey infrastructure elsewhere . <p> What choice lies ahead for India 's cities ? <p> As India 's cities prepare to accommodate hundreds of millions of additional residents , the challenge transcends drainage calculations or sea-wall specifications . <p> Will lakes , marshes and floodplains continue to be viewed as desiccated wastelands awaiting conversion into concrete ? Or will urban governance finally learn to accommodate water as a permanent , living element of the urban landscape -- not an adversary to be vanquished , but a force to be respected ? <p> The answer will determine whether India 's cities survive the climate century ahead , or continue to drown in the consequences of their own turpitude.
