@@138890844 <h> How the continuity of history has persisted in our times , and how it has been disrupted <p> Although there are different views regarding when exactly the journey of humanity started , we may consider here this journey in terms of the last about one hundred thousand years of our planet . All through this period there is one continuity in all history . There are so many changes from time to time but in one respect there is a very remarkable continuity even up to this day . <p> This continuity relates to the fact that the welfare of humanity and in fact all life is positively related to the extent to which humanity lives according to the precepts of justice and equality , peace and harmony , protection of environment and of all forms of life . The more the commitment to these precepts , the more the happiness of people and the greater also the possibilities for distress to be minimized . <p> If this was true at the start of the journey of humanity , this is equally true today . In this respect indeed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Of course the extent of the commitment to these precepts differed widely from place to place and from time to time . Even when the record was not good , people could say -- oh we made big mistakes , we must improve in future . <p> The possibility of improvement was always there because , whatever the mistakes being made , the basic life-nurturing conditions were not threatened in any serious way . <p> If we assume the history of humanity to be about 100,000 years , then this was true for about 99,920 years . However about 80 years back , a very significant change occurred , namely that for the first time it became possible that by its own actions humanity can destroy the basic life-nurturing conditions of earth . While this started with nuclear weapons , it gathered strength with about a dozen serious and inter-related man-made environmental problems led by climate change , as well as with several disruptive and destructive technologies , evolving of very fast weapon systems , autonomous and robot weapons and steps taken towards space warfare . <p> Now what has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ so ( about 0.08% of the history of humankind ) is that as the basic life-nurturing conditions are threatened and the factors causing these are accelerating and there are tipping points which should not be crossed ( at the risk of some very harmful changes in the planet perhaps becoming irreversible ) , so we can not go on saying -- sorry that we made mistakes but we 'll improve later . This space of correction that was available earlier may not be available now in several respects . We simply can not go on making serious mistakes as such mistakes made now can harm the basic life- nurturing conditions of the planet in irreversible ways , thereby causing grave harm to all of us people of this generation but even more to the upcoming generations , our own children , as well as to the entirely innocent other forms of life who have to pay a very high price for the follies of humanity ( supposed to be the wisest species ) . <p> So in this context the last 8 decades have a very big discontinuity with the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first time that human actions have led to serious threats emerging for life-nurturing conditions of the planet . <p> Both this continuity and discontinuity of history are present in these times of very high consequence in the history of humanity . Hence considering both these situations , the most important policy on which humanity should focus with great commitment is to protect the basic life nurturing conditions of the planet within a framework of justice and peace . C per decade in several mid- and high-altitude locations , indicating reduced night-time cooling . <p> The authors cautioned that continued warming in Jammu and Kashmir 's mountain regions could have serious implications for glaciers , snow cover , river flows , biodiversity and water security , affecting millions of people dependent on Himalayan water resources . <p> While the study confirms significant warming trends across the region , the researchers noted that observations above 3,000 metres remain limited and called for a denser network of high-altitude weather stations to improve future climate assessments . <p> The findings add to growing evidence that the Western Himalaya is becoming increasingly vulnerable to climate change , underlining the need for stronger adaptation strategies to safeguard the region 's fragile mountain ecosystems and water resources . Toronto-based artist Shahana Rajani asks this question in the film , Lines that World a River . This new iteration of her moving image work , Four Acts of Recovery , offers criticism of colonial cartography around the Indus . Every year , the river could change its course , and each year the British had to revise their maps . Eventually they used hydraulic technologies , irrigation infrastructure and civil engineering so that the Indus stayed its course . This exercise was carried out in other parts of the subcontinent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ new nation states , followed by the rise of hydroelectric ambitions and the ongoing threat of climate change have destabilised the rhythm of the river and that of the fishing communities that live along it . The drying of creeks and rising sea levels that threaten to engulf the delta are also accompanied by flooding and submerging of sacred shrines and sites that were of spiritual and mystical significance to the communities . <p> Through her work , Rajani looks at alternate ways of mapping the shape-shifting landscape through the intergenerational transfer of knowledge within the fisherfolk , many of whom are already displaced or are at the risk of it . Their wisdom and traditions form a bridge between " between ecologies erstwhile and those critically endangered at present " . The moving image work is part of the new exhibition , The Wall is Water , curated by Anushka Rajendran at the Prameya Art Foundation ( PRAF ) -- a nomadic institutional framework for the arts working out of New Delhi . @@138905198 <h> Monsoon is here and so are the mosquitoes <h> Share : <p> X <p> Likeother insects and the rest of the organisms , including humans , on this planet , mosquitoes are also trying to pass on their gene pool to the next generation to increase their fitness and survival . A majority of the mosquitoes are pollinators . Flowers are their primary source of energy . <p> There are over 3500 species of mosquitoes worldwide , and a vast majority are capable of pollination . Hardly a few species live near humans and started exploring humans as their blood meal substitute to make eggs . In doing so , unintentionally ( from mosquito 's side ) viruses and a few parasitic forms come in contact with humans . <p> The proliferation of viruses and parasitic forms in our blood system can lead to various diseases including dengue , malaria , and chikungunya . SITs include engineering the male mosquito and releasing it in the field . These genetically modified males will mate with the wild females and during this process a lethal gene is passed on , and this will cause female offspring to die before reaching maturity . <p> WBM are based on a cytoplasmic incompatibility technique where male mosquitoes are infected with a naturally occurring strain of endosymbiont . These endosymbionts negatively effects egg hatching due to sperm-egg incompatibility . GDs engineer a gene to be inherited at super-Mendelian rates which means nearly one hundred per cent of offspring 's lead to sterility . Many countries around the globe have gone in for such modern biotechnology centred mosquito control strategies . The high-pressure system acts like a lid , preventing the hot air from escaping and allowing temperatures at the surface to rise . <p> As the trapped air sinks , it compresses and warms further . At the same time , the high-pressure system blocks cooler air , cloud cover and rainfall from moving into the region . With little wind and abundant sunshine , the ground absorbs more heat , creating a self-reinforcing cycle that drives temperatures even higher . <h> Why it creates prolonged extreme heat <p> Heat domes are associated with persistent heatwaves because the stagnant high-pressure system can remain in place for days or even weeks . Its goal is to make sure that buying and selling wildlife across borders does not drive species towards extinction . Today , the convention covers more than 40,000 species of animals and plants . <p> The Animals Committee is made up of scientists and technical experts . Their job is to examine the latest evidence on wildlife populations and international trade , identify species that may be at risk , and advise countries on how trade can be managed without harming wild populations . They also review whether countries are following CITES rules and whether more scientific information is needed before future decisions are taken . <p> The recommendations made here will shape the decisions that governments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) , the convention 's highest decision-making body . <p> The meeting is important as wildlife trade is worth billions of dollars every year . @@138905979 <h> 2047 Vs 2049 : India and China race towards two very different dreams <p> History has an uncanny habit of mocking long-term predictions . Thirty years ago , in the mid-1990s , few economists imagined that China would become the world 's manufacturing powerhouse , accounting for nearly a third of global industrial output . Equally , few believed India , then still wrestling with the after-effects of its 1991 balance-of-payments crisis , would emerge as one of the world 's fastest-growing major economies and the fourth largest by GDP . <p> The world changed dramatically in three decades . The Soviet Union vanished . China joined the World Trade Organization and transformed global supply chains . India liberalised its economy and built a globally competitive information technology industry . The internet revolution , smartphones , artificial intelligence , biotechnology and renewable energy reshaped commerce faster than governments could regulate them . <p> That history should inject a note of humility into today 's grand national visions . China has unveiled a long-term blueprint aimed at becoming a fully developed , technologically dominant and militarily modern nation by 2049 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Republic of China . India , under Prime Minister Narendra Modi , has articulated its own ambition of becoming a Viksit Bharat , or developed nation , by 2047 , marking one hundred years of independence . <p> Both are ambitious . Both seek to inspire national confidence . Both are designed to mobilise governments , businesses and citizens around a common purpose . Yet neither Xi Jinping nor Narendra Modi is likely to be politically present when those milestones arrive . The leaders who inherit these visions will confront a world that may bear little resemblance to today 's geopolitical and economic landscape . That is both the strength -- and the weakness -- of long-term national planning . <p> China 's Long March to 2049 . When the Communist Party of China marked the anniversary of its founding , it celebrated far more than political longevity . It celebrated one of history 's most extraordinary economic transformations . When Deng Xiaoping launched his " Reform and Opening Up " programme in 1978 , China was an impoverished agrarian economy isolated from global markets . The reforms dismantled collective @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , attracted foreign investment and integrated China into global manufacturing . The results transformed the global economy . China lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty , became the world 's factory , accumulated massive foreign exchange reserves and emerged as the world 's second-largest economy , trailing only the United States . <p> Its ambitions no longer stop there . The " China 2049 " vision extends well beyond economic growth . Beijing seeks leadership in artificial intelligence , quantum computing , semiconductors , robotics , biotechnology , aerospace , electric vehicles , advanced manufacturing and green energy . It also seeks military modernisation capable of projecting power well beyond East Asia . Infrastructure initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative , expansion of high-speed rail , digital connectivity and strategic investments across Asia , Africa and Latin America reflect China 's intention to shape -- not merely participate in -- the international order . Its objective is not simply prosperity . It is an influence . <p> The government aims to increase manufacturing 's contribution to GDP , strengthen logistics , modernise agriculture , improve healthcare and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ India also enjoys an important geopolitical advantage . Many Western nations increasingly view India as an indispensable strategic partner in balancing China 's growing influence in the Indo-Pacific . That has translated into stronger defence cooperation , technology partnerships and investment opportunities . <p> The contrast between the two countries is striking . China relied on disciplined state planning , export-led industrialisation and massive public investment . India relies more heavily on markets , entrepreneurship and democratic institutions . China built infrastructure first and consumption later . India 's domestic consumption has grown alongside infrastructure development . China became rich before growing old . India hopes to become rich while remaining relatively young . Neither model is inherently superior . Each reflects different political systems , historical experiences and social structures . <p> India has made remarkable progress in digital public infrastructure , software services , fintech and space technology , yet it still faces major challenges in manufacturing productivity , education quality , labour participation , urban planning and healthcare . Bridging that gap will require decades of sustained reforms . <p> Yet history teaches that thirty years is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stagnation after the 1980s . Few anticipated the collapse of the Soviet Union . The 2008 financial crisis transformed confidence in Western capitalism . COVID-19 disrupted global supply chains overnight . Artificial intelligence now threatens to redefine entire industries . Climate change is altering agriculture , migration , insurance and energy systems . <p> Geopolitical conflicts increasingly reshape trade flows . Who can confidently predict what the world economy will resemble in 2047 or 2049 ? China itself faces daunting structural challenges . Its population is shrinking . The workforce is ageing . The property sector remains under pressure . Local government debt has risen sharply . International tensions have encouraged several multinational companies to diversify manufacturing beyond China . India faces its own uncertainties . It must generate millions of productive jobs annually , improve learning outcomes , reduce regional disparities , increase female labour participation , manage rapid urbanisation and ensure that economic growth becomes more inclusive . <p> Neither country 's future is guaranteed . Leadership Beyond Xi and Modi . Perhaps the most fascinating aspect of both visions is that neither Xi Jinping nor Narendra Modi @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inevitably outlive their architects . The leaders governing China in 2049 and India in 2047 may have entirely different priorities . Global crises could force dramatic revisions . Technological revolutions may reshape national competitiveness in ways unimaginable today . Entire industries may disappear while new ones emerge . Political transitions could alter economic strategies . History rarely follows straight lines . <p> The India-China relationship is often portrayed as a zero-sum contest . Reality is more complex . China undoubtedly aims to remain Asia 's dominant economic power and continue widening its technological advantage . India seeks to narrow that gap , expand its own global influence and emerge as an alternative manufacturing and innovation hub . Healthy competition can benefit both countries -- and the wider world . Together they account for more than one-third of humanity . Their economic choices influence global trade , climate policy , commodity markets , technology standards and international institutions . The rise of both countries need not automatically produce confrontation . It could also produce complementary growth if political differences remain manageable . <p> The Final Verdict Belongs to History . Grand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , provide strategic direction and encourage long-term investment . But they are not guaranteed . China 's 2049 blueprint and India 's Viksit Bharat 2047 represent aspirations rather than predetermined outcomes . The next three decades will almost certainly produce financial crises , technological disruptions , geopolitical conflicts and unforeseen breakthroughs that neither Beijing nor New Delhi can fully anticipate today . <p> History reminds us that nations succeed not because they predict the future perfectly , but because they adapt when the future refuses to behave as expected . China enters that future with the confidence of an industrial superpower seeking technological supremacy . India enters it with the optimism of a rising democracy determined to accelerate its transformation . Whether China succeeds in leaving India permanently behind , or whether India narrows the gap through innovation , demographics and democratic resilience , will depend less on today 's political slogans than on the quality of institutions , the willingness to reform , and the ability of future leaders to respond to challenges not yet imagined . <p> By 2047 and 2049 , the names Xi Jinping and Narendra @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that will matter far more is whether the visions they articulated proved durable enough to survive them -- and flexible enough to adapt to a world that , if the past thirty years are any guide , will be almost unrecognisable from the one we inhabit today . @@138912159 <p> The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development ( NABARD ) , the country 's apex development financial institution for agriculture and rural development , celebrates its 45th foundation day , marking more than four decades of dedicated service to rural India . <p> Established on 12 July , 1982 , the NABARD has grown far beyond its traditional role as a provider of rural credit and today stands as a unique institution combining finance , development , supervision , institution building and innovation . <p> In Arunachal Pradesh , the NABARD 's journey has been one of sustained partnership with the state government , banks , cooperative institutions , civil society organisations and , most importantly , rural communities . From building roads and bridges in remote areas to creating irrigation facilities , strengthening rural health and education infrastructure , nurturing tribal orchards , promoting farmer collectives , reviving natural springs , empowering women through self-help groups and taking unique indigenous products to wider markets , the NABARD 's footprint in the state reflects the diversity , potential and aspirations of Arunachal itself . <p> In a geographically @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fundamental to economic opportunity , the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund ( RIDF ) has emerged as one of the NABARD 's most significant contributions . Under the RIDF , the NABARD has sanctioned 534 projects to the Government of Arunachal Pradesh , involving cumulative assistance of Rs 5,116.46 crore . Through the RIDF , the NABARD has partnered with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh in creating critical infrastructure encompassing rural roads and bridges , irrigation , drinking water , flood protection , soil conservation , health facilities , educational institutions and other essential public assets . These investments have done more than create physical infrastructure . A road connects a farmer to a market , a bridge connects a child to a school , an irrigation channel gives a family the confidence to cultivate another crop , and a rural health facility brings essential care closer to communities living in remote areas . This is the larger purpose that guides the NABARD 's infrastructure financing in the state . <p> Credit remains the lifeblood of rural economic activity . Through refinance support to eligible banks and financial institutions , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ horticulture , animal husbandry , fisheries , farm mechanisation , food processing , rural enterprises and other priority sectors . As a development financial institution , the NABARD also performs an important supervisory role over regional rural banks and cooperative banks , helping strengthen governance , compliance , financial soundness and the overall rural credit delivery architecture . Its role extends to grassroots credit planning through district-level potential linked credit plans and the state focus paper , which assess local potential and help translate available resources and opportunities into actionable credit strategies . <p> The NABARD has strengthened agricultural credit flow through refinance support to the Arunachal Pradesh Rural Bank , with cumulative sanctions of Rs 109.56 crore for short-term agricultural loans and Rs 86.05 crore for long-term agricultural loans . <p> Financial inclusion remains central to the NABARD 's development efforts . Through the SHG-bank linkage programme , promotion of joint liability groups , financial literacy initiatives , capacity building and support for digital financial inclusion , the NABARD continues to facilitate greater participation of women , small and marginal farmers and underserved rural households in the formal financial @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ demonstrated how access to savings , credit and collective action can transform lives , and in Arunachal , women-led institutions continue to emerge as important drivers of social and economic change . The NABARD has provided support of Rs 2,890.22 lakh for various financial inclusion initiatives in the state . <p> The NABARD has consistently recognised that the future of small and marginal farmers lies in collective strength . Seventeen farmer-producer organisations ( FPOs ) promoted and supported by the NABARD in Arunachal are enabling farmers to aggregate produce , procure inputs collectively , improve processing and value addition , access institutional finance and negotiate better terms in the marketplace . The effort is not merely to organise farmers , but to help them build viable , professionally managed and sustainable rural enterprises . <p> Arunachal 's tribal communities possess generations of knowledge about forests , farming , biodiversity and natural resources . The NABARD 's Tribal Development Fund interventions , popularly known as WADI or TRIBES projects , build upon this deep relationship between people and land . Through orchard-based livelihood development , participating tribal families are supported in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by intercropping , soil and water conservation , livestock development , capacity building and community institutions . Crops such as arecanut , citrus , spices and other locally suitable horticultural species are helping create long-term livelihood assets for tribal households . A WADI is more than an orchard ; it is a patient investment in a family 's future -- combining income , nutrition , natural resource conservation and dignity . <p> As concerns over soil health , rising input costs and climate variability grow , the NABARD is promoting agroecological and natural farming approaches through its JIVA programme . In Arunachal , the initiative encourages farmers to reduce dependence on external chemical inputs and rediscover locally adapted farming practices based on healthy soil , biodiversity and efficient use of natural resources . Practices involving Jeevamrit , Beejamrit , Ghanjeevamrit , biomass recycling and diversified cropping are being demonstrated at the field level . The objective is not simply to replace one set of inputs with another , but to rebuild the ecological foundations of agriculture and make farming more resilient and economically sustainable . <p> The NABARD 's development @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Internet of Things ( IoT ) , digital tools and emerging technologies in agriculture have the potential to help farmers make better decisions through real-time information on soil moisture , weather conditions , irrigation requirements and crop health . In a state where farms are dispersed and extension services face geographical challenges , technology can help bridge distances . The NABARD 's endeavour is to ensure that innovation remains practical , affordable and relevant to farmers , rather than becoming technology for technology 's sake . <p> The NABARD has sanctioned assistance of Rs 2,853.27 lakh towards various initiatives in the farm sector in Arunachal . <p> For Arunachal , climate change is not an abstract future concern . Changing rainfall patterns , extreme weather events , soil erosion , drying water sources and pressures on traditional farming systems are increasingly visible realities . The NABARD , with its extensive experience in climate finance and natural resource management , is supporting interventions aimed at strengthening the resilience of rural communities . Springshed development and water rejuvenation initiatives are particularly important in the Himalayan landscape . By scientifically treating recharge @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ communities around the protection of natural water sources , such interventions seek to revive springs , enhance groundwater recharge and improve water security . <p> Arunachal possesses an extraordinary wealth of indigenous agricultural produce , handloom traditions , handicrafts , food products and cultural knowledge . The NABARD has been actively supporting the promotion of geographical indications ( GI ) as a means of protecting this rich heritage while creating economic opportunities for producer communities . Eighteen GI products have received GI certification with the NABARD 's support ; 18 more products are in the pipeline . From unique rice varieties and textiles to traditional crafts and agricultural products , GI registration can help establish authenticity , preserve community knowledge and strengthen market identity . <p> However , registration is only the beginning . The NABARD 's efforts increasingly focus on the journey beyond the GI tag-producer organisation , authorized user registration , branding , packaging , traceability , quality assurance and market linkage , so that the benefits ultimately reach the artisans and farmers who have preserved these traditions for generations . <p> These interventions reflect a fundamental shift @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as producers , entrepreneurs and active market participants . <p> Agriculture alone can not absorb the aspirations of a young and increasingly educated rural population . The NABARD therefore places considerable emphasis on rural MSMEs and the off-farm sector through skill development , enterprise promotion and livelihood programmes . Micro enterprise development programmes , livelihood and enterprise development programmes , and skill development programmes have supported rural youths and women in activities ranging from food processing , bakery and tailoring to handicrafts and other locally viable enterprises . The emphasis is on linking skills with entrepreneurship , credit and markets , so that training translates into sustainable livelihoods . <p> The NABARD 's support to rural entrepreneurship also recognises the immense potential of local resources , traditional skills and emerging value chains in creating meaningful employment close to home . Support of Rs 963.78 lakh for the off-farm sector and Rs 245.95 lakh for skill development and capacity building has been granted by the NABARD in the state . <p> Cooperatives have a special relevance in Arunachal , particularly in reaching remote communities and enabling collective economic action . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ including Large-sized Multipurpose Cooperative Societies ( LAMPS ) , through capacity building , governance improvement , business diversification , computerisation and institutional development . Strong cooperatives can serve as vibrant grassroots economic institutions , providing credit , inputs , aggregation , storage , processing , and marketing services . Strengthening these institutions is therefore not merely an administrative exercise ; it is an investment in community-owned rural enterprise . Fourteen LAMPS in the state have been computerised with support from the NABARD . <p> Across the NABARD 's interventions , women are not peripheral beneficiaries but central agents of change . Through SHGs , livelihood programmes , financial literacy , enterprise development and market support , rural women are gaining greater access to finance , skills , income opportunities and collective platforms . The transformation is often quiet but profound : a woman opening her first bank account , an SHG launching a micro enterprise , a producer displaying her products at a rural mart , or a group of women collectively negotiating with a buyer . These individual stories , multiplied across villages , form the real measure of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has always been anchored in partnership-with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh , banks , cooperative institutions , universities , research and technical institutions , NGOs , FPOs , SHGs and community-based organisations . The state 's unique geography , cultural diversity and ecological richness require development solutions that are locally grounded , rather than uniformly imposed . The NABARD 's approach has therefore been to combine finance with field-level development , traditional knowledge with appropriate technology , and institution building with community participation . <p> On its 45th foundation day , the NABARD renews its commitment to walk alongside the people of Arunachal , building infrastructure , strengthening institutions , nurturing enterprise , protecting natural resources and enabling rural communities to shape their own pathways to prosperity . <p> Because when a village prospers , a state grows stronger ; and when rural India moves forward , the nation moves forward . The Water That Once Cooled a City <p> Before urban planners and real estate developers changed the landscape , Indian cities were designed around water . <p> The Qutb Shahi rulers of Hyderabad , who ruled the Deccan from the 16th century , knew something modern planners have forgotten : in a semi-arid region with unpredictable monsoons , having water stored near where people live is essential infrastructure . <p> The Hyderabad tank system , documented by researchers at the Society for Advancement of Creative Integration , consisted of hundreds of tanks linked in cascading chains @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ When rain fell , it moved from tank to tank , filling reservoirs , recharging groundwater , and moderating the microclimate . <p> The system was so effective that even after the catastrophic 1908 floods on the Musi River that killed around 15,000 people , the response was not to abandon the water-based approach but to strengthen it . <p> The last Nizam , Osman Ali Khan , commissioned the legendary civil engineer Sir M Visvesvaraya to design Hyderabad 's flood protection system , which resulted in the construction of Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar reservoirs , structures that protected the city for decades . <p> In Bengaluru , this intelligence evolved in its own unique way . The feudal lord Hiriya Kempegowda , under the Vijayanagara Empire , built an interconnected network of lakes across the plateau that supplied water for drinking and irrigation . <p> At its peak , Bengaluru had around 920 tanks and lakes in the 1960s . The city did not sit beside a major river , so these lakes were the city 's lifeline . <p> Chennai and the nearby districts of Kancheepuram and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ locally as eris . These made it possible for people to live in an area with unpredictable rainfall . <p> These systems also did something important that people did not fully recognise at the time . Thanks to satellite data , temperature measurements , and research , we now know they helped keep these cities cool . <p> Expand <h> 3 . City by City : How the Lakes Disappeared <p> Hyderabad is perhaps the starkest case study in India . <p> The city once called the " City of Lakes " was built by rulers who understood that the Deccan 's semi-arid climate demanded a water-based infrastructure system . The interconnected tank-cascade system they built , consisting of hundreds of linked reservoirs , managed stormwater , recharged groundwater , moderated the microclimate , and irrigated surrounding farmland . <p> Then the real estate market arrived . The boom of the 1990s and 2000s marked a decisive turn , with more than 3,000 water bodies encroached upon , transforming shared environmental assets into land for commercial and residential development . <p> National Remote Sensing Centre satellite data shows that between @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 61 percent , shrinking from 40.35 sq km to just 16 sq km . <p> According to researchers , between 1989 and 2001 alone , the city lost 3,245 hectares of water bodies , roughly 10 times the area of Hussain Sagar . <p> Hussain Sagar , the most iconic lake in Hyderabad , itself has shrunk by more than 40 percent in area . <p> Madhapur , now the heart of Hyderabad 's IT corridor and home to offices of some of the world 's largest technology companies , was once a network of interconnected lakes . <p> Today , only 185 lakes remain within the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation limits . Many of them are silted , polluted , or fed with sewage rather than clean water . <p> The economic loss is calculable . Using global ecosystem service valuation estimates , researchers found that Hyderabad 's lake degradation costs approximately $30.44 million , or about Rs 2,494 crore , annually in lost ecosystem services alone , a figure representing around 65 percent of the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation 's entire budget for 2024-25 . <p> In recognition @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Hyderabad Disaster Response and Asset Protection Agency , on 19 July 2024 , specifically to identify and demolish encroachments on lakes , ponds , and water channels . <p> Whether this institutional response will succeed where decades of environmental law have failed remains an open question . <p> Bengaluru tells a similar story , if anything more dramatic in its temperature data . <p> TV Ramachandra , coordinator of the Energy and Wetlands Research Group at the Indian Institute of Science , put the change in terms no temperature chart can match : <p> " What was 19 ? C in the 1990s became 21 ? C in 2000 . Today , it 's about 36 -- 37 ? C. That is the change . " <p> The city once described as the " Garden City " had a green cover of 68 percent in 1973 . Today , that figure stands at roughly 6 percent . The built-up area grew from 7.3 percent of the city 's footprint in 1965 to 52.4 percent by 2009 . <p> Over the past 25 years , urbanisation in Bengaluru has expanded @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reduction in the area occupied by lakes and wetlands . <p> The National Remote Sensing Centre confirmed that Bengaluru has lost nearly 10 square kilometres of lake area in the past two decades , and average temperatures have climbed by 1.5 ? C during the same period . <p> Of the approximately 920 tanks and lakes the city had in the 1960s , only around 81 are considered to survive today . <p> Dharmambudhi Lake , which had served Bengaluru 's residents for over 500 years under the Hoysalas , Wodeyars , and Kempegowda , was filled in 1969 to hold consumer fairs and later converted into a bus terminus . That trajectory , a functioning ecological asset turned into a transport hub or a housing layout , repeated itself across the city over the next five decades . <p> Chennai is unique in that its 2015 floods and 2019 water crisis arrived as paired consequences of the same policy failure . <p> When the city removed its wetlands to build residential layouts , it removed both its cooling infrastructure and its flood management system . <p> Of the more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its neighbouring districts , authorities now count 3,896 . Chennai city alone has lost nearly 150 water bodies and approximately 2,400 acres of water body area to urbanisation . <p> Successive state governments promoted housing projects by significantly converting water bodies into residential colonies . The city 's wetlands , which once formed natural cooling corridors , were replaced by impermeable rooftops and roads that trap heat . <p> Delhi leads all Indian cities in heat severity . <p> A Delhi government report found that nearly half , specifically 49.1 percent , of the capital 's official water bodies no longer exist . <p> The Yamuna floodplain , once a significant wetland buffer on the eastern edge of the city , has been encroached upon so severely that it now functions as a surface that absorbs and radiates heat rather than moderating it . <p> Expand <h> 4 . Why This Happened <p> The destruction of India 's urban wetlands was not the work of a single villain . It is the cumulative outcome of several overlapping failures that persisted for decades . <p> Land scarcity in fast-growing cities made @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ body surface look like opportunity . <p> Wetlands were classified as " wasteland " in revenue records , making them administratively easier to convert than agricultural or forest land . <p> Urban master plans through the 1980s and 1990s were drawn up with minimal integration of environmental data . As one researcher put it , " urban planning has been devoid of environment planning . " <p> Institutional fragmentation made enforcement nearly impossible . <p> Urban water bodies in most cities fell under multiple jurisdictions : municipal corporations , state revenue departments , irrigation departments , and state governments often held overlapping or contested authority over the same lake . <p> This fragmentation made it easy for encroachments to proceed unchallenged , with no single agency willing to take responsibility . <p> Solid waste disposal compounded the damage . With no organised landfill sites adequate to city-scale waste generation , municipal garbage found its way into lake beds . <p> Untreated sewage was directed into water bodies across every city studied here , killing the aquatic vegetation that drives cooling and turning ecological assets into open sewers . <p> In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accelerated the collapse , as the traditional institutions that once managed these commons dissolved under urban pressure . <p> Legal protections that existed , including the Wetlands Conservation and Management Rules of 2017 , arrived too late for much of the lake network and faced weak enforcement on the ground . <p> Expand <h> 5 . What It Will Take to Rebuild the Buffer <p> The situation is not hopeless , but we need to be honest about how much work real restoration will take . <p> The Central government 's Mission Amrit Sarovar , which focuses on the rejuvenation of village ponds and water bodies , had successfully restored over 68,000 water bodies as of January 2025 through community participation . <p> India 's Ramsar wetland network has grown from 26 sites in 2014 to 96 sites by December 2025 , covering over 13.6 lakh hectares . <p> In January 2025 , Indore and Udaipur became the first Indian cities to receive the Ramsar Convention 's Wetland City Accreditation , which mandates that municipal master plans align with wetland preservation , effectively treating lakes as flood buffers in law @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Institute of Science research group emphasises that restoring the interconnected lake cascade system is crucial . Isolated lake restoration offers limited cooling , while reconnecting channels significantly enhances the effect . <p> Science also points clearly to what needs to happen at scale . A global meta-analysis covering over 100 cities found that green-blue infrastructure such as parks , wetlands , and restored water bodies can lower local temperatures by 2 to 5 ? C , with larger and denser features producing the most significant reductions . <p> For India , where the urban heat crisis is already killing people and where temperatures will continue rising under any credible climate scenario , this is a cost-effective alternative to the billions spent on energy for air conditioning , the health system costs of heat-related illness , and the emergency relief triggered by urban flooding . <p> NITI Aayog warned , as far back as 2018 , that 21 Indian cities including Delhi , Bengaluru , Hyderabad , and Chennai could run out of groundwater by 2030 , affecting 100 million people . This can deteriorate resilience to future heat waves and droughts . <p> " Tropical forests are among the world 's most important carbon sinks . @@138928988 <p> Climate change could significantly worsen urban water affordability by increasing infrastructure costs and household water bills by mid-century , according to a new study published in the journal Nature Sustainability on July 8 , 2026 . <p> The study is the first to comprehensively examine how climate change , aging infrastructure , utility investment decisions and household water demand interact to affect water affordability . While previous research has focused mainly on the costs and reliability of water systems , this study assesses how those rising costs impact households across different income groups . <h> Santa Cruz as example <p> To understand these impacts , the researchers used Santa Cruz , California , as a case study . The coastal city relies on limited local water sources and has already implemented many low-cost conservation measures , leaving expensive infrastructure projects such as desalination or wastewater reuse as the primary options for improving water security . <p> Using a modeling framework developed with data from Santa Cruz 's water department , the researchers found that climate change alone could leave an additional 7-16 per cent of households facing unaffordable water @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ could nearly double the city 's median household water bills . <p> Currently , about 19 per cent of Santa Cruz households already spend more on water than the affordability threshold set by the US Environmental Protection Agency ( EPA ) . Under a moderate climate scenario , this proportion could increase to 26 per cent . In a drier climate requiring additional infrastructure to ensure reliable water supplies , it could rise further to 35 per cent . <p> The burden would fall most heavily on low-income families . Under the study 's most severe dry-climate scenario , the median monthly water bill for the city 's poorest households could rise from around $60 to $111 . More than five per cent of households could end up spending nearly one-third of their income on water , forcing many to choose between paying for water , food , healthcare and other essentials . <p> The study also highlights trade-offs between affordability and water security . Investing early in large desalination facilities would improve water security during droughts but substantially increase household bills . Delaying these investments would reduce short-term costs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ years . <p> The average cost of tap water in the United States has risen three times faster than inflation over the past two decades , mainly due to aging infrastructure and delayed maintenance . Climate change is adding further pressure by increasing the need for costly upgrades and water management measures . <p> Drought and water scarcity remain the biggest threats to urban water supplies . Rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns are making droughts more frequent and severe , reducing the reliability of water sources . <h> In other cities <p> The researchers say their modelling framework can also be applied to other climate-vulnerable cities , such as Los Angeles , San Diego , San Francisco , Cape Town ( South Africa ) , and Melbourne ( Australia ) -- facing vulnerabilities similar to those of Santa Cruz . <p> South Africa , which receives only about 464 mm of rainfall annually -- less than half the global average , is among the world 's driest countries . In 2018 , Cape Town came close to running out of water , forcing authorities to limit residents to 50 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and conservation measures ultimately helped the city avoid " Day Zero . " <p> Melbourne city in Australia , is also facing increasing water stress . Between 1 March and 1 June 2026 , the city 's reservoirs fell by 6.1 per cent ( 111 billion litres ) . Storage levels are 9.5 per cent ( 172.1 billion litres ) lower than a year ago and 24 per cent ( about 432 billion litres ) lower than two years ago , reflecting prolonged dry conditions , record-low inflows and rising water demand . <p> These examples illustrate how climate change is exacerbating water shortages , increasing the costs of maintaining urban water systems , and highlighting the need for long-term investments in resilient water infrastructure and conservation strategies . <p> The study concludes that addressing climate-driven water affordability will require more than local utility action . The researchers also recommend that future climate adaptation planning assess water affordability alongside supply reliability to prevent climate adaptation costs from disproportionately affecting low-income communities .

@@138929081 <p> India is rapidly increasing the amount of ethanol in petrol as part of its push to cut crude oil imports , reduce emissions and boost farmers ' incomes . While social media is flooded with claims that ethanol damages vehicle engines , experts say the reality is far more nuanced . Here 's what every vehicle owner should know . <p> Why is India promoting ethanol ? The move is aimed at achieving three key objectives : reducing dependence on imported crude oil , creating an additional market for farmers ' produce and lowering carbon emissions . Since India imports a large share of its petroleum requirements , ethanol blending is expected to improve energy security while supporting agriculture and the environment . <p> Is ethanol good for engines ? Yes , if the vehicle is designed for it . Ethanol contains a higher oxygen content than petrol , allowing cleaner and more efficient combustion . Modern E20-compatible engines are specifically engineered to optimise combustion and , in some cases , even improve engine performance . This is why most new vehicles are now designed with E20 compatibility in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ manufactured from crops such as sugarcane , maize and rice , as well as agricultural residues and sugar industry by-products . This provides farmers with an additional source of income and creates demand for produce that earlier had limited market value . In many ways , India 's transport sector is becoming increasingly linked to its agricultural economy . <p> What are other countries doing ? India is not alone . The United States has used E10 and E15 blends for years , while Brazil routinely uses E27 , and millions of its flex-fuel vehicles can run on E100 . These examples demonstrate that ethanol can be used successfully when vehicles are designed for higher blends . <p> Why is there a demand for greater clarity on the long-term use of E20 fuel ? K Radhakrishna Holla , President , Karnataka State Travel Operators Association said , " Although the Government has extensively promoted E20 fuel , vehicle manufacturers are yet to provide comprehensive , model-specific information on its long-term impact . To address this gap , we have written to car companies seeking official technical clarifications on engine durability @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ warranty coverage and long-term reliability . The objective is not to oppose the E20 programme , but to ensure consumers receive transparent , manufacturer-authorised information before using E20 fuel over the long term . " <p> What is ethanol-blended fuel ? Ethanol is a biofuel produced from sugarcane , maize , surplus rice , grain residues and by-products of sugar factories . Instead of relying entirely on fossil fuels , India now blends ethanol with petrol . The country has already moved from E10 ( 10% ethanol ) to E20 ( 20% ethanol ) nationwide , recently introduced E85 , and is also exploring the possibility of E100 fuel in the future . <p> Will fuel efficiency reduce ? Slightly . Ethanol has a lower energy content than petrol , so some vehicles may experience a 3% to 7% drop in mileage . However , modern engines equipped with electronic fuel management systems largely compensate for this difference , keeping the impact minimal . <p> Why are there concerns about ethanol ? Most concerns relate to older vehicles , not ethanol itself . Vehicles manufactured before 2018 generally have lower @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ atmosphere , and if a vehicle remains unused for several weeks or months , moisture can accumulate in the fuel system . Over time , this may affect components such as fuel pumps , filters , injectors , sensors and rubber hoses . However , experts say these issues develop gradually and depend on factors such as vehicle age , maintenance , fuel quality and usage patterns . <p> How does ethanol benefit the environment ? Since ethanol is produced from renewable plant sources , it is considered a cleaner fuel . It reduces emissions of carbon monoxide and several harmful pollutants , helping improve urban air quality . Many countries have expanded ethanol use as part of their strategy to combat climate change . <p> What should vehicle owners do ? Experts recommend a few simple precautions : avoid leaving vehicles unused for long periods , use only the fuel recommended by the manufacturer , inspect fuel filters and pumps regularly , replace ageing rubber hoses and seals in older vehicles when required , service vehicles at authorised centres and rely on manufacturer guidelines instead of unverified social media @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ biofuel experts , there is no conclusive scientific evidence that ethanol alone damages engines . Equally , it is incorrect to claim that ethanol has no impact at all . Vehicle design , age , maintenance practices and fuel quality together determine performance . Older petrol vehicles can generally handle E10 , while most vehicles manufactured after 2023 are designed to run safely on E20 . Experts add that new-generation E20-compatible vehicles are unlikely to face any significant technical issues , making ethanol an important step towards cleaner transport , stronger farm incomes and greater energy independence for India .
