@@138945460 <h> Design Without Discipline : The Role of Incentives and Enforcement in India 's Carbon Market <h> Design Without Discipline : The Role of Incentives and Enforcement in India 's Carbon Market <p> Carbon markets , including India 's own Carbon Credit Trading Scheme ( CCTS ) , are increasingly becoming relevant emission control policy tools for governments to meet their domestic climate goals . The relevance , purpose , and integrity of these markets , however , are limited to the economic principles of incentives that govern a market and the subsequent enforcement mechanisms that are necessary for a carbon market to function as such . These elements must be designed within the structure of the market for it to operate towards its goal . This paper discusses the hurdles to optimising the economic incentive and enforcement mechanism for carbon markets , specifically in the case of India 's CCTS . The paper discusses three issues : the recurring problems in global carbon markets ; the design choices that India has made to counter these hurdles ; and whether those choices are adequate to overcome the obstacles . <h> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ institutions that enforce them . Across the world , emissions trading systems ( ETSs ) have often faltered not because their economic logic was flawed , but because the conditions required for that logic to function -- credible enforcement , meaningful price signals , and robust monitoring -- were absent. 1 , 2 Oversupply , weak penalties , unambitious targets , and institutional fragility have undermined schemes , from Brussels to Beijing. 3 , 4 , 5 <p> India is launching its Carbon Credit Trading Scheme ( CCTS ) against this backdrop . The ICM Portal went live in March 2026 , initiating the formal transition from the Perform , Achieve and Trade ( PAT ) scheme to the CCTS. 6 That transition carries baggage . PAT 's decade-long record was marked by limited emissions reductions , persistent non-compliance , and a price discovery mechanism that functioned poorly. 7 The entities entering the CCTS are the same ones that operated under PAT , yet they have little reason to believe that the rules have fundamentally changed. 8 <p> Once fully notified , the CCTS will cover some 740 entities and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one of the world 's largest emissions trading systems. 9 Amidst mounting climate stress and geopolitical tensions , the stakes are correspondingly high . This paper examines whether the CCTS 's design is sufficient to address the two deficiencies that have historically weakened carbon markets : inadequate economic incentives and weak external enforcement . <p> To understand the role of economic incentives and enforcement in the functioning of a carbon market , this paper is organised around three research questions : <p> 1 ) In what ways have inadequate economic incentives and weak enforcement emerged as recurring challenges in emissions trading systems globally ? <p> 2 ) What design choices has India incorporated into the CCTS to address these challenges ? <p> 3 ) Are these design choices adequate to overcome them ? <h> The Indian Carbon Market <p> In March 2026 , Union Power Minister Manohar Lal launched the Indian Carbon Market ( ICM ) Portal , marking the regulatory beginning of the ICM. 10 Although the market has been under development since 2023 -- with detailed procedures for its compliance and offset mechanisms released in 2024-2511 and target-setting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the portal 's launch formally initiates the registration process for Obligated Entities ( OEs ) ahead of the first trading cycle . Announced at the Bharat Electricity Summit 2026 on 21 March , the trading cycle is scheduled to begin four months after . <p> Starting in April 2025 , two rounds of target-setting exercises and stakeholder consultations were conducted . Final notifications for the 2025-26 and 2026-27 compliance periods were issued in October 2025 and January 2026 for seven of the nine sectors covered under the CCTS : aluminium , chlor-alkali , cement , fertiliser , iron and steel , pulp and paper , petrochemicals , petroleum refining , and textiles. 13 At the time of writing this paper , final targets for iron and steel and fertilisers remain pending . With targets applying retrospectively to 2025-26 and prospectively to 2026-27 , the transition from the PAT to the CCTS is now underway . As it was under PAT , designated consumers will be transitioned into Obligated Entities under the new system. 14 <p> Over the same period , methodologies for the offset mechanism underwent multiple rounds of review @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ continue to be developed . There is a marked improvement over PAT-era administrative timelines , suggesting that CCTS will likely avoid the procedural delays that plagued PAT , although this will be gleaned only when the trading cycle begins . <p> The ICM has a multi-stakeholder institutional governance framework with the National Steering Committee for the ICM ( NSC-ICM ) as the overseeing and advisory body , chaired by the Secretary of the Ministry of Power and co-chaired by the Secretary of the Ministry of Environment , Forest , and Climate Change . The Bureau of Energy Efficiency ( BEE ) works as the primary administrative body in charge of setting targets and all procedures necessary for market functioning . The Grid Controller of India ( GCI ) , the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission ( CERC ) , and the Central Pollution Control Board ( CPCB ) of India15 work in tandem with BEE as registry operator , trade regulator , and penalty enforcer , respectively. 16 <p> Note : The colour scheme indicates the ministry under which each agency operates . The GCI , BEE , and CERC fall @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Control Board ( CPCB ) operates under the Ministry of Environment , Forests and Climate Change . The NSC-ICM is a joint committee chaired by representatives of both ministries and includes members from the relevant government agencies . It primarily serves an advisory role to the BEE , with its recommendations indirectly influencing the functions and operations of the GCI , CERC , and CPCB within the CCTS framework . <h> Compliance and Offset Mechanism <p> The foremost feature of the CCTS is its design as a baseline-and-credit system . Under this framework , baselines or targets are set based on 2023-24 emission levels , and Carbon Credit Certificates ( CCCs ) are issued to obligated entities that reduce emissions below these thresholds . These CCCs are tradeable within the ICM framework . <p> Entities that earn CCCs may either sell them in the market for financial gain or bank them for future compliance obligations . Conversely , entities that fail to meet their obligations during a compliance period must surrender credits equivalent to the shortfall , either by using previously banked credits or by purchasing CCCs at prevailing market @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for the compliance mechanism , illustrates this process. 18 Entities that fail to meet these requirements are liable to pay an Environmental Compensation fee. 19 <p> Figure 2 : ICM Key Features <p> Source : Author 's own illustration <p> The ICM integrates the compliance and offset mechanism , allowing CCCs generated through either pathway to be traded within the same market . The offset mechanism provides opportunities for emissions reduction , removal , sequestration , or abatement in sectors and industries that are not currently subject to compliance obligations . Projects under the offset mechanism must undergo an accreditation process to verify the volume of emissions reduced , removed , sequestered , or abated , following which equivalent CCCs are issued . Methodologies for various project types have been developed , although some remain under consideration . To date , nine methodologies across different sectors have been approved and published , along with 17 necessary tools for conducting projects. 20 <p> The CCTS compliance and offset procedures also establish detailed monitoring and verification requirements . OEs must submit monitoring methodologies for approval by the BEE and conduct monitoring on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ guidance on monitoring plans , activity data collection , energy measurement , emissions measurement , and emission factors . While comprehensive , these guidelines also allow flexibility in implementation , taking into account the capacities and operational circumstances of obligated entities . <h> The CCTS Design and PAT 's Problems <p> The choice of a baseline-and-credit system is intentional . It avoids absolute caps , accommodates intensity-based targets ( per unit of output ) , and allows economic growth to continue alongside emissions reduction . For an emerging economy , this is an advantage . The system is also more equitable than a cap-and-trade model , where an aggregate emissions target is set for the market as a whole . Under the CCTS , targets are determined individually for each entity based on prior performance , capacity , and technological feasibility , with these entity-level baselines cumulatively delivering the desired sector-wide emissions reductions . <p> These advantages , however , are accompanied by two structural vulnerabilities . First , there is a risk of indefinite supply , as credits can continue to be generated so long as entities reduce emissions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ uncertain , as actual emissions reductions depend on the integrity of monitoring , verification , and enforcement . <p> These vulnerabilities were central to the shortcomings of PAT , particularly chronic oversupply and weak enforcement . The data illustrates this clearly . By the time trading opened , 103 lakh Energy Saving Certificates ( ESCerts ) had been issued across the first three PAT cycles against a total purchase obligation of only 52 lakh. 22 This reflected substantial oversupply , driven in part by targets that proved relatively easy to achieve . Compliance rates further exacerbated the problem : of the ESCerts that were required to be purchased , 34 lakh went unacquired. 23 <p> Regulatory decisions did little to strengthen market discipline . Entities that failed to meet their obligations in cycles I and II were not barred from participating in trading during cycle III , weakening incentives to fulfil outstanding commitments . At the same time , certificate performance showed only a weak relationship with environmental outcomes . In both the cement and steel sectors , entities surpassed their energy-efficiency targets by more than 40 percent in each @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these sectors recorded reductions of less than 2 percent relative to output. 24 High levels of ESCert generation therefore coexisted with limited progress on decarbonisation , revealing that certificate generation and emissions reduction were not as closely linked as the scheme 's design had envisaged . <p> The CCTS is vulnerable to similar challenges , not only because these are inherent risks of a baseline-and-credit system , but also because it will regulate many of the same entities that operated under PAT . Over a decade , these entities learned that non-compliance carried few meaningful consequences . Design improvements alone are unlikely to succeed unless those behavioural expectations are fundamentally altered . <p> The transition to the CCTS introduces an additional risk . The conversion of banked ESCerts into CCCs , if undertaken without strict eligibility criteria , could flood the market with legacy credits before a meaningful price signal has emerged . The choice of conversion rates and the design of any parallel operating period between PAT and the CCTS will therefore serve as early indicators of whether the new regime intends to enforce stricter market discipline or whether @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <h> Current Hurdles <p> The primary challenge facing a carbon market is the same as that of any market : the breakdown of price discovery . When prices cease to reflect scarcity and demand , the market stops functioning effectively . India has faced this threat before . Trading at the floor price across multiple PAT cycles signalled a market failure in progress. 25 <p> The roots of this failure can be traced to two interlinked deficiencies : weak economic incentives and inadequate enforcement . Together , they erode the mechanisms that encourage obligated entities to participate meaningfully in a system they are required to join . Without meaningful participation , there is little incentive to pursue deeper decarbonisation . Addressing the factors that undermine these two components in design , monitoring , and execution is therefore the central challenge of any functional emissions trading system that aims to achieve any real environmental benefits . <p> India is not alone in confronting this challenge . Establishing a carbon market that functions effectively has proven difficult for nearly every country that has attempted one . The advantage for India is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lessons from earlier emission trading systems ( ETSs ) are readily available . <h> Lack of Economic Incentive <p> In the absence of perceived monetary gain from trading carbon credits earned , there remains little incentive to induce compliance . This in turn hinders the foundational principle of commodifying emission rights . Understanding these conditions establishes the first necessary component to a motivated market participant . To fulfil the condition of substantial economic incentive , certain factors must be managed . <p> a . Market Instability <p> ETSs in different parts of the world have frequently experienced market instability , at least in the initial phases . ETSs are typically prone to instability via exogenous shocks due to the setup of their supply mechanism . An ETS seeks to curb emissions by limiting the amount that can be emitted . Nonetheless , by its very nature and purpose , the supply of allowances or credits ( essentially , the amount of emissions allowed ) in an ETS does not vary by price , rather it is set by regulatory entities . In baseline-and-credit systems , where credits can continue to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ creation can result in persistent supply-demand mismatch . <p> Market price discovery is a particularly difficult challenge when one considers the factors affecting demand that can be exogenously influenced by variation in regulatory frameworks , economic conditions , credibility of available credits and endogenously affected by marginal abatement costs. 26 Indeed , demand is also governed by obligation and enforcement rather than by price alone . As both supply and demand tend to be relatively inelastic , market prices often require external support to remain stable and meaningful . These market stabilisation mechanisms have been implemented in ETSs globally with varying applications and with the aim of aiding supply-side changes to match demand . <p> The EU ETS , for example , experienced prolonged periods of low prices before introducing measures such as the Market Stabilisation Reserve ( MSR ) , the New Entrants ' Reserve , and a backloading mechanism . The MSR enabled the system to adjust the volume of allowances in circulation , while backloading temporarily postponed the auctioning of allowances during periods of oversupply. 27 The New Entrants ' Reserve set aside allowances for new market @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ demand from disrupting the market. 28 <p> The Korean ETS ( KETS ) , facing similar challenges , supplemented quantity-based measures with price-based interventions . It designated public financial institutions as ' Market Makers ' , enabling them to support trading activity through the use of government-held reserves . An Allocation Committee was also empowered to manage reserve releases and implement price-stabilisation measures under specified conditions , including periods of sustained price increases. 29 <p> In contrast , the guidelines on the Indian Carbon Market and procedure for compliance do not outline any quantity-based stabilisation measures but allude to floor and forbearance prices to be recommended by the BEE and approved by the CERC. 30 While these price brackets allow for control at the extremes , they do not do much to keep the discovery mechanism alive . As seen in the PAT scheme , the isolated existence of price mechanisms allowed the ESCerts to be traded at floor price throughout the cycles . This did not do much to ascertain market functioning and environmental integrity ; it only held the market from collapse . <p> As the CCTS expands @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stringency in setting targets , having supply side measures in place can help the market stay buoyant . At the end , with low prices , economic incentive threatens to entirely disappear , and along with it , motivation to decarbonise goes as well . <p> b . Baselines , Market Supply , and Weak Signalling <p> Unambitious targets and market oversupply often go hand-in-hand . When baselines or caps are low enough , credits can be accrued easily , as emissions can be reduced below baselines without much cost or effort . These easily earned credits can then be used to trade for monetary gain . This can cause an avalanche of credits in the market as the majority of the obligated entities are able to reduce below baselines , and only a minority are left to buy credits . Such an increase in the supply of credits is a formula for extremely low prices as supply far exceeds demand , adding to market instability . <p> Persistently low prices undermine market effectiveness in several ways . They reduce the value of credits for sellers , limiting incentives for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ purchase credits rather than invest in emissions reductions . Low prices may also encourage entities to bank credits instead of trading them , reducing market activity and enabling the postponement of future emissions reductions . In each case , the signal to decarbonise becomes weaker . <p> Excessively stringent targets can create the opposite problem . With targets that are too far from ' business as usual ' , entities may have to put too significant an investment into technology for emissions reduction to meet their obligations . In such a scenario , it may be more cost-effective and low effort for entities to purchase credits in the secondary market , ultimately leading to high demand and low supply with prices soaring too high to be affordable . The outcome can , therefore , be non-compliance and insufficient reductions , making the carbon market counterproductive . Such emission targets can also hinder the competitiveness of firms within the domestic and international markets. 31 Therefore , a careful balance of emission targets is crucial to achieve maximum compliance with subsequent ambition tightening in the future . <p> Easily attainable targets have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ supply and generation of ESCerts but low corresponding emission reductions tell the same story. 32 In contrast , the success of the Surat ETS was attributed to the strict caps that were initially set at 280 tonnes per month , but more importantly , it was attributed to the adjustments created by the Gujarat Pollution Control Board after they realised that the caps were still too easy to achieve . After this , the revised caps were set at 170 tonnes per month , and consequently 20-30 percent of emission reduction was achieved with compliance about 99 percent of the time. 33 This contrast between the PAT 's lenient targets and negligible emission reduction and the Surat ETS 's stricter and stricter caps and high environmental achievement should draw a guiding line for CCTS to follow . <p> Yet , currently , the CCTS seems to be following the PAT path . With the delayed release of final targets and the absence of final targets for some sectors , the final ambition seems to have slipped as compared to the draft targets , causing a potential opportunity cost of about @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ targets are low enough to be achieved simply by cost-saving measures. 34 Nonetheless , with ambition tightening in preceding cycles , it is still possible for the CCTS to redeem itself as a credible decarbonising scheme . <p> c . Low Liquidity , Thin Markets , and Buyer Uncertainty <p> Market instability , oversupply , weak price signals , and regulatory uncertainty can all reduce participation in carbon markets . Frequent policy changes , overlapping institutional responsibilities , and inconsistent enforcement further increase uncertainty among market participants. 35 Such uncertainty can characterise a market with low participation and seasonal trading ( only when it is necessary , for example , towards the end of the trading cycles ) rather than steady market activity throughout a trading cycle . These factors culminate towards thin markets and low liquidity , reducing the lucrative edge and economic incentive as prices remain at the floor . <p> The Korean ETS ( KETS ) is a useful example to understand low liquidity in carbon markets . In an unwilling market , even with Market Stabilisation Mechanisms in place , KETS markets remained relatively ineffective due @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ different governing bodies and agencies in the initial phases of KETS added to the buyer uncertainty with difficulty in coordination and the risk of changing policies. 36 This created an uncertain environment for market players making them less open to sell allowances and rather banking their credits to hedge against the risk of changing policies . Like in the KETS , the PAT scheme also experienced periods of seasonal activity and low liquidity due to non-compliance and extensions of trading cycles , leaving market players with the option to avoid trade unless necessary. 37 <p> For the CCTS , reshaping market behaviour will be critical . Considering India 's past with the PAT scheme and the casual unwillingness to comply among designated consumers , 38 it may be necessary to adhere to stricter timelines and establish an environment of harsh enforcement within the new CCTS . With any delays in the CCTS , there is a risk of allowing entities to presume governance quality and follow the same trading patterns as in the PAT scheme . Moreover , the number of regulatory and institutional entities involved in the execution of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The prospect of trading across multiple power exchanges introduces an additional challenge . While registry mechanisms can prevent double counting and unauthorised sales , they do not guarantee price convergence . It is at present unclear if the different power exchanges in India will be running separate trading sessions with their own pool of buyers and sellers and different clearing prices within the same compliance period . <p> India 's experience under PAT offers a cautionary example . In Cycle III , approximately 1.8 lakh ESCerts were traded across all sessions , 39 and PAT Cycle II saw the same outcome , with all purchases made at the floor price across 40 trading sessions , indicating a persistent absence of genuine price discovery. 40 <p> With demand and supply divided across different markets , thinner markets could lead to a similar price discovery issue , not to mention the possibility of arbitrage in the case of drastically segmented prices . The answers to each of these ambiguities will determine whether the CCTS opens a compliance mechanism in which entities respond to deadlines rather than to price signals . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Power Sector <p> In a baseline-and-credit system , credits can accumulate on the supply side as long as entities continue to overperform beyond their baselines . Demand , however , does not raise organically ; it must be engineered through obligated buyers and coverage design . Therefore , there must be high-emitting sectors that rely on the purchase of credits to fulfil their obligations . <p> The narrower the sectoral coverage , the smaller the pool of obligated buyers . A limited demand base weakens price signals and increases volatility for emissions reductions and undermines environmental integrity . <p> Under the PAT , the thermal power and DISCOM sectors were central to demand generation . Together , they contributed to around 38 percent of total ESCerts issued but were liable for 78 percent of total ESCerts mandated to be purchased. 41 Thermal power accounts for nearly 40 percent of India 's greenhouse-gas emissions , yet the initial phases of the CCTS will cover sectors that contribute only about 10 percent of national emissions . Therefore , the thermal power sector 's absence from the CCTS is a stark absence that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ without precedent . <p> Every major ETS in the world has included electricity generation from the outset . The EU ETS covered power and heat generation in Phase 1 alongside energy-intensive industries like iron , steel , cement , and oil refining ; 42 China 's ETS launched with a sole focus on the power sector spanning 45 percent of its emissions before expanding it to cement , iron and steel , and more ; 43 Korea 's ETS included heat and power from Phase 1 as well ; 44 The California Cap and Trade Program is yet another example of including the electricity-generating sectors from the onset. 45 Indeed it is difficult to find carbon markets that have begun without the power sectors . <p> Especially in India 's case , with domestic coal production on the rise , one can expect absolute electricity production from thermal power to rise as well. 46 With rising emissions from this sector , it seems confusing to exclude the power sector based on India 's climate commitments . With the most widely covered sector , across ETSs globally , missing from the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ loses some more hope . With the central role that the thermal power sector can play in demand generation of credits , excluding it from the initial phase means reducing the likelihood that CCTS will start out with a functioning mechanism . <h> Poor External Enforcement <p> The second piece of the puzzle is external enforcement . Even with well-calibrated baselines and effective market-stabilisation mechanisms , a carbon market may fail to function if compliance obligations are not credibly enforced . In compliance markets , demand is driven not only by economic incentives but also by the expectation that non-compliance will carry meaningful consequences . Obligated entities must be compelled to meet their obligations for demand to materialise and for price discovery to function effectively . This , in turn , requires robust systems for monitoring , verification , and penalty enforcement . <p> a . Monitoring and Verification Challenges <p> On paper , the ICM establishes a detailed framework for monitoring and verification . However , the flexibility built into the system leaves room for ambiguity . Obligated entities are responsible both for monitoring their emissions and for appointing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ large volumes of emissions data , self-reporting is unavoidable . The integrity of the system , therefore , depends heavily on third parties . <p> Although verification agencies must undergo thorough processes to become accredited , once completed , the verification processes carried out by accredited agencies are to be decentralised and not directly monitored by the Bureau . While a decentralised system helps in reducing costs and red tape , this level of flexibility and choice reduces accountability and verification powers . <p> The Bureau retains the authority to appoint another verifying agency to re-check an obligated entity 's data if it has reason to believe that data falsification has occurred. 48 However , due to the mandated procedural timeline , by the time this process is carried out , the compliance period in question will be over , and the emissions reduction meant to be carried out within the period will be forgone . Also , it is quite likely that a falsifying obligated entity may never be reported , in which case non-compliance fees will be forgone as well . Thus , the current system opens room @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and low credibility . This can further lead to buyer uncertainty , low liquidity , thin markets , and price crashes , all of which attribute to weak emission reduction . <p> The Bureau also offers choice in the method of GHG calculations , the method of data collection , the frequency of data collection , and the choice of emission factors. 49 Such choices can be beneficial , as different alternatives provide flexibility across sectors and changing technology . However , complete choice allows for strategic method selection , unfair advantage , inconsistent and incomparable results , and falsification , leading to reduction avoidance . <p> While there are advantages to this flexibility , there is an unwavering trend towards tighter restrictions across baseline-and-credit systems worldwide . Flexibility in choice is still maintained ; however , justification and verification of choices have become stricter through repetitive and regular third-party checks , increased transparency , and more specific monitoring measures . The current level of flexibility offered and the ex-post manner of verification , thus , does not align with the objective of emissions reduction . <p> b . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ compliance is more attractive than non-compliance . As obligations become more stringent , this requires penalties that impose meaningful costs on entities that fail to comply . <p> The target-setting notifications issued by the Ministry of Environment , Forest and Climate Change state that in the event that an obligated entity fails to comply or submit credits equivalent to the shortfall in compliance , it can be charged with an Environmental Compensation fee by the Central Pollution Control Board " equal to twice of the average price at which carbon credit certificate is traded during the trading cycle of that compliance year . " 50 If the purpose of this penalty is to ensure that non-compliance is more costly than compliance , the amount of this penalty may be insufficient . In China 's ETS , penalties for falsification were raised to 5 to 10 times the average market price to ensure compliance . Penalties were imposed on third-party verifiers involved in falsification as well. 51 These compliance regulations led to a 99.5-percent compliance rate. 52 <p> In comparison , the penalties set as part of the ICM seem far @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the PAT scheme . To make any change in market behaviour and entity perception , a heavier penalty needs to be levied . Since the PAT scheme serves as the basis of the CCTS and the former Designated Consumers are going to be converted to the entities obligated under the CCTS , their compliance history should be taken into account while formulating the enforcement regulations for the CCTS . Repeated PAT cycles have failed to establish market price discovery essentially due to non-enforcement of penalties leading to no consequences of non-compliance and therefore no incentive for participating in the market . Non-compliance increased in PAT Cycle II as compared to cycle I , from 9 percent to 56 percent . Quite the opposite of penalising them , these designated consumers were allowed to trade in cycle III. 53 Even after the extensions issued to trading windows , about 51 percent of the total ESCerts that were mandated to be purchased in cycle II were actually purchased . <p> What is more , DCs accounting for 86 percent of the ESCerts mandated to be purchased in cycle III were not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ need for stricter penalties and definitive imposition of penalties . Non-compliance needs to have consequences that directly affect the monetary gains that non-compliant entities accrue by avoiding reductions and further affect their competitiveness . For CCTS to succeed it is crucial that harsher actions are taken , unlike its predecessor . <p> c . Delayed Timelines <p> The PAT scheme has experienced delays in its execution . The first PAT cycle aimed to complete the trading process by July 2017 which ended up extending until January 2018 . In the second cycle , these delays worsened with the issuance of credits postponed by 20 months from the intended date . As a result , trading of cycle II concluded in 2023 as opposed to 2021 . As a domino effect , all subsequent cycles have been running late . Cycle III completed its trading in 2024 instead of 2022 . The issuance of credits for PAT cycles IV , V , and VI were subsequently deferred . <p> Such delays undermine the integrity of the system and have hindered the sincerity with which obligations were viewed and undertaken within the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in that the level of non-compliance increased from 9 percent to 56 percent from PAT cycle I to II. 55 It is , therefore , crucial that the governing authorities ensure timely processing and factor in delay times while setting up the official process timelines . This is all the more necessary to set CCTS apart from the PAT scheme so that the designated consumers that will be graduating to obligated entities under the CCTS are able to identify CCTS as a more stringent protocol than the PAT . However , to avoid such lags in timelines , the root cause of such delays must be addressed . <p> China 's national ETS was repeatedly delayed . A deadline of " within the 12th five-year plan period " ( 2011-2015 ) was postponed to 2016 , then to 2017 , and then again to 2021. 56 Data collection was one of the principal reasons the original launch was severely delayed , 57 and its consequences carried into market behaviour : trading volumes were thin below 100,000 tonnes in most sessions and only increased in late November 2021 when the end-of-year @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ market that opened under time pressure and traded seasonally rather than continuously from the outset . This sounds very similar to the PAT story and makes it even more necessary to equip the CCTS with greater capacity . <p> Considering the current state of CCTS preparations , the likelihood of institutional lag is high . While the process of target setting has moved relatively quickly , the remaining timeline ahead of the first compliance deadline in July 2026 appears insufficient for completing all necessary preparations . Final targets for two sectors are yet to be released . Based on the targets already notified , obligated entities are expected to have already achieved part of their emission reductions for the compliance year 2025-26. 59 That emissions data must then be reviewed by the government before certificates can be issued , and only once that process is complete can trading begin . <p> The Union Power Minister has indicated that trading will commence within four months of the ICM portal launch on 21 March 2026 , placing the expected start sometime around July 2026 at the earliest. 60 Running concurrently with all @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ whose role in certifying the monitoring data submitted by obligated entities is central to the system 's integrity . With this many foundational processes still unresolved and running simultaneously , a functioning market remains some way off . Even minor delays are damaging , not only procedurally but behaviourally : they risk signalling to obligated entities that the enforcement culture of PAT will carry forward into the CCTS , undermining the credibility the new scheme urgently needs to establish . Greater institutional capacity is now required . <p> d . Limited Capacity and Infrastructure <p> Even the most detailed regulatory framework can not achieve its objectives without sufficient capacity . As the experience of PAT demonstrates , limited administrative and technical capacity can translate directly into procedural delays , weakening both compliance and market credibility . <p> The challenge of collecting reliable emissions data , alongside a government reshuffle that transferred ETS responsibility from the National Development and Reform Commission to the newly created Ministry of Ecology and Environment , contributed to the delay in the rollout. 61 Once operating , the data problem persisted . Provincial MEEs sent to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ technical ability and faced a conflict of interest , as many of the largest emitters were state-owned companies critical to local growth and energy security . Penalties for violations were only subject to an administrative fine of up to 30,000 yuan , a ceiling determined by the ministerial-level status of ETS regulations. 62 Insufficient capacity at the provincial level , combined with penalties too weak to deter misconduct , had created exactly the conditions under which enforcement would fail . <p> In India , the ICM portal , launched in March 2026 , represents an important step towards strengthening administrative capacity . The portal enables registration of obligated entities and serves as the central platform for monitoring , reporting , and verification ( MRV ) . 63 Maintained by the BEE , it is also intended to support the functions of the CERC and the GCI . However , digital infrastructure alone is insufficient . Significant institutional resources will still be required to review reported data , issue CCCs , monitor compliance , and oversee trading activity . <p> As yet , trading in CCCs is only allowed on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ approved by the CERC . Therefore , further resources are required to ensure that only over-the-counter trades are taking place to prevent fraudulent activities happening inside and outside the ICM portal . <p> In addition to the many authorities co-governing the internal CCTS mechanism , coordination is necessary interdepartmentally with the National Designated Authority for the Implementation of the Paris Agreement ( NDAIAPA ) for Indian offsets to operate within the international market under Articles 6.2 and 6.4 . India 's past participation in the CDM warrants its utilisation of the Paris Agreement Credit Mechanism to generate climate finance revenues. 64 This will mean that , to some extent , voluntary offsets generated and traded within the CCTS may be used for India 's participation . <p> The ' corresponding adjustment ' as mandated by the guidelines will then be required to ensure no double counting . This will increase institutional burden as projects used for Article 6 will need to be tracked and their corresponding credits must be removed from the CCTS to ensure that those reductions are not used towards India 's NDC . Therefore , it will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with the Designated Authority for the Implementation of the Paris Agreement ( DAIPA ) . <p> Baseline-and-credit systems traditionally depend upon hard price corridors to regulate the market . This is the approach the CCTS is to take as well . That is not to say that baseline and credits can not have combined mechanisms . Credits equivalent to a small percentage of total required yearly emission reductions to meet India 's Nationally Determined Contributions ( NDCs ) can be taken out , and baselines and targets can be calculated after . This can ensure no compromise of environmental integrity while gradually building reserves . In case restrictions are levied on bankable credits , unused ones can be deposited in reserves . Credits can also be borrowed from future circulation ( this would require re-calculation of targets ) to be used for stabilisation purposes . <p> While oversupply needs to be handled , it can not be curbed in a baseline-and-credit system by artificial mechanisms that pull CCCs out of circulation . This is a fundamental difference in the creation rather than allocation of credits in the Indian system . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , CCC generation can be restricted via tightening baselines . Oversupply of CCCs must be interpreted as ' baselines being too easy to cross " . To this end , tightened baselines reduces the number of CCCs that can be generated at prevailing conditions . This can offer increased integrity and price signalling to the market as well . <h> Baseline Tightening <p> Baselines play a dual role in a baseline-and-credit system . They shape price formation while also determining the environmental integrity of the market . Most emissions trading systems begin with relatively lenient targets to facilitate compliance before gradually increasing ambition over time . <p> The aim is to gradually tighten targets . However , to accelerate emissions reductions , a two-tier baseline-setting approach can be used , whereby already efficient entities are incentivised to reduce emissions further , while less efficient entities are given a more gradual pathway to achieve comparable reductions . This approach is used in Alberta 's Technology Innovation and Emissions Reduction Regulation which combines high-performance benchmarks for efficient entities and facility-specific benchmarks based on historical performance. 65 Baseline tightening rates must also be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ annually , while the EU ETS employs a linear reduction factor that began at 2.2 percent and has increased to 4.3 percent. 66 Even if India does not provide a specific rate of tightening , it can forecast the steepness of the tightening slope to aid businesses in planning ahead and investing with long-term goals in mind . <h> More Simplified Operational Structure <p> At present , three different administrative registries govern the system . The BEE hosts the ICM Portal , the registry is operated by the Grid Controller of India , and power exchanges are regulated by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission . While currently , all administrative processes are to be held under the ICM portal , there remains ambiguity in trading platforms and the interoperability of the compliance and offset market . Since CCCs are categorised and operated in separate markets , there is a lack of clarity on whether offset CCCs are eligible for purchase in the compliance market and if the price discovery mechanism will be uniform across these markets and power exchanges. 67 More clarity on operational structure is necessary to establish participant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's revenue-generation framework relies primarily on the Environmental Compensation Fund . This is unreliable due to its dependence on the level of non-compliance and enforcement of penalties . Though unlikely , in the event of perfect compliance , the fund can be left empty , leaving no other revenue collection method . While the CERC notification does note that fees and charges will be collected from participating entities for the upkeep and functioning of the ICM , considering the importance of revenue collection , a more stable source needs to be appointed . Taking inspiration from the Surat ETS , 68 a deposit channel can be used to ascertain stable revenue collection . The non-compliance fees can similarly be deducted from initial deposits , thus leaving a line of revenue open even in cases of perfect compliance . <p> The use of revenues within the CCTS also requires greater clarity . Currently left blank , a plan for usage needs to be devised before the implementation of the CCTS so that operations can be planned ahead . Revenues should be dedicated towards preserving environmental integrity , price-based market stabilisation reserves @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ damages prevention . <h> Expansion in Sector Coverage and Market Participants <p> Many major emitting industries are currently excluded from the CCTS . As the scheme continues to evolve , it presents an opportunity to expand its reach to curb emissions across additional sectors . While such expansion may not be feasible in the initial phase , as the regulatory and verification frameworks are still being refined , the CCTS should ultimately be designed to include electricity , thermal power , and maritime shipping to support their decarbonisation efforts. 69 Expanding sectoral coverage is also critical to maintaining market liquidity by increasing the number of market participants . Nonetheless , this might not be sufficient . Even with stabilisation mechanisms and tightened baselines , in the presence of non-compliance , liquidity can crash . To make market liquidity a driver of the market rather than an effect , some ETSs involve financial institutions that play the role of ' market makers ' , 70 as is the case in the Korean ETS . <p> As market makers , financial players add an additional mechanism of price signalling and information dissemination @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with carbon credits as financial instruments allows external non-obligated financial entities to increase trading activity and thus keep the liquidity and price mechanism afloat as well. 71 While there are concerns about the dilution of integrity , such processes have the potential to help sustain the carbon market as a true market and warrant a closer inspection of their addition into the ICM . <h> Effective Penalty Procedures <p> Reflecting the increasingly stringent regulatory approach adopted by carbon markets worldwide , penalties for non-compliance under both the ICM and the continuing PAT scheme should be strengthened . However , raising the fee amounts on paper is not enough if these are not realised from non-compliers within pre-determined timelines . Under the PAT scheme , non-compliant entities were allowed to continue trading due to the dwindling market activity and the failure of the price discovery mechanism . That in turn set the tone for a lenient environment encouraging greater non-compliance and introducing more difficulty in maintaining stable market activity and functioning . <p> Penalties should not be limited to regulated entities alone , as data manipulation can also involve verification agencies @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ need to be issued to facilitating parties in cases of data manipulation as well. 72 Therefore , to do away with the trend of non-compliance it is necessary that repeat non-compliers are charged with progressively heavier fees . <p> There must be legislation for non-compliant entities to go through heavier checks and verification processes until a compliant attitude is restored to ensure that the severity of the obligations is construed appropriately by the entities . Following the California cap-and-trade programme , there can be a mandated increase in the number of credits to be submitted or equivalent amount of reduction to be done in the next period for each time an entity is non-compliant along with the imposition of monetary penalties. 73 In any case , the BEE has recognised demand generation as a core worry for the domestic carbon market which likely arises with lack of compliance as seen in the PAT scheme . Boosting emphasis on enforcement aligns with these concerns . <h> Increased Transparency and Centralised Verification System <p> The current verification process lacks accountability . With monitoring and verification essentially overseen by the obligated entity , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ public disclosure of emissions data and the methodologies used needs to be mandatory . Further , the proposed verification system is largely decentralised . <p> To add accountability to the verification process , it would be helpful to randomly appoint verifying agencies to obligated entities . Further , regular rotation of verifying agencies to ensure that obligated entities are periodically subjected to new unbiased verifiers can add authenticity and credibility to the verification process . This can help create a clear indication of strict enforcement , making entities more likely to comply . Lastly , a continuous process of verification should be considered as opposed to an ex-post manner by incorporating random in-person checks during the compliance year to ensure that any non-compliant action can be tracked early and necessary changes can be mandated to make sure that reductions are not forgone . Periodic yet arbitrary on-site inspections are necessary as well . <h> Restrictions on CCC Use <p> While bankable credits are important for ensuring market continuity and incentivising for future compliance , restrictions may be necessary in an underdeveloped market to sustain trading activity . To ensure regular @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were allowed to bank up to 10 percent of their annual average from the previous phase in addition to 20,000 more allowances . In case of excess banked allowances , the excess was to be deducted from the free allowances of the next phase . In an instance of irregular thin markets within the CCTS , a provision should be made for such restrictions to ensure a steady supply of credits and the avoidance of seasonal trading to reduce price shocks in secluded periods . <p> Further , credits generated through compliance and offset mechanisms should also be categorised separately because they differ in their underlying attributes , including their generation process and additionality. 74 This has already been implemented on paper , yet the fungibility of offset CCCs with compliance ones is currently undetermined. 75 It is therefore worth considering the implications of a market with inter-tradable credits regardless of the purpose of creation , leaving the likelihood of offsets replacing actual emission reduction quite high . Thus , the true role of the offset market in either diluting integrity or supporting liquidity remains to be examined further . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be needed to manage national registries and handle the metadata necessary for verification . Improved technology use and personnel training will be required to further ensure compatibility of the ICM with international carbon markets to promote international collaboration and working with upcoming international mechanisms like CBAM . The ICM portal is currently used for monitoring and registration processes with the ICM but can be further utilised for offset programmes that align under the Paris Agreement and reduce the likelihood of double counting . <h> Choice of Market System <p> Limiting the overall supply of credits could help restore market balance over time , potentially through a gradual transition to a cap-and-trade system . While intensity-based targets should be retained because of their economic benefits , a cap-and-trade mechanism could provide better control over market supply , especially in the absence of market stabilisation measures . As the market matures , a gradual shift towards stricter emissions caps may therefore become appropriate . Such transitions have been recommended for several intensity-based baseline-and-credit systems , particularly in emerging economies with maturing carbon markets. 76 <p> However , this transition can not be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ largely relies on the national goals of the Indian economy and its stage of development . An emerging market , after all , can not be dampened in production by a cap on emissions that are bound to grow with greater output . Yet , as India works for its Viksit Bharat 2047 goal , this shift to cap-and-trade becomes imminent . <h> Transition from PAT <p> The transition from the PAT scheme to the CCTS raises questions that the current regulatory framework has yet to address . These broadly fall into three areas : the treatment of banked ESCerts , their conversion into CCCs , and the management of the transition while PAT-related processes remain incomplete . <p> The first is the overhang problem . PAT has generated a large pool of banked ESCerts across cycles with no formal mechanism specified for their treatment upon transition . One option is to allow entities to operate under both schemes for a limited period , enabling them to exhaust banked ESCerts before fully migrating to the CCTS . Alternatively , a system of deemed conversion could be introduced , wherein only @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the remainder continuing to trade within PAT , moderating market supply while preserving environmental integrity. 77 <p> The second is the unit conversion problem . ESCerts are denominated in tonnes of oil equivalent saved , whereas CCCs represent one tonne of CO2 equivalent reduced , removed , or avoided . Any conversion between them would require an entity-specific factor accounting for fuel mix , emissions intensity , and additionality , none of which has been formally specified . <p> The third issue only raises concerns for institutional capacity , execution , and administrative burden on the obligated entities . While the compliance periods for PAT have completed , data submissions , verifications , issuance of credits , and final trading are all incomplete processes as yet . These processes will therefore overlap with the implementation of the CCTS . In the event of reduced delays in the CCTS , companies will have to follow the processes under the CCTS and PAT simultaneously . The ambiguity around the overlap of these processes requires greater clarification for a smooth transition . <h> Conclusion <p> This paper examined the hurdles commonly experienced by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is adequately designed to overcome them . A consistent lesson across markets is that effective enforcement underpins a functioning ETS . Without credible enforcement , there is little incentive to participate ; without participation , price discovery fails ; and without price discovery , the market can not generate meaningful economic incentives for emissions reduction . Enforcement and price discovery are therefore mutually reinforcing , together determining whether a carbon market succeeds . <p> India has already experienced these challenges over a decade of the PAT scheme . The CCTS 's more detailed compliance frameworks reflect a conscious effort to address PAT 's shortcomings , with the government 's recognition of these structural weaknesses evident in the new scheme 's design . The entities graduating into the CCTS carry with them a decade of learned behaviour , shaped by a regulatory environment in which non-compliance carried no real consequence . <p> What separates the CCTS from its predecessor will not be determined by design alone , but by the credibility and consistency with which those design choices are enforced . India has the advantage of building its market when the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ documented . Whether it applies them rigorously enough to make the CCTS a genuine decarbonisation mechanism rather than a more elaborate version of what came before remains the question this scheme must answer . <p> Diya Shah is Research Assistant , Centre for Economy and Growth , ORF . <p> All views expressed in this publication are solely those of the author , and do not represent the Observer Research Foundation , either in its entirety or its officials and personnel . <p> Acknowledgement <p> The author acknowledges the use of ChatGPT 5 to conduct a generate high-resolution image for Figure 3 . Through these initiatives , the Quad aims to track dark vessels , safeguard maritime exclusive economic zones , and deter unlawful behaviour . <p> Despite the enduring challenges , the Quad 's role in fostering maritime security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific remains critical because it is anchored in the convergence of security and the region 's evolving developmental priorities . <p> Through these initiatives , the Quad has fostered maritime security cooperation to deliver public goods . As climate change accelerates , perhaps the problem is not simply rising water levels , but an architectural imagination that continues to treat the coast as a fixed edge instead of a dynamic ecology . <p> As indian students studying architecture at Pratt Institute in New York City , our thesis , Churning Systems : Coastal Regeneration for a Shared Ecology , began with a different question : What if Mumbai 's coastline were designed as a living interface rather than a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , one of Mumbai 's oldest fishing settlements , where architecture has evolved through centuries of negotiation with tides , seasons , and the Arabian Sea . Unlike the master-planned districts that increasingly define the city , the Koliwada is incremental , porous , and constantly adapting . Its narrow streets , shared working spaces , elevated thresholds , and flexible waterfront are not accidents of informality but spatial responses to a changing environment . <p> In many ways , it represents a form of climate-responsive urbanism that contemporary architecture is only beginning to rediscover . <p> During our fieldwork , we spent time in Worli Koliwada , documenting its changing shoreline , observing fishing practices , and speaking with members of the Koli community . While conversations often centered on declining fish populations , tidal flooding , and shrinking access to the sea , they also revealed something equally important : a sophisticated understanding of living with water . <p> Rather than viewing these communities as vulnerable populations awaiting intervention , we came to see them as designers of an adaptive urban landscape whose knowledge has been largely overlooked @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ design process . <p> Instead of asking how architecture could protect the settlement from the sea , we asked how architecture could mediate the relationship between them . The project therefore reimagines the shoreline not as infrastructure but as an ecological threshold , capable of accommodating both human activity and natural processes . <p> Inspired by the porous structures of sea sponges , algae , and soft corals , we propose a resilient water 's edge that filters , absorbs , and adapts rather than resists . Wetlands become living infrastructure that improves water quality and restores biodiversity . Flexible fish markets expand and contract with tidal cycles . Modular platforms extend into the water and evolve over time through community participation rather than remaining fixed architectural objects . <p> The ambition is not permanence , but adaptability . <p> That philosophy also extends to construction . <p> Rather than relying exclusively on carbon-intensive materials , the project explores bamboo as a lightweight structural framework that reflects local building traditions while allowing incremental repair and modification . Ferrock , produced from industrial steel waste , offers the possibility of transforming @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and fish waste suggest that architecture can participate in biological cycles instead of interrupting them . <p> Together , these materials support an architecture of regeneration rather than extraction . <p> Equally important is the way the project is assembled . Instead of proposing a singular iconic building , we developed a kit-of-parts system that allows the settlement to evolve gradually . Individual elements can be repaired , expanded , replaced , or adapted as environmental conditions and community needs change . In this sense , architecture becomes less about delivering finished objects and more about designing relationships , processes , and long-term resilience . <p> This approach challenges conventional ideas of permanence that continue to dominate urban development . <p> Decades of reclamation , offshore extraction , industrial development , and large-scale infrastructure have fundamentally altered Mumbai 's coastal ecology . These interventions have generated economic growth , but they have also displaced ecological systems and disproportionately affected communities whose livelihoods depend upon the sea . <p> If architecture is concerned with shaping the built environment , it must also engage with the political and environmental conditions that produce @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ beyond design into questions of environmental justice . We propose exploring legal mechanisms , including a Public Interest Litigation before the Bombay High Court , that acknowledge the cumulative impacts of coastal development on traditional fishing communities while directing future investment toward community-led ecological restoration and climate adaptation . <p> Architecture , in this context , becomes a tool not only for constructing buildings but also for imagining new forms of governance , stewardship , and public responsibility . <p> The conceptual foundation of our work comes from one of India 's oldest narratives . <p> In the myth of Samudra Manthan , gods and demons churn the ocean in search of amrita , the nectar of immortality . Before the nectar appears , poison rises first . The story reminds us that every act of transformation produces consequences that must be confronted before renewal becomes possible . <p> Mumbai is engaged in its own churning today . Through reclamation , infrastructure , industrialization , and <p> climate change , the city continues to reshape its coastline at an unprecedented pace . <p> The question is no longer whether we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ kind of relationship architecture chooses to build between the city and the sea . <p> The Indian principle of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam , " the world is one family , " offers a compelling architectural proposition . It asks us to understand the coastline not as a line dividing human and natural systems , but as shared ground where ecological processes , cultural memory , and urban life continually intersect . <p> Perhaps the future of Mumbai 's coast will not be defined by how effectively we hold the sea back . <p> Perhaps it will be defined by how intelligently we learn to design with it . <p> Lakshya KN and Kriti Malik are Bachelor of Architecture candidates at Pratt Institute , New York . Stormwater drains meant to convey rainwater gradually turn into wastewater channels , contaminating surface water and threatening groundwater quality . <p> The lesson is straightforward but often ignored . @@138959132 <h> India 's evolving Indus strategy is shifting from diplomatic signalling to infrastructure development through Chenab-linked projects , while Pakistan has responded with strong rhetoric over water security . The debate highlights the growing intersection of water management , national security , regional stability and strategic competition in South Asia . <p> Tensions between India and Pakistan over the six-decade-old Indus Waters Treaty ( IWT ) have entered their most dangerous phase since New Delhi placed the agreement in abeyance following the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack . The latest flashpoint came with Pakistan 's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik 's warning that Islamabad would " cut off those hands " seeking to claim Pakistan 's share of the Indus waters . Combined with Pakistan Defence Minister Khawaja Asif 's declaration that Islamabad could " go to war " if its water security were threatened , the rhetoric has transformed what was once a technical water-sharing arrangement into an overt national security confrontation . <p> The escalation comes as India moves beyond diplomatic signalling and begins translating political intent into infrastructure action . The launch of two major Chenab-linked projects worth @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Link Tunnel in Himachal Pradesh and the Rs 268 crore sediment bypass tunnel at the Salal Dam in Jammu and Kashmir -- signals that New Delhi is entering a new phase of hydro-strategic planning . Water , which survived multiple wars as a relatively insulated area of cooperation , is increasingly becoming another arena of geopolitical competition between the two nuclear-armed neighbours . <p> Islamabad has simultaneously intensified efforts to internationalise the dispute by portraying India 's actions as the " weaponisation of water " and invoking climate change , humanitarian concerns and downstream vulnerability to win international sympathy . This strategy is hardly new . From Zafrullah Khan raising the canal water dispute before the United Nations in the early 1950s to Asif Ali Zardari 's 2009 warning that Pakistan 's water crisis could fuel extremism , successive Pakistani governments have attempted to frame the issue as an international rather than a bilateral treaty matter . <p> However , Pakistan 's legal argument is considerably weaker than its political rhetoric suggests . The Indus Waters Treaty grants Pakistan treaty-based rights to utilise specified waters ; it does not confer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Jhelum and Chenab originate in Indian territory , the treaty preserved India 's territorial sovereignty while regulating utilisation of river waters between two sovereign states . This distinction is central to India 's evolving position that greater utilisation of its legitimate share can not automatically be portrayed as depriving Pakistan of its sovereign rights . <p> From Diplomacy To Doctrine <p> The suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty is no longer confined to diplomatic symbolism or retaliatory signalling . More than a year after Pahalgam , India has begun converting policy into infrastructure on the ground . What initially appeared to be a temporary coercive measure is steadily evolving into a broader doctrine of hydro-strategic leverage . The latest projects indicate that India 's approach has entered a more operational phase . The message is unmistakable : New Delhi intends to maximise utilisation of waters that historically flowed downstream with only limited domestic exploitation . <p> End Of Strategic Restraint <p> The significance of this shift extends well beyond engineering . For decades , successive Indian governments argued that restrictive treaty provisions , coupled with inadequate infrastructure , prevented @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Indus Basin waters . The current political and security environment has fundamentally altered that calculation . India 's decision to keep the treaty in abeyance rests on the argument that the agreement was built on an assumption of peaceful coexistence and mutual restraint -- an assumption repeatedly undermined by decades of Pakistan-sponsored cross-border terrorism , culminating in the Pahalgam attack . <p> Chenab Projects Signal Shift <p> Within India , the Chenab-Beas tunnel is being projected as a developmental project that would benefit Himachal Pradesh , Punjab , Haryana , Delhi and Rajasthan by improving water availability while generating nearly 4,000 MW of additional hydropower . Strategically , however , its significance extends far beyond regional development . The project reflects New Delhi 's determination to optimise utilisation of the western rivers through storage , hydropower , flood management and inter-basin transfers rather than allowing vast quantities of water to flow downstream without adequate domestic use . <p> Pakistan 's Growing Concerns <p> Pakistan 's growing anxiety stems not from any immediate prospect of India " turning off the tap " but from the long-term implications of expanding upstream infrastructure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to drastically alter annual river flows overnight . Most existing Indian projects remain run-of-the-river schemes with limited storage . Yet , as barrages , tunnels , sediment-management systems and inter-basin transfer projects gradually expand , India will acquire greater flexibility to regulate the timing and management of flows within the framework of its legitimate rights . In highly seasonal river systems , even modest control over timing can assume considerable strategic significance . <p> Pakistan 's dependence on the Indus system further magnifies these concerns . Nearly 80 to 90 per cent of its agriculture relies directly or indirectly on the basin , while the suspension of hydrological data sharing has introduced additional uncertainty for reservoir operations , irrigation planning and flood forecasting . Consequently , Islamabad 's increasingly aggressive rhetoric reflects not only present realities but also apprehensions about India 's future hydro-management capabilities . <p> India 's Strategic Balance <p> India , however , must also calibrate its strategy carefully . As an upper riparian vis- ? -vis Pakistan and Bangladesh but a lower riparian in relation to China on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej , New Delhi can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ position in future water disputes . It must , therefore , continue presenting its policy as an exercise of legitimate sovereign and treaty rights rather than an attempt to deprive Pakistan of water . <p> Water As Strategic Frontier <p> Ultimately , the real significance of India 's emerging hydro strategy lies not in abruptly choking Pakistan 's water supply -- something geography and existing infrastructure do not presently permit -- but in ending decades of self-imposed restraint that limited India 's utilisation of the western rivers . The Indus Waters Treaty was once regarded as one of the world 's most durable water-sharing agreements because both sides respected its underlying spirit . Today , that foundation has been eroded by persistent cross-border terrorism and deepening strategic mistrust . With India accelerating infrastructure projects and Pakistan openly speaking the language of war , the Indus Basin is no longer merely a water-sharing arrangement . It has become a critical arena where engineering , diplomacy , sovereignty , national security and geopolitical power increasingly intersect , making the future of South Asian stability inseparable from the politics of water .

@@138959416 <p> Climate change discussions in southern Africa often focus on farming , where the effects of environmental shocks are most visible . The debate frequently centres on droughts , floods , declining crop productivity and heat stress affecting livestock systems . This is largely because agriculture is a sector that 's directly exposed to extreme weather events . <p> But food systems involve far more than agricultural production . Between farms and consumers lies the agri-processing sector . This is made up of businesses that transform raw agricultural commodities into consumable food products through activities such as cleaning , milling , preservation , packaging , storage and manufacturing . <p> It connects agricultural production to markets , retailers and households . In South Africa , agri-processing contributes approximately 25 per cent of national manufacturing output and supports more than 300,000 direct jobs . <p> The agri-processing sector is particularly exposed to climate risks because its operations depend on a reliable supply of agricultural raw materials ( crops and livestock ) . This makes it very vulnerable to disruptions caused by droughts , floods , heatwaves and other extreme weather events @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with expertise in food systems , climate change adaptation and agri-processing . We conducted a study in South Africa 's industrial heartland , Gauteng , to find out how businesses in this sector were managing climate change risks and what steps they were taking to adapt . <p> We chose the province because it is one of the country 's most important centres for food processing , logistics and distribution . Disruptions in agri-processing extend far beyond the province . They affect food availability , supply reliability , employment and household food prices across South Africa . <p> Our research involved interviews with 113 agri-processing enterprises . We asked whether they were aware of climate change risks , what they could do to adapt to climate change and what was stopping them from adapting . <p> Most training available to the agri-processors was of little help . This is because it focused on production and running a business , rather than helping people understand climate risks or how to respond to them . <p> We concluded from our findings that merely owning or working in agri-processing participation was not sufficient @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ important role in supporting adaptation . We also studied bakers and businesses that made food products . <p> We found that these enterprises were badly affected by climate-related disruptions , because they were dependent on crops , livestock and other agricultural raw materials , water and energy . <p> These business owners told us that water shortages , rising temperatures , irregular supply of agricultural inputs , and increasing production costs were big problems . Some businesses had taken steps to cope with climate change , such as saving water . <p> They also expanded the range of products they made , including more long-life processed foods @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ extreme heat , improving cooling and ventilation , and using water more efficiently . <p> But many struggled to do more because they lacked money , technical support and access to reliable information about climate risks . <h> The support that agri-processors need to cope with climate shocks <p> Our findings suggest that Gauteng 's agri-processing businesses need more support to understand climate change and prepare for its impacts . This includes better access to information and practical training and support programmes . These will help businesses respond to growing climate risks . <p> Helping businesses adapt will take more than individual companies acting alone . Climate change adaptation needs to be built into the support programmes that businesses already use , such as training , education and advice . It can not be treated as an optional extra . This kind of support is usually delivered through government extension services , industry groups and small business programmes . <p> Any planning for the industry and food production sector must include this kind of training , especially as climate-related disruptions become more common and expensive . <p> Access to climate-focused @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ important . Many business owners are aware that climate change poses a risk . But knowing about the problem does not always mean they know how to respond . Practical guidance , planning tools and expert advice can help businesses move from short-term responses to longer-term preparation . <p> Access to funding will also be important . Adapting to climate change costs money . This could be for new equipment , infrastructure or technologies that can help businesses cope with changing conditions , like heatwaves and floods . <p> At the same time , basic public services need to improve . Reliable electricity , a stable water supply and functioning municipal services are essential for agri-processing businesses in Gauteng . When these systems are unreliable , it is much harder for businesses to prepare for and respond to climate change . <p> Our study also shows that greater support for women-led businesses is needed . Women have more difficulty in accessing finance , technology , markets and climate information . <p> Preparing agri-processing businesses for climate change is not only an environmental issue . Nor is Sonam Wangchuk an ordinary protester . <p> He is neither a career politician seeking electoral relevance nor a partisan activist pursuing ideological battles . He is one of India 's most respected innovators , education reformers , and environmental thinkers . For decades , he has worked quietly to solve real problems faced by ordinary people in one of India 's most difficult terrains . <p> His educational reforms transformed learning in Ladakh by making education more meaningful , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Ice Stupa technology , an ingenious innovation that stores winter water in frozen towers and releases it during spring to irrigate fields facing water scarcity . Long before climate change became a fashionable subject in policy circles , Wangchuk was demonstrating practical solutions for sustainable living . His solar-heated buildings proved that even in the harsh Himalayan winters , modern technology could work with nature instead of against it . His contributions earned him the Ramon Magsaysay Award , often regarded as Asia 's highest public service honour . His life inspired the immensely popular film 3 Idiots , making him a symbol of creativity , courage , and innovation for an entire generation of young Indians . <p> This is someone who has spent his life building rather than breaking , solving rather than complaining , and serving rather than seeking power . <p> When a person of such stature feels compelled to undertake an indefinite fast , one expects a democratic government to pause , listen , and engage . Every cancelled examination means more financial burden , more emotional exhaustion , and more uncertainty . <p> The tragedy is not merely administrative . <p> It is profoundly human . <p> The psychological consequences have become impossible to ignore . Reports of students dying by suicide after examination failures or repeated cancellations have become distressingly frequent . Anxiety , depression , and emotional burnout are increasingly common among aspirants trapped in an endless cycle of preparation , postponement , and disappointment . Social media is filled with voices expressing anger , helplessness , and despair . These are not isolated emotional reactions . They reflect a generation slowly losing faith in institutions that are supposed to reward honesty and hard work . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> He is not fasting for personal gain .
