@@138974764 <p> Etawah , a historic city in southwestern Uttar Pradesh , sits near where the Yamuna and Chambal rivers meet . It 's semi-arid , ravine-carved , and prone to sharp seasonal swings . Over 1.5 million people live here , and like most tier-II and tier-III cities across India , Etawah has been hit hard by rising concrete sprawl , urban heat , and falling water tables . Then something changed . A newly established Etawah Nagar Van under the Nagar Van Yojana ( NVY ) , a national urban forestry scheme , came into the picture . The city saw a rapid green transformation . Here , you can find forest trees , cool air , a soft , pleasant smell , and the sound of birds returning . A degraded , abandoned piece of public land that was once common grazing land has now become a carbon sink , a genuine community space , and , surprisingly , a model for how to get climate finance right . <p> The visitor numbers alone prove it . Mornings bring 100 to 150 people , while evenings see 300 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 600 on weekends . Children run to the swings and slides . Older people come for breathwork . The forest is n't just a project anymore . It 's become something the city actually uses . <p> When people talk about green spaces , they count hectares and saplings . That misses a basic point . What actually matters is whether a place can heal you . <p> One morning , Sunil , an elderly man , told his story . A few months earlier , a serious illness had left him bedridden for nearly three months . He could n't leave the house . When the Nagar Van opened fully with its 5-kilometre walking path , shaded rest spots , and huts , he took his first steps back into the world here . <p> " The air is different here , " he said , looking at the trees around him . " Cleaner . Full of birds . I got so much better . Just being here gave me my strength back . " <p> Now he comes every morning . He 's part of a group @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for yoga , meditation , easy jogging , and the cute huts built as relaxing and resting spots . For them , the forest has become health infrastructure . And they 've started asking for more . They have requested an open-air gym . That matters because it shows people are n't just visiting ; they 're treating it as part of their lives . <p> What separates Etawah from a standard park is its commitment to operating without adding carbon to the atmosphere . The District and Regional Forest Officers set one mandate : this place should be carbon-negative . This assessment is based on a Participatory Rural Appraisal ( PRA ) conducted during site monitoring , evaluating renewable power sources , 70% canopy cover , and three water-storage and groundwater-recharge infrastructure systems . The Van has been cut loose from the coal-heavy grid entirely . A decentralized solar micro-grid powers everything . <p> Lighting and safety . Evening visitors have always avoided large forests because of the fear of wildlife , snakes , and insect bites . Solar lights now line all the pathways . They have extended @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ safe space for women , children , and families . A four-person maintenance team , working in day and night shifts , keeps incidents at zero . <p> Water . Summers in Uttar Pradesh are brutal . Solar pumps draw water without a single litre of diesel or grid electricity . The water feeds into a solar-powered cooling system . Hundreds of walkers get free drinking water every day . <p> Groundwater recharge . The district faces a serious groundwater crisis . Engineers built two water-harvesting ponds with a three-layer structure . The pond excavation uses three layers of materials with different permeability . Surface runoff slows down , urban sediment is filtered out , groundwater recharge accelerates , and the water table stabilizes . <p> Making Climate Finance Work <p> Here 's what matters most for policymakers : how the money was managed . Under the Nagar Van Yojana ( NVY ) , a scheme of the Ministry of Environment , Forest and Climate Change ( MoEFCC ) administered through the National CAMPA ( Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority ) , urban forest funding works out to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hectares , that amounted to ? 2 crore , released in two instalments . The first instalment of ? 1.40 crore was released by National CAMPA following procedural norms , ensuring financial accountability and progress verification . <p> The department treated the ? 2 crore strictly as foundational funding . It covered what mattered : planting and maintaining 2,20,000 trees ( count verified by nursery plantation workers in March 2026 ) , along with installing solar lights , a cooling system , solar pumps , a water-harvesting system , toilets , and basic infrastructure for guards and maintenance staff . They chose native species like Neem , Peepal , and Banyan over exotic ornamentals . That decision paid off : more than 90% of the trees survived . Because these species belong here , maintenance costs also declined . <p> For visitor facilities , the site now has solar water coolers , walking paths , toilets , and parking space , while the forest department works closely with the municipality . They pooled their resources and made them work . <p> The future looks interesting too . Access is free @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ asked people what they 'd be willing to pay , something interesting emerged : residents said they 'd happily pay ? 10 to ? 20 as an entry fee . That voluntary , community-backed micro-transaction could cover the four-person maintenance team and daily operating costs . At the same time , it would shift the forest from a free public good to a modest paid-entry model , carrying the risk of excluding poorer residents who may depend on this low-cost health infrastructure the most . <p> A forest ca n't run on its own . The backbone here is the Joint Forest Management ( JFM ) Committee , which brings the community into the management of the forest and includes representatives from local communities , elected bodies , and forest staff . This structure creates genuine local responsibility and ensures decisions on resource allocation and management priorities reflect community input rather than departmental control alone . <p> It has also created an economy outside the gates . Those 500-600 weekend visitors need food . By evening , vendor stalls line the parking areas , selling sugarcane juice , snacks , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the foot traffic the forest generates . <p> The Etawah Model as a Blueprint for Urban India <p> Big cities spend enormous sums on parks that depend on grid power and water to stay alive . Etawah took a different route . <p> A small city used CAMPA funding as intended . It chose native trees instead of exotics . It was built with a focus on reducing carbon emissions and increasing water recharge . An abandoned plot became a place people genuinely want to visit . What made it work was an engaged District Forest Officer committed to site-level decision-making , direct municipal collaboration on maintenance and facility management , a functional JFM Committee with genuine community participation , and sustained adherence to native-species restoration throughout the three-year establishment phase . <p> What 's worth noting is that it works because nothing here pulls in different directions . The ecological restoration depends on the same trees that lower maintenance costs . The trees that survive generate foot traffic for vendors . The management committee that runs the space consists of people from the local community . Money stays within @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ somewhere else and installed here . It evolved . <p> Other cities could do this . It 's not about being large or having special resources . It 's about choosing the right approach and sticking with it . <p> The writer is a Research Associate at the Ministry of Environment , Forest and Climate Change . Views expressed are personal

@@138976278 <h> Energy News Monitor Volume XXII , Issue 49&amp;50 <h> Published on Jul 14 , 2026 <h> Quick Notes <h> America 's AI Competitiveness : Natural Gas as Strategic Capital <p> Source : International Energy Agency <p> The strategic primacy of abundant , low-cost domestic natural gas is positioning the United States ( US ) as the leader in the global artificial intelligence ( AI ) race . While factors such as semiconductor access , talent pools , algorithmic breakthroughs , and policy frameworks undeniably influence AI outcomes , the foundational enabler remains energy . The United States ' unique position , bolstered by cheap , domestically sourced natural gas powering nearly half its electricity , confers a decisive , structural edge in meeting the insatiable power demands of the AI era . This advantage is not merely incremental but existential . In a domain where marginal differences in compute availability and cost can determine technological supremacy , America 's energy endowment positions it to lead the AI race for the foreseeable future . <h> Energy and AI <p> The computational demands of modern AI are unprecedented . Global data centre ( DC ) electricity consumption , already approximately 415 TWh ( terawatt hour ) in 2024 ( roughly 1.5 percent of worldwide electricity use ) , is projected to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030 under baseline scenarios , with accelerated ( AI-driven ) servers accounting for nearly half of the incremental growth at 30 percent annual rates . To put it in perspective , this is roughly 50 percent of India 's electricity generation in 2024-25 . By one estimate , global DC power demand will increase by 165 percent by the end of the decade relative to 2023 levels , with AI workloads expanding their share significantly . Optimistic projections suggest that in the US alone , AI-related DC power demand could surge more than thirtyfold by 2035 , reaching 123 GW ( gigawatt ) from just 4 GW in 2024 . <p> In a volatile global energy market , exacerbated by recent geopolitical disruptions affecting international energy trade , domestic control over the natural gas supply chain ensures price stability for US AI enterprises . This mitigates the risk of exposure to global commodity price shocks that could otherwise render domestic AI operations economically non-viable . <p> Significance of Natural Gas <p> Natural gas dominates US electricity generation , accounting for over 42 percent of output in recent years , providing dispatchable , flexible baseload and peaking capacity ideally suited to DC needs . The shale revolution has transformed the US into the world 's leading natural gas producer with robust domestic supply chains largely insulated from global geopolitical shocks . Henry Hub ( HH ) spot prices , the US benchmark , have remained remarkably stable and low . In stark contrast , international benchmarks reflect far higher costs and volatility . European ( title transfer facility or TTF in the Netherlands ) and Asian LNG ( liquefied natural gas ) prices have frequently traded at multiples of US levels . As of 1 July 2026 , natural gas benchmark prices at HH were at about US$3.30/mmBtu ( metric million British thermal units ) , Dutch TTF at roughly $15.50/mmBtu , and Asian JKM ( Japan Korea marker ) at around US$16.05/mmBtu . Forecasts for 2026-2027 average approximately US$3.34 -- US$3.60/mmBtu . These figures highlight the stark regional price divergence , with Asia and Europe trading at nearly five times US levels , exacerbated by reliance on imports that increases exposure to disruptions . Even under long-term projections , HH prices remain within approximately US$5-6/mmBtu through the early 2030s despite growing domestic demand . The EIA ( Energy Information Administration , US ) projects that natural gas will continue to supply around 40 percent of US electricity generation throughout the remainder of the decade despite rapid renewable deployment . <p> Beyond the price level , the US position rests on demonstrated production elasticity . Natural gas output is expected to grow to nearly 3.09 billion cubic meters ( BCM ) in 2026 , with the EIA explicitly framing supply as critical to accommodating rising electricity demand driven largely by DCs . LNG export growth of roughly 9 percent in 2026 and 11 percent in 2027 is being absorbed alongside flat-to-modest growth in domestic consumption , with electric power sector demand rising steadily even as residential , commercial , and industrial consumption hold flat or decline . This indicates that the system has meaningful slack to absorb new large-load demand without the kind of acute scarcity pricing seen in import-dependent markets . Indeed , regional oversupply has at times produced negative pricing . From late April to early May 2026 , natural gas price at the Waha Hub near the Permian Basin stayed below -US$2/mmBtu , driven by an influx of associated gas from oil extraction incentivised by elevated global oil prices . Such episodes , while reflecting pipeline bottlenecks rather than unambiguous good news , nonetheless illustrate a domestic resource base so abundant that producers sometimes pay to dispose of supply , a condition with no analogue in Europe or Northeast Asia . <p> The US advantage is not only geological but logistical . The country has about 4.83 million kilometres ( km ) of natural gas pipelines , and the distribution system alone includes roughly 491,000 km of transmission pipelines plus 3.54 million km of distribution pipes , creating a dense and flexible network for moving fuel to power plants and industrial users . This infrastructure reduces delivered-fuel risk for DC clusters and helps explain why gas-linked AI buildouts are increasingly attractive in states with strong gas basins and pipeline access . This infrastructure also supports speed , which is crucial in AI . Electricity projects built around existing gas systems can often move faster than large-scale transmission expansions or new zero-carbon firm power options , making gas a bridge between immediate compute demand and longer-term grid transformation . In a race where time-to-capacity matters , the ability to add power quickly is a strategic asset , not merely an operational convenience . <p> Critics argue that growing LNG exports and expanding AI demand could eventually raise US domestic gas prices . This concern is valid . The EIA projects gradual increases in HH prices as domestic consumption and LNG exports expand . Nevertheless , even these higher projected prices remain substantially below prevailing prices in most competing economies . The US therefore retains a durable structural advantage rather than merely a temporary cyclical benefit . <p> The US advantage is not merely lower energy prices but the interaction between cheap gas and a mature electricity system . This domestic integration minimises transmission losses , import dependencies , and price transmission risks that plague competitors . This existing infrastructure enables rapid deployment of large-scale AI facilities without waiting years for new transmission infrastructure . The strategic logic is reinforced by how capital markets and forecasters are interpreting the AI-gas linkage . Industry analysts project DC demand could drive 84.95 MCM/day or more of incremental natural gas consumption by 2030 , with EIA attributing 2026-2027 power-sector generation growth primarily to large customers including DCs . Separately , under a high-demand scenario , natural gas-fired generation is projected to grow by 7.3 percent between 2025 and 2027 specifically to accommodate the AI buildout , with natural gas positioned as the principal baseload source for new DC load . This is significant as it indicates that natural gas is not merely a passive complement to AI infrastructure but is being actively selected by utilities and hyperscalers as the dispatchable backbone for new computing capacity , precisely because no comparably priced , comparably scalable , comparably dispatchable alternative exists domestically . <p> Natural gas generation offers lower grid-connection costs compared to renewable alternatives . As of 2026 data , grid-connection costs for natural gas have averaged approximately US$24/kW ( kilowatt ) , significantly lower than those for solar or wind , which face steeper geographical and transmission hurdles . The US possesses a robust , pre-existing network of pipelines and storage assets . This structural advantage allows for a faster " time-to-power , " enabling developers to bypass the decade-long permitting delays often associated with building new , large-scale clean energy transmission lines . <p> The strategic imperative for AI firms is to reduce the time from conception to operational deployment . The current market is seeing a shift toward " behind-the-meter " ( BTM ) , electricity that is produced on the customer 's side of the utility meter , rather than by the central grid , known as captive generation in India ) natural gas generation . By co-locating natural gas-fired power plants with DC campuses , firms can secure dedicated , reliable power without waiting for long-term upgrades to the regional grid . This capability acts as a force multiplier for American AI developers , providing a deployment velocity that international competitors , many of whom are heavily reliant on imported energy , struggle to match . BTM gas plants can be deployed in as little as 18 months , compared to multi-year grid interconnection queues . This speed-to-power is decisive for AI projects generating billions in annual revenue , where delays translate directly into lost market share . <p> DCs experience costly outages . One study noted that 78 percent of surveyed DCs had power outages between 2017 and 2020 , with some incidents costing more than US$100,000 each . In this context , firm gas-fired generation has an advantage over intermittent supply options because it can provide continuous load support without depending on storage at very large scale . <p> This is especially important for AI , where downtime does not just interrupt office work ; it can disrupt model training , inference services , and high-value commercial contracts . The value proposition of domestic gas therefore extends beyond fuel cost into system resilience , which is often the binding constraint for compute-intensive facilities . Put differently , cheap gas is not simply an input ; it is an enabler of operational certainty . <p> By contrast , many European countries face simultaneous constraints of higher gas prices , slower grid expansion , longer permitting processes and limited dispatchable generation . Recent analyses note that European electricity prices remain several times higher than US prices , reducing the attractiveness of Europe as a destination for hyperscale AI investment . The vast gap in energy costs is reshaping the global landscape of AI infrastructure investment . According to the International Energy Agency ( IEA ) , the average wholesale electricity price in the European Union in 2025 was about US$95/MWh , roughly twice that in the US . More specifically , in May 2025 , average electricity prices were US$111.65/MWh in the UK , US$88.97/MWh in Germany , US$44.19/MWh in France , and only US$28/MWh in the US . The higher European gas prices mean on-site gas-fired generation costs range from US$190 to US$300/MWh , far exceeding US costs . These price differentials matter because AI investment is highly sensitive to power costs over the life of the asset , not just at the moment of construction . Of US$320 billion in DC projects announced globally in 2025 , the US captured the largest share . As of September 2025 , 23 GW of DC capacity was under construction globally , with roughly 75 percent ( over 17 GW ) located in the US . <p> The US combination of low prices , abundant supply , and an established gas-fired fleet enables quicker grid integration , lower marginal costs for new capacity , and greater resilience , advantages that compound in an AI arms race where training runs and inference scale demand continuous , affordable power . At its core , the AI race is , to a considerable extent , an energy race . The United States ' comparative advantage in natural gas constitutes a critical strategic resource , positioning it to consolidate leadership in this race . <h> Monthly News Commentary : Natural Gas <h> Improvement in LNG Access <h> India <p> LNG <p> Indian LNG ( liquefied natural gas ) carrier Disha has safely transited through the Strait of Hormuz -- the first Indian flagged LNG carrying vessel to exit the war zone in more than three months . @@138988360 <p> Bees are among the world 's most important pollinators , helping sustain ecosystems and supporting the production of many fruits , vegetables , nuts and seeds . Yet bee populations have been declining for years due to habitat loss , pesticides , diseases , parasites and climate change . More recently , another potential threat has entered the conversation : the rapid expansion of data centres . Some beekeepers living near large facilities have reported fewer bees and weaker colonies , raising concerns that electromagnetic fields ( EMFs ) generated by high-powered electrical infrastructure could interfere with the insects ' natural behaviour . While researchers agree that the issue deserves further study , they also caution that the scientific evidence is still evolving and does not yet establish data centres as a confirmed cause of widespread bee declines . <h> Can electromagnetic fields from data centres affect bees ? <p> Honeybees rely on multiple cues to navigate , including the position of the Sun , landmarks , odours and the Earth 's magnetic field . Numerous laboratory studies have explored whether artificial electromagnetic fields generated by power lines , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these natural navigation systems.A scientific review by Environmental Health Sciences examined research on the effects of anthropogenic electromagnetic fields on insects . <p> The review found evidence that exposure to certain EMF frequencies and intensities has been associated with changes in insect behaviour , reduced reproductive success , oxidative stress , DNA damage and altered development under experimental conditions . However , the authors also noted that many studies differed significantly in methodology , making it difficult to draw universal conclusions about real-world impacts.Scientists emphasise that the effects observed in controlled laboratory settings do not necessarily translate directly to environments around operational data centres , where exposure levels can vary considerably . <h> Why are some beekeepers linking data centres to bee declines ? <p> Concerns have grown after some farmers and beekeepers reported noticeable changes in bee activity following the construction of nearby data centres . @@138989028 <p> A tawny pipit , one of the grassland specialist bird species whose habitat is adversely impacted by afforestation in Maharashtra . Siddhant Mhetre via Mongabay . <p> India 's fast disappearing grasslands have long been targeted for afforestation -- a practice that encourages tree planting on " degraded " parcels of land . With their vast and open landscapes , savannahs and grasslands are often considered barren land in need of more dense tree cover . But how does converting grassy , arid land to something woody and canopied transform an ecosystem , and the life within it ? <p> New research from Maharashtra studies how old-growth savannahs , when planted with trees , changes bird populations and distributions . Grasslands and savannahs are estimated to cover 15%-20% of India 's land mass , and yet remain under-researched . <p> The lack of recognition of grassland ecosystems has meant their role in regulating microclimates and hosting endemic biodiversity has largely gone unnoticed . " There are very few studies on dry savannahs in general , and even fewer on the impacts of afforestation on them , " said Abi @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at ATREE and a scholar of India 's grasslands . <p> The study from Maharashtra compared bird species and abundance across undisturbed savannahs and well-established plantations , creating new evidence for how the impacts of afforestation go beyond just changes to tree cover . It found that afforestation rendered the area uninhabitable for grassland specialist species like the Indian courser -- a long-legged bird which scans the grass to forage -- and the tawny pipit , which nests on the ground -- among a host of others . <p> Instead , bird populations were maintained by an influx of other species better adapted to woody and forested habitats . The shift in species composition is a matter of concern because grassland specialists are declining at alarming rates across the country . The 2023 State of India 's Birds report found that across a 30 year period , from 1992 to 2022 , populations of birds occupying open and natural ecosystems declined by half . <p> The recent study renews focus on the importance of landscape-level conservation , which is gradually finding recognition in state policies . New research from Maharashtra studies how afforestation in old-growth savannahs changes bird populations and distributions , particularly affecting savannah specialist species . Image by Siddhant Mhetre . <h> Relic of colonial rule <p> The impulse to plant trees in open natural ecosystems is a legacy of British colonial rule , when grasslands were labelled " wastelands " because -- unlike forests , which could be harvested for timber -- they did not generate revenue for the crown . <p> British policies @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to these lands by encouraging cultivation or afforestation on them , a 2019 study tracing the historical roots of India 's grassland governance , notes . " The colonial misconception of grasslands as degraded forests continued post-independence , creating an ostensible need to ' reforest ' those landscapes that remained , " the paper added . <p> In Maharashtra , this legacy took shape in the form of Gliricidia sepium plantations . This exotic tree with pink flowers and a wide canopy was first brought to India for its ornamental value , and later planted widely in the state in the 1950s to improve fodder availability for livestock and biomass . <p> These plantations also provided the ideal setting to study how afforestation affected local bird populations , said Prabhav Benara , a student of wildlife biology and conservation at National Center for Biological Sciences , and a co-author of the Maharashtra-based study . " Birds are excellent habitat indicators , helping us understand how native biodiversity responds to land-use change , " he said . Benara worked with a team of five other students and researchers on the study @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , a Maharashtra-based NGO dedicated to grassland conservation , who was not part of the study , said research into the state 's grasslands were needed to counter misconceptions about their utility . " <p> The Grasslands Trust 's submissions and trainings on grassland management played a significant role in the state government 's adoption of its new resolution . <h> Winners and losers <p> Afforested patches of G sepium are located close to native , old-growth savannahs in the Pune and Satara districts , making comparison across both habitats viable . <p> The researchers recorded the presence of birds across 15 sites -- each with one old growth savannah and one tree plantation -- and divided them into three categories : savannah specialists ( adapted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wide variety of habitats ) and woodland specialists ( birds that thrive in more densely forested habitats ) . <p> Between December 2023 and February 2024 , a total of 1,079 individual birds belonging to 69 species were recorded across all study sites . Out of these , 22 species were found only in the old-growth savannas , 21 species were found only in the tree plantations , and 26 species were found across both land uses . <p> Old growth savannahs included in the study were qualified by those which showed evidence of abundant native grasses , cattle grazing , and fire use -- methods that humans have used to maintain grasslands for centuries -- but were undisturbed by non-traditional interventions like mining and agriculture . Afforested patches that predominantly contained G sepium , as well as a smaller proportion of Eucalyptus , were also included for comparison . <p> All sites fell across an annual rainfall gradient ranging from 459 mm to 1,007 mm , indicating wide variation in precipitation levels . Woodland specialist species emerged winners , benefiting the most from the afforestation . <p> " Grassland specialist species like the harriers actually play an important role in stabilising the populations of insects , pests , and even rodents , which helps farmers , " said Pawar , adding , " When their habitats change , either due to afforestation or due to trenches , they compete for space or are unable to nest , roost , or properly forage , which causes population decline . " <p> Savannah specialist species like the rufous-tailed lark , tawny pipit , rock bush quail and long-tailed shrike saw the steep declines , according to the study . <h> How rainfall changes the picture <p> Factoring rainfall into the impacts of afforestation brings out an even more nuanced picture @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ example , in areas that received intermediate rainfall ( between 560 and 920mm ) , old-growth savannahs were found to host 11 more species compared to tree plantations . However , in areas with extreme rainfall ( 920 mm of rain and higher ) or extreme dryness ( 560 mm of rain and less ) , afforested patches were found to host more diversity -- up to 22 and 14 more species compared to savannahs . <p> According to the paper , " In the driest rainfall end , tree plantations have sparser canopy and relatively intact endogenous disturbance regimes ( fire and cattle grazing ) , this leads to a mosaic of habitat patches that increases bird diversity in drier plantations ... in comparison to the homogeneous , tree-less , drier old-growth savannas . " In the case of wetter regions , savannah specialists were relatively unaffected because these areas were less likely to host a diversity of them anyway . <p> The worst affected regions by plantations were in the intermediate rainfall zones , where plantations became dense enough to replace grassy understorey . " Tree plantations in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lead to greatest diversity losses -- with savanna specialists being the worst affected , " the paper reads . <p> " It 's not surprising that rainfall plays an important role in species diversity , but an important takeaway is that consistently , they found that savannah species tend to not do well where plantation density increases , " said Vanak from ATREE , adding , " Such insights are often missed in most restoration practices because savannah species are n't treated with as much importance in India . @@138989609 <h> The Next Landslide in the Western Ghats Should Not Surprise Us <h> Heavy rain is not unusual in the Western Ghats . It is an intrinsic part of how this mountain system functions . <p> The Quint is telling the full story of how climate change is reshaping lives in India . Help us do more . Become a member . <p> The first week of July offered a stark reminder that the southwest monsoon is both India 's greatest natural asset and one of its most powerful natural forces . Torrential rain battered the Western Ghats from Kerala to Maharashtra , triggering landslides and flash floods . <p> In Wayanad , a landslide struck a tunnel construction site , while in Maharashtra , the Sahyadri ranges witnessed some of the most intense rainfall in recent decades , leaving highways blocked , railway services disrupted , and several villages temporarily cut off . <p> At first glance , these appear to be separate disasters unfolding in different states . They are not . They are linked by the same mountain chain , the same monsoon system , and a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A low-pressure system moving inland from the Bay of Bengal , an offshore trough along India 's west coast , and favourable monsoon circulation together channelled enormous amounts of moisture from the Arabian Sea towards the Western Ghats . <p> The result was an exceptionally active spell that produced widespread heavy rainfall across Maharashtra and Kerala . <h> Why Did Rainfall Become So Intense ? <p> Mountain meteorology provides an important part of the answer . <p> Extreme rainfall over mountains depends not only on how much moisture is present in the atmosphere , but also on how mountains interact with the airflow . <p> During active monsoon conditions , strong low-level westerly winds continuously transport moisture towards the Western Ghats . As this moisture encounters steep terrain , it is repeatedly lifted , generating new clouds over the same region . <h> Climate Change Is Changing the Climatic Conditions <p> Climate change is not creating the southwest monsoon , nor is it responsible for every landslide . But it is changing the environment in which these weather systems develop . <p> A warmer atmosphere can hold roughly seven percent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ At the same time , the Arabian Sea has warmed significantly over recent decades and is experiencing more frequent marine heatwaves . <p> Together , these changes increase the amount of moisture available to the monsoon circulation . <p> When favourable weather systems develop , they now have access to a larger reservoir of atmospheric moisture , increasing the likelihood of short-duration , high-intensity rainfall . <p> Several studies over the past decade have shown that rainfall extremes over western India are becoming more intense , even if seasonal rainfall totals do not necessarily increase at the same rate . <p> In simple terms , the atmosphere is becoming more efficient at producing intense rainfall events . <h> When Natural Hazards Become Disasters <p> Heavy rainfall is a natural hazard . A disaster occurs when that hazard intersects with vulnerable landscapes and human activities . <h> Planning for the Monsoon We Have , Not the One We Had <p> The point is not to fear the monsoon . The monsoon remains India 's lifeline , sustaining agriculture , rivers , groundwater and ecosystems . But the way we plan and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate changes , our approach to planning must change with it . <p> Whether in the Western Ghats or the Himalayas , we need to build cities and infrastructure designed for weather extremes , not for the climate of the past . <p> We have seen that weather forecasting has improved significantly over the past two decades . <p> Today , meteorologists can often identify the atmospheric conditions favourable for extreme rainfall several days in advance . The next challenge is translating these forecasts into impact-based warnings that consider local geology , soil moisture , slope stability and exposure . <p> Landslide susceptibility mapping , stricter land-use planning , protection of natural drainage systems and climate-resilient infrastructure must become integral to development across the Western Ghats . <p> The mountains have not changed . They continue to respond to the monsoon as they always have . What has changed is the atmosphere above them and the landscape beneath them . <p> A warmer climate is loading the atmosphere with more moisture , while expanding infrastructure and changing land use are increasing exposure to hazards . <p> Unless these two realities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Ghats will become increasingly difficult to manage . <p> From Wayanad to Maharashtra , the message is unmistakable : These are not isolated disasters separated by state boundaries . They are part of a common story unfolding across one of the world 's great mountain systems . One that demands not only better weather forecasts , but wiser decisions about how we live , build and adapt in a changing climate . <p> ( Dr Pratik Kad is a climate scientist specialising in climate dynamics , extreme events , and impacts . Climate change is no longer just creating more patients ; it is attacking the systems meant to keep them alive , warns a new review published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health . <p> The study " The Climate-Health Divide : How Climate Change Will Rewire Health Care Across High- , Middle- , and Low-Income Settings " examines how a warming world will reshape disease patterns , clinical demand , infrastructure , staffing , supply chains and healthcare finance . Its key concept , the climate-health divide , captures one of the defining injustices of the crisis . The same heatwave or flood can be contained where homes are cooled , electricity is stable , transport works and primary care is accessible . Elsewhere , it can trigger dehydration , lost treatment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Climate hazards may be shared , but protection is not . <p> The review warns that no health system is safe , but some are far closer to failure . Wealthy countries face ageing populations and highly technical hospitals dependent on uninterrupted power and complex supply chains . Middle-income countries must expand care without locking themselves into costly , high-emission models . Low-income and conflict-affected settings face the most dangerous collision of all : heat , infection , hunger , displacement and fragile services arriving at the same time . Climate change will not merely test healthcare . It will expose which systems were never built to withstand the future . <h> Climate hazards are becoming everyday clinical demand <p> The study organizes climate-related health pressure through five interacting pathways : extreme heat and weather , changing infectious-disease patterns , food and water insecurity , maternal , child , mental and occupational harm , and disruption to healthcare operations . Together , these pathways show that climate change will not arrive in health systems as one identifiable diagnosis . It will appear as a rising and increasingly unpredictable workload . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cardiovascular strain , dehydration , kidney injury , respiratory illness , sleep disruption and cognitive impairment . It can also alter the risks associated with medications used for heart disease , fluid management and psychiatric conditions . <p> In lower-income settings , the burden is often more continuous and less visible . Agricultural workers , construction labourers , street vendors , pregnant women and residents of informal settlements may experience repeated exposure without diagnosis , compensation or access to reliable water and cooling . The result may be chronic kidney damage , declining labour capacity or worsening maternal health rather than a clearly recorded " heat emergency . " <p> Climate change is also redistributing infectious disease . The study stresses that this is not a simple story of every disease expanding everywhere . Temperature , rainfall , urbanisation , mobility , immunity , sanitation and public-health capacity will shape where risks rise , decline or become seasonal . <h> The same shock will produce radically different health crises <p> The climate-health divide is not simply a divide between rich and poor countries . They lose livelihoods due to climate impacts , while also losing land , water , forests , grazing commons , fisheries and decision-making power in the name of climate solutions . <p> A truly Just Transition must therefore address both crises simultaneously . <p> Understanding the Double Burden <p> First Burden : Climate Change <p> Communities across South Asia are already experiencing : <p> Increasing crop failures due to erratic rainfall and prolonged droughts . <p> Coastal ecosystems are altered for ports and green hydrogen infrastructure . <p> Instead of becoming beneficiaries of climate action , many vulnerable communities become its victims . <p> Climate Justice Beyond @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Respective Capabilities ( CBDR-RC ) recognises that developed countries bear greater historical responsibility for climate change and therefore should undertake deeper emission reductions while providing finance , technology and capacity-building to developing countries . This principle remains fundamental . <p> However , climate justice must also be applied within countries . <p> Large inequalities exist within India and across South Asia . The highest-income households consume far more electricity , transport fuels , steel , cement , air travel , air conditioning and material goods than poorer households . Their carbon footprints are many times higher than those of rural communities living with minimal energy access . <p> Yet the costs of transition often fall disproportionately on those who contributed the least . <p> A Just Transition therefore requires an internal application of CBDR-RC , where responsibilities and costs are shared according to wealth , emissions and capability within societies -- not only between countries . <p> Pastoral communities such as the Rabari , Maldhari and other grazing-dependent groups rely on these landscapes for livestock movement . It is about transforming development pathways so that climate action reduces rather than reproduces inequality . <p> Climate justice must operate across multiple scales -- between developed and developing countries , and equally within nations between high emitters and low emitters , the wealthy and the poor , corporations and communities . <p> The transition to a low-carbon economy will be truly just only when those who contributed least to climate change benefit from the transition , rather than being asked to sacrifice their land , livelihoods , cultures and futures for the benefit of those who consume the most . <p> A genuinely Just Transition therefore demands that renewable energy expansion , climate adaptation and economic transformation be guided by the principles of equity , participation , human rights , ecological sustainability and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ instrument of social justice rather than another source of exclusion and dispossession . <h> Support Countercurrents <p> Countercurrents.org is on annual fundraising drive . @@139004916 <h> Amarnath Yatra : Ecological Questions Kashmir Can No Longer Postpone <p> The debate is not about faith or the pilgrimage , but whether one of the Himalayas ' most fragile ecosystems can continue to bear ever-growing numbers without a transparent scientific assessment of its ecological carrying capacity <p> The Jammu and Kashmir administration 's recent decision to audit facilities along the Amarnath Yatra routes , following an unprecedented rush of pilgrims this year , is a welcome administrative exercise . <p> Reviewing infrastructure , sanitation , logistics and emergency preparedness is essential when lakhs of people undertake a pilgrimage through one of the world 's most fragile mountain environments . <p> Yet this welcome initiative also revives a much larger question that has remained unanswered for well over a decade : has anyone scientifically established the ecological carrying capacity of the Amarnath Yatra ? <p> That question is neither new nor political . It is scientific . And the longer it remains unanswered , the more urgent it becomes . <p> In 2014 , I participated in a discussion hosted by the late Shujaat Bukhari alongside Preet Pal Singh @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Shrine Board , and Dr Tanveer Ahmad Khan , whose doctoral research focused on the Lidder Valley . Watching it today , one is struck less by what has changed than by how many of the questions raised then still await credible answers . <p> The debate was never about opposing the pilgrimage . <p> Kashmir has welcomed the Amarnath Yatra for centuries . Pilgrims have traditionally been received with warmth and hospitality by local communities . The pilgrimage is deeply woven into Kashmir 's composite cultural traditions , and few would question its religious significance . <p> The issue has always been something else : whether the fragile environment that sustains this sacred journey has received the same respect as the pilgrimage itself . <p> In 2014 , I had raised several concerns that remain unresolved even today . <p> One was the continued operation of the Nunwan base camp despite earlier @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ For a substantial part of the tourism season , Pahalgam , one of Kashmir 's premier tourist destinations , effectively functions under Yatra-related administrative arrangements . The consequences are not merely logistical . They directly affect the local economy by displacing high-value visitors whose longer stays generate greater employment and income for local businesses . <p> Another concern is the absence of an independent and transparent scientific study of the carrying capacity of the Yatra route . <p> This is perhaps the most fundamental question . <p> Fragile mountain ecosystems can not be managed through assumptions , administrative convenience or political considerations . They require evidence-based planning grounded in ecological science . Carrying capacity is not an abstract academic concept . It determines how many people , vehicles , helicopters and support infrastructure an ecosystem can sustain before irreversible environmental damage begins to occur . <p> Equally important were the recommendations of the Nitesh Sengupta Committee , many of which deserved careful implementation rather than gradual neglect . Kashmir itself has witnessed repeated episodes of extreme weather that underline the increasing fragility of its environment . <p> It would certainly be simplistic to attribute every environmental event to the Amarnath Yatra . <p> But it would be equally irresponsible to ignore the cumulative impact of growing human intervention in such a sensitive ecological zone . <p> The numbers alone warrant careful reflection . <p> Around @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ figure dropped to nearly 3.5 lakh in 2025 after security concerns arising from the Pahalgam attack . Instead , the region should pursue value-added tourism that attracts visitors who stay longer , contribute more to local livelihoods , generate higher economic returns and impose less pressure on fragile ecological systems . @@139006601 <p> NEW DELHI : India has emerged as one of the global hotspots for climate change-driven sleep loss , with residents in cities especially across South India are losing between 78 and 91 hours of sleep annually , of which eight to nine of those hours attributed to climate change . <p> A new analysis by Climate Central , covering 107 Indian cities , found that Tamil Nadu records the highest climate change-driven sleep loss , with an additional 7.9 hours per person each year . <p> Cities traditionally known for cooler nights , such as Bengaluru and Dehradun , have become warmer , resulting in an additional nine hours of sleep loss over the past five years . <p> In the 1970s , residents of Bengaluru lost 59 hours of sleep annually . That figure rose to 67 hours in 2025 , with the additional eight hours linked to climate change -- the highest increase among India 's metro cities . <p> Similarly , sleep loss in Dehradun increased by 10% over the same period . <p> Globally , the average person lost nearly 56 hours of sleep annually @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ warming caused by climate change between the 1970s and 2025 . <p> The analysis is the first to cover all 1,338 major cities worldwide . It examined rising temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels and quantified their impact on sleep using the latest climate attribution science . <p> The study also found that temperature-related sleep loss attributable to climate change has at least doubled since the early 1970s , with significant implications for public health . <p> It found that India 's metro cities , including Chennai , lost 93 hours of sleep annually , while Mumbai ( 84 hours ) and Kolkata ( 80 hours ) recorded some of the highest overall sleep losses among major metros . <p> People in cities across the Middle East experienced the highest levels of climate change-attributed sleep loss between 2020 and 2025 . <p> Cities in Saudi Arabia , Oman and the United Arab Emirates lost between 55 and 87 hours of sleep annually because of higher nighttime temperatures , with 12 to 16 of those lost hours attributed to climate change . <p> Climate change-linked sleep losses were also @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ India and several countries in Southeast Asia lost between 78 and 91 hours of sleep annually because of higher nighttime temperatures , including about eight to nine hours attributable to climate change . <p> Similarly , in cities across West Africa , including those in Niger , Nigeria and Burkina Faso , people lost 65 hours of sleep or more each year , including about 10 to 11 hours linked to climate change .

@@139007406 <p> In October 2025 , China expanded its export control regime , pivoting from regulating raw materials to controlling the entire supply chain , including magnets , processing equipment , technology transfers , and even foreign-made goods containing Chinese-origin inputs . Given India 's extensive reliance on Chinese rare-earth imports , this development poses acute risks to India 's electric vehicle ( EV ) , semiconductor , clean energy , and defence manufacturing industries . The country 's participation in international partnerships such as the Quad Critical Minerals Initiative , Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement , and the Australia-Canada-India Technology and Innovation Partnership , and domestic initiatives such as the National Critical Mineral Mission and production-linked incentives ( PLI ) , reflect a strategic goal to build resilient supply chains . This paper examines China 's weaponisation of the supply of rare earths through strategic chokepoints and the global response to this development , as well as the impact on India 's strategic autonomy and its policy responses . <h> Introduction <p> ' Chokepoints ' are the specific , dominant nodes in the global economy where one nation holds control @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1 Chokepoints can be both tangible and intangible , and they are integral to great-power competition , often used by some countries to maintain their positions in the global hierarchy. 2 For instance , the United States ( US ) has managed to remain dominant with its strong currency and its clout in the global financial architecture . Since central banks worldwide hold about 60 percent of their total foreign currency reserves in US dollars , Washington has created a key chokepoint through its currency , which is the preferred medium of exchange for international trade and finance. 3 The other chokepoint in the US 's arsenal is the international finance architecture -- the Clearing House Interbank Payments System and the Federal Reserve 's Fedwire system -- that clears cross-border payments. 4 The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication ( or SWIFT ) , which facilitates interbank payments through codes and standardised formats , shares data with the US to track third-party compliance with sanctions. 5 If entities are barred from these systems , it becomes difficult for them to trade globally . <p> The US 's primacy in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ objectives even when the entities targeted are outside its jurisdiction . In 2015 , the French bank BNP Paribas was fined US$9 billion for processing transactions through the US system on behalf of Cuban , Iranian , and Sudanese entities that were subject to American economic sanctions. 6 Businesses outside the financial sector have also been in the crosshairs of US authorities ; for instance , the Chinese firm ZTE was fined US$2 billion for violating US export controls by reselling US technology to Iran. 7 Similarly , in its war with the US and Israel , Iran has used the Strait of Hormuz as a chokepoint by blocking the waterway , through which nearly 20 percent of the world 's oil and liquefied natural gas transits , leading to a severe global energy shock. 8 <p> China is similarly mobilising its resources and nurturing chokepoints , 9 the impulses for which are perhaps coming from ancient Chinese strategic thought , specifically Sun Tzu 's doctrine of subduing rivals without fighting . Several factors have shaped China 's ' chokepoint toolkit ' . First , it responded to rising tariffs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) with retaliatory levies and foreign-exchange depreciation , but the limitations of these instruments led Beijing to develop a strategy centred on export controls on resources such as critical minerals and rare earths. 10 <p> Second , as global opinion turned against China in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic , it recognised that deglobalisation was accelerating , with countries looking inward with respect to industrial production . President Xi Jinping spoke about enhancing China 's position in industries and sectors where it had an advantage , and strengthening its " advantages in the entire industrial chain " in sectors like high-speed railways , electricity-generation machinery , new energy , and communication equipment. 11 He directed efforts to increase the dependence of international industrial chains on China , thereby building a strong " countermeasure " and " deterrent capability " against deliberate supply disruptions by foreign parties. 12 <h> Operationalising the Chokepoint Toolkit <p> China 's dominance of rare-earth elements is the result of decades of deliberate industrial policy , vertical integration , and investment in the most pollution-intensive parts of the value chain . According to the US Geological @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ related rare-earth concentrates , and it also dominates the conversion , separation , and alloying stages that turn ore into usable materials. 13 Other studies have corroborated this assessment , with China 's processing capacity estimated in the 70 -- 90 percent range , depending on which stage of the chain is measured. 14 <p> Since rare-earth elements are essential to civilian clean-energy transitions and military technologies , this concentration creates a strategic lever : control of supplies and , perhaps more importantly , control of the ability to turn ore into high-value magnets and alloys gives a country an outsized influence over downstream industries . Given the dual-use nature of rare earths , their weaponisation as a chokepoint poses national security and economic concerns for importing countries. 15 <p> Chinese efforts to put its chokepoint toolkit into action began with the Export Control Law in December 2020 . The legislation restricts the export of sophisticated technology and " strategic materials " to specific companies and empowers the Chinese government to act against nations or regions that violate its national security or interests. 16 Under the law , exports of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The inclusion of the term ' interests ' in the law indicates that the party-state has leeway to move against entities it seeks to penalise . <p> In 2021 , China released a white paper supporting export controls to regulate trade in science and technology to protect economic and national security. 17 China also worked on measures to consolidate its mining and extraction capacity . Also in 2021 , the Aluminium Corporation of China , China Minmetals Corporation , and Ganzhou Rare Earth Group were merged to form the State-owned China Rare Earth Group. 18 In December 2025 , it revised its Foreign Trade Law to include safeguarding national sovereignty and national security. 19 The law empowers the state to ban or restrict international trade in services that may be linked to activities that endanger China 's sovereignty and security . The law bars individuals and organisations from providing agency , freight , or other support to help circumvent such measures . In April 2025 , China announced restrictions on the exports of the rare-earth elements , samarium , gadolinium , terbium , dysprosium , lutetium , scandium , and yttrium. 23 <p> In some cases , Chinese officials have directed companies to share confidential or proprietary information related to product designs in exchange for access to minerals. 24 This development turned the spotlight on strategic vulnerabilities , as these minerals are critical ingredients in the production of permanent magnets that are widely used in EVs , clean-energy equipment , and arms manufacturing. 25 China produces up to 60 percent of the world 's rare earths but processes nearly 90 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the world and then acquiring a near-monopoly over extraction and processing , China is using its economic resources as a chokepoint . <p> China 's October 2025 decision to expand export controls on rare earths , artificial diamonds , magnetic materials , processing equipment , and related technologies -- followed by a one-year suspension of the restrictions after the US agreed to reduce its tariffs on China27 -- underscores how deeply global supply chains depend on Chinese regulatory choices . China 's global dominance in mining , processing , and downstream manufacturing allows export licensing , compliance rules , and even extraterritorial provisions to function as powerful tools of statecraft rather than mere trade policy . While the temporary suspension has eased immediate pressure on the semiconductor , EV , clean energy , and defence manufacturing sectors , it has not dismantled the underlying control architecture . Instead , it reinforces uncertainty and incentivises diversification , stockpiling , and allied cooperation , albeit at high cost and over long timelines to make supply chains resilient . <p> Between 2023 and 2025 , China expanded the ambit of its export-control instruments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , magnet technologies , and even extraterritorial clauses that can affect goods containing Chinese inputs or made with Chinese technology abroad . Many of these restrictions operate more as licensing , screening , and administrative controls that increase the transaction costs and uncertainty for multinational supply chains and foreign customers than as outright prohibitions. 28 <p> The immediate consequences of such policy moves are uncertainty , re-pricing , and accelerated attempts by importers to diversify . At the same time , it also reveals the deeper practical difficulties of diversification : building separation and refining plants and magnet-making capacity is capital-intensive , technically demanding , environmentally fraught , and time-consuming . Even where mines can be opened outside China , the ' upstream ' mine output is of limited strategic value unless the ' midstream ' chemical separation and metallurgical capacity can be established. 29 ( for instance , a magnet or a sputtering target ) containing Chinese-origin rare-earth materials -- even if only in trace amounts -- will require a Chinese export licence if the Chinese-origin Chinese-origin rare-earth inputs is subject to Chinese export-licensing requirements. 40 In addition , the controls included a " 50 percent rule " ( or affiliate rule ) : licence applications will likely be denied if the importer or end-user ( or its affiliates or subsidiaries with greater than or equal to 50 percent ownership ) appears on China 's export-control entity list or ' watch list ' . 41 Exports destined for military end-users or defence-related industries are subject to outright prohibition. 42 Meanwhile , items intended for semiconductor , artificial intelligence ( AI ) , or other advanced technology applications -- including chips with =14 nm logic or =256-layer memory -- will be subject to case-by-case review. 43 <p> MOFCOM has justified @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ global instability and military conflicts since medium- and heavy-rare-earth elements , super-hard materials , and related technologies can have military uses. 44 Additionally , it has stressed that the facilitation measures -- for example , general licenses or licence exemptions -- for legitimate civilian trade. 46 The recent control measure package thus represents a qualitative escalation over previous measures , which primarily targeted upstream raw materials and certain processed metals. 47 As such , China appears to have adopted a framework analogous to other export-control regimes , such as the US 's Foreign Direct Product Rule ( FDPR ) . The FDPR was introduced in 1959 to control the export of US technology ; it essentially stipulates that if a product is made using American technology , the US has the power to stop it from being sold , including products made abroad . The FDPR was used in 2022 to stop China from obtaining advanced chips. 48 Similarly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but also re-exports , foreign-origin goods , and third-country manufacturing using Chinese inputs. 49 <p> China 's October 2025 announcement has injected uncertainty into the global high-tech and semiconductor supply chain. 50 The reason for the ban is to impact fab capacity , because many advanced-chip fabs rely on sputtering targets , polishing media , or diamond-based sawing and grinding , which often incorporate rare-earth or super-hard-material inputs . The licensing requirement and potential export delays or denials pose a real risk to fabrication timelines. 51 Even a small disruption in the supply chain of these important inputs can have a ripple effect across global electronics production . <p> EV and battery manufacturers are also under pressure . Permanent magnets made from rare-earth alloys remain critical for many EV motor designs , while battery supply chains often depend on precursor materials and processing , some of which now fall under China 's export-license regime. 52 Since China still controls an estimated 80 -- 90 percent of global rare-earth refining and magnet production capacity , alternative supply chains are limited and will take years to scale and be competitive , particularly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ battery makers may face higher input costs , renegotiated contracts , and possibly delayed production , especially if they can not secure long-term supply agreements or find substitute materials. 54 <p> Indeed , China has repeatedly used the flow of rare earths as a chokepoint to gain the upper hand over rivals in geopolitical spats . For instance , Beijing had imposed similar curbs on rare-earth exports in 2024 for United States to control the export of dual-use items such as gallium and germanium. 56 China has also weaponised rare earths against Japan , after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi framed the Taiwan contingency as an existential issue for Tokyo that would require its military intervention . In January 2026 , Beijing responded by banning export of " all dual-use items " for military users that contribute to improving its defence capabilities , in compliance with the Export Control Law , specifically citing Tokyo 's interference in its internal affairs and the violation of the One-China principle. 57 Japan 's annual nominal and real GDP will decline by 0.11 percent if the restrictions last for three months and 0.43 percent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to Counter China 's Rare-Earth Dominance <p> China 's chokehold on rare-earth elements is not a geological accident ; it is a result of decades-long strategic investment . According to 2024 data , China extracted about 270,000 tonnes of rare-earth oxide equivalent , while the US produced only about 45,000 tonnes. 59 Beijing controls 90 percent of global processing and 94 percent of the world 's permanent magnets . Against this backdrop , allied countries are seeking to construct alternative supply chains. 60 <p> For instance , Australia 's Lynas Rare Earths is the world 's largest non-Chinese supplier of rare-earth elements . Following China 's 2010 de-facto suspension of rare-earth exports , which the Chinese government officially denied , Japan financed the Lynas Advanced Materials Plant in Malaysia despite the absence of substantial commercial incentives at the time. 61 Rare-earth elements are procured from Mount Weld in Australia , refined in Malaysia , processed in Japan , and turned into final products across United States , East and Southeast Asia. a Australia has also passed a law that provides 10 percent production tax credits for the processing and refining @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and investment. 62 <p> The US Department of War has invested over US$439 million to strengthen domestic rare earth supply chains since 2020 , supporting key initiatives led by MP Materials , Lynas USA , and eVAC Magnetics. 63 In July 2025 , the Department of War entered into an agreement to become the largest stakeholder in California 's Mountain Pass ( the US 's only operational mine ) , guaranteeing minimum prices for its neodymium and praseodymium and committing to build a new facility to scale up upstream and midstream processing capacity. 64 Additionally , MP Materials is building a manufacturing facility in Fort Worth , Texas , to produce neodymium-iron-boron ( NdFeB ) magnets for EVs and defence applications , with the goal of establishing a fully integrated mine-to-magnet supply chain. 65 <p> In parallel , Japan has a long-term investment in Vietnam . In 2012 , the Japan Organisation for Metal and Energy Security ( JOGMEC ) established the Japan-Vietnam Rare Earth Research Centre to create a processing foothold outside China . The CRMA seeks to achieve 10 percent extraction , 40 percent processing , and 25 percent recycling capacity by 2030 , while capping single-country dependencies at 65 percent across the value chain. 70 The European Union ( EU ) also provided a ? 18.7-million ( US$21.59 million ) grant to the Canadian firm Neo Performance Materials for its rare-earth magnet facility in Narva , Estonia , which has an initial capacity of 2,000 metric tonnes per year. 71 With @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ investment , France 's Caremag SAS is building a facility that can extract heavy rare earths such as dysprosium and terbium , the first such plant outside China . By implementing the CRMA strategic project pipeline , the EU 's dependence on China for rare-earth extraction is projected to fall from 95 percent as of 2024 to 42 percent by 2030. 72 <p> Collectively , efforts across these countries represent a coordinated , multi-nodal attempt to fracture China 's dominance in vertical integration . Australia is supplying upstream ore , Japan is providing processing and technical expertise , Vietnam is poised as an emerging alternative refining hub , and Europe is building downstream magnet manufacturing capacity . <h> Addressing India 's Critical Dependencies <p> India holds the world 's third-largest reserves of rare earths ( around 8 percent of global reserves ) and yet contributes less than 1 percent of the global rare-earth mining output. 73 It has nearly 35 percent of the world 's beach and sand mineral deposits , which are a significant source of rare earths. 74 India 's rare-earth resources are largely embedded in monazite-bearing sand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Kerala , West Bengal , Jharkhand , Gujarat , and Maharashtra , containing 13.15 million tonnes of rare-earth oxides. 75 <p> The source of India 's production gap is regulatory . Between 1950 and 2025 , India Rare Earths Ltd ( IREL ) enjoyed a state-backed monopoly over the mining and processing of key rare-earth minerals , including monazite and beach sand , until the government allowed the private sector to enter rare-earth exploration , refining , and processing. 76 IREL operates mineral separation plants at Chavara ( Kerala ) , Manavalakurichi ( Tamil Nadu ) , and Chhatarpur ( Odisha ) , with a 10,000-11,200 MT processing capacity annually ; however , the actual output is far lower due to cluster of legacy constraints. b <p> Consequently , India is an import-dependent country for nearly all its lithium , cobalt , and nickel requirements , as well as its permanent magnet needs ( see Tables 1 , 2 , and 3 , and Figure 1 ) . India imported over 53,000 metric tonnes of rare-earth magnets in FY 2024-25 alone. 77 India imports nearly 90 percent of its @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and defence supply chains at risk. 78 China accounted for between 59.6 percent and 81.3 percent of India 's permanent magnet imports by value and between 84.8 percent and 90.4 percent by quantity during 2022-23 and 2024-25 . India 's EV sector depends on NdFeB permanent magnets for traction motors , and the defence sector relies on them for radar , sonar , and missile guidance. 79 However , India lacks the technological and industrial infrastructure to refine heavy rare earths that are essential for high-temperature permanent magnets . <h> India 's Response and Mitigation Strategy <p> India 's response to China 's tightening of rare-earth and related export controls has been comprehensive ( ranging from high-level missions , industry incentives , regulatory reforms , stockpiling , and research funding ) , designed to reduce import dependence , build domestic capability , and shore up resilience across critical sectors such as EVs , batteries , and defence . Central to these efforts is the National Critical Mineral Mission ( NCMM ) , launched in early 2025 with an initial outlay of INR 163 billion ( US$1.71 billion ) and a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) over seven years , which aims to secure stable access to critical minerals , including rare-earth elements , lithium , cobalt , and nickel. 84 It integrates exploration , mining , processing , refining , recycling , research and development ( R&amp;D ) , and strategic reserves under one umbrella to foster an end-to-end value chain in India and reduce reliance on imports , particularly from dominant suppliers like China. 85 It includes policy and regulatory reforms such as simplifying mining approvals through a single-window clearance system , auctioning critical mineral blocks , and establishing centres of excellence for research at premier institutions. 86 <p> Additionally , economic , industrial , and fiscal measures seek to cultivate domestic and near-term capacity in strategic supply chains . The government has introduced production-linked incentive ( PLI ) schemes and dedicated magnet-manufacturing incentives , cumulatively worth several million rupees , to catalyse indigenous permanent magnet production. 87 These incentive schemes offer capital subsidies , tax benefits , and support for advanced processing equipment , helping offset the cost disadvantage vis- ? -vis cheaper Chinese imports . IREL has also commissioned a rare-earth @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ participation to scale up manufacturing capacity , although heavy rare-earth inputs currently still need to be imported. 88 <p> At the same time , India is boosting its strategic stockpile of critical minerals and magnets to buffer short-term supply shocks , even as industry groups have urged broader reforms to align incentives , logistics , and standards to attract investment across the entire magnet and battery ecosystem. 89 To supplement industrial responses , the government is also promoting research and human capital development in critical materials science . Research institutes are receiving funding for advanced materials R&amp;D , including efforts to improve rare-earth extraction and separation technologies , high-strength magnet design , and recycling of end-of-life products and industrial waste , which align with the International Energy Agency 's recommendations that emphasise recycling and circular-economy approaches as viable tools to alleviate import pressures in the medium term. 90 Furthermore , to push for strategic stockpiling , the government has moved to classify rare-earth production and processing as ' strategic projects ' , thereby expediting approvals by prioritising them in defence and national security contexts . The Ministry of Defence has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ defence minerals. 91 <p> In November 2025 , the Union Cabinet approved the Scheme to Promote Manufacturing of Sintered Rare Earth Permanent Magnets with a financial outlay of INR 72.8 billion ( US$763 million , comprising US$676.35 million in sales-linked incentives over five years and US$78.64 in capital subsidy ) , targeting 6,000 MTPA of integrated rare-earth permanent magnet manufacturing capacity distributed across up to five beneficiaries through global competitive bidding. 92 Complementing this , the 2026 -- 27 Union Budget announced the creation of dedicated rare-earth corridors in Odisha , Kerala , Andhra Pradesh , and Tamil Nadu to promote mining , processing , research , and manufacturing in a geographically concentrated value-chain cluster. 93 <p> On the regulatory front , India amended the Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation ( MMDR ) Act in March 2025 , permitting private players to explore and mine rare-earth elements. 94 In September 2025 , the Ministry of Environment , Forests , and Climate Change issued a memorandum exempting critical mineral mining projects -- including rare-earth elements , lithium , cobalt , and graphite -- from mandatory public hearings , citing national @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 95 <p> The private sector 's response to these reforms and the supply shock has been substantial : Mahindra &amp; Mahindra , anticipating prolonged disruption , secured nine months of rare-earth magnet inventory through alternative sourcing channels while mobilising an internal engineering effort to develop NdFeB-free architectures for its traction motors and power steering systems ; 96 Sona BLW Precision Forgings shifted to alternative motor designs using light rare-earth magnets and developed rare-earth-free motors ; 97 Bosch India explored non-heavy rare-earth magnet motors ; 98 and Bajaj Auto began evaluating ferrite magnet motors for its motor scooter range to structurally reduce dependence on Chinese heavy rare earths. 99 Broader industrial interest has coalesced around the rare-earth permanent magnets scheme , with Mahindra &amp;
