@@139115496 <h> India 's ethanol revolution : A climate-friendly model for the world <p> The world today stands at a critical juncture in its fight against climate change , adopting a transition towards cleaner energy , biofuels , particularly ethanol , that have emerged as one of the most practical and scalable solutions . <p> The world today stands at a critical juncture in its fight against climate change , adopting a transition towards cleaner energy , biofuels , particularly ethanol , that have emerged as one of the most practical and scalable solutions . Rising temperatures , frequent extreme weather events , melting glaciers and increasing air pollution has shown us frequent calamities like flash flood , erosion , landslides , wildfire and more , and have forced nations to rethink their dependence on fossil fuels . Transportation alone accounts for nearly one-fourth of global carbon dioxide emissions , making the decarbonisation of the transport sector an urgent necessity . While electric vehicles and green hydrogen represent the future of mobility , ethanol offers an immediate and affordable pathway to reduce fossil fuel consumption and lower emissions . <p> Recognising @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's most ambitious ethanol blending policy and energy initiatives undertaken by any major developing economy . By simultaneously addressing energy security , rural prosperity and decarbonization , it offers a holistic model that few countries have matched . Ethanol 's oxygen-rich composition enables cleaner combustion , reducing emissions of carbon monoxide , unburnt hydrocarbons and particulate matter , while its renewable origin helps lower life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions when produced sustainably . India 's rapid progress in expanding ethanol production capacity , achieving nationwide E20 availability ahead of schedule , and promoting flex-fuel vehicles demonstrates how climate action can be aligned with economic development and farmer welfare . Unlike many countries that have focused solely on mandates , India is building an integrated ecosystem encompassing feedstocks , distilleries , vehicle technology and distribution infrastructure , a lesson drawn from global successes such as Brazil . In this sense , India 's approach represents one of the world 's most comprehensive and replicable models for the sustainable use of biofuels . <p> Ethanol is an alcohol produced from renewable resources such as sugarcane , molasses , maize and agricultural residues . Unlike @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for millions of years , ethanol is derived from plants that absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere during their growth . Consequently , when ethanol is burned , much of the carbon released is part of a short biological carbon cycle rather than introducing entirely new fossil carbon into the atmosphere . Ethanol is also known as an oxygenated fuel because it contains oxygen within its molecular structure . This oxygen enables more complete combustion in engines , resulting in lower carbon monoxide emissions , lower unburnt hydrocarbon emissions , reduced soot formation , cleaner engine operation and improved combustion efficiency . <p> While the overall climate benefits depend upon sustainable production methods , ethanol remains one of the most effective low-carbon fuels currently available for large-scale use in internal combustion engines . <p> The push towards ethanol is closely linked to global climate commitments under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change . At COP27 in Egypt , countries emphasised reducing greenhouse-gas emissions from transportation through multiple pathways , including biofuels . At COP28 in Dubai , nations agreed to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where appropriate . This has made ethanol a key component of the global clean-energy transition . <p> Brazil is universally regarded as the world 's most successful ethanol story . Following the oil crisis of the 1970s , Brazil launched the Pr ? - ? lcool Programme in 1975 to reduce dependence on imported oil and utilise its abundant sugarcane resources . Over five decades , the country built an entire ecosystem around ethanol , including flex-fuel vehicles , dedicated ethanol pumps , stable long-term policies , massive investments in sugarcane production and processing . Today , more than 80 percent of new vehicles sold in Brazil are flex-fuel vehicles capable of running on petrol or high-ethanol blends . The country dramatically reduced its oil imports and built one of the world 's most competitive biofuel industries . <p> The United States is today the world 's largest producer of ethanol , primarily using corn as feedstock . Nearly all gasoline sold in the country contains ethanol blends , and millions of flex-fuel vehicles use E85 fuel . The programme has strengthened rural economies and reduced gasoline consumption . Thailand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ support and vehicle compatibility measures . The country now widely uses E10 , E20 and E85 blends and is regarded as one of Asia 's most successful biofuel programmes . Sweden used ethanol as a transition fuel while developing its electric-vehicle ecosystem . The country demonstrated that ethanol and electric vehicles are not competitors but complementary technologies in the broader decarbonisation journey . <p> India 's ethanol programme may well represent the most balanced ethanol model seen globally . Unlike Brazil , which relies overwhelmingly on sugarcane , or the United States , which primarily uses corn , India has developed a multi-feedstock strategy that includes sugarcane juice , molasses , maize , damaged food grains , agricultural residues . This diversified approach reduces risks arising from crop failures and improves long-term sustainability . Moreover , India is not treating ethanol as a standalone solution . Instead , it has adopted a multi-technology approach -- electric vehicles for urban mobility , ethanol and flex-fuel vehicles for liquid-fuel transportation , compressed bio-gas for commercial applications , green hydrogen for heavy industries and long-distance transport . Few countries have attempted such an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ capacity dramatically . Earlier , the country struggled to produce enough ethanol even for E10 blending . Today , installed capacity has increased to approximately 1,700 crore litres annually , and India has reached aggregate E20 blending ahead of its original schedule . This achievement is remarkable for a developing country of India 's size and complexity . <p> The introduction of ethanol blending in India is not merely an energy policy -- it is a transformational national strategy . In the coming decades , as nations seek practical solutions to save the planet while ensuring economic growth , India 's ethanol revolution may well be remembered as one of the defining examples of how a developing country led the world towards a cleaner and more sustainable future .

It is effective in preventing dengue among people aged four to 60 years . <p> " Dengue is a growing public health challenge , and India needs sustained , evidence-based prevention . The latest seven-year data for QDENGA show continued protection against dengue infection and hospitalisation , " stated Mahendra Nayak , Head @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ release . <p> The market approval for Takeda 's vaccine comes after rigorous clinical trials and testing , both globally and in India , to understand the efficacy of the vaccine . Qdenga is currently the only available vaccine in the world for dengue , a viral infection that is transmitted through the bite of the female Aedes aegypti mosquito . <p> According to a press release shared by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India , their vaccine has undergone 19 different Phase I , II , and III trials with a total of 28,000 participants across the world . <p> Two doses of the Qdenga vaccine showed 90% efficacy against dengue-related hospitalisation 18 months after the last dose was administered , and 84% efficacy 4.5 years after . The vaccine also showed 80.2% efficacy against symptomatic , laboratory-confirmed dengue one year after the second dose . <p> Even as Qdenga becomes the first dengue vaccine to be sold in India , another vaccine called DengiAll by an Indian company Panacea Biotech is currently under trials and will be sent for a market approval soon . <p> What is Qdenga ? <p> Qdenga @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by using a weakened version of the original virus strain , which triggers an immune response in the body . Since dengue has four different strains -- DEN1 , DEN2 , DEN3 , and DEN4 -- any dengue vaccine needs to ensure that it is effective against each of these strains . <p> Takeda 's vaccine is built on a DEN2 virus strain ; however , it also has structural proteins from DEN1 , DEN3 , and DEN4 , making it effective against all four strains of the virus . It has two doses , which are administered three months apart , and its efficacy does not depend on whether a person has already been infected with dengue or not . <p> The most common symptoms of dengue are fever , nausea , and flu-like symptoms . Severe dengue , however , can even cause blood haemorrhage and is a life-threatening disease . <p> Globally , more than 14 million cases of dengue are reported every year . @@139138066 <h> Without Social Commitment , Can We Truly Call Ourselves Social Beings ? <p> Human beings are often described as social creatures , a proposition that traces back to Aristotle . Yet in an age marked by widening inequality , ecological crises , digital isolation , and the weakening of democratic institutions , the meaning of being a " social being " deserves renewed examination . If our lives are fundamentally interconnected , can we legitimately claim to be social beings while neglecting our responsibilities to one another ? <p> In a thoughtful reflection , Pon Chandran argues that being social is not merely a matter of living alongside others . It requires conscious commitments that uphold justice , dignity , and collective well-being . Social existence , he suggests , is not an automatic condition of human life but an ethical practice that demands solidarity , participation , and accountability . <p> From Charity to Solidarity <p> A central argument is the distinction between charity and solidarity . Charity often assumes a relationship between giver and receiver , where assistance flows from those with surplus to those in need @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that everyone 's well-being is interconnected . <p> Economic insecurity , systemic discrimination , and climate change do not affect isolated individuals alone ; they shape the fabric of society itself . Standing with vulnerable communities , therefore , is not an act of generosity but a recognition of shared humanity and shared interests . Every individual becomes an equal stakeholder whose rights and dignity deserve protection . <p> Social Commitment in Everyday Life <p> Social responsibility extends far beyond political slogans . Chandran identifies three interconnected levels through which social commitments can be expressed . <p> The article also addresses an enduring tension : how can individuals remain committed to society without sacrificing their own well-being ? <p> Long-term social engagement , Chandran argues , requires healthy boundaries . Activists and socially conscious citizens should avoid burnout by recognising that sustainable commitment is more valuable than short-lived self-sacrifice . Equally important is democratic humility -- the willingness to listen , debate , and occasionally compromise personal preferences in pursuit of the common good . <p> This understanding rejects both selfish individualism and self-destructive martyrdom , offering instead a model @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Resisting Modern Alienation <p> Contemporary economic and technological systems increasingly encourage competition , isolation , and dependence on digital platforms . Chandran sees social commitment as a form of resistance to this growing alienation . <p> He calls for reclaiming real-world spaces where people can organise collectively , build relationships , and exercise democratic participation . Equally important is maintaining digital sovereignty by refusing to let algorithms dictate social interactions or shape public consciousness without scrutiny . <p> The second part of Chandran 's inquiry explores a deeper philosophical question : can genuine individual freedom exist without systemic responsibility ? <p> His answer is unequivocal . Freedom , he argues , requires more than the absence of external interference . People who lack education , healthcare , decent work , or economic security may possess formal legal rights but can not meaningfully exercise them . True liberty depends upon social institutions that create the material conditions necessary for individuals to realise their potential . <p> This distinction reflects the difference between negative liberty -- the mere absence of restraint -- and positive liberty , the actual capacity to lead a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ manipulation and corporate surveillance increasingly influence public opinion and personal autonomy . Effective regulation becomes necessary not to curtail liberty but to defend it . Similarly , freedoms such as dissent and free speech survive only when society collectively commits itself to protecting those who exercise them . <p> Quoting Rosa Luxemburg 's observation that " Freedom is always the freedom of the one who thinks differently , " Chandran concludes that democratic institutions must create conditions where diverse voices can flourish . Systemic accountability , rather than limiting liberty , becomes its strongest safeguard . <p> Reclaiming the Meaning of Being Social <p> The essay ultimately challenges readers to reconsider a familiar assumption . Simply living among others does not make us social beings in any meaningful sense . Genuine social existence requires active participation in creating a society founded on justice , equality , mutual care , and democratic responsibility . <p> In a world increasingly shaped by individualism and fragmentation , Chandran argues that social commitments are not optional moral virtues . They are the very conditions that make both collective life and individual freedom possible . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ human rights activist associated with the People 's Union for Civil Liberties ( PUCL ) , Coimbatore . @@139141670 <h> DCGI clears India 's first dengue vaccine QDENGA <p> New Delhi : India has approved its first vaccine to prevent dengue , with the Drug Controller General of India ( DCGI ) granting market authorisation to Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India Pvt Ltd for QDENGA ( TAK-003 ) . The approval gives the country its first licensed vaccine against a disease that places millions at risk every year and accounts for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden . Health experts say the vaccine could become an important addition to India 's dengue prevention efforts , alongside mosquito control , surveillance , early diagnosis and public awareness . QDENGA is a live attenuated tetravalent vaccine developed by Japan 's Takeda . It is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes , DENV-1 , DENV-2 , DENV-3 and DENV-4 . Unlike the earlier dengue vaccine Dengvaxia , QDENGA can be given regardless of whether a person has previously been infected with dengue and does not require pre-vaccination blood testing , a feature that could simplify large-scale vaccination programmes . <p> The vaccine has been approved in India for people aged @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 0.5 ml subcutaneous injection in a two-dose schedule , with the second dose given three months after the first . <p> Takeda said the approval is based on its global clinical development programme , which included 19 Phase I , II and III clinical trials involving more than 28,000 participants from both dengue-endemic and non-endemic regions . The authorisation is also supported by findings from the Phase III DEN-302 trial conducted in India , which evaluated the vaccine 's safety and immune response in participants aged 4 to 60 years . <p> The company also cited long-term findings from the pivotal TIDES Phase III trial , which enrolled more than 20,000 children and adolescents across eight dengue-endemic countries . After 4.5 years of follow-up , the vaccine demonstrated 84 per cent protection against dengue-related hospitalisation and around 61 per cent protection against virologically confirmed dengue . Takeda said the latest seven-year data continue to show protection against dengue infection and hospitalisation across all four virus serotypes . <p> " Since its launch in 2022 , QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries , with more than 32 million doses distributed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strengthening dengue prevention in India , " said Mahender Nayak , Head of Intercontinental Markets at Takeda . <p> QDENGA has already received approvals in more than 40 countries , including the European Union , the United Kingdom , Brazil , Indonesia and Argentina . It has also received World Health Organization prequalification , confirming that it meets international standards for quality , safety and efficacy . The certification allows procurement through agencies such as UNICEF and the Pan American Health Organization to support wider access . <p> The WHO recommends the vaccine for use in dengue-endemic settings and supports its introduction in public immunisation programmes in areas with high transmission without requiring pre-vaccination screening . <p> Goh Choo Beng , Medical Affairs Head , Southeast Asia and India Cluster at Takeda , said India faces a significant dengue burden , with all four virus serotypes circulating in several parts of the country . <p> " QDENGA is designed to protect against all four serotypes , regardless of prior exposure . Its approval represents an important step in strengthening India 's comprehensive approach to dengue prevention , alongside vector control @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , " Beng said . <p> India has witnessed a sharp rise in dengue cases over the past two decades , driven by rapid urbanisation , population growth , climate change and changing mosquito habitats . Seasonal outbreaks continue to strain healthcare facilities , particularly during the monsoon and post-monsoon months . <p> While the approval introduces a new preventive option , health authorities and experts maintain that vaccination alone can not eliminate dengue . They say mosquito control , removal of breeding sites , personal protection against mosquito bites , disease surveillance , timely diagnosis and access to healthcare will remain central to reducing transmission , especially as all four dengue virus serotypes continue to circulate . <p> Takeda has partnered with Hyderabad-based Biological E to manufacture up to 50 million doses annually in India , a move expected to improve supply and potentially lower costs over time . However , the company has not yet announced the vaccine 's price or timeline for commercial availability , and it remains unclear whether it will initially be offered through the private market or later be included in government immunisation programmes .

@@139156240 <p> A ? 2,600 crore tunnel under the Himalayas . Five accelerated hydropower projects . A treaty placed in abeyance . Pakistan threatening war . India 's Chenab push is the most consequential shift in South Asian water politics in six decades -- and the infrastructure is already under construction <p> Pakistan 's Climate Change Minister and Defence Minister have both threatened war over India 's moves . <p> The Indus Waters Treaty has survived two full-scale wars , multiple military standoffs , and six decades of fractious India-Pakistan relations . It was brokered by the World Bank and signed in 1960 , and is widely cited as one of the world 's most durable transboundary water agreements . <p> In May 2025 , following the Pahalgam terrorist attack , India placed it in abeyance . In the months since , what began as a diplomatic signal has been converted into concrete infrastructure -- tunnels , dams , and hydropower facilities on the Chenab River that are designed to outlast any future diplomatic settlement . <h> Why Is The Chenab River Central To India 's Strategy ? <p> Of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ treaty -- the Indus , Jhelum , and Chenab -- the Chenab is the most strategically accessible for India . The Chenab has been central to hydroelectric production , with projects such as Baglihar and Dul Hasti already operational . <p> Its upper tributaries , the Chandra and Bhaga , flow through Himachal Pradesh 's Lahaul-Spiti region before converging into the Chenab . That geography places the river 's headwaters within comparatively accessible terrain at a point that sits physically upstream of the treaty 's most sensitive allocation questions . <p> The Chenab-Beas Link Tunnel project aims to divert surplus water from the Chandra River in Lahaul-Spiti through an 8.7-kilometre underground tunnel beneath the Pir Panjal range into the Beas basin . Once through the tunnel and into the Beas , the diverted water enters the eastern river system -- the three rivers allocated to India under the 1960 treaty -- and can be used freely for irrigation and storage . <h> What Projects Are Being Accelerated ? <p> India has accelerated several strategic hydropower and river-linking projects on the Chenab river system . The Indian government has issued notifications @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2026 . The project is estimated at around ? 2,600 crore . Beyond the tunnel , India is accelerating work on multiple hydropower projects on the Chenab : Ratle ( 850 MW ) , Pakal Dul ( 1,000 MW ) , Kiru ( 624 MW ) , and Kwar ( 540 MW ) . <p> The Sawalkot Dam , with 1.8 million acre-feet of proposed storage , stands as a pivotal post-treaty project . Once completed , it could irrigate tens of thousands of hectares and contribute to downstream diversions . <h> How Does The Indus Waters Treaty Limit India 's Use Of Western Rivers ? <p> The Indus Waters Treaty divides the six rivers of the Indus system between India and Pakistan . The three eastern rivers -- Ravi , Beas , and Sutlej -- were allocated to India . The three western rivers -- Indus , Jhelum , and Chenab -- were allocated to Pakistan , with India permitted only limited uses : run-of-the-river hydropower projects ( which can not impound significant quantities of water ) , limited irrigation in specific areas , and certain domestic uses . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ India was prohibited from building dams on western rivers that would impound significant volumes of water , and from diverting western river flows into eastern . For six decades , treaty sensitivities , political caution , and the World Bank 's dispute-resolution oversight kept these restrictions largely in place , even during periods of severe India-Pakistan tension . India 's suspension of the treaty has changed that calculus . <h> Why Is India Seeking Renegotiation ? <p> India has advanced three arguments for renegotiation or abeyance of the treaty . The first is security : the treaty was negotiated when terrorism was not a feature of India-Pakistan relations , and India has argued that Pakistan 's use of non-state actors to attack Indian territory fundamentally changes the basis of bilateral treaties , including IWT . The Pahalgam attack , which killed 26 civilians in April 2025 , provided the most recent and most severe provocation . <p> The second argument is changed circumstances : India 's population has grown substantially since 1960 , its water needs in Jammu &amp; Kashmir and downstream states have expanded , and climate change is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ could not have anticipated . India argues that a 65-year-old treaty should be open to renegotiation to reflect these changed realities . <p> The third is asymmetry : India has argued that Pakistan has systematically obstructed treaty implementation , filed frivolous disputes at international arbitration , and refused to participate in dispute resolution mechanisms in good faith . Placing the treaty in abeyance , in this framing , is not aggression but a response to Pakistan 's own failure to honour treaty obligations . <h> What Does This Mean For Pakistan ? <p> Pakistan 's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik has warned that Islamabad would ' cut off those hands ' seeking to claim Pakistan 's share of the Indus waters . Pakistan Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has declared that Islamabad could ' go to war ' if its water security were threatened . The rhetoric reflects the depth of Pakistan 's strategic anxiety . <p> Any significant reduction in Chenab and Indus flows would have direct , catastrophic consequences for Pakistani agriculture . <p> However , Pakistan 's legal argument is considerably weaker than its political rhetoric suggests . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ specified waters ; it does not confer sovereign ownership over the rivers themselves . Since the Indus , Jhelum , and Chenab originate in Indian territory , the treaty preserved India 's territorial sovereignty while regulating utilisation of river waters between two sovereign states . <h> Could This Permanently Change South Asia 's Water Politics ? <p> The question is not whether India 's Chenab push will affect South Asian water politics -- it already has . The question is whether the infrastructure being built now will outlast whatever diplomatic settlement eventually follows , and whether that creates irreversible facts on the ground that any future Indian government would find it politically impossible to reverse . <p> For South Asia 's water politics broadly , the collapse of the IWT framework -- even partial and temporary -- removes the most successful model of transboundary water management on the subcontinent . The Brahmaputra , where China is India 's upstream neighbour , the Cauvery , where India has its own internal interstate water disputes , and the Teesta , where India and Bangladesh share a river and an incomplete treaty , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ template breaks down . <p> If India succeeds in converting treaty suspension into permanent upstream advantage , every other downstream country in South Asia will be recalculating its water security assumptions .

@@139156657 <h> Economic growth is often misunderstood as merely producing and consuming larger quantities of physical goods <p> The twenty-first century presents humanity with one of the most profound policy dilemmas in modern history : how can societies continue to improve living standards while preserving the ecological systems upon which life itself depends ? Climate change , biodiversity loss , depletion of natural resources and increasing pollution have intensified concerns about whether continuous economic growth is compatible with a planet possessing finite ecological limits . <p> The concern is neither new nor unfounded . Scientific evidence overwhelmingly demonstrates that global temperatures are rising , extreme weather events are becoming more frequent , sea levels continue to increase , and natural ecosystems are under unprecedented stress . <p> Fossil fuels still dominate global energy consumption , while the extraction of minerals , metals and other natural resources has expanded dramatically over the past five decades . These realities have prompted many scholars to question whether the prevailing economic model can remain sustainable in the long run . <p> However , an equally important question deserves careful consideration : Does the existence of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ come to an end ? <p> The answer depends upon how economic growth is understood . <p> Economic growth is often misunderstood as merely producing and consuming larger quantities of physical goods . While this description broadly characterised the Industrial Revolution , the structure of modern economies has undergone a remarkable transformation . <p> Consequently , it is essential to distinguish between growth in material consumption and growth in economic value . A nation may continue to become wealthier through improvements in productivity , technology , human capital and innovation without proportionately increasing its extraction of natural resources . <p> This does not imply that technology alone can solve every environmental problem . The well-known " rebound effect " reminds us that gains in efficiency may sometimes encourage greater overall consumption . Nevertheless , the appropriate policy response is not to abandon economic growth altogether but to ensure that technological advancement is accompanied by sound regulatory frameworks , effective pricing of environmental externalities , resource efficiency and responsible consumption . <p> Equally important is recognising that economic growth remains indispensable for many developing countries . Millions of people continue to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ education , clean drinking water and reliable electricity . For these societies , sustained economic growth is not merely an economic aspiration but a prerequisite for reducing poverty , improving public health and expanding human capabilities . <p> Environmental sustainability should therefore complement development rather than replace it . The challenge before policymakers is not whether economies should grow , but how they should grow . <p> Economic performance itself also requires broader measurement . Gross Domestic Product remains an important indicator of production and income , but it does not capture environmental degradation , public health , educational attainment , social equity or ecological resilience . Complementing GDP with indicators measuring natural capital , environmental quality , human development and social well-being would provide governments with a more comprehensive understanding of national progress . <p> The objective , therefore , should not be unlimited material expansion , nor deliberate economic contraction . Rather , it should be sustainable prosperity -- an economic system that continuously improves human well-being while respecting ecological limits . <p> The real challenge of this century is not choosing between economic growth and environmental protection @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ economic progress is increasingly decoupled from excessive resource consumption , fossil fuel dependence and environmental degradation . <p> Human civilisation has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing circumstances through science , innovation and prudent public policy . The transition toward a low-carbon , resource-efficient and knowledge-driven economy offers an opportunity to reconcile prosperity with planetary stewardship . <p> Countries that successfully integrate technological innovation , environmental responsibility , social equity and sound governance will not merely survive the coming decades -- they will define the future of sustainable development .

@@139168124 <p> Recent weeks have seen a flurry of reports from public health authorities and scientists that estimate the deaths caused by Europe 's record-breakingsummer heatwaves . <p> In France , the national public health agency reported 2,025 excess deaths over the week where the heatwave peaked in June . <p> Authorities in Germany and Netherlands put the excess death toll during the same seven-day period at 5,753 and 533 , respectively . <p> An analysis from climate scientists in Carbon Brief found that France saw more than 2,700 heat-related deaths over 17 days in June . <p> Separate research estimated there had been 2,700 heat-related deaths in the UK 's May and June heatwaves -- 42% of which had been caused by human-caused climate change . <p> There are a number of methods for how academics and governments tally deaths caused by extreme heat , each with their own advantages and drawbacks . <p> Here , Carbon Brief looks at the different ways scientists and public health authorities have calculated the death toll of Europe 's record-breaking summer heat . <p> How established is the science of calculating heat deaths @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ between heat and mortality for nearly a century . <p> A pioneering study published in 1923 by geographer Ellsworth Huntington and economist Margaret Justin that looked at mortality data for New York City over 1882-88 found that deaths increased rapidly as temperatures rose above 17C . <p> As global temperatures have risen in response to human-caused carbon emissions , scientists have increasingly sought to understand how warming could impact mortality . <p> Over the past decade , a growing number of studies have gone a step further , by estimating the number of deaths caused by a specific heatwave event and then attributing a percentage or number of those deaths to human-caused climate change . <p> The study estimated that 506 of the 735 summer fatalities in Paris and 64 of the 315 in London were a result of human influence on the climate . <p> More recently , a study in Climatic Change found that 27% of deaths in a 2018 heatwave in Zurich , Switzerland were linked to human-caused climate change and a paper in Science Advances estimated that 11-15% of deaths in a 2021 heatwave in British @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is really only in the last five to 10 years that we have seen this , partly because it does require interdisciplinary expertise . You need people who know how to run the epidemiological models and you need a climate analysis of the counterfactual world without climate change , which is its own effort . " <p> What are the different approaches to counting heat deaths ? <p> A central challenge in estimating deaths from a heatwave is that heat is rarely recorded as the primary cause of death on death certificates . <p> However , exposure to high temperatures has wide-ranging effects on the human body , including the strain of keeping cool . This effort places pressure on the heart and kidneys . <p> As a result , public health authorities and scientists can not depend on death certificates for a full count of heat-related deaths . They instead estimate heat deaths using a number of different approaches , each with assumptions baked into their calculations . <p> " We do n't know what the heat-related deaths are , so we rely on different models to describe the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from heatwaves similar to those from air pollution , he says : <p> " This sort of health-impact assessment has been done for years on studies related to deaths from air pollution , which have the same problem . Air pollution , until very recently , was not recorded on death certificates . <p> " However , for air pollution , the scientific literature is much larger , so no one questions that air pollution is toxic and kills . This sort of messaging for heat is more recent . " <p> There are , broadly speaking , two approaches to calculating deaths during a heatwave . <p> The first involves counting the number of excess deaths relative to a period in the past . <p> This method -- often referred to as an " excess deaths " approach -- looks at how many people died during a particular time period compared to a baseline period where there was no heatwave . <p> To do this , public health authorities and researchers rely on official death figures reported by country authorities . <p> The second method uses long-term mortality data @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a given place . The model that emerges can be used to infer the number of deaths from a heatwave in that place . <p> Dr Callahan -- working with Prof Andrew Dessler , director of the Texas Center for Extreme Weather at Texas A&amp;M University -- used this method to estimate that more than 2,700 people had died in France over a 17-day period in June in an analysis for Carbon Brief . <p> The majority of the figures released in the wake of Europe 's June heatwave have relied on these two methods . <p> There is a third way to calculate heat deaths , which is to look at official counts of deaths attributed on death certificates to heatstroke . <p> Callahan tells Carbon Brief that the " death-certificate coding " appears to have fallen out of favour in Europe -- which he says is a " smart move " given that it does not provide a " full accounting " . <p> Nevertheless , some public health authorities are still using this method . For example , in the wake of the heatwave in the US @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in New Jersey and three people in New York had died from " heat-related illnesses " . <p> Scientists tell Carbon Brief the excess deaths and statistical modelling approaches both have advantages and drawbacks . ( This was a slight increase from preliminary Destatis figures released a week earlier , covered by Bloomberg . ) <p> The Netherlands similarly calculates excess deaths by comparing death figures against an average of deaths in a similar period during unspecified " previous years " . <p> This is 577 more deaths than the 3,049 expected at that time of year , it said . ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ deaths reported on 4 July by NL Times based on preliminary figures from NVIM . ) <p> Callahan says that the excess deaths approach has the benefit of being rapid and relatively uncomplicated : <p> " It is something that public health authorities can put out fairly quickly without having to run a fancy model and do coding like the academic scientists do . It is a short-term , high-impact , rapid estimate of mortality . " <p> The drawback to the approach is that it is impossible to decipher what percentage of these " all-mortality " excess deaths are , in fact , heat-related . <p> Imperial College 's Konstantinoudis notes that the public often " feels more comfortable " with the excess deaths approach over the statistical modelling approach because the data it is using -- the official death numbers -- is based on real-world data . <p> However , he stresses that excess deaths figures are based on a series of assumptions , including the reference period picked by researchers and how the numbers are interpreted . <p> Statisticians and researchers have to make a series of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ baseline . For example , the baseline period could be the week before a heatwave , the same week a year before -- or an average of the same week across multiple years in the past . If averaging mortality of a similar period across a number of previous years , they must decide how much " weight " , or influence , each year should have . <p> They must also decide how to account for spikes in deaths during the Covid-19 pandemic years , as well as the gradual rise in average temperatures due to global warming . <p> A notable example of how assumptions can skew excess death figures came during this period , when the WHO estimated in 2022 that Germany had seen 195,000 excess deaths over two years of pandemic . <p> However , after statisticians and epidemiologists pointed out the assumptions in the model were not suited to Germany 's demographics , the WHO retracted the figure and eventually reduced it to 122,000 and then later to 102,000 . <p> Konstantinoudis explains : <p> " Covid taught us that it is complicated . Depending @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ you get different results ... There is a scientific basis , but we should acknowledge the assumptions . " <p> What are the pros and cons of the ' statistical modelling ' method ? <p> In the statistical modelling approach , researchers use models to determine the specific relationship between mortality and temperature for a particular location and then apply it to temperatures observed during a heatwave . <p> This allows them to estimate the overall number of deaths that were caused by a heatwave . <p> Previousresearch has revealed that , in most places of the world , there is a U-shaped response of mortality to temperature -- where deaths increase rapidly in cold or hot conditions as daily maximum temperatures depart further from an " optimum temperature " . <p> Relationship between daily high temperature and all-cause mortality rates in France , estimated using data over 2004-19 . @@139168147 <h> It 's inspiring to see the World Inequality Lab researchers directly engage in the post-growth debate with a grand vision of global economic convergence . We can only hope it spurs a peaceful mass citizens ' movement to overcome the inevitable opposition of the ultra-rich , writes Share The World 's Resources ( STWR ) <p> At the World Inequality Conference in June , the renowned economist Thomas Piketty and a team of 45 researchers from the World Inequality Lab unveiled the Global Justice Report . It 's a highly impressive and eloquent proposal to achieve ' equality and prosperity within planetary boundaries ' by the end of the century . Based on a fully quantified roadmap derived from extensive macroeconomic analysis , the 135-page report sets forth an ambitious vision : to construct a global economy that shares global wealth and achieves high well-being for all while rapidly decarbonising energy systems , thereby maintaining emissions within the relatively safe limits of 1.8 ? C. <p> This hopeful outlook provides a welcome antidote to our times , in which the world is already reeling from climate breakdown , geo-economic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ core aim of the proposal is to achieve full income convergence across all countries by 2100 , centred around a target level of ? 5,000 ( about $5,700 ) per month for every person . To achieve this , the bottom 50 percent of humanity need to increase their global wealth share from 2 percent to 30 percent . The top 0.001 percent , in contrast , would see their wealth fall from 6 percent to 0.05 percent -- a ' striking redistribution ' , to quote the report , which would essentially abolish the billionaire class . <p> A Global Justice Fund serves to administer this immense effort at international economic sharing , financed by a global wealth tax and a top income tax levied on the richest 1 percent of the world 's population . Some of the revenue raised would go into a World Sovereign Fund , which is projected to accumulate assets equivalent to 60 percent of world GDP and replace tax revenue as the main source of financing . Country dividends are designed to be distributed on an equal per-capita basis , therefore providing more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ than currently allocated to development aid . These funds also come with strong conditionalities in terms of climate investments , inequality targets , and health and education expenditures . <p> A vision of sufficiency <p> The main novelty of the report is to put the concept of sufficiency at the centre of its analysis , rightly arguing that we can not stay within a 2 ? C carbon budget if the entire human population adopts a rich-world lifestyle of high private consumption . Sufficiency , as the report defines it , therefore requires more than halving average working time to 1,000 hours , roughly the equivalent of a two-and-a-half-day standard week . <p> This needs to be accompanied by a significant shift from material to immaterial sectors , such as health and education , which in turn would help refocus the economy toward low-consumption activities . A substantial change in food habits and reduced meat consumption could also allow for a strict deforestation ban , freeing up arable land while scaling down high-emitting agricultural practices . At the same time , sufficiency in production and consumption patterns must be combined @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and enabled by the Global Justice Fund . <p> All this can read , at times , as a wish list of sustainability concepts and policies long espoused by environmental thinkers . But the work of the Global Justice Project is far wider in scope than Piketty 's best-selling tome , Capital in the Twenty-First Century , which famously used vast historical and economic data to argue the case for a progressive global tax on wealth . Back in 2015 , we at STWR and others criticised the book for failing to take seriously the ecological limits to growth and planetary boundaries . So it 's inspiring to see the World Inequality Lab authors directly engaging in this debate , fully denouncing the rhetoric of ' green growth ' that assumes we can address environmental challenges by indefinitely increasing the size of the pie without reducing inequality , consuming less or sharing resources globally . <p> Sharing environmental space <p> Their new report argues that technology alone is not enough to achieve rapid decarbonisation . They acknowledge that to manage the green transition globally within a strict carbon budget , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ radically downscale their resource and energy demands with near-zero growth in GDP . This will clear the ecological and carbon space needed for poorer countries of the Global South to continue growing their economies , enabling a fast energy transition while guaranteeing essential public services and a decent standard of living to all people . <p> It is hardly a novel framing of the issue , but the report emphasises how their Sustainable Convergence Scenario entails a form of ' class-based reparatory justice ' , in that the very rich -- who have benefited the most from fossil-based global economic growth in recent decades -- will primarily fund the Global Justice Platform . What 's more , the proposal is somewhat aligned with the concept of climate equity , and effectively translates the principle of ' common but differentiated responsibilities ' into quantitative policies for addressing climate change . <p> Another strength of the report is how it connects macroeconomic and environmental projections directly to questions of international institutional reform . It centrally highlights the need for a broader overhaul and democratisation of the global economic and monetary system , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Central Bank that issues its own reserve currency . This would eliminate the exorbitant privilege of the US dollar and other major currencies that can borrow at much lower rates , ending a massive reverse redistribution of wealth from Global South countries to the Global North . <p> All other international institutions would be governed by strict rules and equal voting rights , further eradicating the special privileges and veto powers of dominant nations . A new international order would include the reform of World Trade Organisation rules and a reset of dispute settlement mechanisms . And the large financial resources allocated to the Global Justice Fund would de facto underwrite a major restructuring of the entire UN system , strengthening its many agencies , human rights protections and international laws . <p> From plutocracy to democracy <p> As the report affirms , these proposals to transform global governance from ' plutocracy to democracy ' are closely related to many other existing frameworks and initiatives . The Bridgetown Initiative in 2022 , for example , also stresses the complementary role of global wealth taxation and international monetary reform . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tax system and curbing illicit financial flows , while the G20 initiatives led by Brazil and South Africa also champion global wealth taxes to fund climate policies and green energy transitions . <p> There are numerous other networks and organisations that aim toward similar tax and governance reforms , such as the work of Progressive International with their Program of Action on the Construction of a New International Economic Order . The Stiglitz Commission of 2010 and Brandt Commission of 1980 are gladly cited by the Global Justice Report as complementary discussions surrounding the reform of the international monetary and reserve system . <p> Above all , the report authors deservedly mention the Roadmap for Eradicating Poverty Beyond Growth -- a major project coordinated by the former UN Special Rapporteur on extreme poverty and human rights , Olivier De Schutter , that puts forward an exhaustive policy toolkit for building a global economy with human rights and ecological justice at its core . Thomas Piketty and many other prominent economists have put their names to this plan , which is one of the most comprehensive policy documents of recent years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ increased South-South cooperation , reparative climate finance and support for universal social protection floors . De Schutter 's pioneering proposal for a Global Fund for Social Protection is arguably a less utopian prospect for closing chronic financing gaps in low-income countries , building upon existing structures like the UN 's International Labour Organisation and seeking more immediately viable sources of international financing . <p> The operative question , as always , is how the political conditions will arise to implement these policies as an alternative to the far-right techno-authoritarian vision being championed by reactionary political elites and their billionaire supporters . Together , they describe a more complex hazard profile than most existing food safety testing protocols , calibrated for single category risks , were ever designed to catch in a single pass . <p> Most testing protocols were built around a specific question , whether a product contains a particular pathogen or exceeds a particular pesticide threshold , he says , and that single variable approach made sense when the risks themselves were relatively independent of each other . <p> What @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is forcing those risks to interact in ways a single category test simply can not capture . @@139185109 <h> Why removing salmon could change Kamchatka 's entire ecosystem <p> Bear Sits on the Shore of Kuril Lake and Looks at Ilinsky Vulcan ( iStock ) <p> Far away in Russia 's northeast lies the Kamchatka Peninsula , one of the last truly wild places on Earth . Snow-covered volcanoes rise above dense forests . Brown bears roam riverbanks . Steller 's sea eagles wait patiently on tall trees . Crystal-clear rivers cut through valleys that have changed little for thousands of years.This landscape appears to be shaped by mountains , glaciers , and weather . But scientists say another force keeps this wilderness alive : salmon.Every year , millions of Pacific salmon leave the ocean and return to the exact rivers where they were born . They battle currents , leap waterfalls , escape predators , lay their eggs , and then die . It may sound like a tragic ending , but it is also the beginning of new life for almost everything around them . <h> A fish that feeds forests , not just rivers <p> Most people think salmon are important because they are food @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spend years growing in the nutrient-rich Pacific Ocean . During that time , they store valuable nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus inside their bodies . When they swim back upstream to spawn , they carry those marine nutrients hundreds of kilometres inland . <p> After spawning , Pacific salmon die naturally . Their bodies slowly decompose in rivers and along riverbanks , releasing those nutrients into the soil and water.Scientists studying the Kol River in Kamchatka found that nearby willow and cottonwood trees contain marine nitrogen that originally came from salmon . Even insects , microbes , fungi , and aquatic plants depend on this nutrient cycle.In other words , the forests are being fertilised by fish.Without returning salmon , rivers would receive far fewer nutrients each year . Over time , forests could grow less vigorously , insects would decline , and the food web would begin to weaken . <h> Bears , eagles and countless animals depend on salmon <p> Kamchatka supports one of the world 's largest populations of brown bears . During the salmon season , bears gather along rivers to feed on fish rich @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fish . They often drag salmon into nearby forests and consume only the fattiest parts , leaving the rest behind.Those leftovers become food for scavengers and eventually break down into the soil , spreading marine nutrients well beyond the riverbanks.The effects would ripple through the ecosystem in ways that are difficult to reverse . <h> The danger is bigger than losing one species <p> One remarkable finding from scientists working in Kamchatka is that salmon help create the very conditions future salmon need to survive.Healthy forests shade rivers , keeping the water cool . Fallen trees create pools where young fish can hide from predators . Leaves that fall into streams feed insects , which later become food for juvenile salmon.Everything is connected.Professor Kirill Kuzishchin of Moscow State University , who has studied the Kol River ecosystem , summed it up simply : " Everything is connected . " If salmon disappear , rivers lose nutrients . Weaker rivers support fewer insects and fewer young fish . That means even fewer salmon return in future generations . It becomes a cycle of decline . <h> Human choices , not nature @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ least one-fifth of the world 's wild Pacific salmon spawning populations , making it globally important for conservation.The problem is that salmon today face challenges largely created by people rather than by nature.Salmon are under mounting pressure from illegal fishing , overharvesting , and poaching driven by the caviar trade , plus roads pushing into once-remote areas and industrial development . On top of that , scientists warn climate change could shift river temperatures and water flow , adding yet another wildcard.Disclaimer : This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only . It is based on scientific research and documented observations of Kamchatka 's ecosystems . Ecological systems are complex , and conservation outcomes depend on multiple environmental , social , and policy factors . <p> The TOI Lifestyle Desk is a dynamic team of dedicated journalists who , with unwavering passion and commitment , sift through the pulse of the nation to curate a vibrant tapestry of lifestyle news for The Times of India readers . One of India 's largest engineering projects , the Rs 44,605-crore Ken-Betwa Link Project , had begun reshaping the landscape . <p> Advertisement <p> After decades of uncertainty , the project to link the Ken and Betwa rivers has entered a decisive phase , triggering a race to evacuate nearly 2,000 families across 10 villages -- a rushed deadline that has fuelled protests across the submergence zone as residents challenge compensation surveys , eligibility lists and the terms on which they are being asked to leave . <p> For the administration , the remaining months are about meeting engineering timelines , completing rehabilitation and clearing the reservoir before the next phase of construction . For the many families still living in the shadow of the Daudhan dam -- one of the main architectural features under the project -- it 's a struggle of a different kind : proving , through Aadhaar cards , school certificates , revenue records and decades-old family registers , that they belong to the places they are being asked to abandon . <h> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's rivers dates back to the early 1980s . The National Water Development Agency , set up in 1982 to examine the feasibility of interlinking river basins , identified the Ken-Betwa Link , as a priority project . The project , India 's first inter-basin river link , aims to transfer water from the Ken to the Betwa basin . <p> Advertisement <p> A feasibility report followed in 1995 , and in August 2005 , Madhya Pradesh , Uttar Pradesh and the Centre agreed to prepare a Detailed Project Report . The Union Cabinet finally approved the project in December 2021 , transforming the landscape around the rivers into construction sites . <p> Officials say that once ready , the project will irrigate 9.04 lakh hectares , utilise more than 4,843 million cubic metres of water , generate 103 MW of hydropower and 27 MW of solar energy , and supply nearly 194 million cubic metres of drinking water each year . <p> The irrigation network will extend across some of the most parched districts of Bundelkhand such as Chhatarpur , Tikamgarh , Panna , Damoh , Vidisha , Sagar @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Banda , Mahoba , Jhansi and Lalitpur in Uttar Pradesh . <p> Ongoing construction at the site of the Daudhan reservoir , which is proposed to have a gross storage capacity of 2,953 million cubic metres . ( Source : Express Photo ) <p> At the heart of the project is the Daudhan dam planned across the Ken river in Madhya Pradesh -- a structure that stretches for more than 2 km . The reservoir of the dam is designed to hold 2,853 million cubic metres of water , while two proposed power stations at the site are expected to generate more than 219 million units of electricity annually . <p> Water from the Daudhan reservoir will flow through a 218.6-km link canal ( which gives the Ken-Betwa Link project its name ) into the Betwa basin . The network also includes other irrigational structures such as the Lower Orr Project , the Kotha Barrage , the Bina Complex Multipurpose Project across Sagar and Raisen districts and the restored Ken Canal System in Uttar Pradesh . <p> Construction gathered pace in April 2025 . Acquisition proceedings covering nearly 28 hectares are underway , with notifications issued in some cases and records still being processed in others . Water pipelines , electricity lines and government structures within the project 's right of way also remain incomplete , said a project engineer . <p> But the biggest set of unresolved tasks concerns rehabilitation . Villages within the submergence zone must be evacuated before construction can proceed in full . <p> Water from the Daudhan reservoir will flow through a 218.6-km link canal ( which gives the Ken-Betwa Link project its name ) into the Betwa basin . @@139185581 <p> Prices of palm oil , which forms the bulk of India 's edible oil imports , have risen for five straight months . ( Pexels Photo ) <p> Summary <p> India 's domestic edible oil industry is worried about the surge in edible oil imports from Nepal which , they say , is distorting the market . They also want the government to verify that the duty-free benefit is not being misused . <p> This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.Subscribe to enjoy similar stories . <p> Duty-free imports of refined edible oils from Nepal to India , the world 's largest edible oil importer , surged 17-fold to 804,000 tonnes in 2025 from 47,295 tonnes in 2023 . These imports touched 284,976 tonnes in the first five months of 2026 , posing a key concern for India 's vegetable oil industry . Mint explains the jump in the backdrop of Nepal 's limited edible oil domestic production . <h> Why are Indian edible oil producers concerned over duty-free imports from Nepal ? <p> According to the industry , the surge in imports from Nepal distorts the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for Indian processors . <p> Imports from Nepal enjoy preferential treatment under the South Asian Free Trade Area agreement , which allows member countries to export eligible goods at concessional or zero customs duty , provided they meet the prescribed rules of origin . <p> Comparatively , India levies import duty of 16.5% on crude edible oils and 35.75% on refined oil for countries under the most favoured nation route . <h> How does the surge affect India 's domestic refining industry ? <p> India , the world 's largest importer of edible oils , remains structurally dependent on overseas supplies as domestic production meets only 40% of its total requirement . India imports about 60% of its edible oil consumption of 24 million-25 million tonnes annually . <p> India primarily imports crude edible oil rather than refined oil as part of its value-addition strategy . Crude oils such as palm , soybean and sunflower are processed at domestic refineries before reaching consumers . This policy supports local refining capacity , generates employment , attracts investment and creates demand for allied industries such as packaging and logistics . <p> India @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on crude oils to ensure that value-addition takes place within India . However , the rapid increase in duty-free imports of refined edible oils from Nepal has altered this balance . <p> The rising volume of duty-free imports also has implications for customs revenue , estimated by the industry at ? 2,000 crore-2,500 crore annually . <h> How are oilseed farmers affected ? <p> Domestic refining creates demand for locally produced oilseeds such as soybean and mustard , which support millions of Indian farmers . If refiners lose market share to imported refined oil , domestic crushing and refining operations could slow , reducing demand for locally produced oilseeds . <p> Lower refining activity reduces demand for domestically produced oilseeds -- particularly soybean and mustard -- exerting downward pressure on farm-gate prices and affecting farmer incomes in major producing states such as Madhya Pradesh , Maharashtra and Rajasthan . This undermines the objectives of the National Mission on Edible Oils , minimum support price operations and the government 's vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat by weakening the domestic oilseed value chain . <h> Do the imports raise concerns over rules of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ agreement , products qualify for duty-free access if they meet the prescribed rules of origin . This ensures sufficient value addition in the exporting country and is intended to prevent the routing of goods made in a non-member country to claim duty-free access . <p> Experts said Nepal has limited domestic production of palm oil and soybean , making it important for Indian authorities to verify whether the refined oils it exports satisfy origin requirements . <h> What has the industry asked the government to do ? <p> The industry has urged the government to review the surge in duty-free refined edible oil imports from Nepal . <p> The industry has called for stricter implementation of rules of origin and to verify that imports from Nepal meet the rules of origin prescribed under the South Asian Free Trade Area agreement . Verification would ensure that preferential tariffs are extended only to products that genuinely qualify for the benefit . <p> It has also called for a review of the current tariff structure to preserve incentives for domestic refining . The objective is not to restrict legitimate trade with Nepal but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and maintain a level playing field for domestic refiners . <h> About the Author <p> Vijay C. @@139186790 <p> Traditional and Indigenous food knowledge can help build healthier and more sustainable food systems , according to a new study . <p> Researchers from the University of East Anglia 's ( UEA ) Schools of Global Development and Education and Lifelong Learning looked at 39 peer-reviewed studies from around the world , a statement by the UEA said . <p> The scientists found that while Indigenous and traditional food knowledge is increasingly recognised as a solution to interconnected crises such as climate change , biodiversity loss , and poor health and nutrition , health and nutrition education and practice continue to be dominated by top-down , medicalised approaches . <p> They examined how food systems literacy - defined as the knowledge , skills and communication practices that help people engage with food systems - can be strengthened to support healthier , more equitable and environmentally sustainable outcomes . <p> They say this is an important , though often overlooked element of food systems resilience , involving nuanced knowledge of different elements of the food system , from food production to preparation and consumption . <p> The review , published @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ explored how different worldviews and approaches to knowledge production influence health and nutrition interventions involving Indigenous communities . <p> The findings suggest that culturally grounded and participatory approaches are essential for improving food systems literacy and supporting communities to maintain and revitalise traditional food practices . <p> Lead author Nitya Rao , of the School of Global Development , said : " Existing food systems are failing to adequately address global hunger and malnutrition , with over 600 million people projected to face food insecurity by 2030 . <p> " By identifying both challenges and examples of good practice , our review provides important insights for policymakers , educators , health practitioners and community organisations seeking to develop more inclusive approaches to food and nutrition education . <p> " As governments and organisations seek solutions to the interconnected challenges of climate change , biodiversity loss and public health , the findings suggest that greater attention to Indigenous knowledge systems could help create food systems that are more sustainable , resilient , equitable and better equipped to meet future challenges . " <p> Drawing on case studies from Indigenous communities across @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ diverse forms of knowledge and fostering meaningful participation by these communities in the design and delivery of health and nutrition initiatives . <p> Integrating local and Indigenous languages also improves communication , cultural relevance , and inclusivity in both research and health promotion . <p> The researchers gave the examples of integrating the perspectives of the K'iche ' Maya indigenous group into Guatemalan Food Guidelines and co-designing a mobile health app with Maori and Pasifika partners using culturally grounded language , narratives , and visuals . <p> In contrast , the review noted that conventional health and nutrition programmes often prioritise technical and biomedical knowledge , which can overlook cultural contexts and the value of Indigenous expertise . This can limit community engagement and reduce the effectiveness of interventions , it said . <p> While linguistic diversity and the lack of equivalent biomedical terminology do present challenges , interpreter services and community-led health promotion can help bridge knowledge gaps and support equitable care . The studies highlight the need to reconcile Indigenous and Western health worldviews through collaborative approaches . <p> Communication methods such as storytelling , talking circles , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and smartphone apps were found to enhance engagement and support effective health and nutrition interventions . <p> Rao , who is also Director of the Norwich Institute for Sustainable Development , added : " Reclaiming and recognising Indigenous knowledge , values and practices to address the different elements of nutrition and health involves recognising intergenerational and wider social relations , and engaging everyone from the elders , healers , educators and farmers to service providers , policymakers and academics , to together raise issues and find solutions . " <p> The authors concluded that strengthening food systems literacy through collaborative , culturally relevant and community-led approaches , offers significant opportunities to improve health and wellbeing , while also supporting broader environmental and social goals .

These elements are essential to the manufacture of rare-earth permanent magnets -- high-performance components used in electric vehicle ( EV ) motors , wind turbines , consumer electronics , defence equipment , and a growing range of clean-energy technologies . <p> As countries race to decarbonise their economies , demand for these minerals is rising sharply . The powerful magnets that drive EVs rely on rare earth elements , making the automotive sector one of the fastest-growing sources of demand .
