@@139204336 <h> An Assessment of the Taliban 's Foreign Policy <h> An Assessment of the Taliban 's Foreign Policy <p> The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan is today much more favourably placed than when it came to power in August 2021 after overthrowing the then Republic government . While only Russia has granted it de jure recognition so far , the Emirate has met with some success in leveraging the changed international environment and the current global security situation to its advantage , with most of the countries in its region and beyond engaging with it in some capacity , even as it fails to heed international calls for inclusivity and respect for women 's rights . This brief examines the Taliban 's foreign policy since its return to power , focusing particularly on how the regime frames its foreign policy priorities . It attempts to understand the Emirate 's emphasis on a ' balanced , economy-centred ' foreign policy and what this means vis- ? -vis its engagement with the world . <h> Introduction <p> On 9 March 2026 , United States ( US ) Secretary of State Marco Rubio designated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . 1 In his statement , he stressed the Taliban 's " continued " use of terrorist tactics to win concessions and earn ransom . He demanded the release of three US citizens detained by the Taliban and called on it to stop practicing " hostage diplomacy " . The Emirate in its response , urged the United States to resolve the issue appropriately by continuing the constructive discussions that the two sides had held on to the matter. 2 Subsequently , the Taliban released one of the detainees , Dennis Coyle , on humanitarian grounds and in a " spirit of goodwill . " 3 <p> In December 2025 , Australia sanctioned four top Taliban members -- three government ministers and the Supreme Court Chief Justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani -- imposing travel bans on them and freezing their assets in Australia -- for violations of women 's rights. 4 Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said this " autonomous sanctions framework " , was intended to hold the Taliban accountable . In July 2025 , the International Criminal Court ( ICC ) also issued arrest warrants against the Taliban 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ justice , Haqqani , for their persecution of Afghan girls and women . On both these issues , the Emirate released a strongly worded statement , deriding the sanctions as a Western tool to punish nations which hold views different from Western ideals and principles , and explaining the country 's violations of women 's rights as a matter of cultural differences with the West . The spokesperson stressed that its legal system was premised on the principles of Islamic Sharia law , which absolve the current government of any obligations undertaken by previous governments. 5 This mention of sharia and the Quran has been a consistent feature of the Taliban-led Emirate and is reflective of its ideological roots . <p> Running parallel to these censures is a gradual increase in the degree of global engagement with the Islamic Emirate . Russia 's decision to grant it formal recognition in July 2025 -- the first country to do so -- and following this up by signing a military-technical cooperation agreement on 27 May 2026 is the highest degree of diplomatic normalisation by any country . Beyond this , the Taliban @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Iran , the Central Asian Republics , and the countries in the Gulf -- are also growing , with the accreditation of Taliban-appointed ambassadors by many countries . It has also taken over the Republic regime 's consulates in several countries in Europe , including Germany and Spain . While the initial opposition to the Taliban centred on the lack of inclusivity in its government , its clampdown on women 's and minority rights , and its links to transnational terrorist networks , in the almost half a decade since their return , countries have tweaked the importance they assign to these considerations in order to secure their security and strategic considerations . <p> This brief highlights the primary planks on which the regime is engaging with the rest of the world and how it is leveraging the international context and the security situation to lend legitimacy to its rule . <h> Change or Continuity ? <p> In the immediate aftermath of the Taliban 's return , there was much apprehension about what a second regime would mean for regional politics and for other countries ' engagement with Afghanistan @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ policies it had pursued during its first stint in 1996-2001 , especially regarding women , minorities , local governance , and inclusivity . Despite this , global appetite for supporting anti-Taliban resistance grew bleak once the final National Resistance Front ( NRF ) stronghold was toppled in Panjshir . <p> From the start , the Taliban made little concession to world opinion in tangible terms , despite knowing that being inclusive could facilitate global recognition . Their emphasis was on softening the perception of their regime amongst the international community as well as their domestic constituents . While materially things remained as they were -- the first caretaker cabinet , formed in September 2021 , comprised an all-male , Pashtun coterie , 6 women were banned from completing schooling beyond primary school with restrictions placed on their employment as well , supporters of the Republic-era government were hounded and attacked , minorities were targeted -- the refurbished Emirate continued to make strong claims about a changed " Taliban 2.0 " . Almost five years later , the Taliban has solidified its control over the country and disproving assumptions about the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ policy decisions clamping down on the rights of women and minorities and perpetuating its own interpretation of sharia . The pressure tactics adopted by the international community have thus far failed to bring any change in the Taliban 's policies . The case against pressure tactics argues that it pushes the hardliners within the group against engaging with the West while diverting the focus of the pragmatists towards retaining internal consolidation. 7 The persisting distrust between the regime and the West is also seen as a reason why the Taliban are wary of giving in to calls for change from the international community , as they are not certain of being rewarded with the concession they seek . <p> Thus , the Islamic Emirate has retained many aspects of its first regime , though it has also shifted its position in some areas . Unlike during its first stint , when it was virtually closed to the outside world , it has been using Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements , senior leadership press conferences , and social media to establish the principles that define its engagement with the world . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Kabul , the narrative of the group 's victory and the inevitability of its return was in no small measure achieved through its utilisation of social media. 8 Public diplomacy through social media is a major tool through which the Islamic Emirate is making a case for legitimising its regime . The inherited bureaucratic structure also provides it with a framework which is more robust and organised than during its previous tenure . It has also positioned itself as better prepared to govern and engage with the world than during its first stint and has demonstrated complexity in its dealings. 9 <p> The Taliban wants to refine its image , and distance itself from its insurgent past . Hence , visits by leaders of other countries and invitations to visit by neighbouring countries are seen as diplomatic successes. 10 In 2025 , as per the Emirate 's spokesperson , Taliban leaders undertook approximately 99 high-level foreign visits. 11 Ever since it signed the Doha agreement with the US in February 2020 , following which US troops were withdrawn from Afghanistan , every diplomatic engagement it has undertaken has been portrayed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ analyses of its foreign policy had pointed to the Taliban 's lack of understanding of other countries and its inconsistent messaging. 12 It was a closed society , where its perspective could only be gauged by analysing their radio propaganda and their letters to the United Nations ( UN ) . Its main objective then was to achieve de jure recognition and occupy Afghanistan 's seat in the UN General Assembly . The context in which the Taliban first came to power was also different . Three countries -- Pakistan , Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates -- granted it de jure recognition , but beyond those , the Emirate remained globally isolated , more so after it refused to extradite Osama bin Laden following the September 2001 attacks in the US . Attracting investment was also a consideration , though far from successful , as the September 2001 attacks had stopped any possible investment in the mining sector and other areas from private US companies. 13 The then Emir , Mullah Omar , placed Islamic principles above international norms , laws , opinion or organisations , showing no @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's discriminatory policies towards women and assault on individual freedom and rights. 14 The emphasis was on retaining power rather than developing foreign relations and indeed , many maintain that the Taliban 's foreign policy at the time became a victim of its domestic agenda . Lobbying by global women 's groups thwarted any attempts to gain legitimacy. 15 <p> In its second stint , the Taliban has changed as much as the international environment. 16 Though recognition remains an issue , the Emirate has found ways to sidestep it , while doubling down on connectivity and economic engagement even as countries seek ways through which they can secure their strategic interests . But this pragmatism , based on which the Taliban maintains its foreign policy outreach , is also under the shadow of the growing concentration of power by the Emir , with a tussle between the more pragmatic group centred in Kabul and the power centre in Kandahar . <h> State of the Economy <p> The humanitarian situation in Afghanistan when the Taliban took control was dire and has worsened over the past four years . The return @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cessation of humanitarian and development aid under the US Agency for International Development ( USAID ) programmes. 17 As a result , the number of people the United Nations and its agencies can now support with humanitarian assistance in Afghanistan has fallen from 22 million to 12 million ( out of a population of around 43 million ) . Frequent earthquakes , floods and droughts , apart from the pressure created by the continued return of around 6.04 million Afghan refugees between 15 September 2023 to 31 May 2026 from both Iran and Pakistan , have exacerbated the situation , increasing the country 's population by close to 10 to 12 percent and decreasing remittances . While the economy has seen a growth rate of 4.8 percent as per the World Bank 's May Development Update , the structural factors constraining growth continue to persist -- weak income , increasing prices , climate change , a growing population and declining humanitarian assistance -- with no improvement in the standard of living of the people. 18 <p> The Emirate 's perception management emphasises the stability of the country because of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ domestic manufacturing , and the ongoing work on infrastructure projects as markers of development and growth. 19 But the situation on the ground is precarious . The sources of Afghanistan 's annual budget as well as its allocations remain opaque , while there are reports about the diversion of funds towards security- and defence-related expenditures from other heads. 20 The spending in the first half of 2025 saw US$835 million on security-related expenditures , roughly 46 percent of total expenditure , while US$980 million , or approximately 54 percent , was for all other expenditures combined . There is less room for development spending . <h> Understanding the Taliban 's Diplomacy <p> For the Taliban in its second stint , one means of securing domestic legitimacy has been through foreign policy and external engagement . With consistent messaging and advertising of visits to other countries as diplomatic wins , it seeks to solidify its standing domestically and make a case for its transition from an insurgency to a government . Its narrative on social media repeatedly highlights how its predecessor Republic government was a puppet of its " Western masters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ external pressure . Its official website , Al-Emarah , posts articles on visits and regional and international developments , countering all negative reports while further propagating favourable assessments of the regime , like on the state of the economy . The website 's content is supervised by the Cultural Commission , led by the spokesperson of the regime , thus reflecting internal sanction . The group had started posting in English on Twitter ( now X ) from 2011 onwards. 21 The use of social media to present its point of view and its emphasis on countering negative news reflect the growing importance the Emirate attaches to international opinion . Its Deputy Minister for the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice , Sheikh Mohamed Khalif Hanafi , urged the media not to engage in negative propaganda but to bring administrative lapses to the government 's attention and pass on constructive criticism . <p> A major aspect of its outreach is the narrative about its openness towards engaging with the international community . To that end , it highlights the return of security and stability in the country and the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ containment of the growth of the ISKP within the country is seen as an important achievement . The Taliban consider these factors important enough for the Western countries to engage with it , instead of focusing on questions of women 's rights and inclusivity. 22 It also seeks to present its diplomatic outreach as based on a balanced , economically oriented , pragmatic , and non-interfering foreign policy , while committing not to allow its territory to be used to undermine other countries ' security interests . The emphasis is on etching mutually beneficial bilateral ties and engaging in regional forums and initiatives , even if recognition is not immediately forthcoming. 23 As per the United Nations Security Council 's sixteenth Analytics Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team report released in December 2025 , 28 foreign missions and international organisations have representation in Kabul , while the Emirate has 42 representative offices abroad . <h> Incentive to Engage : What is Driving this Engagement ? <p> A factor driving engagement with the regime is the presence of different terror groups within Afghanistan , with certain reports pegging the total number at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ denies the presence of any terror groups within the country , reports about the presence of the Islamic State Khorasan Province ( ISKP ) , Al Qaeda , Al Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent , and the East Turkestan Islamic Movement ( ETIM ) signal the security risks emanating from Afghanistan . While the Taliban has undertaken targeted killings of ISKP members , it still has a presence in the south and east of the country with growing fears about its capability to undertake transnational attacks . Al Qaeda is also intact , prioritising large-scale attacks , and aiding and assisting other terror groups in training and advice . As per the UN , the AQIS also has a presence in southeastern Afghanistan. 24 <p> Contrary to what the Emirate says , the ISKP has been targeting recruits from the Central Asian countries , which are also concerned about the growing movement of fighters from their countries to Afghanistan . Thus , the country 's unfortunate location as a hub for different terror groups is seen as a major driver for engagement. 25 China , for example , shares a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which has been a transit point for ETIM militants to enter China. a , 26 Following the breakup of the erstwhile Union of Soviet Socialist Republics ( USSR ) , Russia no longer borders Afghanistan , but it still fears that members of the ISKP and related militant groups , could target it. 27 <p> In September 2023 , China appointed an ambassador to Afghanistan , Zhao Xing , becoming the first country to do so . In turn , the Emirate appointed Bilal Karimi in December , whose credentials were subsequently accepted by Chinese President Xi Jinping . Russia granted de jure recognition to the regime in July 2025 , becoming the first country to do so . The ISKP had already launched attacks on Russian interests in Afghanistan as well as attacks within Russia . In January 2026 , Moscow also accepted the credentials of the Taliban 's ambassador to the country . On 27 May 2026 , the two sides signed a military defence deal . While the details about the deal have not been made public , it is seen as a technical military deal , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Taliban possess with no mention of a mutual security assurance. 28 Notwithstanding this , the Taliban 's leaders perceive and project this as a strong signalling from a major partner . The timing of the agreement is also particularly pertinent because of the situation at its volatile border with Pakistan , with the two countries engaged in a crisis since February . <p> The Central Asian Republics -- Kazakhstan , Kyrgyzstan , Turkmenistan , Uzbekistan and Tajikistan -- have also engaged with the Emirate to mitigate their security risks. 29 Kazakhstan removed the group from its terror list in December 2023 and Uzbekistan has increased its engagements with the country . While Tajikistan 's engagement has been comparatively more limited than that of the other republics , recent attacks targeting Chinese personnel and drug smuggling networks late last year have led to talks between the two sides . @@139247365 <h> 8 people entered a sealed glass world believing they could survive for two years . Then the oxygen began to disappear <p> Deep in the Arizona desert near Oracle sits one of the strangest experiments ever built , a sealed , 3.14-acre glass and steel enclosure called Biosphere 2 . Constructed between 1987 and 1991 at a cost of roughly $150 million , funded largely by Texas billionaire Edward Bass , it was designed to test whether humans could live inside a fully self-sustaining artificial ecosystem , complete with its own ocean , rainforest , desert , savannah and farmland . On 26 September 1991 , four men and four women , known as biospherians , sealed themselves inside for what was meant to be a two-year mission . What followed became one of the most closely watched , and ultimately most controversial , science experiments of the decade . <h> Why Biosphere 2 was built in the first place <p> The facility took its name from the idea that Earth itself is Biosphere 1 , and this artificial version was meant to model it in miniature . According @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the project , the enclosure was built as a materially closed ecological system , meaning almost nothing was meant to pass between the inside and outside world except sunlight . Beyond its scientific goals , the project was also framed as an early test of the kind of closed life support systems that future space colonies on the moon or Mars might eventually require , with the crew farming their own food and recycling their own water , waste and air . <h> How oxygen quietly began disappearing from the sealed atmosphere <p> Roughly three months into the mission , the crew began noticing a troubling pattern in their regular air quality tests : oxygen levels that had started at a normal 20.9 per cent were steadily falling . According to the peer-reviewed paper titled Oxygen loss in Biosphere 2 , published in Eos , Transactions American Geophysical Union , by researcher Jeffrey Severinghaus and colleagues including Wallace Broecker of Columbia University 's Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory , oxygen levels dropped from 21 per cent to just 14 per cent over the first sixteen months of closure , a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crew inside . <h> The chemistry that explained the missing oxygen <p> The mystery deepened because the drop in oxygen did not match up with a corresponding rise in carbon dioxide , the gas normally released whenever oxygen is consumed through respiration . Severinghaus and his co-authors identified the cause : microbes in the facility 's unusually rich soil were consuming oxygen at a much faster rate than expected , but crucially , the carbon dioxide they produced was reacting with calcium hydroxide in the building 's exposed concrete to form calcium carbonate , a process called carbonation . This meant carbon was effectively being locked away into the walls themselves , masking the true scale of the oxygen loss and making the problem far harder to diagnose in real time . <h> A crew breathing air equivalent to a Himalayan peak <p> By January 1993 , conditions inside had become severe enough that outside intervention was required . Mark Nelson , one of the original eight crew members , later wrote for the University of Arizona Press that the crew had been living with oxygen levels around 14 per @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ elevation , despite the facility itself sitting at only around 3,900 feet in southern Arizona . Nelson described the moment Mission Control finally pumped supplemental oxygen into the sealed structure , raising internal levels to 26 per cent , higher than Earth 's normal atmosphere , and recalled feeling decades younger within minutes , along with hearing the sound of crew members running for the first time in many months . <h> Why the intervention mattered for the project 's scientific standing <p> The need for outside oxygen fundamentally changed how the mission was judged . As a demonstration of a truly self-sustaining closed habitat , the first mission did not succeed on its own terms , since a system that requires external resupply to keep its occupants safe can not be considered fully closed . At the same time , the episode produced a genuinely valuable scientific finding : the interaction between rich soil , microbial respiration and curing concrete had not been anticipated at the design stage , and diagnosing it added real , lasting insight into how closed ecological systems actually behave under sustained real-world conditions . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ oxygen crisis , tension within the crew itself became a major part of the story . According to NPR 's coverage of the project , disagreements among the eight biospherians over how the project should be managed became international headline material , often overshadowing the underlying science entirely . By the time the crew emerged in September 1993 after completing their full two-year mission , the original group had split into two factions that reportedly were no longer on speaking terms with each other , following stress from cramped shared quarters , food shortages caused by lower-than-expected crop yields , and disputes over the project 's direction . <h> What happened to Biosphere 2 after the first mission ended <p> A second , shorter mission began in 1994 but lasted only about six months before being cut short . Ownership of the facility subsequently changed hands several times , and Columbia University took over managing its research programme for a period in the mid to late 1990s before eventually stepping back . In 2007 , the facility was donated to the University of Arizona , which continues to operate it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ now employing dozens of staff , including researchers studying rainforest dynamics , ocean acidification and climate change using the same sealed biomes originally built for the Biospheres . <h> A troubled experiment that still shapes science today <p> Despite its rocky beginnings and lingering reputation as a 1990s punchline , complete with tell-all books and a Pauly Shore film loosely inspired by the project , Biosphere 2 's core scientific legacy has held up in ways its early critics may not have anticipated . The facility demonstrated that life support in a closed system can not be neatly separated into biological and mechanical components , since the ecosystem , the machinery meant to support it , and even the building materials themselves all interact in ways that are difficult to predict in advance . More than three decades later , that hard-won lesson continues to inform research into life support systems for future long-duration space missions , even as the story of the crew 's two years sealed inside a shrinking supply of breathable air remains the detail most people still remember first . <p> At TOI World Desk , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sifts through the vast tapestry of global events to bring you the latest news and diverse perspectives round the clock . With an unwavering commitment to accuracy , depth , and timeliness , we strive to keep you informed about the ever-evolving world , delivering a nuanced understanding of international affairs to our readers . " <h> TAMING THE HILSA <p> In 2012 , Samanta and his colleagues embarked on what many considered an improbable scientific challenge : recreating enough of the ilish 's life cycle in captivity to secure its future . <p> The challenge was formidable . Hilsa is not rohu or catla -- species that have been bred in captivity for decades . A migratory fish that spends much of its life traversing the sea , estuaries and rivers , the ilish had never adapted easily to ponds . Before scientists could even think of breeding it , they first had to answer a more fundamental question : could the fish survive -- and grow -- in captivity ? <p> That question shaped the first phase of a multi-institutional ICAR project between 2012-17 , led by ICAR-CIFRI , Barrackpore , with key contributions from ICAR-CIBA , Kakdwip , ICAR-CIFA , Rahara , and ICAR-CIFE , Kolkata . While CIFRI continued studying the hilsa in its natural habitat -- its migration , spawning grounds and dwindling river population -- its sister institutes specialising in aquaculture focused on a different @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Earlier experiments had hinted that it was possible , but only briefly . This time , the researchers followed the fish over a much longer period . By the end of the project , they had crossed what Samanta calls the first major hurdle : they knew the ilish could survive and grow in captivity . <p> If the first phase established that it could survive in captivity , the second , between 2021-24 , set itself a more ambitious goal : could it complete its life cycle there ? The researchers began with wild brood fish caught during the spawning season . At the spawning grounds , eggs from female hilsa were fertilised with milt from males before being carefully packed in oxygenated bags and transported to research centres in Rahara , Kolaghat and Kakdwip . There , scientists attempted to raise them through every stage of life -- from microscopic larvae and fry to fingerlings and , eventually , sexually mature adults . <p> That meant doing something no one had attempted successfully : recreating , inside ponds and laboratories , the conditions that nature ordinarily provides @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sustained on naturally occurring plankton before being gradually weaned onto specially formulated feed . <p> Researchers experimented with different combinations of proteins , fatty acids and oils in an attempt to mimic the nutrition the fish would normally accumulate during its annual migration between the sea and the river . Different centres also tested how the fish responded to freshwater , brackish water and intermediate salinity . <p> The breakthroughs came one after another . The captive-reared fish not only survived but grew to adulthood . Males matured . Females , too , developed eggs . Using ultrasound scans instead of sacrificing the brood fish , scientists could monitor the development of their reproductive organs over time . " We now have the confidence , " Samanta says . " But the last step is the hardest . " <p> That final step has proved elusive . After inducing the captive-reared fish to breed , researchers watched fertilised eggs divide normally under the microscope -- one cell becoming two , then four , then many more . Four hours later , the development stopped . The embryo never progressed further @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's funding cycle came to an end , although some of the work has continued through institutional support at partner institutes . " We now know it can be done , " Samanta says . " What we need is patience , and a sustained , long-term effort . " <p> Samanta is careful to distinguish the project from an attempt to turn the ilish into just another farmed fish . For him , the larger objective is twofold : conserving a species in decline while safeguarding the livelihoods of the fishing communities that depend on it . If captive breeding can eventually be perfected , he says , the fish need not remain in ponds at all . Juveniles could instead be released back into rivers -- a practice known as ranching -- to replenish depleted wild populations . But he is equally clear that captive breeding can not , by itself , reverse the decline . @@139248718 <h> AI can reshape environmental governance <p> As India confronts growing challenges of water stress , climate change and rapid urbanisation , AI can become a powerful instrument for integrating environmental data , anticipating risks and strengthening governance itself <p> Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming central to India 's development story . Through the IndiaAI Mission and investments in digital infrastructure , data centres and advanced computing , India has made clear its ambition to become a global AI leader . <p> Increasingly , the national conversation has moved beyond AI models and computing power to how AI can strengthen institutions , improve productivity and address real-world development challenges . Yet one important area has received relatively little attention : environmental governance . <p> This deserves greater focus because environmental governance sits at the intersection of economic growth , climate resilience and public welfare . Decisions on water , agriculture , infrastructure , urbanisation and disaster preparedness increasingly shape India 's long-term development trajectory . As environmental risks become economic risks , the quality of environmental governance will increasingly influence the quality of growth itself . <p> Much of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , particularly the energy and water needed to support computing infrastructure . Those concerns are legitimate and deserve attention . But they capture only one side of the story . <p> An equally important question is how AI can strengthen governments ' ability to understand and manage the natural systems on which development depends . <p> Environmental governance has long faced a challenge not of data scarcity but of data integration . India today generates enormous amounts of information on rainfall , rivers , groundwater , weather , land use and ecosystems . The challenge has been bringing these different streams of information together in ways that support timely public decisions . Valuable information exists , but it often remains fragmented across institutions and programmes . <p> Today , advances in satellite imagery , geospatial technologies , sensor networks , cloud computing and AI make it possible to analyse multiple environmental datasets simultaneously , identify patterns that would otherwise remain hidden and generate more timely insights for decision-making . This is more than better monitoring . It enables governments to anticipate risks , understand how different systems interact and respond @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ clearest illustration . India is home to nearly 18 per cent of the world 's population but has only around 4 per cent of its freshwater resources . Groundwater acts as a critical buffer against monsoon variability , supporting more than 60 per cent of irrigation and around 85 per cent of rural drinking water . As climate variability increases , managing this resource is becoming more complex . <p> Yet decisions relating to river basins , groundwater , irrigation , urban water supply and disaster management are often informed by separate datasets , institutions and planning processes , even though water does not recognise administrative boundaries . <p> Integrating satellite imagery from ISRO , hydrological observations under the National Hydrology Project , groundwater assessments by the Central Ground Water Board , weather forecasts , reservoir operations and water quality monitoring into shared decision-support systems would enable policymakers to understand how river basins are evolving and intervene earlier . <p> Water is only one example . These impacts extend far beyond health , affecting education , labour , agriculture , fisheries and social well-being . <p> Education has been disrupted , with 22 to 24 school days lost to heat during the 2023-24 academic year , prompting the country 's first nationwide heat-related class suspensions . <h> Economic losses <p> Greenpeace highlighted the significant economic costs of rising temperatures . Of the country 's 2.3 million registered fisherfolk , around 1.9 million are small-scale or municipal fishers , with poverty rates of 27.4-30.6 per cent , nearly double the national average . <p> Greenpeace 's focus group discussions found that extreme heat is shortening fishing hours , forcing fishers to return to shore earlier and reducing catches as fish move to deeper , cooler waters . @@139249096 <p> We stand at a cross-roads . Unsustainable growth is driving us towards climate catastrophe , while inequitable growth is fuelling increased poverty , increased marginalisation and increased anger . Our learning in India is that growth that is not affordable or , in other words , equitable , can not be sustainable . <p> Consider air pollution . Delhi has become synonymous with toxic air . This is not for want of action . All coal plants have been shut ; pet coke import ( incidentally which the US exports because it is too toxic for local use ) has been banned ; and we are moving towards the cleanest fuels and vehicle technologies . But it is not good enough . Each winter , pollution returns with a vengeance . My colleagues estimate that air pollution in Delhi has fallen by 25 per cent over the past three years , as compared to the previous three ; but levels still need to decline by 65 per cent to get what you can call , clean air . And this is when air pollution is a great equaliser . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ; between the rural and urban populations . This is different from water pollution , where the rich can turn to bottled water . The middle-classes of the city may buy air purifiers , but they still breathe in the same airshed that contains toxins from the cars of the rich as well as the biomass-based stoves of the poor . <p> This is where the question of what we do next , becomes critical . We can continue to do what the rest of the world has done to combat pollution from each vehicle : improve the quality of fuel and even consider moving to electric vehicles . But these incremental actions would keep us spending and keep us behind the pollution crisis . The reason is simple : today , less than 20 per cent of my city drive in cars to work ; roughly 25 per cent own cars . But these 25 per cent vehicle owners take 90 per cent of the road space . This will mean combining affordability and convenience and safety . <p> Transformative action is also needed in case of energy . Today , many households in my world still use biomass to cook food . Women are exposed to toxic air pollutants . The problem is this pollution , which is killing poor people , is also contaminating the airshed of the rich and those owning SUVs . @@139260477 <h> Saving the Planet Starts from Our Food Plates <p> Last summer , while visiting my mother 's village in Haryana , I noticed something unusual at lunch . The meal consisted of millet rotis , lentils , seasonal vegetables and homemade curd . Curious , I asked why there was no rice on the table . My mother smiled and said , " When I was young , we ate what the land could easily grow . It was healthier for us and kinder to nature . " At that moment , her words seemed like a lesson from the past . Today , however , they sound remarkably relevant to the future . <p> This simple observation reflects a larger truth : food is not merely a matter of taste or habit . It is a powerful entry point into questions of sustainability , health , agricultural resilience and environmental responsibility . As the world confronts climate change , environmental degradation and persistent malnutrition , the choices we make on our plates have become more important than ever . Saving the planet begins not just in international climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The contemporary food system is under immense pressure to produce more , faster and cheaper . Yet this model has generated serious ecological and social costs . Agriculture consumes a large share of freshwater resources and contributes substantially to greenhouse gas emissions . Intensive farming practices , excessive use of chemical fertilizers and the expansion of monoculture crops have degraded soil quality and reduced biodiversity . At the same time , millions continue to suffer from undernutrition , while obesity and diet-related non-communicable diseases are rising globally . This contradiction reveals a central weakness in present food systems : they often prioritize productivity over sustainability and quantity over quality . More food does not necessarily mean better food , and more output does not necessarily mean better outcomes . <p> One of the most overlooked dimensions of this crisis is the invisibility of environmental costs in everyday food culture . For decades , food has primarily been viewed through the lens of taste , affordability and nutrition , while its environmental consequences remained largely hidden from public consciousness . This is why food literacy must now go beyond calories and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Another serious issue is post-harvest loss . In India , a substantial share of harvested produce is lost before it reaches consumers because of inadequate storage , poor transportation and weak cold-chain infrastructure . Estimates suggest that around 15 to 30 percent of food can be lost between farm and fork . Such losses are not merely technical inefficiencies . They represent a profound waste of land , water , energy , labor and fertilizer . When food is spoiled after harvest , the environmental costs of producing it are already irreversible . In a country where food insecurity still persists , these losses are especially troubling because they reveal a contradiction between abundance and access . The significance of post-harvest loss is often underestimated in policy debates , yet it should be central to any serious discussion on sustainable food systems . <p> The environmental consequences of current agricultural practices are also visible in changing landscapes . In delta regions , including parts of the Ganga basin , soil salinity has increased , making cultivation more difficult and less predictable . Salinity reduces soil fertility , affects crop @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ successfully grown . The rise in salinity also highlights a broader point : agriculture is deeply shaped by place . A crop that performs well in one region may fail in another . A food system built on water-intensive crops and uniform production models may not remain viable under conditions of climate variability , soil stress and resource scarcity . This is why local adaptation matters . Agricultural sustainability must be grounded in ecological suitability rather than blind uniformity . In this context , millets deserve renewed attention . They are hardy , nutritious and generally more water-efficient than many other staple crops . Choosing such foods is not an exercise in nostalgia ; it is an evidence-based response to the twin challenges of climate change and malnutrition . <p> Consumer choice , however , can not bear the entire burden of transformation . If food systems are to become more sustainable , governments , institutions and markets must also change . Schools and colleges should teach students not only about healthy eating but also about sustainable eating . Agricultural policy should reward biodiversity , soil conservation and climate resilience @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ short , must become environmental education . <p> At the same time , consumers do have real power . When people choose seasonal , local and minimally processed foods , they help reduce the environmental footprint of their diets . When they waste less food , they conserve the resources embedded in every meal . When they support traditional crops and diverse farming systems , they contribute to agricultural resilience . Individual choices may seem small , but collectively they shape markets , incentives and norms . In that sense , the plate becomes a site of environmental politics . <p> This is why the wisdom embedded in older food traditions deserves renewed respect . My mother 's remark in the village was not simply a sentimental observation . It reflected a practical truth about eating with the land rather than against it . Her generation may not have used the vocabulary of carbon footprints or sustainable diets , but they understood limits , seasonality and locality . Today , in the face of an ecological crisis , that understanding is more valuable than ever . <p> Saving the planet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cooperation . Yet it will also require something simpler and more immediate : a rethinking of everyday meals . The future of climate action may well depend on decisions made at breakfast , lunch and dinner . If we begin there , we may discover that sustainability is not an abstract ideal but a daily practice . And perhaps , in learning to eat more wisely , we may also learn to live more responsibly . <h> Related Posts <p> Social hierarchies based on gender , race , appearance , and status are often learned rather than inevitable . One 's relative status has profound effects on attention , memory , social interactions , health , and wellness . " <p> How Social Hierarchies Become Internalized <p> The ranking of people within social structures is reflected through everyday cues long before they are formalized into law or policy ; appearance , dress , grooming , posture , and social performance become the visible indicators that categorize people . <p> The desire to alter one 's appearance , beyond health and financial considerations , to avoid anticipated bias fuels several industries , including entertainment , fashion , cosmetics , and plastic surgery . @@139267576 <p> Extreme weather events have become increasingly common across the world over the past few decades . Floods , landslides , heat waves , cyclones , and episodes of exceptionally heavy rainfall are occurring more frequently than before . Scientists attribute this growing trend largely to climate change and the rising global temperature . Among these extreme weather events , a cloudburst is one of the most sudden , localised , and destructive natural phenomena . Although it usually affects only a small geographical area and lasts for a short period , it can unleash enormous devastation within minutes . A cloudburst can transform a calm mountain valley into a torrent of floodwater , washing away homes , roads , bridges , agricultural fields , forests , and even entire settlements . <p> Cloudbursts occur in many parts of the world , particularly in mountainous regions where the landscape strongly influences weather patterns . In India , they are most common in the Himalayan states , including Uttarakhand , Himachal Pradesh , Jammu and Kashmir , Sikkim , and Arunachal Pradesh . Recent years have also seen similar incidents reported @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ primarily focused in hilly areas , frequently reach well beyond the mountains . Rivers carrying giant volumes of water from the Himalayas frequently overflow into the plains , causing severe floods downstream . Destructive floods have repeatedly struck Assam , partly due to intense rainfall and cloudburst events in the Himalayan catchments . The recent flooding in districts such as Charaideo , Sivasagar , and Jorhat once again demonstrated how weather events occurring hundreds of kilometres away can have serious consequences for downstream regions . <p> According to the India Meteorological Department ( IMD ) , a cloudburst is generally defined as rainfall exceeding 100 millimetres within one hour over an area of approximately 20-30 square kilometres . Unlike widespread heavy rainfall , a cloudburst is highly localised , meaning neighbouring areas may receive little or no rain while the affected location experiences an extraordinary downpour . The rainfall intensity is so high that natural drainage systems are unable to carry away the water quickly , leading to flash floods and widespread destruction . The word " cloudburst " often creates the impression that a cloud physically explodes . In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ refers to the sudden release of an exceptionally large amount of rainwater from a cloud over a very short period . The rainfall is so intense that it appears as though the cloud has burst open . Understanding a cloudburst requires understanding how clouds are formed . Solar energy continuously heats water in oceans , seas , rivers , lakes , wetlands , soil , and vegetation . This water evaporates into the atmosphere as water vapour . Warm air can hold more moisture than cold air , so the rising warm air carries large amounts of water vapour upward . As it rises to higher altitudes , the air cools because atmospheric temperature decreases with height . The water vapour then condenses around tiny particles such as dust , smoke , pollen , or sea salt to form microscopic water droplets and ice crystals . Billions of these droplets and crystals combine to create clouds . <p> Meteorologists classify clouds according to their altitude and appearance . Low-level clouds include stratus , stratocumulus , cumulus , nimbostratus , and cumulonimbus , while middle-level clouds include altostratus and altocumulus . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ consist mainly of ice crystals because temperatures at those heights are extremely low . Among all cloud types , the towering Cumulonimbus cloud is the most significant because it produces thunderstorms , lightning , hail , strong winds , and the heaviest rainfall . These enormous clouds may extend from near the Earth 's surface to heights of 12-18 kilometres , making them among the tallest weather systems in the atmosphere . <p> Rainfall is a normal part of the Earth 's hydrological cycle . Under ordinary conditions , tiny water droplets inside a cloud gradually merge into larger droplets . Once they become sufficiently heavy , gravity pulls them toward the Earth 's surface as rain . However , the process is dramatically different during a cloudburst . Within a rapidly developing thunderstorm , an enormous quantity of water accumulates inside a Cumulonimbus cloud . When atmospheric conditions can no longer support this stored moisture , most of the water is released almost simultaneously over a small area , producing an exceptionally intense downpour . Mountainous regions are especially vulnerable to cloudbursts because of a process known as orographic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Bay of Bengal or the Arabian Sea is forced to rise when it encounters mountain slopes . As the air rises , it cools rapidly , causing large quantities of water vapour to condense . Strong upward air currents continue supplying additional moisture , allowing the cloud to grow rapidly . Inside the cloud , water droplets and ice particles collide repeatedly , forming increasingly larger droplets . Eventually , the cloud reaches a point where it can no longer retain its enormous water content . The accumulated water then falls almost instantly , producing a cloudburst . These events - thunder , lightning , hailstorms , and powerful winds - frequently accompany these events , further increasing the damage . Thunder , lightning , hailstorms , and powerful winds often accompany these events , which further increase the damage . <p> The Himalayan region is considered one of the world 's most vulnerable zones for cloudbursts . Its steep slopes , narrow valleys , and fragile geological structure create ideal conditions for flash floods and landslides . Rainwater from intense storms can not spread over a broad area and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Himalayas are geologically young mountains , making them more susceptible to landslides during heavy rainfall . Human activities such as deforestation , hill cutting , unplanned urbanisation , road construction , tourism-related infrastructure , and hydropower projects have significantly increased environmental vulnerability in these regions . Forecasting cloudbursts remains one of the greatest challenges in weather science . Unlike cyclones , which develop over several days and cover vast areas , cloudbursts form rapidly and affect only a limited region . Although modern forecasting systems use weather satellites , Doppler weather radars , automatic weather stations , high-resolution numerical weather prediction models , and artificial intelligence-based forecasting techniques , accurately predicting the exact location and timing of every cloudburst is still beyond present scientific capability . Nevertheless , continuous improvements in weather observation networks have significantly enhanced early warning systems for heavy rainfall . <p> Scientific studies indicate that climate change is increasing the likelihood of extreme rainfall events worldwide . According to the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship , the atmosphere can hold about 7 percent more water vapour for every 1 ? C increase in temperature . As global temperatures continue @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of moisture , increasing the potential for exceptionally intense rainfall . Although climate change can not be blamed for every individual cloudburst , researchers agree that global warming is creating conditions that favour more frequent and intense extreme precipitation events . India has experienced several catastrophic cloudburst disasters . One of the most devastating occurred in June 2013 in Kedarnath , Uttarakhand , where intense rainfall triggered flash floods and landslides that claimed more than 6,000 lives . The overflowing Mandakini River and the sudden release of water from Chorabari Lake caused widespread destruction of homes , roads , bridges , and pilgrimage centres . Another tragic cloudburst occurred in Leh , Ladakh , in August 2010 , when a sudden night-time downpour triggered devastating flash floods and mudslides , killing over 250 people . More recently , Himachal Pradesh has experienced repeated cloudbursts that have severely damaged villages , highways , bridges , and hydropower infrastructure , causing significant economic losses . <p> Although cloudbursts can not be prevented , their impacts can be greatly minimised through effective planning and preparedness . Strengthening weather forecasting systems , expanding the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in vulnerable areas , improving early warning systems , and enhancing disaster response capabilities are essential . Equally important are environmentally responsible land-use planning , protection of forests and wetlands , restoration of natural drainage channels , strict regulation of construction activities in hazard-prone areas , and greater public awareness regarding disaster preparedness . A cloudburst serves as a powerful reminder that the same rain that sustains life can also become one of nature 's most destructive forces under exceptional circumstances . As the climate continues to change , understanding the science behind cloudbursts is becoming increasingly important . Greater investment in scientific research , modern forecasting technology , environmental conservation , sustainable development , and community preparedness will play a crucial role in reducing future loss of life and property . A scientifically informed society is better equipped to face such natural hazards and build resilience against the growing challenges posed by extreme weather .

@@139276958 <p> Sleep loss is increasing across 107 Indian cities with Chennai being the worst hit . ( Istockphoto ) <p> Summary <p> In this edition , we discuss how people living in 107 Indian cities are suffering from sleep loss due to rising nighttime heat <p> This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.Subscribe to enjoy similar stories . <p> Climate Change and You is a fortnightly newsletter written by Bibek Bhattacharya and Sayantan Bera . Subscribe to the newsletter to get it directly in your inbox . <p> Dear reader , <p> It 's getting harder to get a good night 's sleep . For many , modern lifestyle choices are to blame , but for most Indians suffering from sleepless nights , the cause is a dangerous rise in nighttime heat . As global temperatures rise due to climate change , nights are getting steadily hotter . Latest studies show that both the number of warm days and warm nights are increasing every decade across India . <p> Earlier this month , the international climate attribution body , Climate Central , released a new report that tracks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Costing People Sleep , the report analyses data from 1,338 major cities from across the world . Globally , people have lost an average of nearly 56 hours of sleep per year due to high temperatures between 2020 and 2025 . Over 10% of those hours of lost sleep can be definitively attributed to climate change . In fact , temperature-related sleep loss has at least doubled since the early 1970s . <p> View full Image <p> Climate change is driving greater sleep loss every year across the world . ( Courtesy Climate Central ) <p> A good 107 of India 's cities were also a part of the survey , and the report reveals that the country is emerging as a global hotspot of sleep loss . Warmer nights fuelled by climate change are wreaking havoc here , especially in hotter regions like southern India , where people living across cities are losing about 78-91 hours of sleep annually . Of this , at least 8-9 hours can be directly attributed to climate change . Tamil Nadu recorded the highest number of hours lost due to global heating , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the most sleep-deprived city in the country , with 93 hours lost per person annually . <p> Among other cities , Mumbai lost 84 hours of sleep annually , while Kolkata lost 80 hours . However , Bengaluru has emerged as the Indian city with the strongest signal , with sleep loss rising by 8 hours per person per year . Among states , Maharashtra , with 22 cities on the list , and Uttar Pradesh , with 11 cities , have also emerged as hotspots . Poor sleep is a major public health crisis , a leading cause for cardiovascular disease , weakened immunity , and poorer mental health . <h> STATE OF THE CLIMATE <p> View full Image <p> Extreme heat is causing job loss and rising cost of living in India 's agriculture and construction sectors . ( Istockphoto ) <h> The price Indians pay for extreme heat <p> Adelphi Global , a Berlin-based think tank on environmental and development policy , released a report earlier this month titled Heat , Health and the Increasing Cost of Living . The report analyses how extreme heat is affecting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ finds that rising temperatures are causing significant income losses due to reduced working hours , especially affecting informal workers in agriculture and construction . <p> Based on data from the World Bank , the International Labour Organization , World Meteorological Organization , World Health Organization and others , the report concludes that heat stress is not only reducing the income of people , but simultaneously raising costs , especially in the form of rising health expenses to counter heat-related illnesses . Globally , between 1992 and 2013 alone , there were economic losses of up to $50 trillion due to global warming , and approximately 546,000 annual deaths from extreme heat between 2012 and 2021 . The equivalent of 35 million full-time jobs were lost between 1981 and 2010 due to extreme heat caused by the climate crisis . <p> View full Image <p> The number of working days lost in India 's agriculture and construction sector due to heat . @@139277443 <h> Follow Us <p> For decades , the UAE has depended heavily on imported food . To reduce that dependence , it is investing in technologies that can strengthen food security , diversify its economy and make food production more sustainable <p> The UAE has set an ambitious goal under its National Food Security Strategy 2051 -- to become the world 's most food-secure nation by 2051 . For decades , the Gulf nation has depended heavily on imported food . To reduce that dependence , it is investing in technologies that can strengthen food security , diversify its economy and make food production more sustainable . <p> One of the technologies at the heart of this effort is precision fermentation . <p> What is precision fermentation ? <p> Precision fermentation is almost like the philosopher 's stone -- not because it magically turns lead into gold , but because it transforms simple ingredients such as sugar , with the help of engineered microbes , into products of immense value . These include insulin , dairy proteins , egg proteins and other high-value biomolecules . Unlike the mythical alchemy of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ biology and biotechnology . <p> Unlike traditional fermentation -- which uses microbes to make foods such as yogurt , beer and bread -- or biomass fermentation , where the microbes themselves become the final product , precision fermentation instructs microbes to produce one specific ingredient . The technology is not new . Recombinant insulin , first produced in the early 1980s by inserting the human insulin gene into E. coli bacteria , is one of its earliest success stories . However , the term " precision fermentation " has gained popularity only in recent years as the technology has expanded into food production . <p> Supporters say precision fermentation could dramatically reduce the land and water needed to produce food . It can also lower greenhouse gas emissions , make food production less vulnerable to climate change , and allow countries to produce key food ingredients locally instead of importing them . <p> The UAE , especially Abu Dhabi , is positioning itself as a regional hub for precision fermentation and alternative proteins . <p> In 2022 , US-Australian food-tech company Change Foods partnered with KEZAD Group ( Khalifa Economic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ precision fermentation . In 2024 , Abu Dhabi-based Novel Foods Group announced the first phase of a nearly $500 million biotechnology production hub . The facility will focus on producing brazzein , a naturally occurring sweet protein from a West African plant that is hundreds of times sweeter than sugar but contains no calories . <p> A year later , precision fermentation companies Vivici and The Every Company signed agreements with the Abu Dhabi Investment Office ( ADIO ) to explore a shared industrial-scale facility with a production capacity of around four million litres . Vivici specialises in animal-free whey proteins , while The Every Company produces animal-free egg proteins . <p> Most of these projects are still in the planning or early development stage , which is typical for large biotechnology investments . But together they signal the UAE 's intent to move beyond importing food and become a global centre for producing the next generation of sustainable food ingredients . <p> The Emirati government is also working to make it easier for such products to reach the market . The Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) , and ADIO are developing a streamlined regulatory framework for novel foods , including precision fermentation products and cultivated proteins . <h> TAGS <p> Disclaimer : Comments posted here are the sole responsibility of the user and do not reflect the views of THE WEEK . Such events can rapidly raise river levels , trigger landslides and leave authorities with little time to issue warnings or conduct evacuations . <p> Experts have warned that high-intensity rainfall events exceeding 50 mm or 100 mm in a day are likely to become more frequent as temperatures rise . <h> The Role of Erosion , Siltation And Encroachment <p> The Brahmaputra carries enormous quantities of sediment from the Himalayas . After entering the Assam plains near Pasighat , the river 's slope becomes gentler , reducing its ability to carry sand and silt . <p> This sediment settles on the riverbed , reducing its water-carrying capacity and pushing water towards surrounding floodplains . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and increased the amount of loose material entering rivers . Encroachment on wetlands , river channels and natural drainage routes has further reduced the space available for floodwaters to spread safely .

@@139277922 <p> The WHO now treats extreme heat as an occupational risk demanding accountability . Indian law , even after the new labour codes , still treats it as weather . That gap is where the duty of care goes to die . <p> When roughly 45,000 factory workers walked off the floor in Noida and Greater Noida this April , the stated demands were wages , fixed hours and overtime , and the state read the protest , which turned violent by its fourth day , as a law-and-order problem . But the workers at its centre , in garment , footwear and electronics units , are precisely the population Indian field research identifies as bearing the highest occupational heat burden . One survey of garment workers across Delhi NCR , Tamil Nadu and Gujarat found nearly nine in ten reporting heat-related symptoms in the previous year . Heat was not the banner they marched under , but it runs through the twelve-hour shifts they were marching against . It is time Indian law caught up with that reality . <p> The World Health Organization has given the issue an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ environmental health risks in workplaces and major events , developed within its Sport for Health programme with FIFA and in partnership with the World Meteorological Organization and the ILO , treats extreme heat , air pollution and UV exposure as occupational and environmental health risks requiring protocols and accountability . The ILO estimates 2.4 billion workers are exposed to excessive heat , with losses equivalent to 80 million full-time jobs projected annually by 2030 . The legal question that follows is simple to ask and hard to answer in India today : when heat harms or kills a worker , who owes a duty of care , and how is it enforced ? <p> The statutory gap after the labour codes <p> India brought its consolidated labour codes into force in November 2025 . The Occupational Safety , Health and Working Conditions Code , 2020 ( OSHWC Code ) , operative from 21 November 2025 , was the natural vehicle to codify heat protection . It largely did not . The Factories Act , 1948 , which the Code subsumes , at least treated heat as a health matter , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ injury . The Code addresses workplace temperature substantively only in narrow contexts such as dock work ; where heat safety appears , it reads as discretionary welfare rather than a binding , inspectable technical mandate . <p> Three structural features deepen the problem . First , heat-related illness and death are not clearly recognised as occupational hazards , so they are treated closer to acts of nature than to preventable risks a duty-holder must control . Second , the Code permits exemptions for establishments in defined circumstances , often framed around economic activity . Third , its factory protections turn on worker-count thresholds that can exclude the smallest , hottest , least-ventilated MSME units , exactly where danger concentrates . The result is that a large share of India 's informal and outdoor workforce , numbering in the hundreds of millions , sits outside meaningful protection , even as analyses classify a majority of Indian districts as heat-prone and heatwaves reach humid zones that once rarely saw them . <p> There is , however , a seed within the Code itself . It gives an employee the right to flag @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ health , obliging the employer to take remedial action . Read purposively , extreme heat can constitute exactly such an imminent danger . Operationalising this , through rules that define heat thresholds , mandate acclimatisation , rest , shade and hydration , and protect the right to pause work in dangerous conditions without loss of pay , would begin to address the piece-rate trap that keeps workers labouring through the heat because they can not afford to stop . <p> Advisories are not enforceable rights <p> The common reassurance is that India already has more than 200 Heat Action Plans across some 23 states , with colour-coded warnings , cooling-shelter guidance and advice to shift work away from the midday peak . These are genuine achievements of public health administration . But most operate as advisories rather than enforceable obligations , and are generally not notified under the Disaster Management Act , 2005 . Municipalities typically face no penalty for failing to open a shelter or run a water station , and responsibility is dispersed across agencies . Two further gaps compound this : heatwaves are not on India 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ funding , and frameworks lean on dry-bulb temperature while giving less weight to humid heat , even though human tolerance falls sharply as humidity rises . <p> The constitutional anchor : Ranjitsinh and its unfinished business <p> In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India ( 2024 ) , a three-judge bench of the Supreme Court recognised a distinct fundamental right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change , rooted in Article 21 and Article 14 , expressly noting the disproportionate burden borne by the poor and marginalised and calling for both mitigation and adaptation . It is a significant advance in principle . But the same judgment flagged that India has no umbrella climate legislation . The Court , in effect , declared the right 's arrival while noting there was no statutory road to it . <p> Heat protection for workers and event-goers is among the most concrete places to build that road . The right can be operationalised by giving Heat Action Plans statutory backing with named enforcing agencies and penalties , by weighing the notification of heatwaves as a disaster to unlock funding and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ heat provisions into mandatory , humidity-aware standards through the rules . India has also not ratified ILO Convention 155 , the instrument most associated with enforceable domestic occupational-safety obligations ; comparative benchmarks such as California 's WBGT-based work-rest and acclimatisation standards and France 's droit de retrait show what enforceable heat law looks like in practice . <p> What works : templates India helped pioneer <p> The templates are not hypothetical , and several are Indian . After a 2010 heatwave that caused an excess of 1,344 all-cause deaths in a single month , Ahmedabad built South Asia 's first Heat Action Plan with the Indian Institute of Public Health-Gandhinagar , the NRDC and the Public Health Foundation of India ; a pilot evaluation credited it with avoiding roughly 1,190 deaths a year . Odisha , which built India 's first state heat plan after the 1998 heatwave , targets the most vulnerable using socioeconomic data ; Rajasthan pioneered a rural-focused approach . Abroad , Freetown appointed Africa 's first chief heat officer , and Seville became the first city to name and categorise heatwaves by health impact . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Information Network , the Arsht-Rock Resilience Center , and , at home , the NDMA and the Ministry of Health 's National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health . <p> A whole-of-government duty , and community at every level <p> Extreme heat is the textbook problem no single ministry can own , which is why it falls between them . Disaster management ( NDMA and state authorities ) already leads on Heat Action Plans ; health ( MoHFW , NCDC and NPCCHH ) runs heat-illness surveillance and hospital preparedness ; the IMD issues forecasts and alerts ; labour owns the OSHWC Code and its rules ; and housing , power , environment , finance and local bodies each hold a piece . A genuine whole-of-government response means each proactively owning its slice and sharing expertise , with a named coordinator , on the global chief heat officer model , so accountability is assigned rather than diluted . India 's State and District Task Forces on Climate Change and Human Health already exist to convene these actors . Beneath government , the response must be co-designed with those most exposed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Mitra volunteers , unions and employer associations , local bodies and women 's self-help groups . Ahmedabad worked because it was built with slum communities , not handed down to them . <p> Adaptation is not enough <p> All of the above is adaptation . It is necessary and insufficient . The IPCC is unambiguous that limiting warming near 1.5 degrees Celsius requires global emissions to fall about 43 percent by 2030 and reach net-zero carbon dioxide around 2050 . India 's Panchamrit pledges and net-zero-by-2070 commitment are real , as is its fair claim to climate justice under common but differentiated responsibilities , since the historic emissions driving today 's heat were overwhelmingly not ours . But pledges are not reductions , and the finance and technology long promised to the global South remain the missing half of the bargain . Heat is only the most immediate face of a wider cascade of rising seas , melting Himalayan glaciers and food insecurity . Adaptation decides how many survive the heat already here ; mitigation decides how much worse it gets . <p> India 's extreme heat is being governed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and public health crisis , and that distinction is precisely the difference between an advisory and an enforceable right . The WHO gives us the framework , the Supreme Court the principle , Ahmedabad and Seville the templates , and our own ministries and frontline workers the machinery . What remains is the will to bind it together with clear liability , and to reach the people most exposed to the heat and least heard in the making of the law . <p> Purva Singh is a public health law and policy advisor and the founder of Bhagwani Consultancy , Delhi NCR . A member of the Bar of Delhi ( D/395/2010 ) , she has recently published a column in the Bar &amp; Bench , an Op-Ed in the Outlook Magazine and written in several national legal journals . She has coordinated and coauthored several chapters for the second edition of the Report on tobacco control for the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare . Views are personal .
