@@139291448 <p> The annual floods in Assam have long been described as a natural disaster . That description , while partly accurate , has become increasingly inadequate . Flooding is indeed intrinsic to the hydrology of the Brahmaputra basin , one of world 's largest and most sediment-laden river systems . Yet the growing frequency of flash floods , prolonged inundation and repeated failures of infrastructure point to a deeper problem . Much of the devastation witnessed today is not merely the consequence of excessive rainfall or swollen rivers but of engineering systems that have failed to evolve with changing climatic and hydrological realities . <p> The Brahmaputra is unlike most rivers . Carrying one of the highest sediment loads in the world , it constantly alters its morphology through erosion , channel migration and deposition . Traditional flood-control structures designed several decades ago were based on historical flow patterns and rainfall intensities that no longer reflect present conditions . Climate change has introduced greater hydrological uncertainty , with extreme rainfall events becoming more frequent both within Assam and in the upper catchments of Arunachal Pradesh , Bhutan and Tibet . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accelerated siltation and flash flooding that overwhelms existing infrastructure . <p> Engineering responses , however , have remained largely reactive . <p> For decades , embankments have formed the backbone of Assam 's flood-control strategy . They undoubtedly protect agricultural land and settlements under normal flood conditions . Yet embankments alone can not provide a comprehensive solution . Many have exceeded their design life , suffer from inadequate maintenance and are increasingly vulnerable to piping , toe erosion , slope instability and overtopping during extreme flood events . Repeated breaches demonstrate that structural defences without systematic asset management eventually become liabilities rather than safeguards . <p> The challenge is compounded by sedimentation . As riverbeds aggrade because of continuous sediment deposition , the effective carrying capacity of channels declines . Consequently , even moderate increases in discharge can trigger overbank flooding . Merely strengthening embankments without addressing sediment management resembles raising the walls of a container while ignoring the material accumulating inside it . <p> Community participation should also become an engineering consideration rather than merely a disaster-management objective . Local knowledge regarding historical flood paths , erosion zones and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ improve maintenance of drainage channels , embankments and local flood-control structures while strengthening public ownership of resilience measures . <p> The fundamental lesson is that floods can not be eliminated from Assam , nor should that be the objective . Floodplains are dynamic ecological systems , and seasonal flooding remains essential for agriculture , fisheries and wetland ecosystems . The goal should instead be to reduce flood risk through better engineering , improved planning and climate-adaptive infrastructure . <p> Assam 's flood challenge is therefore not simply a battle against water . It is a test of whether engineering can work with natural systems instead of attempting to overpower them . Stronger embankments will remain necessary , but they are no longer sufficient . Scientific river management , resilient urban drainage , modern hydrological modeling , sediment management and nature-based infrastructure must together form the foundation of a new flood policy . <p> Climate change has made yesterday 's engineering assumptions obsolete . The next generation of flood management must therefore be designed not for the river that once existed , but for the river that Assam will increasingly confront @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ move from an annual cycle of disaster response to a long-term strategy of resilience. 
@@139291450 <p> Floods are among the most familiar natural disasters in Assam , yet the greatest suffering often begins only after the waters start to recede . Public attention generally focuses on overflowing rivers , submerged villages , rescue operations and relief camps . While these images capture the immediate scale of destruction , they reveal only one part of a much larger crisis . Once the floodwaters withdraw , thousands of families are left to confront a different kind of disaster that receives far less attention . Homes stand buried under thick layers of mud , drinking water sources become contaminated , agricultural fields are rendered unusable , roads and bridges remain damaged , schools stay closed , healthcare services struggle to function , and economic activity comes to a standstill . For many flood-affected families , this period is more painful than the flood itself because survival is no longer dependent on rescue alone but on rebuilding an entire way of life from almost nothing . The recent floods in Upper Assam , particularly across Sivasagar , Charaideo and Jorhat districts , once again demonstrated how rapidly such disasters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the neighbouring hill regions , rivers such as the Dikhow , Disang , Jaji and Bhogdoi overflowed within hours , breaching embankments and causing widespread devastation . Such events also highlight the changing character of floods under the influence of climate change . Instead of gradual flooding that once allowed communities time to prepare , sudden surges now leave little opportunity for evacuation or protection of property . However , extreme weather alone can not explain the increasing scale of destruction . Years of deforestation in upstream catchments , encroachment upon wetlands , poor drainage planning , heavy siltation of rivers , unscientific embankment construction and unplanned urban expansion have collectively transformed seasonal floods into recurring humanitarian emergencies . Unless these structural failures are acknowledged alongside natural causes , every monsoon will continue to produce similar tragedies , and post-flood suffering will remain an unavoidable feature of life across large parts of Assam . <p> Once floodwaters recede , the immediate challenge shifts from rescue to public health and sanitation . This transition is frequently underestimated despite being one of the most dangerous phases of the disaster cycle . Wells @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ become contaminated by sewage , decomposing animal carcasses and accumulated waste . Thousands of families , having no alternative , are compelled to consume unsafe water , creating ideal conditions for outbreaks of diarrhoea , cholera , typhoid and other water-borne diseases . Children , pregnant women and elderly people become particularly vulnerable because their immunity is comparatively weaker . Simultaneously , stagnant pools of water provide ideal breeding grounds for mosquitoes , resulting in increased transmission of malaria , dengue and Japanese Encephalitis , diseases that have repeatedly posed serious threats in Assam . Flood-affected communities also experience skin infections , fungal diseases , eye infections and leptospirosis due to prolonged exposure to contaminated water and mud . Healthcare facilities themselves often remain partially dysfunctional because floodwaters damage hospitals , rural health centres , medical equipment and transport infrastructure . Doctors and healthcare workers struggle to reach remote villages where roads have collapsed or bridges have been washed away . Essential medicines , vaccines and emergency supplies frequently arrive late when they are needed most . Electricity disruptions further complicate medical treatment by affecting refrigeration systems , communication networks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sanitation systems . Damaged toilets force many families into open defecation , increasing environmental contamination and accelerating disease transmission . Waste management also becomes a serious concern as plastic debris , household refuse and dead livestock accumulate across villages , creating hazardous living conditions . These circumstances demonstrate that post-flood recovery is not merely about restoring damaged infrastructure but about preventing a secondary humanitarian crisis driven by disease , inadequate sanitation and insufficient public health preparedness . Strengthening healthcare resilience before disasters occur is therefore just as important as improving flood control measures themselves . <p> The economic and social consequences that emerge after floods often persist long after public attention has shifted elsewhere . Agriculture , which remains the backbone of rural Assam , suffers extensive damage as standing crops are destroyed and fertile farmland becomes covered with thick deposits of sand rather than nutrient-rich silt . Such fields frequently remain uncultivable for several years , depriving farming families of their principal source of income . Livestock losses further deepen rural distress because cattle , poultry , pigs and goats represent both economic assets and household security . Fisheries @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cultivated fish escape into floodwaters . Small rural enterprises , local markets and transport networks struggle to recover because damaged roads interrupt supply chains and raise the prices of essential commodities . Families burdened with outstanding agricultural loans or microfinance debt often face enormous financial uncertainty , compelling many working-age members to migrate temporarily or permanently to urban centres and other states in search of employment . Yet the damage extends well beyond economics . Schools frequently remain closed for weeks because classrooms serve as relief camps or require extensive repairs . Thousands of students lose textbooks , learning materials and school uniforms , interrupting their education and increasing the risk of long-term academic setbacks . Psychological trauma also deserves greater recognition within disaster management policies . Watching homes collapse , livelihoods disappear and years of savings vanish within a single day leaves lasting emotional scars . Anxiety , depression and uncertainty become common experiences among flood survivors , particularly those who have repeatedly endured similar disasters . Women and children face additional risks associated with insecurity , displacement and disruptions to community support systems . Inadequate relief distribution , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ public confidence . Rebuilding confidence among affected communities is therefore as important as rebuilding damaged houses and roads . <p> Reducing post-flood suffering requires a comprehensive strategy that combines scientific planning , environmental responsibility and institutional preparedness . Flood management can not remain confined to emergency rescue operations conducted after rivers overflow . It must begin months before the monsoon through continuous river dredging where scientifically justified , regular maintenance of embankments , restoration of wetlands , protection of natural drainage channels and strict regulation of construction activities in flood-prone areas . Equally important is the conservation of forests in upstream catchments because healthy ecosystems reduce soil erosion and moderate runoff entering downstream rivers . Schools should receive priority in rehabilitation so that children 's education resumes without unnecessary delay . @@139299673 <h> Scientists tracked the world 's mangroves from the 1980s to 2023 and found natural regrowth has quietly reversed decades of decline <p> Mangroves have long been considered one of the planet 's most threatened ecosystems . These dense forests along tropical and subtropical coastlines were steadily being lost to urban expansion , shrimp farming , agriculture , pollution and climate change . Each year thousands of hectares were lost , threatening wildlife , fisheries and coastal communities that depended on them . But a striking new study suggests the narrative is beginning to change.According to online media reports , scientists who analyzed satellite images spanning more than four decades -- from the 1980s to 2023 -- say mangrove forests are coming back in many parts of the world . Published in the journal Science , the research found that the historic decline in mangroves has been largely offset by natural regrowth and expansion , with global mangrove losses now slowing dramatically . <p> The results are one of the most positive conservation stories in recent years , showing that with protection , restoration and community support , nature has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that would not vanish across the globe <p> Using decades of satellite imagery , researchers tracked annual changes in the extent and canopy health of mangroves . Rather than continuing the steep decline recorded in the late 20th century , they found that mangrove forests have entered a period of relative stability . <p> An unexpected element of this turnaround has been natural regeneration , where forests come back on their own with very little human help . On several continents , new mangroves have been reported growing around major rivers , estuaries and deltas.The results also corroborate the findings of the United Nations Environment Programme 's ( UNEP ) 2023 report , The Decade of Mangrove Forest Change , which found that global mangrove losses had largely plateaued while gains were increasingly frequent in many coastal areas . <h> Why mangroves matter more than we know <p> Why mangroves matter more than we know <p> Mangrove trees make up less than 1 percent of the world 's tropical forests , but they are one of the planet 's most valuable ecosystems . According to environment experts , they are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ natural protection from storms , coastal erosion and flooding . Their complex root systems trap sediments , stabilize shorelines and improve water quality.If experts are to be believed , mangroves are also called climate heroes . They sequester vast amounts of carbon , both in their trees and in the soil beneath them -- sometimes called " blue carbon . " Mangrove forests are thought to store many times more carbon per hectare than many terrestrial forests , making them an important tool in the fight against climate change.Mangroves are not just good for the environment but also for the livelihood of millions of people . According to UNEP , healthy mangrove ecosystems support fisheries , tourism and resilience to disasters with almost 2.4 billion people living within 100 kilometres of the world 's coastlines . More than 1,500 species of fish , birds , reptiles , mammals and invertebrates live in mangrove habitats . <h> Is science taking conservation in a new direction ? <p> Is science taking conservation in a new direction ? <p> Well , the answer is yes . Based on original data from 1,579 children across 1,370 households in Medell ? n , Colombia , the research finds that displacement leaves lasting cognitive , physical and mental health effects that can not be explained by poverty alone . @@139309230 <h> The NEET movement must become the beginning of a new Republic <p> Every generation inherits a defining political moment that compels it to decide whether it will merely protest injustice or undertake the far more difficult task of transforming the society that produces it . India 's young people may now be approaching such a moment . The NEET scandal , which rightly provoked widespread anger among students and parents across the country , has been presented by the government as an unfortunate aberration -- a criminal conspiracy to be corrected through arrests , administrative tightening and promises of greater vigilance . Such an explanation is politically convenient because it isolates the problem from the larger failures of governance . Yet the very scale of the public response suggests that the country is reacting not simply to an examination scandal but to something far deeper . NEET has become the prism through which millions of young Indians are expressing accumulated frustration over unemployment , institutional decay , corruption , declining public accountability and the growing belief that the promise of equal opportunity is steadily being withdrawn . Those measures may satisfy the immediate demand for accountability , but they would leave untouched the conditions that have repeatedly produced examination fraud , recruitment scams and public distrust . India has witnessed paper leaks before . Recruitment examinations have been cancelled before . Corruption in educational administration has surfaced before . Each scandal has generated outrage , official assurances and a return to business as usual . What distinguishes the present moment is that the youth are beginning to understand that these are not isolated incidents but recurring expressions of a deeper political and institutional disorder . If that understanding matures , the movement will cease to be about NEET and become a democratic challenge to the manner in which the Republic itself is being governed . <p> There is a tendency within governments confronted by public anger to reduce structural failures to the actions of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the convenient scapegoats . A few officials are suspended , a committee is appointed , and the political leadership proclaims that decisive action has been taken . Such responses deliberately narrow the public imagination . They encourage citizens to believe that corruption is the work of a few dishonest actors rather than a symptom of institutions that have become vulnerable because transparency , accountability and public oversight have steadily weakened . The question therefore is not simply who leaked examination papers , but why systems entrusted with the future of millions have become so fragile that organised criminal networks are able to penetrate them repeatedly . That question can not be answered by police investigations alone . It demands political investigation into the health of public institutions themselves . <p> The movement should therefore resist every attempt to confine its demands within the boundaries of educational reform . The erosion of confidence is therefore moral as much as administrative . When citizens cease to believe that public institutions operate fairly , the legitimacy of democratic governance itself begins to weaken . <p> This is the point at which the movement faces its greatest historical responsibility . Every significant democratic movement eventually reaches a crossroads where it must decide whether it seeks reform within the existing order or transformation of the conditions that repeatedly generate injustice . Reform is necessary , but reform alone rarely changes the underlying logic of governance . It repairs damaged mechanisms while leaving intact the political culture that produced them . Economic development that excludes large sections of society eventually undermines its own legitimacy . A programme for democratic transformation must therefore place equal emphasis upon social justice , equal opportunity , labour rights , gender equality , minority rights , the dignity of Dalit and Adivasi communities , and the elimination of discrimination in every sphere of public life . Similarly , environmental sustainability can not remain an afterthought . The generation now entering adulthood will inherit a world profoundly shaped by climate change , ecological degradation and the reckless exploitation of natural resources . Development must therefore be measured not only by economic output but by its capacity to preserve the ecological foundations upon which future generations will depend . <p> The movement itself must embody the democratic values it seeks to advance . Rather , it should create a broad democratic coalition in which every participant contributes experience , organisational strength and political imagination while recognising the autonomous leadership of the youth movement that gave birth to the initiative . @@139309293 <p> The student movement in India is encouraging at a time when the country has experienced a significant democratic decline ( Figure 1 ) . Students have been protesting against a poorly governed educational system in which examination paper leaks have become commonplace . They have received support not only from their parents but also from farmers and broader sections of the non-student population . Their protests have been strengthened by the organizational skills of Left students . The protesting students have suffered at the hands of a brutal security apparatus employed by an authoritarian government , even though their protests have been peaceful . <p> The student movement in India raises important questions about education and its relationship to the wider society . The protests demonstrate that decades of communal politics promoted by right-wing forces inside and outside the state have not extinguished people 's democratic and egalitarian instincts . The government 's violent response to the student movement suggests that , whether a protest is peaceful or not , if it challenges the state ( or corporate power ) beyond the level of tolerance of the system , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it is likely to be met with state brutality . The state remains the violent machine that exists to maintain capitalist class rule . <p> The vast majority of people -- around 75 percent -- suffer because of a free-market economic policy that serves corporate interests , introduced by the liberal predecessors of today 's right-wing rulers . To distract attention from the failures of this policy and to weaken people 's movements against it , the government promotes a divisive ideology based on the claim that the religion of the majority is superior to those of minorities and that the nation belongs to the majority religious community . Yet the overwhelming majority of the population -- again , around 75 percent or so -- do not accept this divisive ideology . To implement these two mutually reinforcing policies , the government must rely increasingly on authoritarian methods . <p> An authoritarian government has little need to be accountable when it makes mistakes . It judges its own performance and invariably concludes that it is satisfactory , even when it falls far short of meeting people 's needs . Because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ little incentive to perform its functions competently -- for example , to conduct examinations properly or provide public services effectively . Its elected representatives and bureaucrats may be highly incompetent and yet retain their positions simply because they promote the government 's right-wing ideology , demonstrate loyalty to the supreme leader , or remain close to those in power . Authoritarian governments are therefore prone to incompetence . Examination paper leaks , lack of accountability , and brutality against peaceful protesters -- as well as actions such as changing electoral rolls to disenfranchise millions and facilitating the near-complete capture of major parts of the state -- are all manifestations of authoritarian governance . <p> It is to be hoped that the movement will not only raise the political consciousness of students and other sections of the population but also win its immediate demands . However , education is one moment in the social reproduction of capitalist society , so educational struggles can not achieve lasting victories unless they develop into struggles over the wider conditions of social reproduction . The struggle for education -- which has emerged as an important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ appeared to be in decline -- must therefore be linked to broader struggles against exploitation , unemployment , inequality , and attacks on democratic rights . This article develops that argument by examining how employment , state spending , democratic rights , environmental conditions , and other dimensions of social reproduction shape education and student struggles . <p> Education as a part of the wider society <p> Society as a process does not just exist . It has to continue to exist . Social relations and conditions need to be reproduced . Social reproduction refers to continued existence of bodily and mental conditions of an individual . To continue to live as a flourishing human being , one has to eat and drink and have access to shelter , healthcare and transit , a favourable/sustainable physical environment , and a safe built environment and social spaces , as well as culture , including education . <p> Education is indeed a key moment in the social reproduction . Therefore , every major determinant of social reproduction -- employment , wages , housing , access to food , agriculture , democracy , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and political right to self-determination or independence -- also becomes a determinant of education . <p> Students are future workers -- wage earners , salaried employees , and small-scale self-employed producers . Many of them work part-time . Many also work to save money before returning to school or college . Most students ' parents are workers or small-scale ( self-employed ) producers of goods and services . Students ' lives are therefore closely connected to what happens in the world of work ( or employment ) . Educational demands can not be permanently secured unless the social conditions that produce problems concerning education along with other problems are transformed . <p> There are two major attributes of students . Students are citizens , even if they are citizens in an unequal and exploitative society where the state basically works for and on behalf of the employing and exploiting class and where the state imposes many obstacles to the people exercising their rights as citizens . Everything that affects students as citizens affects them as students qua students . This attribute of students emerges from people 's relationship with the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is being a worker/employee , i.e. as owner of labour power , and that attribute emerges from students ' relation to their employer . Labour power is their mental and physical ability to work . As a key component of social reproduction , education -- like health -- contributes to the production and reproduction of labour power . Everything that affects labour power as such eventually affects education . <p> Education is part of the value of labour power because it provides , directly or indirectly , the technical and non-technical skills and other abilities needed to work . The quality of education therefore shapes the post-student lives of today 's students . Moreover , it is not enough to have a good education . If there are no jobs available , what is the value of a good education ? Education is therefore connected to all the other areas of life that shape people 's economic conditions , the conditions of the parents of current students and of the future workers who are currently students . Thus , education not only reproduces labour power ; it is also shaped @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is further shaped by the fact that the state is bound by the logic of profit-making . Students ' lives -- like those of their parents -- are shaped by what the state provides to , or takes away from , people , and by how democratically the state functions . Therefore , students ' lives depend on much more than what happens within the educational sector . How ? <p> Social Determinants of Education <p> Education depends on students ' innate abilities and hard work . But there are more fundamental determinants of education . As with health , these are the social determinants of education . <p> Education depends on the material conditions of students and their parents <p> A basic premise of any rational analysis is that one has to eat , drink , have shelter , and meet other basic needs in order to live as a human being and fulfil one 's potential . In our society , meeting these needs requires money because most goods and services have to be purchased . A hungry stomach can not support an active mind . <p> Students @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ educational institutions , although some students also contribute through their own earnings . To the extent that parents finance their children 's education -- and often do so with great difficulty , including by selling their land or cutting back on their own subsistence needs -- students can not pursue their education unless their parents have adequate incomes . Adequate incomes , in turn , require expanded opportunities for secure employment with adequate wages . Moreover , without such opportunities , many of those who are currently students will remain unemployed or underemployed after completing their education . The value of a corruption-free examination system becomes limited if there are no secure , well-paying jobs . <p> Everyone must have access to employment with an adequate wage which can support educational and other needs . The expansion of secure employment opportunities with adequate wages requires a people-oriented economic development . This requires that the public sector , small-scale production ( in both rural and urban areas ) , and cooperatives expand and create secure , socially useful , and sustainable employment , and that common people exercise greater control over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to be sustainable . Environmental degradation , including climate change , affects students and their parents . Consequently , students ' lives , both during and after their education , will continue to be adversely affected unless the state addresses environmental change . <p> Many students have parents who are affected by what I call ' expanded primitive accumulation ' ( EPA ) , which is forcibly orchestrated and defended by the state . This includes the privatization of government-owned companies , leading to job losses . Students and their parents depend on the public provision of healthcare , public transportation , and other essential services . The withdrawal of these services , itself a form of EPA , lowers the living standards of both students and their parents . EPA includes forcible dispossession of small-scale owners of land -- many of whom are Adivasis -- to make way for corporate industrialization . EPA also includes people losing access to their land and homes because of urban redevelopment , special economic zones , corporate mining , forest clearance , eco-tourism , solar projects , and infrastructure projects , all of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ people , whose children are in colleges and universities , suffer because they do not receive remunerative prices for their agricultural products , which undermines their livelihoods . This occurs partly because the state has withdrawn much of its earlier support , and such withdrawal is a form of EPA . Many farmers and self-employed in urban enterprises also suffer because of unequal foreign competition as earlier protection is withdrawn . Unless a country has economic sovereignty , parents ' incomes are adversely affected , and this in turn affects students . Unless EPA is halted , many students can not fully live the lives of students . <p> Education depends on state spending priorities <p> To the extent that educational institutions support students through scholarships and bursaries , there must be greater public funding of universities . Without expanded university funding , employment opportunities for students who aspire to academic careers will remain limited . <p> The state must invest in education at all levels . The Indian state invests far less than the minimum 6 -- 8 percent of GNP that it should . Eliminating inflated expenditure on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , loan write-offs and government contracts at inflated prices ) , government advertisements aimed at merely celebrating its own so-called achievements , and money used by ruling parties to buy legislators from competing parties as well as for direct transfer of limited amount of cash to selected voters which effectively serves as a bribe for votes , in place of creating collective means of subsistence ( state-funded quality education , schools , transit system , parks , etc. ) -- all these would make more resources available for education and other needs . Therefore , demands for such reductions -- or , in some cases , elimination -- must be part of the struggle to improve education . <p> Education depends on democratic rights and an accountable state <p> Unless the communalization of society and of the state is halted , and unless attacks on secularism and egalitarian values are reversed , the curriculum will become less scientific and less socially relevant , teachers will continue to be appointed because of their loyalty to a right-wing agenda rather than their intellectual qualifications , and campuses will increasingly be filled with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ division without any scientific basis . Without the protection of democratic rights , even the struggle for immediate concessions to students becomes difficult . <p> Students and their parents ' lives will improve if the functioning of the various branches of the state is democratized so that politicians , bureaucrats , police officers , and other public officials are accountable to the people . No one should have to rely on bribes or personal connections in order to enjoy their rights or obtain public services . <p> Education involves the production of ideas that are innovative , grounded in reason , empirically verifiable , and critical of ideas , individuals , and institutions that produce and disseminate inadequate knowledge . Therefore , freedom of the media , academic freedom , the protection of minorities , and secularism all create conditions conducive to education . <p> Education does not happen only in classrooms or conference halls . An important part of education takes place in the spaces of everyday life . It takes place in sites of protest against injustice ; against attacks on the scientific attitude ; against attacks on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scientific value has not been established ; and against attacks on human decency , secularism , and egalitarianism . For people to participate fully in these spaces of public life , they must be safe for everyone , including women , disabled people , and other oppressed groups , and there must be no violent repression by the state . <p> The Political Implications <p> The point of the above discussion is that education is connected to many other key areas of life . Therefore , demands for a corruption-free examination system and affordable education , important though they are , must be seen as part of a broader set of demands that , when realized , will improve the lives of students today , the lives of their parents , and the post-student lives of those who are students today . <p> As the student movement grows , and if it seeks lasting change , it must broaden its demands beyond education alone . It must defend the interests of students as students , as well as the interests of workers and small-scale owners -- the social groups to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which today 's students themselves will belong after completing their education . Therefore , the struggles of students must be united with the struggles of workers , peasants , Adivasis , women , minorities , and all other oppressed people . <p> Just as it is important that workers ' and small-scale producers ' struggles for immediate concessions develop into broader social struggles , similarly students ' struggle may begin with immediate demands ( e.g. resignation of a Minister or a bureaucrat ) and then logically extend into a programme of wider social transformation . <p> Students ' demands should therefore include , among others : <p> Expand access to affordable , high-quality corruption-free education system at every level ; <p> Stop the privatization and commercialization of education ; <p> Stop the communalization and obscurantization of education and society ; <p> Guarantee every person -- including every educated person -- a job suited to their abilities , with a living wage automatically adjusted for inflation ; <p> Provide affordable housing , universal healthcare , and accessible public transportation for all , including students ; <p> Guarantee nutritious food for all @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Ensure remunerative prices for peasants whose income supports many students and others who produce food and agricultural raw materials ; <p> Promote small-scale production , cooperatives , and the public sector to create secure and socially useful employment to income of all to create opportunities for the students as future workers and for the parents of current students ; <p> Establish greater people 's control over large-scale enterprises ; <p> Fight climate change while creating secure , well-paid climate jobs ; <p> Reduce military expenditure and redirect resources toward education as well as toward healthcare , housing , and other social needs ; <p> Pursue an independent foreign policy and protect the country 's productive capacities from unequal international competition in order to stop loss of jobs and income that affects the parents of current students and students as future workers ; <p> End the forcible dispossession of peasants , Adivasis , and all other communities ; <p> Invest substantially in science and promote thinking based on reason , evidence , and critical inquiry ; <p> Protect democratic rights , including the rights to organize , assemble , speak @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and independent media ; <p> Make every government functionary accountable to ordinary people , whether formally educated or not ; Adopt zero tolerance toward bribery and corruption at every level . <p> Note : From one angle , the above list includes immediate demands , institutional reforms , and strategic goals . From another angle , these are democratic demands , economic demands , social welfare demands , developmental demands , and anti-imperialist demands . <p> Conclusion <p> Students are not just students . They are future workers . Many of them are already workers . They are citizens with rights . Education is part of society , and the governance of education is part of the governance of society as a whole . Therefore , demands concerning education -- such as corruption-free examinations , affordable education , and so on -- must be understood as part of a broader set of demands for social change . Students should avoid educational sectionalism -- the idea that they should fight only for educational demands . The struggle for education necessarily expands into a struggle over society as a whole . A @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ social and political horizon . <p> Governments generally respond to protests through four strategies : coercion , concession , consent , and confusion . They use brutality and seek to instill fear . They make limited concessions -- for example , by transferring an official or forcing a politician to resign . Such concessions can create consent or an unwarranted sense of trust when the regime says , ' Look , we listened to you . We are not as bad as you think . ' Often , however , these concessions are temporary or reversible . Governments also try to convince protesters and the wider public that conditions are not as bad as they believe ; that the nation is above all else ; and that protest is anti-national or even opposed to a particular religion or other identity . They also create confusion by changing their responses unpredictably -- for example , by alternating between police repression , offers of negotiation , promises of new policies , attempts to buy off movement leaders , and other tactics . Therefore , students need a broader understanding of society as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- including the democratization of the state and the defense of democratic rights -- as well as to egalitarianism . It is equally important to recognize that students have an objective material interest in broader social transformation -- in the world of work and employment and in the way the state functions -- because both their education and their post-education lives depend on it . Students should support workers and peasants not only out of solidarity but also because the conditions under which workers and peasants -- including many students ' parents -- live directly shape the conditions under which students study . Without democratic rights throughout society , students ' ability to organize and to learn through collective action is limited . Without state support for science , the quality of education suffers . Without the public provision of healthcare , housing , and public transportation , and without effective state action to address climate change , students ' lives are adversely affected . And so on . <p> The struggle of students must be not only for a corruption-free and affordable education but also for such values and practices as decency in public life , democracy , egalitarianism , and secularism . When this broader struggle reveals the forces opposed to these values and practices , it must become a struggle against those forces -- corporate power and the state that defends it . <p> That requires more than jokes and mimicry or periodic protests that last a month or two and then dissolve after securing a few concessions . It requires rigorous theory , the courage to draw practical lessons from theory , skillful agitation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ limits of a mere popular-front-type -- that is , multi-class -- mobilization and , consequently , the need for a mobilization based on the political leadership of the exploited classes : workers and small-scale producers , including peasants . <p> It will also reveal the need to move beyond a democratic consciousness , which informs the struggle for democratic rights , and beyond an economic ( trade-union ) consciousness , which guides the struggle for economic rights from employers and the state , including the struggle for an efficient , corruption-free education system , toward a political or class consciousness . Such a consciousness enables students and others to understand that the fundamental interests of the corporate class and the political-bureaucratic elite allied with it are incompatible with the fundamental interests of most students and their parents , who depend on wages and salaries or on small-scale farming and other forms of petty production . <p> Significant and lasting concessions , whether in education or in any other sphere , are always the by-product of a process of political mobilization that goes beyond immediate demands . @@139314185 <p> The arrival of the monsoon in Assam has long been synonymous with the swelling of the Brahmaputra , an annual phenomenon that sustains the region 's rich biodiversity and agricultural plains . However , what was once a natural cycle of inundation and renewal has morphed into a recurring humanitarian and ecological catastrophe . As we witness the devastating floods of July 2026 , the tragedy unfolding across Upper Assam is not merely a seasonal interruption but a stark indictment of systemic vulnerabilities , climate change , and human mismanagement . While it is convenient to blame the relentless rains and the inherent volatility of the Brahmaputra river system , a rigorous analysis of the crisis reveals that the intensifying devastation is profoundly rooted in our collective actions and oversights . The time has come to elevate our discourse from temporary relief measures to long-term accountability and holistic river basin management . <p> The current situation in Upper Assam paints a grim picture of displacement and loss . Recent reports from July 2026 indicate that the floodwaters have affected over 7.27 lakh people across more than a dozen districts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ particularly Sivasagar , Charaideo , Jorhat , Lakhimpur , and Dhemaji , have borne the brunt of the deluge . Sivasagar has emerged as the worst-affected epicenter , with over 3.75 lakh residents impacted and hundreds of villages completely submerged . The geographical landscape of the region is literally being rearranged by the sheer force of the water . In Dhemaji , for instance , the Dikhari River recently changed its course entirely , slicing through settlements , destroying vital infrastructure , and washing away agricultural lands . Families have lost their homes , livestock , and livelihoods , forced to seek refuge on elevated bamboo platforms or in state-run relief camps . For these communities , the river 's fury is an existential threat that wipes out years of socioeconomic progress in a matter of days . To understand the magnitude of this disaster , one must look beyond the immediate meteorology and examine the complex hydrology of the Brahmaputra alongside our historical interventions . The Brahmaputra is one of the world 's largest and most dynamic rivers , carrying an immense volume of water and vast amounts of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hits the relatively flat plains of Assam , the river loses its velocity , depositing sediment on its bed and naturally raising the water level . However , human interference has drastically exacerbated this natural vulnerability . For decades , the primary strategy for flood management in Assam has been the construction of embankments . Since the 1950s , over 400 embankments have been built along the Brahmaputra and its tributaries . Research indicates that a vast majority of these earthen structures have long outlived their intended lifespans , many are fragile , poorly maintained , and highly susceptible to breaches during peak flow . We have essentially tried to cage a dynamic , sediment-loaded river within aging mud walls , resulting in catastrophic breaches that unleash high-velocity water into unsuspecting villages . Furthermore , the ecological degradation in the catchment areas significantly amplifies the flood risk . Rampant deforestation , unscientific mining , and aggressive road construction in neighboring hilly states have loosened the topsoil . During heavy rainfall , this soil is washed into the tributaries , severely silting the riverbeds of the Subansiri , Burhi Dihing , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ urban centers like Dibrugarh and Jorhat , the situation is further compounded by unplanned urbanization . The encroachment of wetlands , the filling up of natural drainage channels , and the cementing of floodplains have left the rainwater with nowhere to go , leading to severe urban flooding . The destruction we are witnessing in Upper Assam is thus a cumulative result of ecological apathy and unscientific infrastructure development . Recognizing our responsibility in this crisis requires a fundamental paradigm shift in how we interact with the riverine ecosystem . The current model of reactionary disaster management heavily reliant on the heroic , albeit temporary , rescue operations by the National Disaster Response Force ( NDRF ) and the State Disaster Response Force ( SDRF ) is unsustainable in isolation . While emergency evacuations and relief distribution centers are crucial for immediate survival , they do not cure the underlying disease . As researchers and floodplain experts advocate , we must transition to a comprehensive , basin-wide management approach . The Brahmaputra must be treated as an integrated ecological system rather than a series of isolated hazard points . This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ releases , alongside the modernization of our hydrological infrastructure . Our collective responsibility extends from policymakers to ordinary citizens . The government has recently signaled a shift toward long-term flood mitigation projects , such as massive investments in permanent urban drainage solutions and resilient infrastructure . However , these structural measures must be complemented by behavioral and policy changes . We need strictly enforced floodplain zoning laws to prevent residential and commercial construction in highly vulnerable areas . Agricultural practices must adapt to the flood cycles by promoting flood-resistant crop varieties and shifting away from water-intensive farming in erosion-prone zones . Additionally , traditional ecological knowledge should be integrated into modern engineering ; local communities have historically known how to live with the river , utilizing stilt houses and sustainable wetland management practices that have been largely sidelined by rapid urbanization . <p> The recurring floods in Upper Assam serve as a powerful and tragic reminder that nature can not be engineered into submission without consequences . As the floodwaters of 2026 eventually recede , leaving behind a trail of silt and sorrow , we can not afford to succumb @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Assam lies in acknowledging our past ecological missteps and committing to sustainable , climate-adaptive development . By prioritizing environmental conservation , upgrading aging riverine infrastructure with scientific rigor , and fostering community resilience , we can mitigate the devastating impacts of the monsoon . It is our moral and civic duty to ensure that the mighty Brahmaputra remains a source of life and prosperity for the state , rather than a harbinger of annual despair .

They serve as natural buffers against cyclones , storm surges and coastal erosion while supporting fisheries , biodiversity and local livelihoods . <p> India 's gain of 118,000 hectares places it behind only Australia in terms of net mangrove expansion since 1985 . @@139324870 <p> Climate change is likely to widen the gap between rich and poor countries , with wealthier people using more air conditioning while poorer communities face rising heat-related deaths , a new report has warned . <p> The report by the Climate Impact Lab says temperature changes linked to climate change could contribute to about 430,000 additional deaths each year by 2050 , compared with historical conditions . It says 10 times more of those deaths are likely to occur in poorer countries than in richer ones . <p> The findings highlight the unequal ability of countries and communities to adapt to extreme heat . Cooling , particularly air conditioning , is already a crucial way to reduce the health risks of high temperatures . But the report says many of the places facing the most dangerous heat will also have the least access to reliable and affordable electricity . <p> " Air conditioning is a life saver , " said Michael Greenstone , co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and a professor at the University of Chicago . But he said many countries would be unable to respond to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The report projects that electricity use for cooling will grow seven times more in middle-income countries than in low-income countries because of climate change . In low-income countries , the projected increase in electricity use per person would be enough to power only a single LED bulb for four months . <p> Stylised relationship between energy consumption and temperature for the richest 20% and poorest 80% of the world 's population for electricity and heating fuels Climate Impact Lab <p> The report identifies areas in 18 countries , home to 676 million people , that face what it calls a " mortality-cooling trap " : high heat risk combined with very limited growth in electricity consumption . These areas are expected to account for about 377,000 heat-related deaths annually by 2050 . <p> Most of these countries are in northern sub-Saharan Africa , including Niger , Mali , Burkina Faso and Chad . Others are in southern Asia , including Pakistan , Bangladesh , Nepal and Myanmar . <p> The report contrasts Niger with Saudi Arabia , noting that both face high temperatures , but Saudi Arabia is far @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2050 , communities in Niger are projected to lose 27,000 more lives annually because of a warmer climate than Saudi Arabia . <p> Ashwin Rode , a fellow at the Climate Impact Lab , said the findings identified the places most at risk of heat deaths and least able to use air conditioning to protect people . <p> The report says improving electricity access will be essential , but not enough on its own . It calls for heat early warning systems , heat action plans , expanded healthcare , urban greening and targeted social protection programmes . <p> It also argues that electricity market reforms should be treated as part of climate adaptation , because reliable and affordable power will determine how many lives can be saved as temperatures rise . 
@@139324872 <p> Climate change is affecting cities more and more . This creates major challenges , but it also gives fast-growing cities , especially in sub-Saharan Africa , the chance to adapt to global warming in new and better ways . <p> Cities rely on roads , pipes and flood barriers to work well when a climate disaster strikes . This is physical infrastructure . But they also rely heavily on social infrastructure . This is the public spaces , relationships , and community networks that help people connect , organise and respond collectively to crises . <p> Parks , squares and community gardens are social infrastructure . They 're more than just places to relax . They help cities cope with climate change by lowering temperatures , providing cool spaces during heat waves , and reducing flooding . <p> We are a team of town planners and architects who studied how parks , squares and community gardens help communities in Tshwane , South Africa 's fourth biggest city by population , cope with climate change . We looked at three spaces to understand how good design and planning can make @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ weather , heavy rain and flooding . <p> Our study found that these spaces do much more than help cities cope with heat and flooding . They bring people together , strengthen community ties and provide places for support programmes that help vulnerable residents , like unhoused people . <p> Involving marginalised groups and local communities in creating and maintaining the green spaces also helps build a stronger sense of belonging and shared responsibility . <p> We also found the most effective public spaces for climate change adaptation are those that are created with communities , not just for them . Creating these spaces together means they can change over time as the climate and people 's needs change , with local residents and leaders working together to set up what works best in the local area . <h> How three public spaces are helping Tshwane adapt to climate change <p> Tshwane is projected to become increasingly hotter and dryer . It 's also experiencing increasing urbanisation pressures due to migration from rural areas . <p> Our first case study was Moja Gabedi , a former derelict and illegal dumpsite @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ space had been rehabilitated and in 2020 , urban farming was introduced . A wide variety of crops are now grown there , ranging from vegetables and fruit to herbs . <p> We found , after visiting the site several times and interviewing the people involved in the development and maintenance of the park , that the site supports food security and the social reintegration of vulnerable individuals . <p> At the time of the study , Moja Gabedi provided fresh food for a transitional shelter for people recovering from drug addiction who were previously homeless . The park also accommodated psychological and social services helping those individuals to reintegrate into society . It helps the surrounding area too , as it is highly vegetated and includes ponds that cool the immediate environment . <p> The second case study was Muckleneuk Commons . It is a small , community park , specifically planned along a central route through which commuters walk to and from work . It has a drinking fountain , central gathering space and iconic sculpture in an indigenous garden , where pedestrians can rest on their journey @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the first municipal park established in 1874 when Tshwane was Pretoria . This park is still managed by the municipality today . It follows a typical classic Victorian layout with a series of historic trees and buildings on site . <p> This park has experienced many changes over time , from being the first botanical garden in the city , to accommodating support services for unhoused people . However , our research found that the local community had not been drawn in enough to run the park . Social support projects were not happening as much as they could be . Despite this , Burgers Park remains a vital refuge for many users , including the local unhoused community . <p> Together , these case studies show that public spaces play an important role in building transformative resilience . This is where green spaces help cities recover from shocks such as floods or heatwaves , and also where the need to adapt to climate change becomes a chance to create stronger , more equitable communities . <p> By studying these public spaces and speaking to the people who created and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ better and also support local initiatives that bring about positive change . <h> People are key to climate-ready public spaces <p> Because adapting to climate change happens at the local level , public spaces can help communities prepare for and respond to its impacts . They bring people together , strengthen neighbourhoods and create a sense of belonging . When people feel connected to a place , they are more likely to look after it and support one another during difficult times . <p> A key finding of our study is that how public spaces are created is just as important as what they look like . The decisions about what happens there , who is involved and how the space will be used shape its success . The best public spaces are created with local communities and are based on a deep understanding of the area 's history , people and needs . <p> Including local communities in developing green spaces that help cities adapt to climate change is essential . When we involve people in the process of making places in our cities , we allow individuals to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to a place , they are more likely to care for it and support one another during difficult times . <p> Our research found that local champions are essential . These are people who share a clear vision for a place and help turn it into reality . They are also willing to learn , adapt and respond quickly as people 's needs change or as floods , heatwaves and other pressures affect the community , helping the place and the community continue to grow and thrive over time . <p> Cities can unlock the potential of their communities to regenerate public spaces and help the city adapt to climate change . But to do this , cities need to stop focusing on green spaces as purely physical or environmental and recognise them as social infrastructure . In this way , public spaces will evolve to meet the changing needs of society through ongoing co-creation and collaboration .

@@139325282 <p> New Delhi , July 27 ( IANS ) Climate-driven temperature changes are on track to cause about 430,000 more deaths annually by 2050 , with 10 times more deaths occurring in poor countries than in richer countries . How many of those lives can be saved largely depends on access to energy , particularly the electricity needed for cooling . Yet , a new Climate Impact Lab report on Monday found that many of the regions most impacted by extreme heat will also lack the resources to power the cooling needed to adapt . <p> " Air conditioning is a life saver , and climate change will no doubt lead to more AC adoption in today 's wealthy countries . Our research finds , however , that in too many countries around the world people will not be able to respond in the same way . The result is one of climate 's great cruelties -- lots of death in the very countries that have contributed the least to climate change , " said Michael Greenstone , a co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and the Milton Friedman Distinguished @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> " These findings are a clarion bell that many countries do not have much time to improve the functioning of their electricity markets so they deliver inexpensive and reliable energy and identify other successful adaptations that can save lives . " <p> The report finds that today only the world 's richest have the resources needed to power cooling . As the world warms , many middle-income countries will see their economies grow enough and their energy markets mature enough to support greater consumption of electricity and access to cooling . <p> Electricity used for cooling is projected to grow seven times more in middle-income than in low-income countries due to climate change . In fact , the growth of electricity use per person due to a warming climate in low-income countries is projected to be so small it would only be enough to power a single LED bulb for four months . <p> The same poor countries projected to see so little increase in electricity also tend to be hotter than other countries . The report identifies areas in 18 countries -- home to 676 million people -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and lack of cooling . <p> Due to hotter temperatures and little projected increase in energy consumption , around 3,77,000 people in these areas are set to die annually by 2050 . All of these people live in either low-income or lower middle-income countries today , mostly in northern sub-Saharan Africa such as Niger , Mali , Burkina Faso and Chad . <p> The rest live in Southern Asia , including Pakistan , Bangladesh , Nepal and Myanmar . These trapped countries sit in stark contrast to their wealthier neighbours . <p> For example , countries across the Gulf like Bahrain , Kuwait , UAE and Saudia Arabia are equally as hot as sub-Saharan Africa . But Gulf countries consume much more electricity for cooling and are projected to have big increases , leading to far fewer deaths . <p> Take Niger and Saudi Arabia . The projected increase in electricity use per person in Niger will be 1/9th that of Saudi Arabia , and communities in Niger will lose 27,000 more lives annually in 2050 due to a warmer climate than its wealthier counterpart . <p> " We 've @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ die from the heat and least able to power up ACs to save them , so people and governments can zero in on saving the greatest number of lives , " said Ashwin Rode , a fellow at the Climate Impact Lab and director of scientific research at the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago ( EPIC ) . <p> " Communities will need to find ways to protect people from heat like improved energy access , employing heat early warning systems and action plans , expanded healthcare access , and targeted social programs . But as of now , many adaptation approaches remain untested . We 're working to change that . " <p> The Climate Impact Lab is developing a global playbook of data-driven , adaptation priorities and tested adaptation strategies for funders national and local governments , and the people that will increasingly face climate risks . <h> Weekly Poll Question <h> Connect with us <h> Intro footer <p> The Morung Express <p> The Morung Express is a people-oriented alternative newspaper based in Nagaland that was conceived from the Naga people 's historical realities and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from the well-recognized concept that the core of a free press is based on " qualitative and investigative " journalism . @@139338480 <p> The recent flash floods that swept across parts of Jammu &amp; Kashmir once again exposed the fragility of the Himalayan landscape . As rescue teams worked to restore connectivity , another question resurfaced : Are human interventions making Kashmir 's rivers more vulnerable to extreme weather ? <p> Scientists are clear that flash floods are primarily triggered by intense rainfall , cloudbursts and climate change . Yet they also caution that human activities including unregulated riverbed mining , deforestation , encroachment on floodplains and unplanned development can amplify the destructive effects of these natural events by weakening the resilience of river systems . <p> Among these concerns , riverbed mining has emerged as one of the most contentious environmental issues in Jammu &amp; Kashmir . Rivers naturally carry boulders , gravel and sand that regulate water flow , strengthen riverbanks and recharge groundwater . These materials are crucial elements that give the rivers their stability . <p> Government reports placed before the NGT estimated that between 10.62 lakh and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gravel and sand had been extracted from stretches of the Sukhnag between 2020 and December 2024 . This is roughly equivalent to one lakh dumper loads of RBM . Expert inspections also documented excavation reaching up to 5.22 metres below the riverbed in certain locations , far beyond what scientists consider environmentally sustainable . <p> Earlier proceedings before the Tribunal also recorded findings that illegal mining had taken place in the Sukhnag , affected water sources and caused losses to downstream trout farms . The NGT further noted that numerous short-term mining permits had been issued while examining whether environmental clearances and statutory safeguards had been complied with . <p> The Sukhnag case has since become one of the most important environmental litigations in Jammu &amp; Kashmir . It demonstrates how judicial intervention can bring scientific scrutiny to environmental disputes and reinforce the principle that natural resources are held in trust for the public . <p> The recent flash floods should serve as a warning , not only about a changing climate but also about the cumulative impact of human actions on fragile mountain ecosystems . Protecting rivers is not simply an environmental obligation , it is a prerequisite for sustainable development and the security of future generations . 
@@139343753 <p> IN A first-of-its-kind initiative in India , scientists have begun ' Restoring Forests ' on abandoned opencast coal mines using a scientific ecological approach that goes far beyond conventional tree plantation . Under this special project , instead of merely increasing green cover , the project lays emphasis to revive biodiversity , improve soil health and recreate the ecological functions of natural forests . The ambitious restoration programme , funded by the Coal India Limited ( CIL ) , is being implemented across coal-mining areas operated by South Eastern Coalfields Limited ( SECL ) and Western Coalfields Limited ( WCL ) in Madhya Pradesh , Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra states . As a matter of fact , these three states account for 18 of the 39 coal mine sites selected nationwide for ecological restoration studies . According to Dr Avinash Jain , Scientist-F and Head of the Forest Ecology &amp; Climate Change Division , ICFRE-Tropical Forest Research Institute ( TFRI ) , Jabalpur , the project has been launched under the direction of Dr Sanjeev Bhatia , National Project Coordinator of Centre of Excellence on Sustainable Land Management ( CoE-SLM @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ecological restoration programme dedicated to restoring mined landscapes . Unlike traditional plantation drives , the project is designed to recreate entire ecosystems . Scientists have spent nearly two years studying soil characteristics , native vegetation , climatic conditions and biodiversity before preparing restoration plans for individual sites . <p> The idea is to restore landscapes according to their original ecological conditions rather than planting the same species everywhere . So far , 13 mining sites have been handed over to TFRI for restoration , with plantation activities already underway at 10 locations . The programme covers nearly 90 hectares , with each restoration site spread across about five hectares . The restoration model combines native trees , shrubs and grasses to resemble natural forests . Around 25 saplings and nine shrubs are being planted in each plantation block , while species selection varies according to local topography and agro-climatic conditions . On steep slopes , bamboo and other soil-binding species are being planted to prevent erosion , alongside rainwater harvesting measures to conserve moisture . To support the programme , TFRI has raised around two lakh quality saplings in its @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nearly 12,500 plants , researchers say the success of the project will not be measured by plantation numbers alone . Instead , they will monitor plant survival , soil improvement , biodiversity recovery and the gradual return of natural ecological processes . <p> Scientists believe the restored landscapes could eventually support wildlife , improve water conservation and even provide sustainable livelihood opportunities through medicinal plants , agroforestry and silvipastoral systems where suitable . As India continues to depend on coal for energy , the project offers a scientific roadmap for balancing resource extraction with environmental recovery . If successful , it could become a national model for transforming degraded mining areas into self-sustaining forest ecosystems .

@@139352997 <h> Scientists warn oxygen is disappearing from Earth 's oceans , rivers and lakes , and the damage could last for centuries <p> Oxygen levels are quietly falling across oceans , coastal waters , rivers , lakes and streams around the world , and scientists are warning that this decline deserves far more attention than it currently gets . A new review led by researchers at the University of California San Diego 's Scripps Institution of Oceanography argues that aquatic deoxygenation , the loss of dissolved oxygen from marine and freshwater environments , should be formally recognised as a critical planetary process under threat , joining a select group of nine processes already used to track how close Earth is moving toward dangerous , unstable conditions . The researchers say some of the resulting damage could last for centuries and may not be reversible within a human lifetime . <h> What the Planetary Boundaries framework is and why scientists want to expand it <p> According to a press release from Scripps Institution of Oceanography , the Planetary Boundaries framework was first introduced in 2009 to identify major Earth systems and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ needed to keep the planet stable . The framework currently includes nine processes , covering climate change , ocean acidification , biodiversity loss , atmospheric aerosol loading , stratospheric ozone depletion , freshwater change , land use change , chemical pollution and biogeochemical flows such as the nitrogen cycle . <p> The new review , led by Scripps alumna Erica Ferrer alongside senior author Lisa Levin and many more , argues that dissolved oxygen deserves to be added as a tenth boundary . The researchers say oxygen loss is closely connected to nearly every one of the existing nine categories , meaning it can not be properly understood or managed in isolation from the other pressures already being tracked . <h> Why oxygen is disappearing from oceans and freshwater systems <p> The review , published in the journal Limnology and Oceanography , identifies human-caused warming , excess nutrient pollution and changes in the natural circulation that carries oxygen into deeper water as the main drivers of aquatic deoxygenation . Warmer water simply holds less dissolved oxygen than cooler water , while nutrient pollution from agriculture and wastewater fuels algae blooms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ circulation can also disrupt the natural mixing process that normally carries oxygen-rich surface water down into deeper layers.These combined pressures are already affecting a wide range of species . According to the study , declining oxygen levels threaten organisms ranging from microbes to fish and sharks , and even disrupt some of the chemical processes that help regulate Earth 's climate . Marine mammals are not spared either , since although they breathe air at the surface , oxygen loss can still reshape their habitats and disrupt the food webs and prey populations they rely on . <h> How the idea for this study began at a UN climate conference <p> Ferrer and Levin developed the idea for the review after attending COP25 , the United Nations Climate Change Conference held in Madrid in 2019 . The researchers said they wanted their work to push policymakers and scientists toward treating aquatic oxygen loss as part of a connected system of environmental pressures , rather than as a standalone regional problem confined to specific water bodies.Ferrer described the goal of the study as elevating the profile of aquatic deoxygenation as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and lakes need oxygen to function normally , and that the stability of the wider planet depends on the stability of these aquatic systems . Levin , a biological oceanographer at Scripps , echoed this , saying that formally recognising oxygen loss within the Planetary Boundaries framework would help researchers better understand its wider impact on Earth system stability . <h> What adding a tenth planetary boundary could mean going forward <p> If aquatic deoxygenation is formally added to the Planetary Boundaries framework , it would mark the first change to the list since it was introduced in 2009 . Researchers hope this recognition would push funding agencies , policymakers and scientists to study oxygen loss alongside climate change , pollution and biodiversity loss rather than treating it as a separate , lower priority concern.Ferrer carried out much of this research as part of her doctoral work at Scripps , with support from the National Science Foundation 's Graduate Research Fellowship Program along with funding from Scripps and the University of California San Diego . The study 's authors say that mitigating the effects of aquatic oxygen loss is not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ represents a critical piece of maintaining both biodiversity and climate stability at a planetary scale , making the case for why this quiet , often overlooked crisis deserves a permanent place in how scientists track the health of the entire planet . <p> The TOI Science Desk stands as an inquisitive team of journalists , ceaselessly delving into the realms of discovery to curate a captivating collection of news , features , and articles from the vast and ever-evolving world of science for the readers of The Times of India .
