@@139353063 <p> As the 30-year term of the 1996 Ganga Water Treaty between India and Bangladesh approaches its conclusion , discussions about its future are gathering momentum . Much of the public debate is about whether the treaty will be renewed or revised . But a more consequential question is , what kind of agreement will it be ? The political , institutional and ecological conditions that produced the 1996 treaty are vastly different . The negotiations are likely to be about much more than water sharing at Farakka . <p> The 1996 treaty had a single-point agenda of water sharing , following India 's decision to build the Farakka barrage . The treaty provided a flow-dependent water-sharing arrangement that includes a 50:50 pro-rata sharing when the flows at Farakka dip below a limit . Bangladesh has often expressed its dissatisfaction about not receiving its due share during the dry seasons . <p> Advertisement <p> The next Ganga Treaty is not likely to be restricted to this one specific transborder issue . It will transcend territories and borders , within and outside , enlarging the scope of negotiations . The negotiations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Bangladesh . But they can also offer new opportunities for robust water diplomacy and enduring relations between India and Bangladesh . <p> There are two reasons why the negotiations will have an expanded agenda . <p> First , politics have become more complex . The 1996 treaty , signed after decades of deliberations , reflected a particular political moment of relatively stable bilateral relations . The treaty emerged from sustained Track 1 and Track 2 engagements that built trust and goodwill . Today , the negotiations are likely to be shaped as much by domestic political dynamics as by bilateral diplomatic considerations . Dhaka will find it challenging to navigate the antagonistic sentiment towards India at home . In India , too , the federal politics surrounding Ganga water-sharing are no less complex . West Bengal 's resistance prioritising its own needs and Bihar 's allegations of siltation upstream of Farakka leading to floods will both pose challenges . <p> Advertisement <p> Second , the agenda has expanded beyond Farakka . Besides the Teesta , the recent protracted source of tension , disagreements over multiple shared rivers in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the concerns are unlikely to be just about water-resources sharing and development . The scope will expand to growing water-related risks , with greater uncertainty due to climate change . Climate change pushes the agenda beyond bilateral water allocations to regional-level responses to managing Himalayan glaciers , hydrological extremes , ecosystem resilience and shared vulnerabilities . <p> These changes have a few critical practical implications for the negotiations . <p> First , there is a need to avoid what political geographers call the " territorial trap " -- the assumption that negotiations occur between the two sovereigns , represented by Delhi and Dhaka . Water diplomacy can not be separated from internal diplomacy efforts , both in India and Bangladesh . Dhaka must figure out a way to navigate the polarised politics within . Further , posturing has its limits as a bargaining strategy . Signalling closer engagement with China in the Teesta basin may strengthen Bangladesh 's negotiating position in the short term , but it also risks securitising negotiations and narrowing opportunities to explore mutual benefits . As the downstream riparian , Dhaka 's long-term interests are better @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ India , too , will need to invest in some amount of federal diplomacy despite the conducive equations after the recent elections in Bihar and West Bengal . Getting the states on board will not be easy . Water is an emotive subject and can offer opportunities for the parties in opposition to mobilise resistance from within . <p> Second , shared rivers create indispensable interdependencies -- a less acknowledged but essential characteristic of transboundary rivers . It is not a zero-sum game when water-sharing considerations accompany those of coping with collective risks . The negotiations must build on this for an enduring bilateral relationship . The interdependencies may not always be bilateral . They may transcend to become regional in character . Framing it as interdependencies shifts the focus to shared gains . Better management of floods , fisheries , inland navigation for trade , improved flood forecasting , and joint ecological restoration efforts could create benefits that extend beyond questions of water allocation . <p> Third , an enabling response to the first two is to invest in institutional avenues . Both India and Bangladesh will need to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in support of negotiations . Bilateral institutions need revisiting as well . Earlier institutional choices of the overarching Joint Rivers Commission and the Joint Committee for implementing the Ganga Treaty will not be adequate . They were conceived to implement agreements , not to manage uncertainties . The changed realities and greater uncertainties , including water availability , will need robust and resilient transborder institutions to address the enhanced scope of issues -- water sharing , data collection and monitoring , dispute resolution , responding to risks , etc . <p> Finally , both countries will have to reinvent the political capital that made the 1996 treaty possible , and reinvest in it . The treaty negotiations can be a means to do it . Alongside Track 1 diplomacy , both countries should encourage Track 2 dialogues to generate ideas , sustain dialogue and build intellectual and political constituencies to support the dialogue . The 1996 treaty benefitted from such engagement . The Centre for Policy Research was among those at the forefront of such initiatives and contributed to developing a working draft of the treaty . <p> The negotiations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ India and Bangladesh jointly championed when SAARC was conceived . The institutional form may have to evolve beyond SAARC , but the underlying strategic rationale has become stronger . The next Ganga Treaty , therefore , presents an opportunity not merely to renew a bilateral water-sharing arrangement but to reimagine a regional strategic vision to address challenges of this new age of shared vulnerabilities and fragmented global economy . <p> The writer is president and chief executive , Centre for Policy Research , New Delhi . @@139355286 <h> Water bankruptcy : A looming global crisis <p> The world is entering an era of water bankruptcy . Countries have spent beyond their sustainable water budgets for so long that critical water assets are now depleted , leaving the world to face huge economic , social , and environmental costs . According to a UN report , the Earth has entered an " era of water bankruptcy " due to over-consumption and global warming , with three in four people living in countries facing water shortages , contamination , or drought . <p> The report found that most regions are overdrawing their annual income of rainwater and snowmelt and are now dipping into groundwater savings that can take thousands of years to replenish . Seventy percent of major aquifers are declining , and many of these changes are irreversible . In basin after basin , long-term water use has exceeded renewable inflows and safe depletion limits -- in effect , the planet has run up a water debt . <p> The problem is set to worsen with climate change , population growth , and technological expansion , all of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ water resources can still be protected , many places may have already crossed the point of no return . Rivers , lakes , wetlands , soil , and glaciers have , in numerous cases , been damaged beyond realistic hope of full recovery . <p> A Slow-Building Crisis <p> Like financial bankruptcy , water bankruptcy builds gradually . It is not merely a metaphor for water shortage -- it is a chronic condition that develops when a place uses more water than nature can reliably replenish , and when damage to the natural assets that store and filter water , such as aquifers and wetlands , becomes difficult to reverse . <p> The world is now confronting an era in which the water table is deepening and supplies are growing scarcer , posing a serious threat to humanity . Every effort must be made to ensure judicious use of water -- for human and animal needs alike , and in the course of everyday activity . Yet despite such efforts , the world continues to struggle with dwindling water sources . Water is indispensable to human and animal life , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It is a matter of grave concern that the globe is rapidly heading toward water insolvency . Nearly four billion people experience severe water scarcity for at least one month a year , and more than two billion lack access to safe drinking water . Driven by climate change , population growth , and unsustainable consumption , 70 percent of major aquifers are in decline , threatening both food production and ecosystems . By 2030 , water scarcity could displace 700 million people ; in 2025 alone , 1.8 billion people faced absolute water scarcity . <p> Key Drivers of the Crisis <p> Global overuse : According to the UN University , humanity continues to draw on water as though it were an infinite resource , rather than the finite , renewable one it actually is . <p> Climate change and ecological damage : Rising temperatures are melting glaciers , shrinking snowpack , and fuelling longer , more intense droughts . What were once seen as temporary crises are becoming prolonged -- in many places , near-permanent -- signalling a decisive shift into water bankruptcy . <p> Nearly half the global population -- about four billion people -- now lives with severe water scarcity for at least one month each year . The consequences are visible well beyond that : dry reservoirs , sinking cities , crop failures , water rationing , and more frequent wildfires and dust storms in drying regions . The huge amount of heat generated by wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly , carrying smoke , ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere . As the air rises , it cools and the water vapour condenses into a cloud . If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable , that cloud can grow into a towering cumulonimbus -- the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms.Turbulent winds created by the fire clouds can send embers shooting off in all directions , making wildfires unpredictable and harder to fight . Lightning strikes can also spark more blazes . Pyrocumulonimbus are more likely when there are extremely dangerous conditions such as high temperatures , strong winds and little moisture.Scientists have predicted that climate change is likely to increase the chances of such events . @@139371114 <h> Utilising Urban Planning to Address Climate Change as a Health Crisis <h> Utilising Urban Planning to Address Climate Change as a Health Crisis <p> There is widespread evidence that the climate crisis is also a health crisis : extreme heat , increasing emissions , recurring disasters like floods and landslides , and changing climatic conditions affect vector-borne disease patterns and impact health outcomes . In the absence of participatory grassroots urban planning , culturally-appropriate design , and climate- and health-centric crisis preparedness , large populations in the Global South are bearing the disproportionate consequences . This brief examines three mechanisms through which urban planning can address climate-health outcomes in Indian cities : 1 ) climate communication and education through participatory and cultural activities ; 2 ) disaster recovery , involving pre-positioning of relevant emergency health infrastructure , community networks , and planning for post-disaster response ; and 3 ) resilience building . It studies the impact of the long- and short-term challenges to illustrate the compounded effect of the climate crisis , while noting the importance of ecological considerations for biodiversity protection . <h> Introduction <p> The direct link @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ health is widely acknowledged by institutions such as the World Health Organization ( WHO ) 1 and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) , 2 which formalised their alignment on the subject during the UN Climate Change Conference ( COP28 ) in 2023 . The IPCC Assessment Report 6 of the same year concluded that climate change is a " threat to human wellbeing and planetary health , " and that delayed actions will close " the rapidly narrowing window " to secure a liveable future . Climate change is already causing adverse impacts on human health through heat stress , food and water insecurity , infectious diseases , and mental health burdens. 3 <p> The greenhouse effect and rising temperatures in urban spaces are linked to numerous health issues : increased deaths from dehydration and heat strokes , illnesses due to epidemic outbreaks , kidney stresses due to chronic dehydration , and assorted cardiovascular issues due to chronic heat exposure. 4 Environmental toxicity from unregulated transport and construction emissions , waste/effluents from assorted industries , and poor solid waste management has resulted in water-borne pollutants that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are partially the result of unplanned , vehicle-oriented urbanisation across the country , prioritising tourism infrastructure , and focusing on gross domestic product ( GDP ) rather than ecological well-being and human development . <p> To be sure , the climate crisis is not experienced equally , and within the Global South , cities are at higher risk of disaster vulnerability due to continued excessive construction , transport-related emissions , and growing population density . WHO maintains , " Climate change , pandemics and rising inequalities remain a threat and underscore the urgency for building resilient health systems . " 5 Much remains to be done to tackle the ever-growing burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases. 6 <p> Between 1995-2004 , extreme weather events such as intense heatwaves and storms accounted for 66 percent of the global climate impact , with the Global South bearing disproportionate losses due to its many vulnerabilities. 7 The losses beyond labour productivity are less quantifiable . Ninety percent of urban population growth is projected to be in Asia and Africa , 8 increasing the exposure of vulnerable communities that already lack climate resilience . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lower emissions per capita . <p> The impact is gravest on those who lack the agency to participate in planning or economic processes : children , migrants , refugees , the poor , and other vulnerable groups . Infants and the elderly have been exposed to 7.7 and 8.4 heatwave days per year , respectively. 9 Unprecedented heatwaves in 2023 ( following the global breach of the 1.5 ? C threshold ) exposed people to unbearable heat stress as well as more frequent , extreme , and recurring weather-related disasters. 10 <p> Studies by WHO11 and IPCC12 indicate that the impact of climate change in India is worse than in other countries. 13 Indeed , Indian cities epitomise the Global South 's climate-health nexus , where dense populations collide with unplanned growth , amplifying threats like heatwaves , floods , droughts , and pollution . In mega-cities including Delhi and Mumbai , levels of emissions measured as AQI ( Air Quality Index ) , specifically of PM2.5 , far exceed WHO standards . According to The Lancet , air pollution from burning coal , as well as oil and gas @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ million Indians in 2022 , an estimated 38-percent increase since 2010 ; 14 fossil fuels alone are responsible for some 750,000 of those deaths . WHO projects 250,000 additional global deaths yearly from 2030 -- 2050 due to climate-attributable malnutrition , malaria , diarrhoea , and heat stress . The urban heat island ( UHI ) effect -- where concrete can raise temperatures 5-12 ? C above rural baselines and trap heat overnight , preventing recovery -- is seen in the 20-30 percent increase in hospital admissions during peak temperature periods. 15 The loss of tree cover further compounds the effect of heat traps in cities. 16 <h> Climate Change and Health in Urban India : An Integrated Systems View <p> The health impacts of climate change in Indian cities are the interconnected consequences of unplanned urbanisation , the loss of natural systems , and inadequate community-based planning and preparedness . A single planning failure , such as unregulated construction in a floodplain , can generate interrelated and recurring health crises . For example , destroyed drains are prone to waterlogging that breeds disease vectors ; construction dust and debris @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of green cover removes carbon traps and intensifies UHI ; and forced displacement ( even temporary ) generates psychosocial stress and mental health burdens . These impacts compound each other in ways that thematic policy silos can not capture . Thus , understanding the socio-political and ecological networks as an integrated system requiring a multifaceted approach is essential for effective disaster management . Supporting assorted networks for disaster response and preparedness across demographics is especially important , as is leveraging arts and culture to make it context-specific . <p> Devising an integrated systems framework means demonstrating how human and environmental health impacts are not disparate problems but are interconnected consequences of the same planning failures . Instead of identifying separate health impacts , it contextualises how a planning decision affects assorted health outcomes that tend to compound each other . <h> Political Economy Constraints in Urban Climate Governance <p> Inequalities and poverty in cities of the Global South have accentuated these populations ' vulnerability . The United Nations Development Programme ( UNDP ) reports : " As the impacts of climate change escalate , they can perpetuate or even aggravate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and between countries . Marginalised communities , who are least equipped to cope with the effects , often bear the brunt of these impacts . " <h> The Danger of Growth-First Planning Incentives <p> India 's urban governance has systemically prioritised GDP-linked infrastructure over climate-adaptive land use. 17 The pursuit of growth and profit maximisation has led to the overexploitation of resources , excessive greenhouse gas emissions , and wide-ranging environmental degradation . Development norms increasingly view the environment as a resource ; tourism and GDP-led development have therefore displaced human well-being indicators like health in the hierarchy of priorities . As a result , environmental and human well-being are now at the mercy of competitive market and consumption patterns , compounded by fiscally poor and unaccountable governance . <h> Unsustainable Real Estate and Infrastructure Lock-In <p> Highways , high-rises , and parking infrastructure , once built , are very expensive to retrofit for climate resilience. 18 Yet , urban planning is often leveraged to accommodate private vehicles rather than people . Heat-trapping materials like metal , glass , and concrete are predominant . Pedestrians tend to experience them at pavements , benches , bus stops , and other smaller infrastructure . A lack of thoughtful design and the use of inappropriate , heat-trapping materials create a heat lock-in effect , which only tends to worsen with time . <h> Failures of Fragmented Fiscal Governance <p> Bahadur and Tanner and other scholars19 highlight a lack of targeted financing mechanisms ; 20 fractured responsibilities across municipal bodies and state agencies mean that no single entity is accountable for climate health impact . The shortage of urban planners and regulatory frameworks results in land use zoning that ignores informal settlements or the health of natural resources . Top-down approaches also tend to bypass local governments while prioritising national benchmarks over city-specific issues . Limited public participation and rigid hierarchies present easy adaptability , while the views and experiences of vulnerable groups are often omitted in mainstream planning . As one analyst observes , " Urban India 's future will depend on bridging the chasm between legal provisions and lived realities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 21 <h> Urban Planning As Intervention : Three Mechanisms <p> Urban planning as an interdisciplinary field offers a way to direct and design resilience for land , infrastructure , and services as they become increasingly urban . Planners use diverse disciplines for policy , such as land use , transport , and housing that may benefit health . In the context of disaster risk reduction ( DRR ) , they may also be used to democratise public spaces and strengthen networks for preparedness through creative scenario building . <p> The question of how to involve communities and other groups , particularly those that are more vulnerable in climate and health action and preparedness , becomes more pertinent during discussions about leveraging urban planning as an intervention . The work of Mariana Mazzicato22 suggests leveraging the role of arts and culture as integral to processes like development and infrastructure . Governments may also leverage experts and specialists ( including , for instance , conservationists rather than contractors ) . This section examines three specific mechanisms through which grassroots urban planning can address the climate-health nexus in Indian cities . <h> Climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ play an important and engaging role in explaining climate science ( including health risks ) , which requires as much communication and organising support as possible and can not be left up to either government or businesses . Tapping into the ideas , knowledge , and insights of those who understand context is crucial for future resilience and effective responses to climate change : for instance , vernacular forms of architecture are an effective path towards climate-resilient construction . <p> In India , such approaches can directly complement existing policy instruments and urban realities . Under Heat Action Plans ( HAPs ) adopted by cities like Ahmedabad , Nagpur , and Bhubaneswar , art-led community engagement can support education and communication , which is particularly important given the country 's linguistic diversity . The use of colour-coded murals , shaded public installations , and locally intelligible signages can convey heat-risk alerts , cooling behaviours , and access to water or shelters . Hand-drawn maps of contingency plans such as where to get clean water or backup power supplies are also useful . <p> In smaller Indian towns , where infrastructure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advisories , co-created visual tools and participatory design efforts can improve awareness of flood risks , sanitation-related health threats , and evacuation routes , while strengthening community resilience . In coastal cities such as Mumbai , Chennai , Kochi , and Visakhapatnam , public art and spatial design can help efficiently communicate concerns about sea-level rise , storm-surge risks , and the importance of mangrove or wetland conservation , while reinforcing resilience through culturally grounded narratives . Art and design ought to be embedded in grassroots urban planning to better translate national and municipal climate strategies into actionable , community-level resilience across India 's diverse urban landscapes . <p> Under the National Disaster Management Authority ( NDMA ) guidelines , participatory visual communication and community-designed public spaces can help strengthen disaster preparedness , early warning dissemination , and post-disaster recovery , particularly in high-risk urban wards . Within AMRUT ( Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation ) , such approaches can support water security , heat mitigation , and green infrastructure goals through neighbourhood-scale design solutions and citizen science or other engagement around nature-based interventions . <p> The Smart @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , tactical urbanism , and climate-responsive design as tools for inclusive resilience rather than purely technological optimisation which tends to fail under current climate conditions . In coastal cities , in alignment with the Coastal Regulation Zone ( CRZ ) framework , art and design can enhance public awareness of no-development zones , ecosystem buffers , and climate risks , while reinforcing community stewardship of mangroves , wetlands , and shoreline commons . Embedding these practices within formal programmes can bridge the gap between national policy intent and lived urban experience , ensuring that climate resilience is not only planned , but also socially understood and locally sustained in urban Indian settings . <h> Grassroots Urban Planning and Design <p> As a multidisciplinary field , urban planning serves to both guide and direct the development and design of land , infrastructure , and services as places increasingly become urban . Planners utilise diverse disciplines for policy , including land use , transportation , housing , public spaces , and environmental considerations that benefit health. 23 <p> Urban planning in India remains a struggle due to rapid urbanisation , which tends @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ including fractured governance , often lead to unplanned and unregulated growth and sprawl , inefficient use of resources , and other social inequities . The scale of illegal and informal construction amplifies existing issues of traffic congestion and water scarcity as central plans often fail to consider or adapt to local needs . Seventy percent of urban development is unauthorised . Meanwhile , top-down approaches often bypass local governments or prioritise the national agenda over city-specific problems . The smart cities mission , for instance , in Kochi , reflected central government plans rather than local demands. 24 Limited public participation and rigid hierarchies prevent easy adaptability , while the views of vulnerable groups are often omitted in mainstream planning.In practice , India 's urban planning remains extremely fragmented , reliant on outdated land-use zoning and short-term projects that tend to omit integrated , long-term visions of sustainability . There is a need for proactive , grassroots , and more holistic planning that incorporates climate resilience into masterplans . Heat Action Plans from Pune and Ahmedabad offer examples of linking economic development with health and climate strategies. 25 Integrated urban @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ address interconnected issues such as waste management and heat stress . <p> A large share of urban India 's population lives in moderate to high seismic zones , where enforcement of building and safety codes remains weak . High-rise buildings often do not comply with standards . Rapid , often unplanned vertical growth in cities has led to an increased likelihood of damage vis-a-vis disasters like flash floods or earthquakes . However , the flaw of top-down urban planning is not just a misalignment of national designs and plans , but a lack of consideration for the smaller infrastructures that non-motorised transport and pedestrian users of the city experience : pavements , benches , and other common infrastructure have not been thoughtfully designed and are often made of heat-trapping materials such as metal and glass . <p> These plans tend to miss out on efficacy due to limited public input and misalignment with local needs : insufficient community engagement , high costs with low returns , and centralised priorities tend to impose standard , uniform decisions that are disconnected from on-ground realities . The use of materials , methods , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can create dead zonesa that overlook access to food , nutritional , social and green space requirements for communities . <p> There are often few or no mechanisms for inclusive demographic involvement , and a shortage of urban planners ( 1 per 100,000 people ) , as well as fractured governance , further add to the challenges. 26 Regulatory frameworks tend to emphasise land-use zoning over climate resilience or inclusive growth , ignoring informal settlements and natural resources , for instance . Failing to address local needs often results in inefficient or misplaced implementation ; there is also a general lack of accountability and coordination between national , state , and local priorities . <h> Disaster Recovery and Emergency Health System Preparedness <p> Disaster preparedness is a policy realm that offers the possibility of multi-stakeholder engagement for practical purposes . In the context of India 's climate change challenges , resilient urban planning should build upon people 's insights and knowledge about the places in which they live. 27 Disaster relief and resilience ( DRR ) plans based on grassroots urban planning should become a policy goal for Indian cities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ engaging communities and organising resources in case of emergency across space . Urban planning in the context of DRR can help democratise public spaces and enable conversations about preparedness through creative scenario building . This might facilitate the re-establishing of ties that have been eroded through the atomisation of people in the modern world . The current urban planning status quo begs the question of how better to involve communities and grassroots groups in climate and health action and planning processes . <p> In 2010 , a heatwave in Ahmedabad caused over 1,300 deaths , forcing the city to develop a Heat Action Plan that included a tiered and colour-coded warning system which offered information about cooling shelters ; how to access health workers ; and even leveraging colorful murals to communicate to low-literacy communities . This resulted in a 25-percent reduction in heat-related mortality . The causal chain here would be : planning art-based interventions that are tiered warnings and leverage community infrastructure to reduce ambient exposure during heatwaves , thus reducing mortality and allowing for institutional capacity to be scaled in other cities . In DRR , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ led by governments , NGOs , or private actors . Researchers like Greenfield , 28 Acciavati , 29 and Wahl30 offer compendiums of unique approaches to not just grassroots organising , but also of citizen science that serves as an independent form of monitoring and accountability . <p> A 2015 study of flood response in Chennai demonstrated how self-organised community networks offered the fastest and most effective relief in place of overwhelmed state responses . Informal settlement mapping helped direct relief to the most vulnerable , and art-based education helped raise awareness about waterborne disease risks . The lesson here is that communities with prior participatory mapping experience were substantially more prepared and resilient . Chennai 's post-flood management relied on community networks and integrating art for awareness-raising. 31 <p> DRR relies upon decentralised networks that are effectively able to leverage first responders . Integrated urban planning approaches that combine communication , engagement , and emissions reduction can address interrelated issues such as waste management and heat stress . <h> 1 . Institutional Integration <p> Funds , volunteers , and other resources must be allocated to research and address the climate change-air pollution-public health nexus as a priority . Indian cities require independent ground monitoring mechanisms to observe changing disease burdens and transmission patterns , as well as to assess related health impacts . This requires appropriate local agency to respond to the various needs that might arise . Within budgets , funds must also be allocated for post-disaster recovery and relief planning by supporting existing networks and organisations -- this leverages grassroots insights and knowledge . <h> 2 . Reforms in the Built Environment <p> Urban planning and design may be used to delineate and preserve green spaces in cities , particularly forests as critical infrastructure and protect them from exploitation . Financial support @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ resilient is an important area of regulation and financing . Planning smaller design interventions or infrastructures for people , like shaded pavements and tree-lined parks , can offer passive cooling through shade and sprinklers.Urban spaces are to be planned for people , and not cars , through land-use planning : planning of low-emission zones ( LEZs ) ; conserving carbon-trapping forest areas ; and designing green spaces that encourage shade through tree cover . It would also include an adequate number of clinics and hospitals , training networks of first responders and ASHA workers , and designing the outreach for health-related messaging . <p> Regulating emissions for vehicles and industries through pollution controls and buy-back schemes could be useful in creating a shift towards greener and cleaner energy economies across sectors . This could be based on financial incentives for public transport or e-vehicle use , as well as disincentives and similar financial mechanisms to dissuade private vehicles from parts of the city at specific hours . Transport modes can also be accessibility-based : for instance , younger people should be encouraged to use public transport to increase active living @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ given priority for private vehicle use . Car-free zones can be created for safer play and its interrelated benefits . <h> 3 . Multilevel and Decentralised Network Support <p> Research has demonstrated that urban cooling may be guided by nature to reduce the UHI effect exacerbated by construction and urbanisation . Nature-based solutions ( NbS ) offer cooling effects that can be achieved at the intersection of green and blue solutions. b Tree canopies offer shade and also allow for evaporation , which can reduce peak summer temperatures . Water bodies are heat sinks , while wind channels can help disperse hot air , and lighter colours will reflect more heat . Naturally porous materials like slate can promote evapotranspiration . NbS can therefore lower urban temperatures by offering shade and promoting evapotranspiration , while acting as heat sinks . It is also important to encourage the conservation of forests -- not just for the benefits of tree cover , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ traps . Wild spaces are crucial within urban areas , and are often the result of concerted urban planning decisions . <p> Investing nationally and locally in cleaner energy sources for buildings and transport , while supporting a shift in available technologies in the economy , is crucial . Framing this as being beneficial for healthier urban planning could also incorporate designing child-friendly , safe streets that allow for active living . This is dire , since road accidents cause an estimated 1.19 million deaths annually . Meanwhile , trapped pollutants from increasingly heavy traffic and unregulated pollution from industries including construction , are harmful to pedestrian commuters as well as nearby communities . Accountability and coordination , as well as fiscal allocation amongst assorted actors living in urban and rural spaces , is key to developing effective resilience building plans , which promote the well-being of communities . <p> Urban planning priorities ought to support grassroots , self-organised groups , citizen scientists , and other specialists/researchers whose findings may be relevant but beyond the scope of government work . This includes NGOs and other civil society networks . All @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ relief and responses , which will require assorted forms of creativity to be inclusive . The Global South is home to more than 15 percent of the world 's flora and 12 percent of the fauna . These regions are simultaneously experiencing some of the most disproportionate biodiversity decline and climate change vulnerabilities , globally. 36 By resisting the urge to homogenise and paying attention to varied socioeconomic and political contexts , policymakers -- with the help of assorted specialists -- can more effectively prepare for a resilient future . <p> The four pillars outlined in this brief can offer policymakers pragmatic pathways to connect health impact assessments with disaster responses via targeted grassroots preparedness . @@139383007 <h> The world 's biggest oxygen producer is n't the Amazon . It 's the ocean filled with tiny invisible life <p> The first place people consider when thinking about the source of the oxygen that humans breathe is usually the big rainforest areas like the Amazon . Although forests play a very important role in storing carbon and conserving biodiversity and climate , the oceans provide a greater share of the oxygen in the atmosphere than forests . Almost half of the oxygen generated on earth is generated by oceans . According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration ( NOAA ) Ocean Service , these tiny organisms form the foundation of marine ecosystems while quietly generating the oxygen that sustains life across the planet . <h> Microscopic phytoplankton are the ocean 's oxygen factories <p> In the oceans , more than 70% of the available oxygen is produced by the process of photosynthesis through tiny organisms called phytoplanktons.They exist on the top surface of the ocean and depend on sunlight , water , and carbon dioxide for the process of photosynthesis to produce oxygen . As per @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Ocean Service , it has been found that these minute organisms are responsible for producing 50% or even more oxygen on the earth , which is invisible to the naked eye . <h> Why the Amazon is n't called the planet 's ' lungs ' <p> The Amazon rainforest is often referred to as the " lungs of the Earth " , but scientists say the description can be misleading.Forests certainly produce oxygen through photosynthesis , yet they also consume large amounts of it through respiration by plants , animals and microorganisms , as well as through the decomposition of dead organic matter . <p> Over long periods , much of the oxygen produced within mature forests is balanced by these natural processes.By contrast , the ocean 's vast populations of phytoplankton continuously contribute enormous quantities of oxygen to the atmosphere while also forming the base of marine food webs . As NOAA Ocean Service explains , marine photosynthesis plays a central role in maintaining the balance of atmospheric gases that support life on Earth . <h> The tiny organisms that support entire ecosystems <p> Besides producing oxygen , phytoplanktons @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the food chain of the ocean , serving as food for tiny animals called zooplanktons which become food for fishes , whales , birds and other marine creatures.As the vast majority of life in the ocean either feeds directly or indirectly on phytoplanktons , it is important to know that the condition of phytoplanktons affects the performance of fishing grounds and marine ecosystems across the world.In addition to their ability to take out carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis , phytoplanktons contribute significantly to Earth 's carbon cycle by sending some of the captured carbon to the bottom of the ocean . <h> Why protecting the ocean protects the air we breathe <p> Although the ocean produces an extraordinary share of the planet 's oxygen , marine ecosystems face increasing pressure from climate change , pollution , ocean acidification and rising sea temperatures . These changes can alter phytoplankton populations and disrupt the delicate balance of marine ecosystems.Scientists continue to monitor phytoplankton using satellites , research vessels and ocean observatories to better understand how environmental change may affect their abundance and productivity . According to NOAA Ocean Service @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ biodiversity but also for maintaining one of Earth 's most important natural systems for oxygen production . <h> A reminder that every second breath begins at sea <p> The ocean 's contribution to life on Earth often goes unnoticed because its greatest oxygen producers are microscopic . Yet every day , trillions of phytoplankton quietly convert sunlight into oxygen , supporting humans and countless other species.While forests remain indispensable for biodiversity , climate regulation and carbon storage , the evidence shows that the ocean is equally vital to our survival . The next time you take a breath , there is a good chance that the oxygen came not from a forest , but from tiny drifting organisms floating near the surface of the sea . <p> The TOI Science Desk stands as an inquisitive team of journalists , ceaselessly delving into the realms of discovery to curate a captivating collection of news , features , and articles from the vast and ever-evolving world of science for the readers of The Times of India . @@139383131 <h> More than 4,000 Kenyan students came together to plant mangroves in a bid to set a Guinness World Record <p> Thousands of students and scouts from Kenya 's coastal region took part in an ambitious attempt to set a new Guinness World Record for the largest number of people planting mangrove trees simultaneously . The event , held at the Jomvu Kuu Mangrove Site in Mombasa County to mark World Mangrove Day , brought together young volunteers , conservation groups and government agencies in a large-scale effort to restore one of the country 's most important coastal ecosystems . While organisers hope the attempt will earn international recognition , the primary objective was to promote mangrove conservation and inspire young people to take an active role in protecting the environment . The initiative highlights the growing role of community-led conservation in tackling climate change , protecting biodiversity and safeguarding coastal communities that depend on healthy mangrove forests . <h> How an attempt to restore Kenya 's coastal forests became a bid to set a new global record <p> The Guinness World Record attempt was organised by the Kenya Forest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Association ( KSA ) . According to local broadcaster Diana Imanene from Kenyans , more than 4,000 participants gathered for the event , with organisers aiming to break the existing world record for simultaneous mangrove tree planting . <p> In order to comply with Guinness World Records regulations , KFS also trained 50 forest rangers to be stewards . Each steward would have been responsible for ensuring that 100 people planting the mangroves were doing so according to the Guinness World Records ' standards . This included making sure that each plant was placed at the correct distance and in the right place . The event was further documented through photography , videos , and witness testimonies . <h> Why mangrove restoration matters <p> Though the world record-breaking was the main event , the message that mangrove reforestation is the larger objective should be remembered . Mangroves help to prevent coastline erosion and minimise the effect of storm surges , as well as serve as habitats for marine life like fish and crabs.These forests are also recognised as one of the world 's most effective natural carbon sinks . By @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ waterlogged soils , mangroves play an important role in helping combat climate change while supporting biodiversity and local livelihoods . <h> Part of Kenya 's wider reforestation efforts <p> The initiative forms part of Kenya 's broader environmental campaign to increase tree cover through the government 's 15 Billion Tree Growing Programme . Forestry officials said restoring mangrove ecosystems is a key element of the country 's climate resilience strategy , particularly along vulnerable sections of the Indian Ocean coastline.Organisers also hope the event will encourage more schools and youth organisations to participate in conservation activities , demonstrating how collective community action can contribute to long-term environmental restoration.Official Guinness verification remains pendingDuring the event itself , the Guinness World Record had not yet been officially bestowed . The documentation from the planting process will be analysed by Guinness World Records , which will then see if the attempt meets all of their verification criteria and award a record based on that decision.In either case , organisers note that the mangrove seedlings that have been planted make up an enduring environmental success story for the Kenyan coast . <p> At TOI @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ passionate writers tirelessly sifts through the vast tapestry of global events to bring you the latest news and diverse perspectives round the clock . @@139383490 <p> Major U.S. coastal cities could face far greater flooding , property damage and pressure to abandon vulnerable neighborhoods if global sea levels approach 6.2 feet of rise by the end of the century , according to research that raises the upper limit well beyond widely used United Nations projections . <p> From Miami and New Orleans to New York and communities along the California coast , higher seas could magnify storm surges , overwhelm existing flood defenses and expose homes , roads , ports and other critical infrastructure to more frequent inundation . Saltwater could also penetrate farther into freshwater supplies and agricultural areas , while some low-lying communities may eventually have to consider managed retreat . <p> The warning stems from research by scientists at Nanyang Technological University ( NTU ) in Singapore and Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands . Their modeling suggests that under a high greenhouse gas emissions scenario , global mean sea level rise by 2100 could fall within a " very likely " range of approximately 1.6 to 6.2 feet . <p> The 6.2-foot figure is not a prediction that oceans will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the upper end of a broader probability range designed to capture severe outcomes that could be missed when planners rely on narrower projections . <p> That distinction is especially important for the United States , where trillions of dollars in homes , businesses and infrastructure are concentrated along coastlines . Decisions being made now about sea walls , drainage networks , ports , highways and new construction could have consequences lasting well into the next century . <h> Live Events <h> Why the new sea level estimate matters for the US <p> The implications of rising seas extend well beyond beaches disappearing beneath the water . <p> As the average sea level increases , coastal flooding can begin from a higher baseline . That means hurricanes and other storms do not necessarily need to become stronger for their storm surges to reach farther inland . <p> The effects will not be identical across the United States . Local land movement , ocean circulation and changes associated with melting polar ice can cause relative sea levels to rise faster in some locations than the global average . <p> Subsidence poses an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , compounding the impact of rising water . <h> Researchers combine two approaches to calculate future risk <p> Scientists have long faced difficulties determining exactly how high oceans could rise because different forecasting methods can produce noticeably different results . <p> Physics-based models simulate processes including glacier loss , ice-sheet changes and the expansion of seawater as oceans warm . While grounded in known physical processes , these models may have difficulty representing some highly uncertain events capable of producing rapid changes . <p> Expert assessments provide another source of information , particularly for potentially high-impact processes that are harder to model . <p> A research team led by NTU senior research fellow Benjamin Grandey developed a statistical " fusion " approach designed to bring those sources together rather than choosing one over the other . <p> The work , involving researchers from NTU and Delft University of Technology , was published in Earth 's Future in December 2024 and used underlying data associated with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change 's Sixth Assessment Report . <h> How high could sea levels actually rise ? <p> Under a lower-emissions pathway @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ roughly 1.0 to 3.3 feet of sea level rise by 2100 . <p> Under high emissions , the range widened considerably to approximately 1.6 to 6.2 feet . <p> The researchers ' probability framework differs from the one used for some headline IPCC projections , so the figures can not simply be compared as equivalent forecasts . The IPCC 's comparable high-emissions range reaches roughly 3.3 feet at a 66% probability threshold . <p> The significance of the new work lies largely in its treatment of uncertainty . By widening the range , researchers can account for potentially devastating outcomes that may have relatively low probabilities but enormous consequences . <h> Flood defenses may need to prepare for worse scenarios <p> For U.S. cities , a wider range of possible sea level rise could change how officials think about infrastructure built to last for many decades . <p> A seawall , bridge or transit system designed around a lower estimate could prove inadequate if actual sea level rise approaches the higher end of the range . <p> Coastal planners can instead use severe scenarios to stress-test projects and determine whether @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Rising seas could also worsen saltwater intrusion into freshwater aquifers and agricultural land and accelerate the loss of wetlands that naturally provide some protection against storms . <p> In the most vulnerable communities , repeatedly rebuilding after floods may eventually become more expensive than relocating people and infrastructure -- a process generally known as managed retreat . <p> The researchers do not argue that such an outcome is inevitable across U.S. coastal cities . Instead , the expanded projections underline the scale of uncertainty confronting communities making long-term decisions today . <p> For cities with infrastructure expected to remain in use through 2100 and beyond , the question is no longer only how much sea levels are likely to rise . Planners may increasingly have to consider what happens if the more extreme projections become reality .

@@139396461 <h> The Right to Water : Reimagining the Cauvery Dispute through Ecological Federalism <p> The Cauvery dispute is often portrayed as a contest between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu over the distribution of river water . Such a narrative , however , obscures the deeper constitutional , ecological , and developmental challenges confronting India . The issue is no longer simply about allocating a fixed quantity of water between two States . It is about governing a shared and increasingly fragile natural resource in an era marked by climate change , rapid urbanisation , ecological degradation and growing water insecurity . The real challenge is to move beyond litigation and political confrontation towards a model of cooperative and ecologically sustainable river basin governance . <p> The Journey So Far <p> The origins of the dispute lie in the agreements of 1892 and 1924 between the princely State of Mysore and the Madras Presidency . While these agreements reflected the political realities of colonial India , they became increasingly contested after Independence as developmental priorities evolved . Karnataka sought to expand irrigation and provide water for its growing urban centres , whereas @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ agriculture depended upon assured downstream flows . <p> To resolve the dispute , the Union Government established the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal in 1990 under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act , 1956 . Following extensive hydrological assessments and legal deliberations , the Tribunal delivered its final award in 2007 . <p> In 2018 , the Supreme Court marginally modified the allocation by recognising Bengaluru 's growing drinking water needs while substantially affirming the Tribunal 's framework . More significantly , it directed the establishment of the Cauvery Water Management Authority ( CWMA ) to supervise reservoir operations and ensure compliance with the water-sharing arrangement . <p> Despite these institutional interventions , disputes recur almost every deficient monsoon . This persistence demonstrates that legal adjudication alone can not resolve conflicts rooted in environmental uncertainty and competing developmental demands . The Cauvery has become not merely a legal dispute but a test of India 's capacity for ecological governance under conditions of climatic stress . <p> Constitutional and Human Rights Perspectives <p> The Constitution places water under Entry 17 of the State List , yet recognises that inter-State rivers require collective @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Parliament to enact legislation for resolving inter-State river disputes , leading to the enactment of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act , 1956 . <p> Beyond this institutional framework lies the broader constitutional philosophy of cooperative federalism , which requires States to function as partners rather than competitors in managing shared natural resources . The Supreme Court has also interpreted Article 21 , the Right to Life , as encompassing the Right to Water , thereby recognising access to adequate and safe water as integral to human dignity , public health , and sustainable development . <p> Although international water law primarily regulates rivers shared between sovereign States , its principles offer valuable guidance for India 's federal structure . <p> The 1997 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses is founded upon two complementary principles : equitable and reasonable utilisation , ensuring that all riparian regions receive a fair share of available water , and the obligation not to cause significant harm , requiring upstream and downstream users alike to avoid actions that seriously prejudice others . <p> The future of the Cauvery @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that no longer exist . Climate variability requires a transition from fixed water-sharing arrangements to adaptive water governance , where allocations respond to scientifically measured inflows , reservoir storage , and seasonal rainfall . <p> Agricultural policy must also adapt to emerging climatic realities . Precision irrigation , micro-irrigation technologies , crop diversification , and climate-resilient farming practices can substantially reduce water demand without compromising farmers ' livelihoods . Sustainable agriculture is therefore not merely an economic necessity but an essential component of long-term water security . <p> Finally , India requires a permanent Cauvery Basin Council comprising scientists , engineers , environmental experts , economists , farmers ' organisations , civil society representatives , and governments of both States . River governance should become a continuous process of dialogue , scientific assessment , and collaborative planning rather than a cycle of litigation and political mobilisation . <p> From Water Sharing to Shared Stewardship <p> Courts can determine legal entitlements , but they can not create rainfall . Governments can frame regulations , yet they can not command the monsoon . The future of the Cauvery ultimately depends upon replacing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is not merely an economic resource flowing through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu ; it is a common ecological inheritance sustaining agriculture , biodiversity , livelihoods and cultural memory across generations . Protecting it therefore demands a shift from competitive federalism to ecological federalism , where constitutional values , scientific knowledge , environmental sustainability and inter-State cooperation become mutually reinforcing . <p> A durable solution is neither " more for Karnataka " nor " more for Tamil Nadu . " It is enough for both , achieved through constitutional morality , climate-sensitive governance , scientific transparency , ecological restoration and equitable sharing . Only when the Cauvery is governed as a shared river basin rather than contested political territory can it cease to symbolise conflict and instead become a model of cooperative federalism in twenty-first-century India . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Advocate Sudhakar Shunmugam hails from Mela Puthaneri village in Tirunelveli District , Tamil Nadu , South India . @@139396486 <h> Trump 's ... energy policy , and what it 's going to cost us all <p> We talk regularly about Big Oil , but it would probably make more sense to at least occasionally refer to it as Big Gas -- many of the same players are involved , of course , and the two are often found in the same places , but it 's been clear for some time that oil is not a growth industry . The rapid rise of EVs in most of the world undercuts projections of future use -- we 're at or near the top of the plateau now , and by 2030 or so the amount of oil we use should be going down . <p> That 's why the hydrocarbon industry 's growth story has been largely about natural gas . It 's used for many things -- heating , cooking -- but above all for generating electricity , and it 's on that ground that the fossil fuel industry has set out to build its market , stressing constantly that it is clean and cheap . Two important new @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ claims really are . <p> The first comes from a Center for Climate Integrity team led by Rebecca Leber and Rebecca John . Leber has a long record covering the industry -- her 2020 report in Mother Jones about the industry paying Instagram influencers to plug natural gas was an early landmark in our understanding of pay for play social media , as well as the lengths the industry would go to in order to tell its fibs. ( " #cookingwithgas makes food taste better , " says Camille , an LA-based foodie who poses artfully with her spatula , to her 16,700 followers . " ) <p> But as they document in the new report , which should be read in full , this is a very old story . It turns out that the natural gas industry has been playing the pr game for a very long time . As far back as the 1950s , gas had a bad image : it was known to contribute to respiratory problems when burned indoors ( more on that later ! ) , and to local air pollution . And @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1970s , most of the concern was about carbon dioxide , but there was a growing realization that methane -- which is essentially what natural gas is -- was the smaller but still important sibling greenhouse gas . And so the industry began doing what it did best , which is lying , or to use the technical term , " public relations . " They constructed a whole mythology around natural gas , turning it into the fossil fuel equivalent of the " other white meat . " <p> In the late 1980s , the gas industry and major oil companies started to brand gas as a " bridge fuel " -- a clean-burning transition fuel to a renewable energy future . In reality , they planned a long-term future for natural gas , while simultaneously undermining renewables , obstructing the destination to which gas ' " bridge " was supposed to lead . Over the next 20 years , the industry effectively solidified the bridge fuel myth by co-opting the science and oversight originally intended to keep carbon and methane emissions in check . <p> Working together in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ several major environmental groups , the industry managed to temper concerns about methane using strategies crafted by the same firms that for decades undermined the scientific consensus about the harms of tobacco . AGA and allied groups aggressively challenged the science around methane through industry-funded studies and the creation of the objective-sounding Gas Research Institute . <p> But their approach was multi-dimensional . While muddying the waters on the industry 's methane problem , the gas industry was careful not to deny the issue of climate change outright , instead focusing attention on carbon dioxide . It paired this with relentlessly promoting the concept of gas as clean -- certainly cleaner than coal or oil -- and positioning gas as a bridge fuel and climate solution . In the process , the gas industry solidified partnerships with EPA with the explicit goal of fending off regulations in favor of voluntary emissions management , while also recruiting environmental organizations that would lend legitimacy to their arguments . <p> I want to highlight the effectiveness of this strategy with a story about ... me . In 1988 , before this campaign took @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sometimes called the first book for a general audience on climate change . And in it I wrote : <p> A common suggestion is to replace much of the coal and oil we burn with natural gas , since it produces only about half as much carbon dioxide . But it natural gas -- methane -- escapes into the atmosphere before it burns , it traps solar radiation more efficiently than co2 ... As a result , switching to natural gas may have no effect on the greenhouse effect . It might even make it worse . <p> So give me credit for knowing this crucial science when I was 27 . <p> But not really , because I think I more or less forgot it over the next two decades , as the gas industry rearranged the terms of the debate , and turned it into the lesser of two climate evils , the " bridge " to a future of cleaner energy . This argument was bought wholesale by politicians , especially Democratic ones -- if you go read Barack Obama 's State of the Union addresses , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as both an economic boon and a way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions ; we were replacing coal with something cleaner . I wrote some early pieces on their work for the New York Review of Books , and then published a long piece in the Nation that made the same point I 'd made more than a quarter-century earlier . <p> Our combined emissions of methane and carbon dioxide have gone steadily and sharply up during the Obama years . It makes clear that the industry is running out of the really cheap stuff -- the fracked gas from the Permian and Appalachian shales that it 's been pumping for the last two decades . Many of those wells are playing out fast , and now it 's going to need to turn to the more " geologically complex " Haynesville shale of east Texas and Louisiana , and that will drive up costs -- especially since more and more of the gas is , at least theoretically , going to be exported to Asia as the industry builds out massive shipping terminals along the Gulf of Mexico . <p> If industry succeeds in locking in unprecedented demand for U.S. gas by expanding exports and domestic consumption , U.S. supply may be pushed to its limits . Gas supply can only meet such high levels of demand if prices rise to cover the higher production costs of marginal gas supplies . This connects rising dependence on gas to rising energy costs . U.S. consumers and those in LNG-importing countries must push policymakers to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reliable , affordable renewable energy <p> The numbers are fairly startling : <p> Between 2026 and 2040 , the average wholesale price of gas could be 80 percent higher than during the past decade of U.S. LNG exports , a decade when energy price volatility was already causing hardship in the U.S. and LNGimporting countries . @@139400140 <p> Jammu and Kashmir has been under near-continuous assault from the cloudbursts and flash floods in recent weeks . They are tearing through the hilly areas , causing landslides , Chenab has crossed the danger mark , highways have been disrupted ; and at least 30 people are dead and properties partially or fully damaged . <p> None of this is unfamiliar . Almost the same sequence played out last year . What repeats each monsoon is not only the weather but the gap it exposes . The institutions closest to the ground and best placed to notice the first warning signals are also the ones that are least equipped , structurally , to report or act . <p> Jammu and Kashmir 's Panchayats are , in institutional terms , newly built and were never designed with the environment in mind at all . The Jammu and Kashmir Panchayati Raj Act of 1989 kept local self-government largely nominal . The 73rd Constitutional Amendment , which gave Panchayati Raj Institutions constitutional status and real devolved powers across the rest of the country , now extended to Jammu and Kashmir has made @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ feet , working out basic questions of authority and capacity under conditions of bureaucratic caution and continuing security sensitivity even as climate disaster risks , as repeated incidents show , in this region are far more profound . <p> This important connection between a young institution , a fragile mountain landscape , and a warming climate has been largely absent from the growing literature on " ecological democracy . " Scholars from Robyn Eckersley , who has argued for an eco-centric political theory , to John Dryzek , who has described a " democracy without boundaries " folding environmental stewardship into democratic participation . <p> Much of this literature has built this field around mature Western democracies or India 's longer established Panchayati Raj states . Jammu and Kashmir , where local self-government is still new in any operational sense , has barely featured in it . <p> Jammu and Kashmir is located in one of the world 's most ecologically fragile zones . The Himalayas are geologically young and prone to landslides , flash floods and glacial retreat , changes that unfold at a scale too fine-grained for a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Only communities living directly on that land tend to notice a drying spring , an eroding slope , or a shrinking pasture early enough to act . <p> Climate change is not an abstract concern . Shifting snowfall , erratic monsoons and glacial melt are already unsettling agriculture , water supply and livestock-based livelihoods . When ecological disruption turns immediately into food and water insecurity for rural households , environmental decision-making can not be left to experts sitting elsewhere . It has to sit where the consequences land . <p> Panchayati Raj Institutions , however , were built for roads , sanitation and welfare delivery , not environmental stewardship . Without a deliberate ecological mandate , Panchayats carry no obligation to weigh ecological cost against short-term development gains , so unregulated construction , unsustainable tourism and resource overuse happen by default rather than informed local choice . <p> The same gap shows up in tourism and resource extraction . State-level regulation , enforced from a distance , is usually too slow to stop damage as it happens . A Panchayat with genuine ecological authority could act as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is deliberately built into the institution rather than assumed to follow automatically from its existence . Because Jammu and Kashmir 's Panchayats are still being built , this is an unusually open moment to do exactly that . <p> Ecological democracy , in this sense , means a decentralised , participatory system of governance in which citizens actively take part in conserving , managing and sustainably using natural resources , while pursuing environmental justice and intergenerational equity . It widens governance beyond political accountability and service delivery to include environmental accountability as well . <p> Evidence of Climate Change <p> Meteorological records show Jammu and Kashmir 's annual temperatures rose by roughly 0.8 ? C between 1980 and 2016 , with daytime highs in Kashmir and night-time lows in Jammu both rising steadily . Under a high-emissions scenario , researchers project average annual temperatures could rise a further 5.2 ? C in Kashmir , 4.8 ? C in Jammu and 6.5 ? C in Ladakh by the century 's end , with glacier cover across the region shrinking by as much as 85 percent . <p> The glaciers are already @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Kashmir Himalayas and a key source for the Jhelum basin 's Lidder and Sind rivers , has retreated by roughly 2.85 kilometres since 1857 , with the pace accelerating sharply after 2000 ; it lost close to a quarter of its ice cover between 1962 and 2018 alone . Because meltwater from glaciers like this feeds irrigation , drinking water and hydropower downstream , that retreat becomes resource pressure for the very communties Panchayats exist to serve . <p> Rainfall patterns are shifting too . What once fell across two months in the Kashmir Valley is now compressed into spells as short as ten days , producing a punishing cycle of drought-like dry spells followed by the kind of intense , flood-inducing bursts now battering Poonch and Rajouri . Srinagar recorded its hottest July day in 25 years in 2024 , alongside one of its warmest nights in over a century . <p> None of this is a future risk . It is a measured trend , which strengthens the case for ecological accountability into local government , while these institutions are still taking shape . <p> Jammu and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a significant proportion of its rural population maintains a close relationship with natural resources . Forests provide fuelwood , fodder , medicinal plants , and livelihood opportunities . Water bodies support agriculture , fisheries , and domestic needs . Pastures sustain livestock-based economies , while biodiversity contributes to ecological balance and tourism potential . Environmental degradation therefore has immediate consequences for the daily lives of rural households . <p> Turning ecological democracy into practical governance calls for instruments designed for institutions this early in their development , not borrowed from systems that assume institutional capacity Jammu and Kashmir 's Panchayats do not yet have . <p> The first is an Ecological Democracy Index , combining measures of environmental governance , natural resource management , waste and pollution control , climate resilience and community participation , to let the ecological performance of individual Panchayats be tracked and compared as their powers mature . <p> The second is the Ecological Gram Sabha - a forum dedicated to environmental issues like water conservation , forest protection , biodiversity , climate adaptation , waste management , and sustainable agriculture . This can sit alongside @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Introduced now , while Jammu and Kashmir 's Panchayati Raj structure is still being defined , it would build ecological concerns into grassroots democracy from the outset , rather than retrofit them later . <p> Composite vulnerability indices are not new to Himalayan research ; similar tools already exist for farming communities in Himachal Pradesh and for villages in Kashmir 's own Kupwara district . What would be new is building one consistently across all of Jammu and Kashmir 's districts on common indicators , treating health and education access as core measures alongside climate and livelihood . <p> Women belong at the centre of this framework , not the margins . They are typically the ones who fetch water and fuelwood and manage household resources . Young people are equally central , well placed to lead biodiversity mapping , environmental monitoring and eco-tourism initiatives . <p> Tourism regulation is a related opportunity . Panchayats empowered to manage waste , regulate activity and protect sensitive sites could let communities benefit economically from tourism without absorbing all of its ecological cost . <p> Timing is Crucial <p> What makes ecological democracy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ itself , which has a long history in Western green political theory . It is the timing . The region 's Panchayati Raj Institutions are still newly operational ; their powers still being negotiated . Embedding ecological participation , an Ecological Democracy Index and Ecological Gram Sabhas into that formative period , rather than into an already-mature system of local government , is the more pragmatic thing to do . <p> As rain keeps falling this week , rivers keep rising , and rescue teams keep searching hillsides in Poonch for the missing , that argument stops being academic . @@139404627 <h> Liquid trees and solid gases , the things we do for the environment <p> Nigel Pereira on two inventions that seem to be mind-boggling as they seem to change the natural state of the resource in question . <p> With deforestation and the burning of fossil fuels now widely accepted as prime causes of climate change and extreme weather , scientists worldwide are leveraging technology to tip the scales back into balance . Two of these inventions in particular seem to be mind-boggling due to the fact that they seem to change the natural state of the resource in question . <p> Trees , without a doubt , are one of our most critical natural resources , crucial to maintaining our soil , preventing floods , and keeping our air breathable . Trees , however , are tall and solid , and even if it was possible to melt one and pour it into a tank , we probably would n't think of doing it . <h> The LIQUID 3 <p> In a 2019 report , Serbia was ranked as the number 1 country in Europe with the highest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was also ranked 28 in the world for worst air quality . To combat this issue , the source of which is concentrated in urban areas , scientists in Serbia have developed a liquid tree called LIQUID 3 . <p> Developed by Dr. Ivan Spasojevic , author and Ph.D . in Biophysical sciences , the LIQUID 3 is a 600-liter clear tank called a photo-bioreactor filled with a green liquid made up of loads of microalgae in water . The microalgae basically do the job a tree would do by converting carbon dioxide to oxygen through the process of photosynthesis , but a lot better . <p> The advantage microalgae have over trees is that it is 10 to 50 times more efficient at turning carbon dioxide into oxygen and a single 600-liter unit can do the job of two ten-year-old trees or about 200 square meters of grass . <p> Dr. Spasojevic explains that while his invention is n't meant to replace trees , it can be used in highly polluted areas where it is difficult to grow trees due to poor air and soil quality . This is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the LIQUID 3 does n't need soil . Additionally , he goes on to explain how the only maintenance required is removing the biomass created by the algae which can then be used as a fertilizer . <h> Solidified Natural Gas <p> Global carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) emissions from energy combustion and industrial processes reached a new all-time high of 36.8 billion tonnes . Belgrade , in particular , was ranked one of the dirtiest cities in Serbia due to two coal power plants that were ranked among the 10 dirtiest plants in Europe . Now while natural gas has evolved into a key stepping stone between fossil fuels and cleaner renewable sources of energy , problems related to transporting and storing natural gas remain . <p> The dangers related to gas leaks as well as expensive , pressurized tanks and the related equipment to pump natural gas safely are the reason why you have to drive for a while before you come to a gas station that sells CNG or compressed natural gas . <p> While researchers around the world are actively working to solve this problem , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ along with his team members from the Dalian University of Technology and the Indian Institute of Technology , Chennai , believe they have the answer . Solidified Natural Gas , or natural gas hydrates are created by trapping gases such as methane inside water molecules in a way that they ca n't get out . The procedure which involves additives as well as specific temperature and pressure conditions , produces a material that not only is solid but can also be stored safely without expensive equipment and the risks associated with flammable pressurized gases . While these gas hydrates can only be produced in limited quantities for laboratory experiments as of now , it 's definitely a step in the right direction . <h> Too close to home <p> While it 's great to read about the crazy things people are doing with technology in order to mitigate carbon footprints that only seem to be getting bigger , it 's important to remember that there is nothing better than the real deal when it comes to nature . So while we do need to come up with more ingenious ways to reverse the damage being done , not doing the damage in the first place should be the priority . <p> With a background in Linux system administration , Nigel Pereira began his career with Symantec Antivirus Tech Support .
